en: Śrī:
In the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra, the beginning of the third section; now begins the section on the Sārālaṅkāra (the Ornament of Essence).
That very [progression] is called "the essence" by the wise when there is a successive increase in excellence.

That very same chain, when describing a progressive excellence where each subsequent member surpasses the preceding one, is called the figure *sāra*. This very same figure is designated as *udāra* by the author of the *Sarvasva*. Accordingly, its definition is: "The progressive enhancement [of excellence] is *udāra*. They maintain that this figure is of two kinds, according to whether its subject matter consists of a single entity or multiple entities. In the case of a single subject, the recourse to different states is necessary, because excellence is invariably dependent upon distinction.

For no entity whatsoever can become greater than itself with respect to itself without some distinction such as state (*avasthā*) and so forth. Regarding this, the author of the *Vimarśinī* states that there is a fourfold classification based on whether the subsequent superiority occurs by way of essential nature (*svarūpa*) or by way of an attribute (*dharma*).
In that regard, an example of progressive excellence within a single object by way of its own nature is as follows:
"May that Trivikrama protect us, whose upward-reaching splendor gradually increased—first appearing like a crest-jewel of diamonds, then a necklace of pearls, and finally a girdle of gems. (1407)
In this [verse], there is a progressive excellence of the one and only Blessed One, characterized by His various distinct states and His essential nature.
As it is said:

"O Blessed One, the sun, possessing the luster of Your feet at its rising, then shedding its childhood as it attains the beauty of golden bracelets, and finally matured with its crest-jewel, performs its play for You. (1408)
Or again:

"O Lady, the moon, when it is a mere crescent, attains a resemblance to the curve of your toenails; yet when full, it becomes like the splendor of your face—indeed, purity leads to ever-increasing excellence. (1409)

In this case, since the superiority of the sun and moon as characterized by each successive subsequent state is stated in relation to their respective preceding states, there is identity of subject matter; the distinction here, however, is that this is headed by an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle).

As you were proceeding to the site of Bali’s sacrifice, O Upendra, your foot shone like a lotus upon the ground; meanwhile, the umbrella of Indra was raised aloft, as was the great canopy over the worlds.

In this case, since the Lord’s foot—which in its prior state was small in size like a land-lotus—is described as being distinguished by a progressively greater magnitude like an umbrella and so forth, its excellence is expressed; thus, there is identity of subject matter.

O Blessed One, your majesty blazed forth like a lamp through the Dharma at first, then like a forest fire, and finally like the sun at the end of a Yuga; it consumed Virādha, Mārīca, and the Ten-faced Rāvaṇa.
Here, there is a progressive intensification of the majesty of the Blessed One alone, by way of prioritizing the attribute of its being brilliantly illuminated.

Just as my devotion toward you, O Madhusūdana, having first sprouted, then put forth leaves, then formed buds, and finally blossomed, gradually becomes great and bears fruit that is free from blemish.
In this passage, the progressive excellence of devotion itself is depicted by prioritizing its quality of greatness.

If, in this case, the figure of speech *paryāya*—characterized by the sequential residence of multiple superstrates upon a single substratum—is perceived here, then let it indeed be so perceived. However, that does not in the least diminish the *sāra*, which consists in the progressive excellence of each subsequent element relative to the preceding one.

The excellence of multiple objects by way of their own nature is as follows: "She who dwells upon the peak of the Silver Mountain (Kailāsa), and she who dwells upon his peak (Śiva), and he whose chest is marked by the lac-dye from her feet—he is Śiva; may that Lakṣmī be victorious! (1413)
In this regard, there is a progressive excellence among many [categories], each subsequent one being superior to the preceding one by its very nature.

According to the Dharma, among living beings humans are the best; among humans, the wise Brahmins; among them, those marked by the discus, O Acyuta; and among them, those who have placed the burden of their lives upon Your feet.

Just as a knot is better than ignorance, therefore one who is skilled in wearing it is better; than him, the man of knowledge; than him, one whose mind is resolute; and even better than him, O Acyuta, is one who knows the true nature [of the Self]. || 1415 ||

"Skilled in its retention" (taddhāraṇe kṛtī) means he has mastered the memorization of the text. The suffix *ini* is applied to the word *kṛta* in the sense of the agent according to the rule "iṣṭādibhyaśca. The locative case in the word *taddhāraṇe* is used for the object of a verbal derivative ending in *kta* that implies an action toward an object, according to the rule "ktasyenviṣayasya karmaṇyupasaṅkhyānam. "Those who possess knots" (*granthinaḥ*) refers to those who have performed the study of books. In these two examples, there is a progressive excellence from one to the next, characterized by the quality of superiority among humans and so forth, as well as among knots and so forth. Furthermore, in the first example, among all beings, living creatures are superior; among living creatures, those who live by their intellect are superior.
Among the intelligent, men are the best; among men, Brahmins are traditionally held to be the best.
The shadow of such sayings of Manu is placed before us. In the second [verse], however:
"Those who merely memorize are superior to the ignorant; those who retain [the texts] are better than those who merely memorize;
those who possess knowledge are superior to those who merely retain them; and those who practice with resolve are superior to those who possess knowledge."
Thus it should be understood that the sequence of Manu’s statements has been declared; all of this constitutes the excellence of praiseworthy dharma.
The excellence of an unpraiseworthy quality is as follows:
"O Lord, if you are indeed the Sovereign, then you purify this heart of mine—which is more soiled than a buffalo, more soiled than a crow, and more soiled than a mass of darkness. (1416)
An example of both types [of contradiction] is as follows:

"The surface of the earth is vast; greater than that is the sky, and greater than that is the cosmic egg; greater than that is the water in a pit; and greater than that, O Hari, is my sin—how can this be, O Hari? (1417)

This is the second person singular of the optative (liṅ) from the root *hṛ* (to take away). Here, in the context of pits and water, "extreme vastness" is a praiseworthy quality; however, in the actual subject matter at hand, it is a sin and thus not praiseworthy.

In this regard, it should be noted that because a chain (*śṛṅkhalā*) is not aesthetically pleasing when applied to a single subject, *sāra* (the "essence" figure) animated by it does not attain beauty; for since the chain requires natural distinctions, it fails to manifest when the distinction is merely produced by circumstances such as place and time. For this very reason, other authorities have accepted the ornament named *vardhamānaka* (the "ascending") in this context, defining it thus: "The *vardhamānaka* occurs when there is an increase in both form and quality."

Therefore, while the *kāraṇamālā* (chain of causes) and others have a single subject as their scope—just as a chain does—it is not possible to say the same for *sāra* (the essence), because that would entail the undesirable consequence of admitting other figures of speech within a single subject. However, the definition of *sāra* is appropriately stated as: "The essence (*sāra*) consists in the excellence [of each subsequent element] over the preceding one, by way of its quality (*guṇa*) or its nature (*svarūpa*). This is the meaning: when there is excellence over each preceding element through either its quality or its nature, it is called *sāra*. Thus, since it is sometimes animated by a chain (*śṛṅkhalā*) and sometimes independent, its having multiple subjects as well as a single subject is well-established.

Thus, since the distinctness of the aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) of figures based on chains (*śṛṅkhalā*) is established by experience, their status as separate figures is proven; yet, just as non-contradiction (*abheda*), similarity (*sādharmya*), and so forth are merely vitalizing elements for other figures, it is appropriate that the chain itself be considered such a vitalizer rather than a separate figure. For if it were so, then non-contradiction and the others would also incur the status of separate figures. However, in cases such as the complete (*pūrṇā*) and elliptical (*luptā*) [similes], there is no distinctness of charm apart from the charm of the simile itself—this is the traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*).

Now, what is this *vicchitti* (distinction)? It is said: *Vicchitti* should be understood as either the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*) residing in the poem—acting as the cause for the mutual distinction or differentiation among the figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*) through the relation of being produced—or, alternatively, it is the aesthetic charm (*camatkāritā*) resulting from that very state of being produced.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, the Chapter on the "Essence," in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Figure of Speech "Respective Order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*):
"Where the connection of objects is stated according to the order of their mention, the ancients called that 'Respective Order' (*yathāsaṃkhya*); others have termed it 'Sequence' (*krama*)."

The term *yathāsaṃkhyam* (according to order) is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "not exceeding" (*anativṛtti*) the meaning of the objects [enumerated]. Since the non-exceeding of the number occurs through a sequence—namely, that the first [object] is connected with the first [correspondent], the second with the second, and so forth—the very etymological meaning (*yogārtha*) constitutes its definition. Others have designated this as the figure of speech *krama* (sequence). It is of two kinds: verbal (*śābda*) and implied (*ārtha*).

In that case, when there is a sequential connection between non-compounded elements and non-compounded elements, the relation is verbal (*śābda*), because the sequential relationship is not obscured. However, where two groups are expressed by means of a compound, and first one group is generally connected with the other group, and subsequently—through a consideration of the following-up of the meaning—the connection of the individual members of those groups occurs sequentially, there the relation is semantic (*ārtha*).
O Lord of the Bull Hill, O Viṣṇu, just as you sprinkle, scorch, nourish, and steal away the thirst, the heart, the happiness, and the suffering of those who bow before you. 1418.

O Viṣṇu, Lord of Vṛṣādri! You *pruṣṇāsi*—that is, you satisfy (*pūrayasi*) the thirst of those who bow before you; you *pluṣṇāsi*—that is, you dwell within their hearts (the meaning being that you serve them, or you cause affection for yourself within them). This is derived from the two roots *pruṣ* and *pluṣ* belonging to the *krayādi* class, used here in the present tense (*laṭ*). Furthermore, you *puṣṇāsi* happiness and you *muṣṇāsi* suffering;

these two roots, *puṣ* (to nourish) and *muṣ* (to steal), also belong to the *krayādi* class. Here, the actions beginning with *pruṣṇāsi* are connected respectively with "thirst" and the others. In this case, the connection is verbal (*śābda*), because there is a sequential connection between the uncompounded verbs and their respective objects.

Just as the lotus is surpassed by the luster of your eyes and the stainless orb of the moon by the luster of your face, so too, O Kamalā, surely even the water has been conquered by you, for it enters into great caverns.

The "great cave" (mahābila) is the vast hollow of the atmosphere; as Amarasimha states: "The great cave is the gateway of the clouds. The distinction is that this [instance] contains a verbal *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), whereas the previous one was pure (*śuddha*).
Just as it is said:

"Of these two who are devotees of Śrī Kālī, the first here is a drinker of wine (surapa), while the other will become a drinker of liquor (surāpa); the former is most radiant, yet he is intoxicated by his own nature, whereas this [latter] is the opposite of that form. (1420)

Regarding the two devotees of Śrī-Lakṣmī and Kālī-Durgā: here, between these two, the former, the devotee of Śrī, shall be a *surapaḥ*—meaning a lord of the gods (*devādhīśa*) or equal to one—and for that very reason, he shall be most radiant (*bhāsvattamaḥ*), exceedingly luminous and possessed of great splendor. But the latter, the devotee of Kālī, shall be a *surāpaḥ*; this means he is not a protector (*na-pātī*) of the *sura*s (gods), thus a non-protector of the gods. The true sense is that he is a *surāpa*, meaning a drinker of *surā* (liquor).

The sense is that the practice of the left-hand path (vāmācāra) is well-known among the Kālika lay-devotees (*upāsakas*). [The word *matta*] is derived from the roots *pā* "to protect" and *pā* "to drink" by means of the suffix *ka* according to the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*. For this very reason, he is *matta*, meaning "intoxicated" or "possessed of pride.

[The word *svabhāḥ* is analyzed as: one whose *bhāḥ* (splendor) does not exist is *abhāḥ*; one who is thoroughly *abhāḥ* is *svabhāḥ*, meaning "devoid of excessive brilliance. The sense is that one who drinks liquor cannot possess the splendor of Brahman (*brahmatejas*). Thus, *mattasvabhāvaḥ* is a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of two qualifying words. To the question, "Why is there a disparity between these two? he says: *tadākāra*.

Because this person, who is designated last as a devotee of Kālī, is opposed to her form—that is, opposed to the form of the first-designated devotee of Śrī (meaning opposed to her conduct)—the sense being that there is an extreme distance between virtuous conduct (*sadācāra*) and wicked conduct (*vāmācāra*). In the alternative sense, the word "surāpa" (liquor-drinker) is opposed to its own form; that is, it is opposed in form to the word "surapa" by virtue of its middle letter, the vowel *ā*—the sense being that it is of a contrary nature.

The sense is that because of the presence of the vowel *ā* in the middle, its form is contrary to the word *surapa*. Thus, this word *mattasvabhāva* is the opposite (*vipratīpa*) or reverse (*pratiloma*) of the nature of the word *bhāsvattama*, which possesses that same form. The meaning—that the very word *bhāsvattama*, when viewed in reverse order, results in *mattasvabhā*—also nourishes an extraordinary aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*). Here too, the figure is purely verbal (*śābda*). The distinction from the previous [type] is indeed clear.
Just so,
O Mother, for those who have taken refuge in you as well as for other embodied beings, there exists here before our very eyes the distinction between vast sovereignty and meager sovereignty.

"Vipula-aiśvarya" means sovereignty over the earth; "virala-aiśvarya" means one of meager fortune. Here, between these two—those who have taken refuge in you and those who have taken refuge in others, or between their respective fortunes—the difference exists right before our eyes (*purata eva*). The meaning is that it is clearly manifest. In the alternative sense, the meaning is also striking: that the difference lies right at the beginning of the words "vipula-aiśvarya" and "virala-aiśvarya," namely, by the letters *pu* and *ra*. Here too, the distinction is purely verbal (*śābda*).

May the husband and wife—who dwell respectively upon the lotus and the ocean, who possess a heart-shining jewel-necklace and a forest-garland, and who move together within the palace of the heart—sport before us as they proceed toward us. 1422.

In this case, since the collective expression beginning with "the dwelling in the lotus and the ocean" first connects with the collective pair consisting of wife and husband, there subsequently arises—by virtue of the requirements of the sense—the understanding that the "lotus" and other terms connect with the "wife," and the "ocean" and other terms connect with the "husband"; thus, the figure of speech is *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence).
Just as Bṛhaspati and Divaspati have been surpassed by the greatness and intellect of you two respectively, even so these two manifest a vast mutual distinction between themselves.

Bṛhaspati and Divaspati—the preceptor and the protector of the gods—have been surpassed equally by the intellectual power and majesty of your devotees, the Bhāgavatas. Even though they are equal in being surpassed, these two, Bṛhaspati and Divaspati, manifest a distinction between one another as if it were great; that is to say, even while there is no difference in their state of being surpassed, they display it as if it were significant. Alternatively, the word *iva* serves as a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṃkāra*).

The underlying intention is that they demonstrate a great distinction consisting of the relationship of teacher and disciple. In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), the words *bṛhaspati* and *divaspati* reveal their distinction through the two syllables *bṛ* and *di* alone, and not through any other letters; such is the meaning. Here too, everything is as before, with the only difference being the description of another meaning based on the word itself. Or, for example: "O Lord, O Blessed One, while the ten-faced Rāvaṇa and Vibhīṣaṇa were respectively hostile and friendly toward You, they became reduced to mere skeletons, O Lord, under the influence of the distinction between the qualities of their own natures. (1424)

"O Lord, O God! Rāvaṇa and Vibhīṣaṇa, who were respectively your adversary and your friend, became *śoṣa-śeṣau*—that is, Rāvaṇa was reduced to mere emaciation (*śoṣa*) and Vibhīṣaṇa remained as a survivor (*śeṣa*). The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) of the roots *śuṣ* (to dry up) and *śiṣ* (to remain). He states the reason for this with the word *tad*."

The construction is as follows: "Due to the distinction (*bhidāvaśāt*)—that is, the difference (*bhedavaśāt*)—between the qualities of their respective natures (*prakṛtiguṇānām*), namely the qualities inherent by nature such as 'hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance' [Gītā 16.4], and those such as 'fearlessness, purity of being, and steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge' [Gītā 16.1] which belong to the divine endowment (*daivasaṃpadguṇānām*) and the demonic endowment (*āsurasaṃpadguṇānām*), there arise for those two, Daśavadana and Vibhīṣaṇa. By the connection with the particle *smā* (indicating the past), the verb *bhavati* is used in the present tense to denote the past (*bhūte laṭ*). Thus, due to his birth from the demonic endowment and his hostility toward the Blessed One, the destruction of Daśānana occurs.

The meaning is that, due to being born with a divine fortune and his friendship with Vibhīṣaṇa, [Rāma] possessed both longevity and supreme welfare as the only remaining possibilities. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), regarding the verbal roots which serve as the bases for the prescription of suffixes, the "qualities" (guṇa) of those two—meaning the qualities prescribed by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* due to their distinction caused by the presence of the suffix *ghañ*—are understood through their differentiation.

The roots *śuṣ* and *śiṣ* are distinct in their original forms (*prakṛti*); their respective *guṇa* substitutes, characterized as the vowels *o* and *e*, are also distinct. It is by virtue of such a distinction that the words *śauṣa* and *śeṣa* are produced—this is the intended meaning. The rest is the same as before.

In this regard, it must be examined whether this [correspondence] can truly be admitted as the path of the figure of speech *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence) or not. For in this matter, which is established by common worldly usage, there is not even a trace of that "creation by the poet’s imagination" which is the very life-breath of poetic ornamentation (*alaṃkāra*). Since that is absent, the designation of it as an "ornament" would be entirely unjustified. Therefore, *yathāsaṃkhya* is merely the absence of the defect known as *apakrama* (lack of sequence). Consequently, the assertions of those who follow the school of Udbhaṭa are as unattractive as counterfeit coins.
By this, the moderns explain that the words of Vāmana—who employs the very term *kramālaṃkāra* (the ornament of sequence) for what is indeed *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence)—are also accounted for.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Figure of Speech "Respective Order" (Yathāsaṃkhya), in the Alaṃkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on the Figure of Speech "Transition" (Paryāya):
Where a single object is described as resorting to multiple substrates in succession, that figure of speech is called Paryāya.

The figure of speech *paryāya* occurs where a single object (*ādheya*) resides successively in multiple locations (*ādhāra*), whether by its own nature or as composed by a poet. Here, the word "successively" (*krameṇa*) is used to exclude the figure *viśeṣa*, for in that case, the connection of the object with multiple locations occurs simultaneously, and thus there is no over-extension [of the definition]. For this very reason, because it relies on succession, the name *paryāya* is etymologically appropriate.
Furthermore, this figure is twofold, depending on whether the cause [of the transference] is explicitly stated or not.
Just as nectar formerly dwelt in the ocean of milk, and thereafter in the charming moon, it now, O Consumer of Madhu, resides within your own deeds.

In this instance, the successive resorting of a single nectar to various receptacles, such as the Ocean of Milk and others, is described. Therein, the existence of the nectar in the Ocean of Milk and the lovely moon is stated as being real in fact; however, its presence in the deeds of the Lord—who is the subject of description—is established solely by the poet’s imagination. This ornament occurs only where there is some requirement for the poet’s creative fancy regarding the sequence of the receptacle, the contained, and their relationship.
But the essential principle is that where everything is established by worldly reality in every respect, no poetic ornament exists.
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem, having placed its foot upon the position of the Lord of the Nectar-Eaters from the ocean of nectar,
took up residence on the peak of the Wind-Eater’s mountain— the very self that is the abode of Ramā. || 1426 ||
In this case, the lack of mention of the instigator is clear. To illustrate its mention:
"The ocean, out of affection for his daughter, bestowed upon her face excellent pearls, most beautiful coral, and the essence of nectar. (1427)

Here, the phrase "by the ocean out of affection" (*vātsalyataḥ*) indicates the causal agent (*prayojaka*). Herein, there is the placement of multiple objects—such as excellent pearls and the like—upon a single substratum, namely the face of the Ocean’s consort (Lakṣmī). The status of the ocean as the substratum is implied (*ārthī*), whereas in the previous examples it was expressed directly (*śābdī*). Furthermore, the distinction is that this [figure] is enlivened by *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of identification), because the teeth and other features are identified (*adhyavasāna*) with pearls and so forth.

Just as the redness residing in coral was, by fate, placed upon your two lips, O Daughter of the Ocean, so too was it subsequently placed upon your pair of lotus-feet out of a desire to proclaim your own maturity.

Here too, the causal agent is indicated [by the phrase] "out of a desire to manifest his own maturity according to the prescribed rule. This entire [instance] is a pure synonym (*śuddhaparyāya*), as it is untouched by contraction or expansion.
An example of a synonym involving contraction (*saṃkocaparyāya*) is as follows:

"O You of countless virtues, Your compassion—which formerly pervaded the entire world and then became attached in certain places to the likes of the aged elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa)—has today, it is said, become bound solely to me. (1429)

This is the statement of a poet who considers that the Blessed One’s compassion is greatest precisely toward himself. Here, because the scope of compassion becomes increasingly restricted by its substratum, this is an instance of the "successive contraction" (saṅkocaparyāya) figure.
O Mother, just as the Gaṅgā flows from the great station of Brahmā and clings to the hollow of the matted locks of Śiva, she then merges into your gentle smile, O Dweller in the Lotus.

In this instance, there is a progressive narrowing of the substratum for the Gaṅgā; the fact that both are animated by hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) is equal in both cases. The distinction is that the previous example is headed by poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), whereas this one, which is about to be described, is headed by the figure of concealment (*īlita*).
An example of the figure *vikāsa* (expansion) is as follows:

"O Mother, that sovereignty which resides in you is connected to the lotus-eyed one [Viṣṇu] by virtue of your relationship; what more need be said? It is likewise connected even to the multitude of gods headed by Tryambaka [Śiva]. (1431)
In the lotus-eyed Lord Śrīnivāsa, there occurs here a transition to another substratum of sovereignty without the abandonment of each preceding substratum; this is a synonym for "expansion."
Just as the hardness of the Kaustubha gem, the kinsman of the sun, was observed only upon your chest, so now, O destroyer of demons, it has arisen in my heart as well due to its sin.

"O slayer of the Daityas! O enemy of the Daityas!"—this is the speech of reproach directed toward the Blessed One by a poet who is weary of the burden of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). Here too, as before, there is a sequence of unfolding; the distinction lies in its being sustained by a double entendre (*śleṣa*) consisting of two meanings—hardness and cruelty—as conveyed by the word *kaṭhoratva*.

Regarding this, the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara* states: "In common usage, the term *paryāya* (succession) is observed to be employed only when, following the destruction of one relation, another relation comes into being; for it is seen exactly so in the example cited by the *Prakāśa*: 'The curve of the hips abandons its thinness, while the waist takes it up.
Furthermore: 'O slender one, that very redness which was previously seen on your bimba-like lips is now seen, O fawn-eyed one, even in your heart.'"

"In this regard, the statement that the mention of a synonym (paryāya) is improper," he said. Others, however, maintain that because the synonym is supported by the example of the verse "bimboṣṭhe," and because the discrepancy between the terminology defined in the treatises on poetics (alaṅkāra-śāstra) and common worldly usage is of no consequence, what was stated [by the former] is simply unskillful.

The meaning is as follows: *paryāya* (succession) consists in the description of multiple substrata (*ādheya*) upon a single locus (*ādhāra*) in succession, or the description of multiple substrata upon a single locus in succession. The word "in succession" (*kramāt*) is used to exclude the figure of speech called *samuccaya* (accumulation), which will be discussed later; for in that case, there is a simultaneous connection (*yaugapadyena anvayaḥ*) of both qualities and actions. It differs from *parivṛtti* (exchange) because there is no exchange; the definition of *parivṛtti* as involving an exchange will be stated immediately hereafter.

Just as I was previously terrified with fear from contemplating the ocean of existence, and then became utterly despondent, so now, through the enumeration of the multitude of Your virtues, O Mādhava, I have become steadfast and find supreme bliss. (1433)

"O Mādhava!"—this is the form of address. Here, first there is the state of being startled by fear, then despondency, then fortitude, and immediately after that, bliss; thus, there is a description of multiple states residing sequentially within a single substratum.

O Blessed One, just as I previously held the delusion that the body is the self, and thereafter the notion of an independent self, so now I am possessed of the delusion that all else besides You is real; I consider myself to have only You as my remainder.

"One who possesses the notion of an independent self" means one who has the delusion that the self is independent. "One who possesses the delusion that others—such as parents, other deities, or others—are the *śeṣa* (the subordinate/dependent)" refers to those who hold such a misconception. Herein is the sequential binding of many qualities to be established within a single substratum: namely, the delusion of the body being the self, the delusion of the self being independent, the delusion of others being the *śeṣa*, and [finally] the state of having the Blessed Lord alone as the *śeṣin* (the primary/dependent).

Just as [a lotus] is first soiled by darkness, then becomes clear through the grace of the Guru, and thereafter attains a green state, yet within that very place my heart has become red—this, O Lotus-eyed One, is a marvel! (1435)

Here, first there is *mālinya* (turbidity), which is ignorance and blackness; then *vaiśadya* (clarity), which is the light of knowledge and whiteness; immediately after, the attainment of *haritatva* (greenness), which is the discernment of the Lord’s true nature and the color green; and then *raktatā* (redness), which is affection for the Lord and the color red. This is a description of multiple superposed attributes (*ādheya*) in a single substratum (*ādhāra*) in succession. It should also be understood that this is a "wondrous" (*citram*) and "marvelous" (*āścaryam*) variegated color (*śabalavarṇa*). The previous example was pure; however, the distinction here is that it is mixed with *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and has its cause (*prayojaka*) presented by the words beginning with *tamas*. As another example:

O Blessed One, if a man who is bold enough to enter another's property as a thief were seen by you and protected by you, he would indeed be one who is courageous in entering another's property as a thief.

He was looked upon by you and cast a sidelong glance at; he was protected (*avita*) and guarded. In the alternative reading, there is a word-break as *vita*, meaning "devoid of the letter *ta*. The construction is to be joined as "he was looked upon" (*dṛṣṭaśca*). [He is one] who takes the property of others...

The meaning is that when the letter *t* is removed from the word *nyapraveśadhīraḥ*, it becomes *parasvasainyapraveśadhīraḥ*. The sense is that one who was previously merely a thief (*stena*) would become a hero (*śūra*) upon being glanced at by Your side-long look. Regarding this, the Teacher [Haribhadra] states in his *Gadyabhāṣya*: "Heroism (*śaurya*) is the capacity to enter fearlessly into a formidable enemy army, even without assistance, as if it were one's own army. This very point is expressed by the passage beginning with *parasvastainya*.

"Skilled" (*dhīra*) means one who is an expert in the act of entering—that is, in the theft or robbery—of another's property; "steadfast" (*dhīra*) means one who possesses fortitude in entering the armies of both enemies and one's own kin. Here, there is a sequential description of both thievery and steadfastness within a single substratum.

O son of Daśaratha, Sītā, when separated from you, became exceedingly distressed; yet, once united with you—who are an ocean of auspicious virtues—she became truly distinguished by her inner stability.

O son of Daśaratha! Sītā, that ocean of auspicious virtues, having become exceedingly restless—meaning her mind became extremely unsteady—upon being separated from you, immediately thereafter became one whose inner self was steady (sthirāntarā), meaning her mind was firm, precisely because she had attained union with you.

In one sense, the word *viśliṣṭā* (separated) is exceedingly beautiful; having attained the state of being without the letter *la* (*al*) within—that is, in its interior—it is thus described as possessing "streams" (*vārāḥ*), meaning multitudes, of auspicious qualities (*guṇāḥ*). This is indeed an epithet of Sītā. Furthermore, when it is stable (*sthirā*) with the letter *śi* (the syllable *śi*) fixed within—that is, in its middle—it becomes *viśiṣṭā* (distinguished). The meaning that the word *viśliṣṭā*, upon the removal of the letter *la* and the stabilization of the letter *śi*, becomes *viśiṣṭā*, is also full of poetic charm.
Here, in a single substratum consisting of Sītā’s form, there is a sequential presentation of two attributes—the flickering and the steady. In both examples, the distinction is indeed clear.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, the Chapter on Synonyms (*paryāya-sara*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Chapter on Exchange (*parivṛtti-alaṅkāra*):
Exchange (*parivṛtti*) is the bartering of objects, which may be equal or unequal.

*Nimaya* means exchange (*vinimaya*). As Amara states: "Paridāna, parīvarta, naimeya, and nimaya [are synonyms]. The figure of speech called *parivṛtti* (exchange) is the taking up of equal objects for equal objects, or unequal objects for unequal objects. Among these, exchange of equals is twofold: the taking up of superior things by superiors, and of inferior things by inferiors.
Exchange of unequals is twofold, consisting of the taking up of an inferior thing by a superior one, and the taking up of a superior thing by an inferior one. Thus, *parivṛtti* is fourfold.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"O crest-jewel of the serpent-mountain (Śiva), having offered this nectar-like hymn to you, the fortunate man receives from you in turn an even greater measure of nectar—just like myself. (1438)

Here, there is an exchange between two similar things—the praise of that which has the nature of nectar and the nectar itself—based on their status as the most excellent. This is accomplished through the identification [of the two] rooted in the pun (*śleṣa*) inherent in the word "amṛta."

Just as a wise man, having somehow fixed his own heart—already trembling with longing—for You, O Sinless One, finds You in return, Your heart likewise trembling with longing for the hearts of those women with beautiful teeth who have heard [Your praises]. (1439)

The wise and learned one [says]: "The *tarala* (quivering) in the heart refers to the lord-gem (*nāyakamaṇi*) situated in the chest; or rather, the truth is that it refers to her whose mind is quivering and fickle. Alternatively: "The Blessed Lord Hari bears his own self—the stainless, ageless, and immortal—within this world in the form of the Kaustubha gem."

Thus, according to the sequence described in the chapter on weapons and ornaments, this is the nature of the Kaustubha gem. "The Self" (ātmānam) refers to one's own inner self (pratyagātmānam). "In some way" (katham api) means by means of great effort due to the extreme fickleness of the heart. "Having placed" (ādhāya) means having fixed [it] upon You. "Of the fair-toothed lady of the Vedas" (śrutisudatyāḥ) means upon her heart, that is, upon her breast; "shining like the central gem of a tremulous necklace" (taralam hāramadhyamaṇivat dīpyamānam) means that which is expounded by the Vedas. Thus, he perceives You as the Supreme Self (paramātmānam).

"Tarala means a gem situated in the middle of a necklace, and it is used in three genders for 'fickle,'" according to the *Ratnamālā*. Here, there is an exchange between the two selves who have become fickle at their hearts, which is enlivened by *parivṛtti* (exchange) and *śleṣa* (punning).

Just as Śiva becomes [liberated] by offering even a mere drop of water or a flower to the Lord of Śrī, what other gain could there be for one who receives from him even a mere drop of water or a flower? (1440)

Śambhu is existence itself. By offering even a mere drop of water—a "drop, a fragment, a particle" (*lavaleśakaṇāṇavaḥ*), according to Amara—and even a single flower, in accordance with the teaching "a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water," one obtains another mere drop of water and a flower; that is to say, one acquires that very sacred water and that very same flower used for worship. The sense is: what gain is there for one who receives an equivalent object by giving an equivalent object? There is no gain at all. This is the intended meaning.

He takes up even a mere drop, a mere fraction, of the "flower of the waters"—for the Vedic scripture states, "The moon is indeed the flower of the waters. This is the actual state of affairs. The sense is that his status as the Moon-crested Lord (Candraśekhara) is due to the greatness of worshipping the Blessed One. Here too, there is an exchange between two equals based on their excellence, which gains its scope through an identification rooted in *śleṣa* (paronomasia). Alternatively, this may serve as an illustration of the variety of exchange to be mentioned later, where an exchange occurs between two equals due to a deficiency [in one].
O Nārāyaṇa, what gain indeed could there be for the people of Vārāṇasī who, having given up such a perishable, material body, receive back a body composed of the elements?

[It refers to] a perishable, material body composed of the five elements; such a perishable body consisting of the five elements. In reality, however, the meaning is that it is a body belonging to a specific class of elemental beings (*bhūtayoni*), as stated in the passage: "Piśācas, Guhyakas, Siddhas, and Bhūtas—these are the classes of divine origins. Although its composition of the five elements (*pāñcabhautikatva*) certainly exists [in this case as well], even if one accepts the previously demonstrated meaning, the intended proof is indeed established.

Nevertheless, it should be noted that the meaning just stated nourishes an excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) through the device of *śleṣa* (paronomasia). For among those residing in Vārāṇasī, the attainment of a "corpse-body" (*bhūtadeha*) after the casting off of the physical body is indeed well-known as an inevitability. Here, there is an exchange between two equal things—the physical body and the "corpse-body"—due to their deficiency [in comparison to the divine]. The fact that this is enlivened by *śleṣa* and other figures is just as before.
The underlying sense is that for residents of Vārāṇasī—unlike residents of cities that are mere fields of manifestation for You—there will be no attainment of a divine, non-material body at the end.
As in another example:
Since the devotees of Giriśa take up such a body as it was at the time of their gift of bodies ending in ashes, O Blessed One, the gain of mere chaff is what results from the granting of husks.

That whose end is ashes—that body (*varṣma*) or limb (*gātra*)—is "ash-ending" (*bhasmānta*). This should be understood from the Vedic scripture, "Now this body ends in ashes," and from the Purāṇic statement, "The physical frame is designated as excrement, worms, and ashes," which indicates that the physical frame becomes known as ashes upon cremation. Alternatively, it means "the nature of ashes.

Or, "that very body which is ash-ending" implies an exchange of equals through ellipsis (*nyūnatayā parivṛttiḥ*). The true meaning, however, is: "that which is beautiful (*anta* = *ramya*) with ashes, or that which has ashes at its end (*ante* = *antike*)."

The *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *anta* means interior, extremity, proximity, destruction, essential nature, and that which is charming. The intended meaning is that [the body] is entirely smeared with ashes. However, the devotees of the Blessed Lord (Bhagavat) assume a divine, non-material form adorned with celestial garlands, unguents, ornaments, garments, and other Brahmanic decorations, as described in such passages as "a hundred [maidservants] with garlands in their hands. The point is that they do not, like the devotees of Giriśa (Śiva), possess a ghostly body smeared with ashes. As it has been said:

Having cast off his former body, which was unshakeable yet rife with disease, onto the mountain of gold, who would not be filled with wonder at the simplicity of that person as he assumes another such body? 1443.

That which possesses immovability (*acala*), fear (*bhaya*), and the conch (*śaṅkha*); that which possesses abundance (*pracura*), the disease (*gada*) or the mace *Kaumodakī* (*gada*). Here too, as before, there is the figure of speech *nyūnasamaparivṛtti*. The underlying meaning is that for a person who casts off their body on Śeṣādri, there arises the attainment of the Lord’s own form (*sārūpya*). Or, as it is said: "Those men who have bestowed their friendship upon the knowers of Brahman receive there the fruits of their good deeds; but those who have entrusted their faults to Him indeed incur the fruits of their evil deeds. (1444)

*Sādhu* here means *kṛtyā*, which refers to action (*kriyā*)—both good and evil actions—according to Amara’s lexicon; thus, *sukṛta* (well-done) is its meaning. Similarly, *pāpakṛtyā* means *duṣkṛta* (ill-done). The word *tatra* (therein) also connects with the second half-verse. "Therein" refers to the realm of Brahmā. *Nyastadveṣāḥ* (those who have cast off hatred) refers to those [enemies] of that knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*). Here, in the first half-verse, there is an exchange of the superior for the equal (*uttamasamaparivṛtti*), while in the second half-verse, there is an exchange of the inferior for the equal (*nyūnasamaparivṛtti*). This is a pure example [of parivṛtti], as in: "His sons inherit his estate; his friends, his good deeds; and his enemies... [inherit his evil deeds].
The phrase "pāpakṛtyām" is a restatement of the meaning of the Vedic scripture (śruti), and thus it differs from the previous examples.

However, those who have been initiated do not regard this as an equal exchange, but rather as an unequal one; and thus their definition of exchange is: "Exchange is the mutual transfer of things that are respectively deficient and excessive."
Third verse:
O Lord, through the abundance of the eightfold yoga, or by the sixfold limbs, or by means of surrender (*prapadana*), some indeed purchase liberation from You, the giver of final release.

In this context, there is a substitution of isolation (*kaivalya*)—which is inferior to the two superior practices of entering upon the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) and the sixfold yoga (*ṣaḍaṅga*)—for that [isolation]. Isolation (*kaivalya*) is the experience of the absolute self (*kevalātman*).
Just as some, having surrendered their wealth—consisting of wives, homes, children, splendor, kingdom, and so forth—to you, O Lord of Veṅkaṭagiri, alas, they attain service unto you. 1446.

Here too, there is an exchange of a greater royal splendor and the like for a lesser service. This was cited with the intention that service is inferior according to the worldly view that "everything dependent on another is suffering. However, those who know Brahman would consider this as an illustration of the very exchange of the greater for the lesser, since, in reality, service to the Lord is superior to the splendors of wife, home, and so forth.
O Lord of the Serpent Hill, the virtuous here, offering their most minute selves unto you, consider themselves as having purchased you—the Great among the great—through the means they have employed.

"The scriptural text, 'This subtle Self is greater than the great,' should be reflected upon here. Those by whom the prescribed means—either the practice of devotion (*bhakti*) or surrender (*prapatti*)—has been performed are so described. They spread forth [the results] as if they were purchased; the sense is that, according to the saying, 'Janārdana is purchased by love (*bhāva*); Janārdana is purchased by devotion (*bhakti*')."
O Lord of Lakṣmī, protector of the distressed, just as the sage Kucela purchased from you immeasurable and manifold riches by giving a handful filled with parched grain, so too [may I obtain them].

In the phrase "from the gift of a handful (prasṛti) full of grain," since it is impossible for the gift to belong to the "handful" which serves as the substantive (viśeṣya), the connection of the gift must be with the "grain" which serves as the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa)—that is, from the giving of grain that fills the handful. This is similar to expressions such as "the heaven-dweller has perished. Indeed, those learned in logic state: "When a prescription or prohibition applies to something qualified, if the substantive is precluded, they transfer to the qualifier. Thus, the vocative word "O protector of the wretched" (dīnāvana) is a qualifier of the term "Lord of Ramā" (ramāpate).
Just as you, O Lord, having given a certain river consisting of words and water to the ocean, received from it a daughter who was a jewel of splendor and a jewel of gems.

"O All-pervading Lord! Having given the river to the ocean"—by this, giving without expectation is expressed; "srotasvinī" means a river. In these three examples, the exchange of the lesser for the greater is evident. These five examples, beginning with "the eight-limbed yoga," are pure.
Or rather,
as the lotus-eyed Lord, out of great curiosity, offers the five-fingered hand to the two sons of the daughter of the Earth, he experiences a thousand-fold joy through them.

Padmāvatī was the daughter of Vasudhā, the goddess Earth; her [son] was someone possessing five branches—though the reality is that it refers to the hand—and he was one whose nature possessed a thousand branches, endowed with infinite branches, and exceedingly vast.
Or rather,
O Acyuta, by offering even a mere blade of grass or a fragment of the earth at Your feet, the wise have attained lordship over the worlds along with abundant retinues.

Having offered even a single leaf such as *tulasī*, a fragment of earth, or a drop of water at Your feet—according to the principle stated in the verse "A leaf, a flower" (*patraṃ puṣpam*)—many have attained sovereignty over the worlds (the waters or the realms), whether as Varuṇa, Indra, or Dhātṛ; that is to say, they acquired a state wherein there are many leaves or petals [in one sense], and in the other sense, a state wherein there are many attendants, such as ministers and retinues. They thus assumed lordship over the worlds, the waters, and the realms.

The qualifier "skilled" (*kṛtin*) contains the intention of a cleverness consisting in the acceptance of an excessively superior object in exchange for the gift of some inferior object. For this very reason, this [figure] is sharpened by the sprout of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *parikara* (poetic elaboration); thus it differs from the previous one, which was embellished by *śleṣa* alone.

Just as a certain moon-faced cowherd girl purchased a priceless, dark-blue gem—the very ornament for the parting of the hair of the young maiden of the Vedas—by offering smooth sprouts of coral. 1452.

*Ślakṣṇaḥ* means small; as Amara states: "The words *ślakṣṇa*, *dabhra*, *kṛśa*, and *tanu* [mean small]. Regarding *yaḥ pravālaḥ*: *pravāla* refers to coral; alternatively, *ślakṣṇa* means smooth or glossy, as Vaijayantī states: "The words *masṛṇa*, *ślakṣṇa*, *soma*, *alaca*, and *cikkaṇa* [mean smooth]. It is the lower lip which is identified (*adhyavasita*) as being that coral; [the result follows] from its being offered. The rest is clear.
Just as the daughter of King Ākāśa, whose mass of luster was devoted to serving the face of the full moon, sought the Lord of the World with two golden jars of supreme quality. 1453.

"Praguṇatamam" means possessing an exceedingly straight nature; according to Amara, "ṛju," "ajihma," and "praguṇa" are synonyms. By this, his lack of awareness regarding the deceptions employed by others is suggested. From the phrase "by the two golden jars and the treasury," it is understood that [the jars] contain a multitude of riches placed within golden pitchers. Here, in the example "Śrutiyuvatī" (The Maiden of the Vedas), because the Lord is superimposed upon the quality of being a dark gem and the lower lip upon the quality of being a smooth coral sprout, there is the figure of speech *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor). This is supported by the figure of *nyūnādhikaparivṛtti* (exchange of the deficient and the excessive).

The distinction is that this [speech] is embellished by the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the form of a metaphor (*rūpaka*)—namely, "by the golden jar and the treasury" in the example "O King Ākāśa"—and by the ornament of *parikara* (the suggestive epithet) in the form of the intentional qualifier "most excellent," according to the stated method.
In these examples, the transaction of giving and taking is purely a poetic invention; it is not real. Where it is real, there is no figure of speech (alaṅkāra).

Just as in a marketplace, some fortunate ones purchase clusters of excellent jewels—which possess rays like those of the sun, meaning they are exceedingly brilliant—for the pleasure of the mind of the Lord of Śrīparvata, using a price equal to their own sons. (1454) In this verse, the giving and receiving are merely products of the poet’s imagination; there is no actual transaction involved.
O Mother of All, the young girls of your house purchase all the rose-apples with clusters of *śambara* gems and the bimba-fruits with heaps of *kuruvinda* rubies. (1455)

The *bimba* fruits—those belonging to your devotees—are found in the houses of children, charming young women, or boys. Although here there is the presence of the *udātta* (the exalted) figure of speech, consisting of a description of prosperous objects, and thus involving giving and taking, nevertheless, these [examples] do not deserve to be cited as illustrations, because the buying is merely literal and has not been brought forth by the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*).

If it is admitted that even such instances of giving and taking possess the quality of being brought forth by the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*), then this too is indeed an example (*udāharaṇa*), and not a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) like the verse beginning with *adhivipaṇi*.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, the "String of Parivṛtti Jewels," in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.

The bimbas—meaning *bimbī* fruits—are present in the houses of your devotees; [the agents] are young girls, charming women, or boys. Although here the transactions of giving and taking are governed by the figure of speech *udātta* (the sublime), which consists of the description of a magnificent object, nevertheless, these are not brought forth by the poet’s creative genius (*pratibhā*). Since the act of purchase is merely factual, such instances do not deserve to be cited as examples [of this figure].

If it is admitted that even such instances of giving and taking possess the quality of being brought forth by the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*), then this too is indeed an example (*udāharaṇa*), and not a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) like the verse beginning with *adhivipaṇi*.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on Exchange (Parivṛtti), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Chapter on Enumeration (Parisaṃkhyā):
"When one thing could be obtained in many ways, the restriction of it to a single instance is what those who travel the path of poetics call Enumeration (Parisaṃkhyā)."

This statement is made here on the occasion of discussing the "one" and the "many. When a single object is simultaneously possible in multiple locations, its restriction to one location—by way of excluding the second—due to its impossibility elsewhere, is *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification). It is called *parisaṃkhyā* because it is a counting (*saṃkhyāna*) of something as being worthy of description by means of the exclusion (*parivarjana*) of something else. This [figure] is first divided into two types: the pure (*śuddhā*) and that preceded by a question (*praśnapūrvikā*). Each of these two is further divided into two types—the semantic (*ārthī*) and the verbal (*śābdī*)—thus resulting in four varieties of this figure.

Although the established principle of the *Pūrvatant*ra (Mīmāṃsā) is that a *niyama* (restriction) excludes an option that might otherwise be obtained, whereas a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) has as its fruit the exclusion of other objects when multiple options are simultaneously available; nevertheless, in this [present] system, the internal distinction between what is optionally obtained and what is invariably obtained is not intended to be expressed, due to the absence of any purpose [for such a distinction]. For this very reason, even in the *Mahābhāṣya*, the term *niyama* is used for *parisaṃkhyā* in the case of the rule "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten. Examples follow in order: [Example of *niyama*: "One should sacrifice with *vrīhi* grain" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "Five five-nailed animals are to be eaten" (*pañca pañcanakhā bhakṣyāḥ*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He wears two garments" (*dve vāsasī paridadhāti*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not eat at night" (*na naktaṃ bhuñjīta*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the rising sun" (*nodyantam ādityam īkṣeta*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the setting sun" (*na nimlocantam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in water" (*na salile saṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected on the ground" (*na bhūmau saṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in a mirror" (*na darpaṇe saṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in a sword" (*na khaḍge saṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in a chariot" (*na rathasaṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in a horse" (*na hayasaṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in a cow" (*na goḥ saṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in a woman" (*na striyāḥ saṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in a man" (*na puruṣasya saṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in a garment" (*na vāsasaḥ saṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in a house" (*na gṛhasaṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in a wall" (*na kuḍyasaṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in a tree" (*na vṛkṣasaṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does not look at the sun reflected in a mountain" (*na parvatasaṃkrāntam*). [Example of *parisaṃkhyā*: "He does
If you have a desire to see him who personally sports with Lakṣmī, behold him; if service is desired, then, my dear, serve him sufficiently.

In this context, since the status of seeing and other such acts—which are indicated by the words *yadi* and *cet* and are prompted by worldly attachment—is already established with respect to the Blessed Lord Śrīnivāsa as well as with respect to other objects, it would follow that the sentence-meaning constituted by the sense of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) would be rendered purposeless. Therefore, the exclusion of those respective acts from having other objects as their focus—expressed in the form "you should not see other objects," and so forth—is postulated as the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*). Consequently, this is an "implicative" (*ārthī*) and "pure" (*śuddhā*) negation.

What is the disease? The bondage of worldly existence (bhava-yoga). Who indeed is the physician? That Primordial Person (puruṣa). What is the abundant medicine? That sovereignty which consists in the recitation of His names.

Here, by the force of the intended meaning (*tātparyamaryādayā*), the sense is understood that the conjunction of the states of existence (*bhava-yoga*) and so forth alone constitutes disease and the like, and nothing else; thus, this is both implied (*ārthīya*) and preceded by a question.

The field is the lineage of the excellent serpent; in this place, one knows it to be a field unlike any other, barren soil. It is the abode of the god Vāsudeva, who is more than a mere form, like a living god himself.

Here, by means of the two words "ūṣarakṣetra" (a saline field) and "savigrahamṛt" (earth with a form), the exclusion of [the comparison to] a divine field and a divine deity is perceived; thus, this is verbal pure [śuddha].
Just as my heart may remain forever attached to the Slayer of Madhu and never at all to wealth, so let there be incomparable devotion to His feet, but never mine in vain ascetic practice.
Austerity (*tapas*) refers to the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such practices. Here too, as before, the exclusion based on the literal meaning (*śābdī vyāvṛttiḥ*) is pure.
Where indeed could there be success in describing the lotus-eyed one’s glories with words? Not even in a most marvelous hymn of praise for the widespread noose of a false king.
Here, the exclusion is verbal and is preceded by a question.

This is the opinion of the ancients. Others, however, maintain that the figure of speech *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) occurs only when the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is intended as a significant meaning; otherwise, it is merely a simple *parisaṃkhyā*. Just as the figure of speech *hetu* (causality) occurs only when causality is intended as a significant meaning, whereas otherwise it is a mere cause, they say that this [figure] has only these two varieties.

Others, however, maintain that even if exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) has a referent, it does not constitute a figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*), because that would lead to the undesired consequence of such status for statements like "five five-nailed animals are edible," "one should sacrifice when the moon is level [with the sun]," and "of *rāt* and *sas*. Rather, only such an exclusion as is fashioned by the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*) is a figure of speech.

O Blessed One, for me, whose sins have been endless since the beginning of creation, this very service to you— being your servant— is indeed my atonement for those evils that are difficult to terminate.

O Blessed One! For the pacification of my endless and insurmountable sins that have persisted from the beginning of creation until now, my very state of being a *śeṣa* (a dependent) to You is itself Your *nirveśa* (acceptance); for me, whose sole remainder is You, Your constant mindfulness as my *śeṣin* (the master/protector) is the true *nirveṣa*—that is, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). The sense is that it is not the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, or other such penances. "If You desire Your own revival—if You have a longing for Your own existence—then always remember Your own servitude to Hari and His nature as the Master."
Just as fire with its uplifted flames, aided by the wind, consumes dry grass,
so does Viṣṇu, residing within the mind, burn away all that is inauspicious for yogis.
For he has indeed expiated even the sins of ten million births,
since, though helpless, he uttered the name of Hari as a prayer for well-being.

Such authoritative sources as these should be considered here. Regarding the phrase *śeṣatayā*, there are two words: *śe* and *ṣatayā*. *Śe* refers to the letter *śa*; *ṣatayā* means "by way of being *ṣa*" (*ṣakāratayā*), that is to say, by the substitution of the letter *ṣa* in place of the letter *śa*. One should also consider a specific poetic figure (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) in the fact that the word *nirveśaḥ* becomes the word *nirveṣaḥ*.
Or, for example:

"While the Lord with lotus-eyes, the auspicious one who protects the earth from blemish during the rite of night, was present, the reputation of 'the time of darkness' (pradoṣatā) arose among the people at the very beginning of the night. (1462)
Śrī, that is Lakṣmī herself, is the night; the meaning is "in the moon" (vidhau) of that night. Or, for example:

"O Hari, while you protect the world, the word 'calamity' has come to mean 'an army without foot-soldiers'; the word 'hardship' (kṛcchra) is heard by people only in connection with the performance of expiatory rites. (1463)

In such instances as these, the word *vipatti* means news of calamity (*vipad-vārtā*). Alternatively, *vipatti* is that in which the foot-soldiers (*pattayaḥ*) have departed; thus, the word *vipatti* [is derived]. *Kṛcchram* means hardship or suffering, such as the *parāka* and other types of penance (*kṛcchra*). This is also seen in the compositions of others, such as: "While he, the subduer of the earth (the King), was ruling, there was heat only in the kitchens. For here, the meaning of the nominative case is unified through the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*), and by means of that, the exclusion of its opposite is established. And so: "If you have a desire to see..."

In this case, let there be *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) because the meaning "nothing else is to be seen" is understood; however, it is not the figure of speech *parisaṅkhyā-alaṃkāra*, because the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is factual (*vāstavika*) and thus does not depend upon the poet’s creative imagination (*pratibhā*). Exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) means delimitation (*vyavaccheda*). But in the verse "What is disease? Association with worldly existence," there is a *dṛḍhāropa-rūpaka* (a firm metaphor based on superimposition) preceded by a question. Otherwise, even in the verse "They say poison is not truly poison; the property of a Brahmin is called poison," there would result the fault of [misapplying] *parisaṅkhyā*.

"Where indeed is the field for the fruitfulness of words? The lineage of the noble serpents (the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*). Here too, there is only pure *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), because, for the reason stated previously, there is no lack of purpose [in the exclusion]. Therefore, they say that examples such as "heat in the kitchens" are alone the illustrations of this [figure].

In reality, however, even if the exclusion is verbal (*śābda*), if there is an excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) through *śleṣa* (punning) and other means brought forth by the poet's genius, the figure of *parisaṃkhyā* is not barred even in such cases.

O Mother, your sovereignty is entirely unimpaired in every respect; you alone are to be served by him. Of what use is that Śauri to us, who has assumed the lordship over the Yadus only in certain places? || 1464 ||

That Śauri, because at some time he assumed a diminished or inferior lordship—where "of the Yadus" (*yadūnām*) is a compound word, though the actual state of affairs is that it refers to the lordship over those belonging to the lineage of Yadu; the word *yadu* is used here figuratively to denote his descendants.

In this case, although the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)—expressed by the words "what is the use of that Śauri?"—is verbal, it is nonetheless supported by the presentation of a reason provided through the figure of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), which is rooted in the identification [of one thing with another] based on the foundation of *śleṣa* (punning). Since the resulting excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) cannot be denied by connoisseurs, the figure of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusion) certainly exists here. Thus, since the figure of *parisaṃkhyā* must necessarily be admitted even in such instances where the exclusion is verbal, its existence elsewhere as well cannot be denied.

Likewise, the figure of speech *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) is quite prevalent even in the verses that will be cited hereafter; for this very reason, the authors of the *Kuvalayānanda* cited the example: "The waning of oil occurs in lamps, not in the hearts of those with arched brows."

Just as there are two things called "wealth" (*vitta*) and "conduct" (*vṛtta*), yet here it is conduct alone that must be protected by your followers, and not wealth—which comes and goes—is it not true that the distinction between these two is thus clearly revealed? (1465)
The word "nanu" is used as an address to the Blessed One. That wealth (*vitta*) comes (*eti*) and goes (*yāti*). The distinction between these two—wealth and conduct (*vṛtta*)—is indeed manifest:
"One should always protect conduct alone; wealth comes and goes.
One who is diminished in wealth is not lost, but one who is diminished in conduct is utterly destroyed."

The meaning is that the distinction (*vailakṣaṇya*) has indeed been explained by the sages who remember [the tradition] in this way. Regarding those two words, *vitta* and *vṛtta*, the difference (*bheda*) consists precisely in the two syllables *vi* and *vṛ*; the suffix *-tas* is used here in the sense of all case-endings (*sārvavibhaktikas-tasi*). Furthermore, the meaning—that the distinction is merely that much, since they are otherwise identical in their other phonemes—is also strikingly beautiful (*camatkārī*).

In this case, although the exclusion expressed by the words "but not wealth" (*na tu vittam*) is verbal in nature, the figure of speech *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) certainly occurs because it is nourished by the excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) that has been established. It should be noted that in this example, the reversal of the application of the terms *vṛtta* and *vitta*—which were understood according to their traditional definitions—is precisely what constitutes the distinction; this is done in accordance with the pursuit of the established charm.

Or rather: "O Leader, if you do not take me, who have come to you for refuge, to yourself, then let the Slayer of Madhu lead even me to that supreme Leader; may you alone be my protection—what need is there for him?"

O Śrī! If you lead—meaning, cause to reach—the Lord, my own dear leader and beloved, who has come to you for refuge; then even this Madhumathana might seek another leader or protector besides himself and not protect me himself, but instead hand me over to another like a load to be carried by a porter (*viṣṭibhāra*). This is the sense. The *liṅ* suffix is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). Therefore...

"You alone must protect"—that is, you must guard [him]. The sense is: "What is there that cannot be accomplished by the Blessed One, who thus causes him to reach another hero? The instrumental case is used because "even an implied action serves as the motivator for a case-ending. In the ultimate sense, however, the meaning is: "If you lead me, who have come for refuge, to your beloved, then do so without delay. The construction is: "This Madhumathana [is] the hero (*nāyaka*). This refers to *nāka*, meaning heaven, formed by removing the letter *ya* from *nāyaka*.

"Paraṃ nākam" means the supreme heaven, the highest ether, that is to say, the divine abode. "Abhigamayet" (may He cause to attain): the sense is that by virtue of His overflowing affection for you, through you—who have become the very instrument of His personal effort—He causes [the soul] to reach His own presence and immediately unites it with the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). Therefore, the sense is that you alone are the primary cause for obtaining such a special attainment. "Avyāḥ" (may He protect). Why is this said? It is out of an extreme abundance of respect for Lakṣmī, and not because of indifference toward the Blessed Lord; this is the secret.
Here too, as before, one should consider how the exclusion [of others] is expressed verbally and so forth.
O Daughter of the Earth, although you entreated him, saying, "Hand me over to my husband," the ten-faced Rāvaṇa delivered only Laṅkā back to him, but not you, his mother.

"To the Lord, the husband, the son of Daśaratha; deliver him, hand him over. According to Amara, "niryātana" means the settling of a debt, giving, or the returning of a deposit. By this, the words of the blessed Sītā—"And you, being diligent, ought to deliver me to him"—are recognized. He delivered Laṅkā itself—that is, he gave it [to Rāma]—but not you.

In reality, however, she made her [the city] "niryātuḥ," meaning one from whom *yātus* (demons) have been expelled or completely eliminated; the form *niryātuḥ* is derived from the word *niryātu-* by applying the rule of *iṣṭhavadbhāva* (treating it like the superlative suffix *iṣṭha*) before the suffix *ṇa*, resulting in the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant). The meaning is that he searched for and dealt with the *rākṣasas*.

Just as the husking of rice occurs only for the heap of grains within a cooking pot, so it is not for those who bow at Your feet, O Blessed One, the bestower of all fruits, for their desires are already fulfilled.

Those who deserve the *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooking) are called *sthālībilīyāḥ*; the meaning is "those fit for cooking. The suffix *cha* is applied after *sthālībila* in the sense of "deserving" (*arha*). Regarding those husks (*tuṣa*), their being "in the heap alone" means the absence of *phalīkaraṇa*—that is, the lack of threshing. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of negation, like the word *nirmakṣika* ("free from flies"). *Phalīkaraṇa* refers to the fine husks of rice and other grains; elsewhere, it means making something useless. Thus, the meaning here is that they are not made useless [by being removed].
While Nārāyaṇa, the cause for the removal of all sins, shines within my heart, if my enemy should still resort to evil deeds, let him do so; it would not affect my mind at all.

If misfortune (*durita*) should resort to hostility (*aritām*) or enmity (*vidveṣam*) toward me, let it do so; if it should strive to cause me distress, let it strive. The sense is that such misfortune alone would be "burned" (*dutam*), scorched—derived from the root *ḍu-du* (meaning "to afflict") with the suffix *kta*. But my mind shall not be burned, for the Lord Hari dwells right there [within it]. In the alternative sense, the word-play is as follows: if the word *duritam* were to lose its status as having the letter 'r' (*aritām*)—that is, if the letter 'r' were absent—it would result in the form *dutam*. This meaning also produces a striking aesthetic effect (*camatkurute*). As in another example:

O Śauri, for me who am wallowing here in this shoreless, terrible, and boundless ocean of saṃsāra, you are not my savior; yet, because of my own fickleness, I myself have become the quicksilver (pārada).
Having obtained refuge in you alone, the wise cross over the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, which is a vessel for infinite afflictions.

The sense is: "even though you have been described as possessing such great power. You are not my ferryman—one who reaches the further shore—for me as I wallow in the shoreless and terrible abyss of saṃsāra. This expresses a reproach: "I do not know [if you fail] due to indifference or due to incapacity. However, the meaning is: "because of my fickleness—that is, my inability to wait for you to reach the further shore—I myself became the ferryman, the one who reached the further shore for you or for me."

In the ultimate sense, however, due to its fickleness and restless nature, I became like mercury—mercury being called *rasa*, *sūta*, and *pārada* (Amara-kośa). The meaning is: "Though I have waited for so long, when will you, who fail to bring me to the further shore of the ocean of existence, carry me across? Therefore, I take refuge in the 'Avatapta-nakula' (the heated stone that does not burn the mongoose). Or as another example: "O Lord, the mountain of gold, though there may be wickedness, anger, or foul-mouthedness during a particular year, never at any time do these exist among those who have taken refuge in You. (1471)

O Blessed One, talk of miserable rebirths and accounts of calamities arise only among the classes of people beginning with the *prādi* [prepositions]; they never manifest among the classes of people beginning with the Brahmins who have taken refuge at the lotus-feet of You.

"News of misfortune" (durgativārtā) refers to news concerning poverty, hell, and so forth; as Medinī states: "Durgati means hell or destitution. "Ill omens" (durupasarga) refers to wicked portents; as Amara states: "Ajanya, utpāta, and upasarga—these three are synonymous and are neuter. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), for the indeclinable *duḥ*, there is "news of movement," meaning its designation as a *gati*; for the prefix *duḥ*, there is the "discourse" or mention [of its status].

The meaning is that because both the designations *upasarga* (prefix) and *gati* (indeclinable particle) are prescribed for the words listed in the *prādi* group by the two rules, "prādayaḥ" and "gatiśca," and because the word *duḥ* is read therein [in the *prādi* list]. Furthermore, the sense that the *viprādi* group is contrary to the *prādi* group should also be supplied as an interpretation.

In these examples, although the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is verbal, it constitutes the figure of speech *parisaṃkhyā* nonetheless, because it possesses an excellence of charm through its fusion with a superimposition of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*) rooted in *śleṣa*. Thus, the figure *parisaṃkhyā* should be understood as twofold, by way of being either implied (*ārthī*) or expressed (*śābdī*). Although earlier authors cited a twofold division of this figure based on whether it is preceded by a question or not, the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* has disregarded it due to the absence of any particular strikingness (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*).

Furthermore, when this figure is enlivened by *śleṣa* (punning), it possesses an exceeding charm; as should be noted, in the verses cited immediately above, an extreme beauty is perceived through the punning of words such as "rendering mercury fruitless" (*pāradaniṣphalīkaraṇa*).

In this figure of *parisaṃkhyā*, there is no fixed rule regarding the sequence of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) and restriction (*niyamana*), just as in the case of concealment (*nihnava*) and attribution (*āropa*) in pure *apahnuti*. Thus, even when the exclusion comes first—as it does in the case of restriction—the figure of *parisaṃkhyā* remains entirely intact.
O Delight of Nanda, you cannot become a source of misfortune by deviating from your true nature; for none other than you—not even Brahmā or Rudra—could do so, of this there is no doubt. (1473)

O Nandanandana, because you would be the opposite of *prakṛti*, you would be a giver of misfortune (*anarthada*) due to being contrary to the nature of *sattva* as described in such passages as, "That which is *sattva* is the Lord Hari; He is the Great Lord, the Puruṣa, the impeller of *sattva*. You would not be the bestower of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) resulting from an abundance of *rajas* and *tamas*.
For it is said: "Whosoever Madhusūdana beholds at the time of birth, he should be known as one of *sattvic* nature; indeed, he is intent upon the goal of liberation."

The sense is this: according to the manner described above, since You are the bestower of the supreme human goal in the form of *niḥśreyasa* (liberation) preceded by the awakening of *sattva*, how could You grant a human goal that is to be abandoned? Anyone other than You—whether the four-faced Brahmā or Rudra—might indeed be such [a giver], but due to their contrary nature, they would be givers of misfortune; of this there is no doubt.
As it is said: "If Brahmā or Rudra sees him being born, his mind is overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*."

The sense is that, according to the manner described, since they incite *rajas* and *tamas*, they would only bestow those human goals that are to be abandoned, and not, like You, bestow the supreme goal of life. In the alternative sense, the word "Nandanandana" (Son of Nanda) would not be "anarthada"—that is, it would not fail to reveal the aforementioned meaning—due to its being read in reverse order (*prātilomyena*) from the stated form of the *prakṛti*. The sense is that even when the *prakṛti* "Nandanandana" is read in reverse order, it does not lose its own inherent meaning.

The sense is that, were there a reversal of nature through the inversion of the prior sequence, the word "Brahmā" would not signify anyone other than you as Brahmā, nor would the word "Rudra" signify Rudra; rather, it would fail to illuminate any meaning whatsoever. Here, one should distinguish that in this case there is exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) preceded by negation, whereas in the previous examples there was restriction (*niyama*) preceded by affirmation.

In these examples, by means of either the inherent nature of things or through the identification based on the foundation of *śleṣa* (punning), the negation of a thing whose relation is well-established in both [contexts] is established by its affirmation in one place. Some, however, maintain that even for a thing whose relation is well-established in one place, its negation is established in another substratum (*dharmin*)—which possesses the same well-known status—by means of the affirmation of a property (*dharma*) in the other. For example:
"O Lord, this earth is exceedingly burdened by him who is envious of you—a man of ill-repute and ill-mannered—not by mountains or by vast *sāla* trees."

It is well known that the excessive burden of the earth belongs only to mountains and the like, and not to a person who is envious of the Blessed One. In this verse, the prescription of such excessive burden for that kind of person and the prohibition of it for mountains and the like constitute a clear instance of the aforementioned variety of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification). Furthermore, it should be noted that this is embellished by *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole), consisting in the assertion of a connection with such a burden for that person, despite the fact that no such connection actually exists.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of Enumeration (Parisaṃkhyā), in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of Option (Vikalpa):
"Option (*vikalpa*) is described as the occurrence of two contradictory possibilities."

"In a single substratum (*dharmī*), because two contradictory properties—which are obtained through their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and are therefore of equal strength—cannot possibly be obtained simultaneously due to their very contradiction, the attainment [of both] results in a merely partial or alternative attainment. This [figure], as the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara* following the *Alaṃkārasarvasva* states, is the opposite of the *samuccaya* (conjunction) about to be described, and is like the *vyatireka* (contrast) to *upamā* (simile).
