For in *samuccaya*, there is the simultaneous existence of both; here, however, it is otherwise, and thus it is its opposite."

The author of the *Vimarśinī* states: The *Dīkṣitas*, however, describe another distinct figure of speech called *Kārakadīpaka*, which they claim stands as the counterpart to the first type of *Samuccaya* (Accumulation) and as the counterpart to the second type of *Samuccaya* that follows immediately after *Samādhi*.

Thus, due to this difference of opinion, it has been deliberated whether [the subject] should be "death or crossing" of the great ocean; for alas, O best of the Raghus, even though you are one who enables the crossing of the ocean of worldly existence, you have [remained] on the shore of the [physical] sea! (1475)

The verse from the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*, "Today let there be either my death or the crossing of the ocean," is intended here. The phrase "due to a difference of opinion" (*matabhedāt*) means "due to an alternative" (*vikalpāt*). It is the ablative case used with the elision of the suffix *-lyap* (i.e., *vibhajya*). The meaning is "having resolved upon an alternative. Furthermore, for the sake of a particular aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*), it may be embellished by the sense that one or the other is adopted based on the mere difference between the letters *ma* and *ta* in the words *maraṇa* (death) and *taraṇa* (crossing).

Perceiving that you have uttered the words for the liberation from the entire mass of sins, I go to you for refuge; the moment has arrived for that [promise], whether it be a deception or a deliverance.

This is a restatement of the meaning of the *Carama-śloka*: "I take refuge in You," while perceiving with full conviction Your word—"I shall liberate you from all sins"—which declares the release from the entire mass of sins. The occasion for that promised liberation from all sins has now arrived; the sense is that it has come about through the acquisition of a person like me, who is a treasure-house of every sin. Whether that word of Yours be a deception or a betrayal, let it be a salvation—a deliverance across the ocean of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*).
O Lord, even if I have committed an offense, I find You through devotion or through surrender; accept me as such, however wretched I may be, or punish me—what does my infamy matter?

"Accept me—who have thus established my resolve and employed the proper means—for protection; or seize me, or restrain me. What dishonor or infamy is there for me? On the contrary, the infamy would be yours alone in the restraint of one who has sought refuge. Here, because there is no perception of a formal comparison (*aupamya*) between death and crossing over, or between deception and saving, or between accepting and restraining, there is merely an option (*vikalpa*), as in the expression: "Whether life or death befall me, I shall never abandon righteousness."
Regarding this, the authors of the *Rasagaṅgādhar* and others maintain that there is no perception of a simile between living and dying.

This example shows that one who has gone for refuge without hesitation should not be harmed by an enemy, even in two ways; O Lord of the Night-rangers, either protect Rāghava in battle or quickly seek refuge with him yourself.

This is the speech of Aṅgada directed toward Rāvaṇa: "This Rāghava would not harm an enemy who has sought refuge in him without hesitation—that is, in such a way that he is free from doubt, thinking 'this one will surely harm me,' because he stands at the very forefront of those whose primary duty is the protection of those who seek refuge. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), it means "without the letter *śa*" (*niśśam*), which refers to the battle (*raṇam*) where the sound *śa* has departed.

"Whichever enemy has come forward for battle, whom would it not afflict? It afflicts every assailant; this is the meaning. Therefore, quickly take refuge with Rāghava—go to him for protection, since the root *pad* preceded by *pra* carries that sense. Alternatively, you should enter—that is, reach—the *āhava*, which is battle."

In this context, regarding the act of surrender (*prapadana*), since it is impossible for the two actions—surrendering to Rāma and fighting with Ahi—to occur simultaneously as the objects enjoined by the two authorities that dictate the performance of peace and war, their occurrence must be understood as successive. The comparison is based on the common attribute of the two actions being fulfilled solely through the result of the act, namely, surrender.

If it is argued that, just as here the similarity between two actions is understood through the identity of the property consisting in *prapatti* (resorting), which is the fruit of the meaning of the verbal root *pad* preceded by the prefix *pra*, so too in expressions such as "let there be life or death," the similarity between the agents—life and death—is likewise fit to be understood through the identity of the property consisting in existence (*sattā*), we reply: it is indeed fit, yet it is not understood. If one asks for what reason this is so, understand that it is because of the absence of the poet’s intention (*tātparya*).

The poet’s intention here is not that death and life are equal; rather, as in the expression "Eat poison, but do not eat in his house," he intends to show that even death is better than the abandonment of dharma, given the excessive aversion toward what is forbidden. And for that purpose, since death has been adopted [as the preferred alternative], the comparison is simply not established because its locus is unintended, so they say.

Thus, in the verse beginning with "either death or deception," the poet's intention is to take up the prohibited course—characterized by the abandonment of the implied promise—and thereby perceive an excess of fault therein; whereas in the verse beginning with "but in that [verse] regarding the excess of devotion," the poet's intention lies in the excess of regard for the prescribed course, namely taking refuge, and not in death or deception. This should be understood likewise in the verse beginning with "by means of devotion."
Just as the heroic monkeys, free from the terror of apprehension, blocked the gates of Laṅkā, so [you] must either restore Sītā or grant a vast battle to the Lord of Kosala.

In this context, within the speech of Sāraṇa addressed to Rāvaṇa—which follows the verse from the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*: "Either give Sītā to him, or offer a fair fight"—there is a description of *vikalpa* (option), characterized by the rejection of one alternative without violating the possibility of obtaining either, regarding the two options of giving Sītā or engaging in battle. These two options, pertaining to Rāvaṇa, are obtained through the authoritative means of peace (*saṃdhi*) and war (*vigraha*), and are therefore of equal strength; yet, because they cannot occur simultaneously, there arises a description of optionality. Here, the simile (*aupamya*) consists in the common attribute of the two actions—giving Sītā and fighting—namely, their shared result in the form of "bestowal" (*vitaraṇa*).
Or as it is said:

"O jewel of the Nāgeśa mountain, this person has approached you out of fear; grant me either worldly enjoyment (bhoga) or spiritual union (yoga)—what difference does this distinction of fear make to you? (1480)

O jewel of the Nāgeśa mountain, O crest-jewel of Śeṣādri, this person has sought refuge in you through the connection with fear—that is, out of a state of dread. Grant me either *bhoga* (worldly happiness) or *yoga* (the path of devotion which causes the cessation of worldly enjoyment), or the experience of your own self; bestow it as you wish by virtue of your unrestrained sovereignty. How difficult could this removal of the fear of one who has sought refuge be for you? This is the meaning. Furthermore, what difference does the distinction between the letters *bha* and *ya* in the words *bhoga* and *yoga* make? It is of no consequence, since they are identical in all other respects. Thus it is said.

Generally speaking, here there is an option (vikalpa) because of the impossibility of the simultaneous occurrence of enjoyment and yoga, which are mutually contradictory. Here too, the comparison between the two actions—enjoyment and yoga—is based on the common property of being accomplished through the act of giving as their respective fruit.

O Lord, since you have undertaken the vow of protecting those who prostrate, I implore you for refuge. Whether my distress be stilled or your fame be increased, the protection of those who bow before you is your sole purpose.
If you protect me, my suffering will be stilled; for as long as one does not go for refuge to You, the destroyer of all sins, there shall be suffering, longing, delusion, and unhappiness.

For it has been said: "If [you do not protect him], your fame—founded upon your dedication to rescuing those who have sought refuge—will perish. Behold: when a protector fails to guard one who has come for shelter, that unprotected person departs taking away all of that protector's merit."
It leads away from heaven, brings dishonor, and destroys strength and valor.

Because of this statement, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the pacification of distress (*ārti-śānti*) and the pacification of fame (*kīrti-śānti*), as both are obtained simultaneously by means of two authorities of equal strength; since they are mutually contradictory, their simultaneous existence is impossible. The comparison should be understood through the common attribute of being a form of pacification applied to both distress and fame.
In some cases, even when the common attribute is omitted, this ornament [simile] occurs provided that the comparison is still understood.
Whether it be little or much, cast aside this dullness consisting of the five senses; you shall enjoy this nurse of the world, or you shall even attain the prosperity ordained by the Creator.

In this instance, the intended comparison is between the act of nourishing (*dhātrī-bhoga*) and the attainment of the Creator’s perfection (*vaidhātra-saṃpat*), both of which are praiseworthy. This is an option (*vikalpa*) between the meanings of two verbal roots (*dhātvartha*), and not between the nourisher and the Creator’s perfection; for since these two are merely factors (*kāraka*), an option between them would be incoherent without their connection to an action. Nor should it be argued that the option is "omitted" (*lupta*) because a common property in the form of the agent has been stated for one of the two root-meanings; for by taking the common property in the form of the agent, no beautiful comparison is produced here.

Otherwise, they say that just as in the verse "Either being slain you shall attain heaven, or having conquered you shall enjoy the earth," the same cognition of comparison would arise even in the case of "Either being slain you shall go to hell, or having conquered you shall enjoy the earth. Thus, in this figure of speech, the seed of its status as an *alaṃkāra* is the beautiful comparison between the two alternatives being considered; for it is only by taking up that [comparison] that the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) unfolds. Otherwise, it would be a mere *vikalpa* (alternation); such is the secret.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, "The Lake of Alternatives," in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.

Here, the intended comparison (*upamā*) is between the attainment of the prosperity of a nurse (*dhātrī-bhoga*) and that of Brahmā (*vaidhātra-saṃpat*), both being regarded as praiseworthy. This is an alternative (*vikalpa*) between the meanings of two verbal roots (*dhātvartha*), and not between the prosperity of the nurse and that of Brahmā; for an alternative is untenable between two things unless they are connected to an action solely by way of being factors (*kāraka*). Nor should it be argued that the comparison is "elliptical" (*luptā*) because a common attribute in the form of the agent (*kartṛ*) has been stated for one of the two root-meanings; for a beautiful comparison is not established here by taking the agent as the common attribute.

Otherwise, they say that just as in the verse "Either slain you shall attain heaven, or having conquered, you shall enjoy the earth," the same cognition of a comparison (*aupamya*) would arise even in the case of "Either slain you shall go to hell, or having conquered, you shall enjoy the earth. Thus, in this figure of speech, the seed of its status as an *alaṃkāra* is the beautiful comparison between the two alternatives being considered; for it is only by taking that [comparison] up that aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) is manifested. Otherwise, however, it would be a mere *vikalpa* (alternative); such is the secret.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Jewel of Ornaments (*alaṅkāramaṇi*), in the *Alaṅkāra-muktāvalī*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of Conjunction (*samuccayālaṅkāra*):
"Conjunction (*samuccaya*) occurs when there is a connection of objects simultaneously."

The term "simultaneity" (*yaugapadyāt*) is intended to exclude [the application of] the rule of corresponding order (*yathāsaṃkhya*), but not to imply that [the two cognitions] must occur in a single moment. Therefore, even if there is a slight difference in time in some cases—according to the analogy of piercing the hundred petals of a lotus flower—there is no loss of their being a conjunction (*samuccaya*). This [conjunction] is twofold, by way of a difference in the substrata (*dharmin*) or an identity of the property (*dharma*). Even in the case of an identity of the property, there is a twofold division: [conjunction] through a relation other than causality when there is a connection with a single property, and [conjunction] through causality when there is a connection with a single property.

Thus, in this threefold [classification], in the first two varieties there is a conjunction of qualities, actions, and both qualities and actions; whereas in the third variety, there is a conjunction of beautiful, ugly, and both beautiful and ugly things with similar [objects]. This very third variety is what was designated by Dīkṣita as the second type of *samuccaya* (conjunction), namely "the conjunction of those sharing a single task through a sense of rivalry" (*ahaṃprathamikā*). The ancients called this very same figure *tatkara*.

As it has been said: "When, for the sake of accomplishing that [same effect], another [cause] should occur in relation to one [cause] which is already performing it. Its existence consists in the rejection of alternative possibilities (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, one should not suspect that this third variety constitutes the figure of speech *samādhi* (the "convenient"), which will be discussed later; for the domain of *samādhi* is where, while an effect is being brought about by one cause, an excellence such as ease is produced by another cause that happens to arrive unexpectedly.

In this third type of combination (*samuccaya*), however, its scope is that case where many [factors], like pigeons on a threshing floor, simultaneously rush forward with the thought "I am first" in order to accomplish a single effect, yet there is no excellence whatsoever in the effect itself.
Among these, an example of concomitance with different substrata (*bhinnadharmyanvaya*) is as follows:

"The sky is brightened by the rays of the autumnal moon, but the Yamunā forest is darkened by the splendor of Kṛṣṇa; the eye of the cowherd maiden is blue from the passion of love, yet it is also copper-red. (1483)
O Infinite One, my pair of eyes yearns for you, my mind, overcome by supreme joy, becomes delirious with delight; tears of rapture flow forth, and through service to you, all fear dissolves.
Here, in the first [type], there is a simultaneous connection with different substrata for the qualities, and in the second, for the actions.
An example of the concomitance with a single property (*ekadharmyanvaya*) is as follows:

"Shining with the luster of excellent jewels, reddened by the glow of his necklace, and smiling with the dark splendor of his own hue, Hari’s chest shines like a wonderful landscape fashioned for the sport of the Goddess Śrī. (1485)

Here, the qualities such as "redness" (āruṇya) and so forth are construed simultaneously with a single substratum in the form of the "large" (uru), through the relation of being located therein (ādheyatā). In the same manner, this should be understood accordingly in the subsequent cases as well.

O Lord, the fortunate man who remembers the flood of your multitude of auspicious qualities finds joy, abandons thirst for other things, censures [worldly life], and rejoices in your preeminence. (1486)
He censures thirst, that is, craving for sense objects; he rejoices, meaning he delights in your own excellence.
O Vāsudeva of inconceivable majesty, alas, when you are not meditated upon for even a single moment, the virtuous person wanders, exhausts himself, suffers intensely, and finds no peace at all.
Herein, the meaning of such authoritative scriptures as "Even for a moment or an instant, Vāsudeva is not meditated upon," and so forth, has been set forth.

O Enemy of Mura, one who is ignorant of You becomes angry with the virtuous, feels malice toward them, and rejoices in evil company; he delights in sense objects, withers away, and cultivates great sin. 1488.

In these three examples, there is a simultaneous connection (anvaya) of actions with a single substratum (dharmin); moreover, in the first two, that substratum is praiseworthy, whereas in the third, it is censurable.
The simultaneous connection of qualities and actions is as follows:

"The face of the Mistress of the World—its eyebrows moving, charmingly sweet, beautiful with its disheveled locks, and its outer corners turned upward—constantly delights the mind of the Lord of the Serpent-Kings. (1489)
In this instance, there is a simultaneous and collective connection of the two qualities—*lalita* and *madhura*—as well as the actions such as "moving the eyebrows," with a single substratum.

Thus, within the second classification characterized by the unity of attributes (*dharmaikya*), the primary variety—consisting of the co-occurrence of multiple attributes within a single substratum through a relation other than causality—has been demonstrated. Within the sub-classification consisting of the co-occurrence of multiple attributes within a single substratum by way of causality, there is the conjunction of excellences with excellences, as follows:

"Your loftiness is proclaimed by auspicious qualities that are not shared by others, such as knowledge, power, sovereignty, and so forth, as well as profundity, steadfastness, courage, and the like. (1490)

In this context, when excellence is possible through even one among knowledge and the other qualities, then qualities such as strength and so forth—whether falling away due to rivalry or for the sake of manifesting excellence—are beautiful.
O Lord of the Mountain, beloved of Kamalā, whose pair of eyes possesses the luster of lotuses and whose form resembles a dark rain cloud— this proclaims your sovereignty over all.

In this context, although the lordship of the universe could have been proclaimed by even one among the three attributes— such as having lotus-eyes well-known from such scriptural passages as "His eyes are like a lotus with petals as yellow as a monkey's bottom," "Hri and Lakshmi are his two wives," and "He stands in the midst of dark clouds"— all three have come together for that purpose as if in competition, and thus they are beautifully combined.
O Infinite One, as I gaze upon you, the arising of love, curiosity, the blending of fragrance, and horripilation unsettle the very limits of my restless mind. (1492)
Here too, as before, the conjunction of the arising of love and so forth is to be understood.
All of this is an illustration of the conjunction of beautiful things with beautiful things. An example of the conjunction of non-beautiful things with non-beautiful things is as follows:

"O Lord, the objects of the senses are indeed difficult to ward off, and my senses are difficult to subdue; moreover, my evil karma is boundless—when these are reflected upon, they cut into my very vitals. (1493)

Here, there is a conjunction (samuccaya) of the unwholesome objects, characterized by their being difficult to ward off, with the unwholesome senses and so forth, characterized by their being difficult to subdue. Although the cutting of the vital points is accomplished by contemplating the single factor of the objects being difficult to ward off, the difficulty of subduing the senses and so forth is also conjoined as it follows as a necessary consequence for that same purpose.
An example of the combination of the beautiful and the ugly:
"Your eye is devoid of description, and your tongue is likewise devoid of description; your ear is devoid of hearing—how then can my mind be inclined toward you? (1494)

In this context, the eyes and other features are not to be censured because they are beautiful by their very nature, and also due to the power of the poetic qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*). Thus, there is a "conjunction of the beautiful and the non-beautiful" (*śobhanāśobhanasamuccaya*), wherein beautiful things are brought within the scope of censure. In the compound *śobhanāśobhanānām*, a *karmadhāraya* is adopted rather than a *dvandva*, for otherwise the fault of "divergence from the associated" (*sahacarabhinnatva*) would arise.
In this way, a conjunction (samuccaya) is possible even for things that are unattractive and attractive, when they come together for the purpose of producing a single effect.

Just as your life-story is a poem consisting of your auspicious name, sung in tender tones, so too even the state of being an animal on your mountain is sufficient for the highest good, O Beloved of Śrī.

In this context, by such authoritative texts as "One should avoid poetic discourse" and "One who is impassioned should not sing," poetic songs and the like—which are inherently unwholesome—are nevertheless combined [with other practices] and rendered wholesome through the power of specific qualifications. The meaning is that on your mountain, even the state of being an animal (tiryaktva) becomes the state of being an animal [only] in the sense of being a servant devoted to your mountain.

O Lord of the Mountain, tears born from meditating upon You, the dullness born from contemplating You, and the faltering voice produced by chanting Your name— these are the path to the state of the virtuous.
In this case, although tears and the like are by nature inauspicious, they become auspicious through the power of their specific differentiation.
Some, however, maintained that there is also a combination of substance and genus; yet that is disregarded by us because it lacks a specific strikingness of effect (*vicchitti*).
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, the Chapter on Accumulation (Samuccaya), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Chapter on the Illuminator by Means of the Case-Function (Kārakadīpaka):
"If there are successive actions occurring within a single case-function..."
That which is performed as a combination (gumbhana) would be the illuminator of the factors of action (kārakadīpaka).

The joining together of successive actions pertaining to a single grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is the figure of speech known as *kārakadīpaka*. Although the grammatical factor (*dharmin*) that serves as the agent (*kāraka*) functions with reference to all the actions being described because they are equally contextual (*prastuta*), it is not appropriate to designate this as *dīpaka*, since it lacks the similarity to *dīpaka* characterized by being incidental (*prāsaṅgika*) to one thing while having been initiated for the sake of another. Nevertheless, it is so designated by resorting to a mere similarity to *dīpaka* based on the fact that a single entity is connected to multiple [actions].

We have already stated at the very occasion of defining the figure *dīpaka* that Daṇḍin, having subsumed *kārakadīpaka* within *dīpaka* itself, has also presented *tulyayogitā* as merely a variety of it. However, in reality, this [figure] deserves to be a distinct ornament like *mālādīpaka*, and should not be subsumed under *dīpaka*; for the soul of the latter—namely, its being based on a comparison (*upamā*)—is absent here. Furthermore, because it stands in opposition to *samuccaya* (conjunction), there exists a specific charm [of its own]. Thus, although this distinction was not made by earlier writers, it has been demonstrated by Dīkṣita, just as he did for the figure *vikalpa* in his *Alaṃkārasarvasva*.
He ascends the bull-like mountain, O Lord, and plunges into that lake; the fortunate man reaches you, then sheds tears of joy, and desires to dwell right there. (1497)

Just as Hari sees her, approaches her, stands near her, speaks with her, laughs, jests with her, converses, touches her, embraces her, and approaches the cowherd girl, he attains non-difference from her. || 1498 ||

*Ālāpa* is conversation; *sallāpa* is mutual discourse. Here, in the first [example], the sequential connection of a single agentive factor (*kartṛ-kāraka*)—in the form of the act of performing—to actions such as "climbing" is established. In the second, the sequential connection of a single agentive factor—in the form of Hari—to actions such as "seeing" is likewise established. Thus, this is the opposite of the first type of *samuccaya* (cumulative conjunction).
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, the Section on the Illuminator of the Case-Relations (*kārakadīpaka*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Section on the Ornament of Resolution (*samādhyalaṅkāra*):
Where the ease of accomplishing some particular effect is described by virtue of the proximity of another cause, there the ornament of resolution is said to reside.

The figure of speech *samādhi* consists in the perfect provision of that facility which belongs to an effect produced by a single cause, through the conjunction of another incidental cause. This [facility] occurs both through the effortless accomplishment of the effect and through the accomplishment of its constituent parts. Its distinction from a particular type of *samuccaya* (accumulation) has already been stated previously.
Just as you, by the power of some accidental merit, desire to uplift one such as I, so too has such an encounter with a holy man come upon me by chance at this very moment. (1499)
Just as Hari perceives her, so too does he approach, stand near, converse, laugh, jest, speak intimately, touch, embrace, and unite with the cowherd girl, becoming non-different from her. (1498)

*Ālāpa* is conversation; *sallāpa* is mutual discourse. Here, in the first [example], the sequential connection of a single agentive factor (*kartṛkāraka*)—in the form of the act of doing—to actions such as "climbing" and so forth is established. In the second, the sequential connection of a single agentive factor—in the form of Hari—to actions such as "seeing" and so forth is likewise established. Thus, this is the opposite of the first type of *samuccaya* (conjunction).
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, the Section on the Illuminator of the Case-Relations (*kārakadīpaka*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Section on the Ornament of Convergence (*samādhyalaṅkāra*):
Where the ease with which a certain effect is accomplished due to the presence of another cause is described, there the ornament of convergence is said to exist.

The figure of speech *samādhi* consists in the perfect provision of that facility which belongs to an effect produced by a single cause, when it is aided by the accidental concurrence of another cause. This [facility] occurs through the effortless accomplishment of the effect and through its accomplishment with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*). Its distinction from a particular type of *samuccaya* (accumulation) has already been stated previously.
Just as you, by the power of some accidental merit, desire to uplift one such as I, so too has such a meeting with a holy man come upon me by chance at this very moment. (1499)
In this regard, the attainment of the Lord’s desire to uplift, which might otherwise be accomplished only through accidental merit, is achieved effortlessly through association with the virtuous.
Or, for instance:
While the beautiful women of Vraja were longing for Śarī to give them a spontaneous embrace, a swarm of bees, drawn by the fragrance of their faces, arrived and rendered him assistance. (1500)

Here, for the cowherd woman who was longing [for her lover], the effortless accomplishment of a self-chosen embrace with Śauri as its object occurs through the coincidence of another cause in the form of the sudden descent of a swarm of bees.

When the vine-like body of Vraja accepted the novel and charming dalliance of Śauri, she then suddenly embraced him with a density intensified by the warbling of cuckoos, even though her embrace was slack.
Here, the completeness of the embrace is established by means of the warbling of cuckoos.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on Samādhi, in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on the Pratyanīka ornament:
"The Pratyanīka is the act of disparaging either a powerful adversary or his partisans."
Or, assistance rendered to one's adversary is termed an "enemy force" (pratyanīka).

In this context, the accomplishment of the Lord’s desire to uplift [the soul], which might otherwise be achieved only through accidental merit, is accomplished without effort through association with the virtuous.
Just as the beautiful women of Vraja longed for Śarī to grant them a spontaneous embrace, a swarm of bees, drawn by the fragrance of their faces, arrived and rendered him assistance.

Here, for the cowherd woman who was longing [for her lover], the effortless accomplishment of an embrace—initiated by herself and directed toward Śauri—is brought about through the coincidence of another cause: the sudden descent of a swarm of bees.

When the vine-like maiden of Vraja accepted the novel and charming flattery of Śauri, she then suddenly embraced him—though it was but a loose embrace—with a density intensified by the warbling of cuckoos.
In this case, the attainment of completeness for the embrace is established by means of the warbling of cuckoos.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on Samādhi, in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on the Pratyanīka ornament:
Disparagement of a powerful adversary, or of his partisans.
Or, assistance rendered to one's adversary is termed a counter-force (pratyanīka).

Where a weak person directly confronts a powerful adversary, the act of confronting that adversary by one who is unable to retaliate is called *pratyanīka* (counter-array). It is so named because it is similar (*sadṛśa*) to an army (*anīka*). Since similarity is established by its very nature, the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti...* (Pāṇini 2.1.6) would already have applied; however, because the word "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) is mentioned again in the rule, the *avyayībhāva* compound is formed even when the quality of similarity is subordinate (*guṇībhūta*).

In the world, an army (*anīka*) is deployed to repel an adversary; if that proves ineffective, one repels someone associated with him; and in the absence of even that, assistance is sought from a powerful opponent of the adversary. Because it is employed as something similar to an army, it is called a "counter-army" (*pratyanīka*). In this context, both the superiority residing in the adversary and the inferiority residing in oneself are understood. Of these, the first is as follows:
It is said that the orb of the Lord of Day, its radiance suddenly eclipsed by your greatness, immediately assumed the form of the Kaustubha gem and entered your heart.
Here, the direct refutation of the opponent's position has been established.
Or rather,
O Śauri, the tāpiñcha flower, having its own color surpassed by your preference, became a mere feather (piñcha) out of indignation and placed itself upon the place where your head rests.

*Tāpiñcha* refers to the flower of the *tāpiñcha* tree (the Tamāla); it is neuter because of the rule "all [words] denoting fruit are [neuter] when devoid of the [gender of the source]. [The phrase] *tvadrucikṛtāt paribhavataḥ* means from the humiliation or defeat caused by your displeasure; *bhraṃśitaḥ* means brought to a fall. Thus, [it describes one] whose facial complexion—that is, the luster of the face—has been cast down, meaning he has attained a loss of color in his countenance. *Piñchaṃ bhūtvā* means having become a tail-feather (*barha*), that is, having manifested in that form.

In this context, the word *tāpiñcha* is *bhraṃśi*, meaning "that which has a fall. That whose essence (*ātman*) or own nature (*svarūpa*) is *tā* is *tātmā*; that whose first syllable is such a *tātmā*, being thus constituted, becomes *piñcha*. The meaning is that by the removal of the present *tā*-vowel, the word *tāpiñcha* is produced as *piñcha*. The rest is easy to understand.

Just as the armor of Śauri, cast aside from his chest with a *kaṭa* sound due to its thickness and swollen with pride, rises upward and, assuming the nature of a *kaṅkaṭa*, subsequently covers that very chest—how wonderful! (1504)

Regarding the words *kapāṭa* and *kavāṭa*, the *Sudhā* commentary accepts the reading *kapāṭa* as primary in the statement "the words *kapāṭa* and *kavāṭa* are synonymous" (*kapāṭamararaṃ tulye*), and demonstrates the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) as "that which splits (*pāṭayati*) the head (*kaṃ*). In this view, the word *kapāṭa* is also included; there is identity between these two forms. In the phrase "cast down by the chest of Śauri" (*urasā apāstam*), the statement that the chest was cast down follows from the description of the chest's similarity to a door-panel (*kavāṭa*) in the verse "one whose chest is like a door-panel and whose neck is constricted" (*kavāṭavakṣāḥ pariṇaddhakaṃdharaḥ*). In the alternative view, however, the distinction lies in the reading *pāstam*.

The meaning is: that [city] in which the wall (*pākāra*) has been cast down and expelled; "cast down" means thrown out. By its "cheek-ness" (*kaṭatayā*), that is, by its being like the cheek of an elephant—Amara states, "the cheek is *kaṭa*"—it was "swollen with rut," meaning swollen with pride or with the flow of temple-ichor (*dānodaka*). Consequently, it was "raising its head upward" (*ūrdhvam añcayat*), meaning lifting up its head; in the alternative sense (of the city), it means "upward" on its upper part.

The analysis of the compound is *kamañca yat*. That which, while becoming the word ending in the nasal *m*—namely, the form *kam*—undergoes the *yaṇ* substitution (by the rule *iṇo yaṇ*) when following the root *iṇ* in the present participle (*śatṛ*), is that whose nature (*ātman*) is *kaṅkaṭa*; thus, being of the nature of armor (*kaṅkaṭātma*), it covers the chest (*uraḥ*). As Amara states: “*uraśchadaḥ kaṅkaṭakaḥ*” (armor is a breastplate). In the alternative sense, it means its perfected form is the word *kaṅkaṭa*. The meaning is that by placing the syllable *kam* at the beginning of the word *kaṭa*, and then applying the *anusvāra* and the *parasavarṇa* (the subsequent homogeneous letter) rules, it is transformed into *kaṅkaṭa*.

Just as a wrestler, unable to defeat another, takes the form of a woman and then triumphs by resting upon her head, so indeed do the women dwelling upon your head, O Son of Nanda, appear to be conquered by you, though they are actually your victors. 1505.

O son of Nanda! This [statement] is intended as a preparation for the defeat of the wrestlers and so forth. The wrestler—Cāṇūra and the others—being incapable of defeating you, who are skilled in wrestling, has assumed womanhood (*strībhūyam*), that is, femininity; the suffix *kyap* is applied here according to the rule "after the root *bhū*, in the sense of state" (*bhuvo bhāve*). The underlying meaning is that having become a *mallī* (a female wrestler), she is derived from the word *malla* with the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* to denote a genus, thus resulting in the form *mallī*. In the alternative sense, it means she has taken on the nature of a *mallī* flower.

From the word *mallī*, by applying the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "produced from" (*vaikārika*), there is elision (*lup*) according to the rule "in the case of flowers and roots, [the suffix] is frequently elided. By the rule "when there is elision (*lup*), the gender and number are like those of the original base," the state of being like the original base (*yuktavadbhāva*) is maintained. Thus, the meaning is: "dwelling upon your head, it conquers you, i.e., overcomes you. In the alternative sense, the meaning is: "it attains excellence by becoming a garland for your head. For indeed, women are said to be your conquerors; the implication is that this is because you are subject to the cowherd girls (*gopavadhū*).

As the teachers have said: "That supreme reality as well is subservient to the cowherd women. The particle *kila* is used here in the sense of reproach (*upālambha*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that he has achieved victory over you—which is difficult to achieve through masculinity—by means of femininity. In all three of these examples, one should note the specific distinction that the direct disparagement of the opponent is animated by an identification based on the foundation of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), rooted in the identity between word and meaning. As for example:

O Mother, you bind that fickle lightning around your neck in the guise of a necklace, together with the clouds, as if she has achieved her purpose by stealing your own luster while clinging to the rain-bearing clouds.

The flickering lightning, having stolen your splendor—your own radiance—is called "fickle" (*capalā*); by this term, its lack of stability and its tendency to act without reflection are illuminated. Being merged within the cloud (*payodhara*), it feels as though its purpose has been fulfilled, thinking, "Henceforth, not even the slightest fear shall arise for me"; thus it "rejoices," which means it exults. In reality, however, it merely shines forth.

You bind that flickering [lightning] around your neck under the guise of a necklace of diamond-jewels, together with the clouds that serve as its support—those clouds which rival its own radiance; in another sense, you fasten it upon your throat along with her breasts (or, in the other sense, you attach it for the sake of ornamentation). The meaning is: "Having bound [it] around the neck of the Ten-necked One," and so forth; in the other sense, it means you place it around the nape of the neck for the purpose of decoration.

Here, the concealment of the lightning-creeper—which serves as the direct rival and possesses its own support—is enlivened by both the identification based on the figure of speech *kaitavāpahnuti* (concealment by pretext) and *śleṣa* (paronomasia); thus, there is a distinction from the previous examples.

O Acyuta, it is as if the moon, unable to conquer your face which surpasses its own slender luster, became the letter *ma* and, turning into a bee, swallowed an elephant—truly, you are the sole refuge for those like me! 1507.

O Acyuta! The *madhukara* is the bee; there is an identity (*tādātmya*) between the two because of the word *madhukara*. By the luster of Your body—the splendor of Your form—it is also understood that it is by even a slight radiance. Having been conquered, the moon, while still being the moon, while its dark spots (*dhūvarṇa*) are vanishing, and at the very moment of its waning, becomes the *makara*—the sea-monster; in the alternative sense, the word *madhukara*, upon the elision of the syllable *dhuka*, becomes *makara*. This is the intended meaning.

"He swallowed the elephant"—that is, he devoured the beast who had you as his sole refuge. Here, the prowess of the bee—who was defeated by the luster of the Lord’s body and was powerless to retaliate—is manifested through his assumption of another form (that of an elephant) against that very elephant who sought refuge in you.

This [verse] possesses a specific charm rooted in the identity between the expressed meaning and the suggested meaning (*śabdārthatādātmya*). The same should be understood for the subsequent examples as well.

O Mother, just as it is said that a boar first approached you out of anger to destroy your victorious earth, yet in the end, having become a cuckoo (*lopa-gata*), he—being a boar in name only (*kola-ssan*)—pierces the earth known by that very name. 1508.

O Mother! That victorious cuckoo, having first approached you—your own counselor—with anger, as if intent on piercing or tearing apart your speech, indeed came into the vicinity of your words; yet in the end, having himself met his destruction, he became a boar (*kola*) and now pierces the earth (*gāṃ*), which bears the name "cow" (*go*). The sense is that this is because of the earth's well-known quality of being easily dug up by him.

In this context, the word *kokila* (cuckoo) is first supported by the syllable *ko*; then, having undergone the loss of the *ki*-syllable (*kilopa*), it reaches the state of *kola*. The compound is formed according to the rule "the second member is *śrita*" (*dvitīyā-śrita*). Finally, at the conclusion, it is joined with the syllable *la*. The meaning is that the word *kokila*, with only the *ki*-syllable elided, results in the form *kola*.

O Blessed One, just as a sugar-cane, having been defeated by a cow and with its face suddenly unseen by others, takes on the nature of a hyena and furiously slaughters those very cows; so too [is the case with the wicked]. 1509.

O Blessed One! This sugarcane has been conquered and surpassed by Your speech; for this very reason, it quickly hides its face from others—meaning that, out of the humiliation caused by defeat, it does not show its face to anyone else. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), "i" refers to the phoneme *i*. Thus, [the word] lacks the phoneme *i*.

In whatever action that [word] might be, such that its face—meaning its beginning—is seen by the letter *ta* and the letter *ra*, it is so described. "Tarakṣutvam" means the state of being a hyena (*mṛgādana*), as Amara states: "The *tarkṣu* is the beast of prey (*mṛgādana*). In the alternative sense, the word *ikṣu* (sugarcane), upon the removal of the vowel *i* and the placement of the letters *ta* and *ra* in that very place, results in the word *tarkṣu*; this is the meaning. "Those named after that" refers to those whose speech is designated by the word *go* (cow); thus, the meaning is "he destroys the cows. As for example: [The verse continues: "In the case of the word *ikṣu*, when the vowel *i* is removed and the letters *ta* and *ra* are placed there, the form *tarkṣu* is produced; this is the sense. Those things designated by that [word], namely those whose verbal designations are expressed by the word *go*, he destroys. As for instance: (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the example.)
O Lord whose crest is like the peak of a serpent, that [darkness] which was hidden by You is now beyond remedy; for at some time during the full moon, darkness eclipses the moon named after You.
The ignorance residing in darkness is Rāhu; this is the agent. Viṣṇu, who exists on the mountain of serpents (Śeṣa), is the object. To him [O Lord], it has been concealed—that is, destroyed—by you.
Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the radiant lamp of knowledge.

Thus it is from the song. The rest is clear. Here, by the Lord, who has become concealed through darkness and is unable to counteract [the enemy], there is the eclipsing of the moon—whose identity as such is imagined through its bearing his name—as being of that [darkness].
Just as the fresh cloud, surpassed by the luster of your body, thunders while remaining below your mountain-abode; for a cloud does not endure its own humiliation.

Here, because the fresh cloud is surpassed by the radiance of the Lord’s body, its inability to rival that [body] results in its surpassing the mountain [upon which it rests]. In both examples, the subjugation of the respective objects is identical; it is supported by the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) inherent in words such as "lower lip" (*adhara*) and "moon" (*vidhu*), and consists in the subjugation of those [objects] which are themselves incapable of directly subjugating their own opposites. However, it should be noted that in the final case, the distinction lies in its being crowned by a *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle).
This [figure] is also seen in cases where there is a subjugation of something related to that which is related to the opponent. For example:
Surely this Svarbhānu, whose head was formerly severed by the Abode of Śrī, now shines following its own radiance and occasionally swallows the orb of the sun.

The term *anuvibhāta* is the genitive singular of the word *bhās*, serving as an adjective for *vibhāvasoḥ*. Here, the resonance of the Vedic text, "Everything shines after Him who shines" (*tameva bhāntamanubhāti sarvam*), is intended. *Maṇḍalam* means the orb; it is also understood to mean the kingdom. The rest is clear. In this context, Svarbhānu—who, having had his head cut off by the Blessed One, was unable to retaliate—obscures the orb of the sun which shines following the light of that [Blessed One]. This is therefore an instance of "obscuration of that which is connected to one connected to the adversary."

O my mother, as if disregarded by the luster of your face, the moon— the white-rayed friend of my eyes— now, having surpassed the lotus, binds those who have taken refuge in it during the night with its dark hue.

The word "tava" (your) and "mukharucā" (by the luster of the face) are connected to both [phrases]. Here, the eye belonging to the face of the Mother of the World—which is the direct adversary—is mentioned; then the lotus related to that [eye] by being its friend; then the bees related to that [lotus]; and finally, the disparagement of those [bees] is expressed. Thus, there is a distinct charm compared to the previous [instance].
The third [type] is as follows:

O Mother of All, your eye, which completely overpowers the blue water-lily with its mass of golden luster, became the arrow of Madana, who—having been defeated by its beauty—desires to take revenge. (1514)

In this instance, the Lord of the Immobile (Śiva), having descended as the *kuvalaya* lotus—which is the very essence of Lakṣmī’s eye—in order to overcome Hari who is his own adversary, provides assistance to Madana, who desires to retaliate against him because he has been surpassed by that [lotus]’s beauty; thus, this is the third variety of *pratyanīka*, consisting of assistance rendered to an opponent.

Here it is argued that since its meaning is already conveyed by the figure of poetic fancy (utprekṣā) based on a cause, this cannot be a distinct figure of speech. In the example "tvadrucikṛtaparibhavataḥ," the causal element is indeed expressed verbally (śābda), while the element of poetic fancy is merely implied (ārtha); in other examples, however, both elements are implied. If it is argued that there is a distinction because in this figure causality is established as a certainty, whereas in the poetic fancy of cause it is a mere possibility, [we reply] that this would result in the poetic fancy of an implied cause being no longer considered a poetic fancy at all.
Since there is no particle such as *iva* to indicate comparison, it is possible to state that the nature of being a cause (*hetutva*) is being ascertained even in that case:
"Though unable to do him any harm, Rāhu, having taken up a physical struggle by seizing [the moon] with his body,
now afflicts the moon— which possesses a form resembling the lovely face of [Rāhu’s] beloved— even today."

Thus, even in the ancient verse cited in the *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, because of the cognition that "Rāhu afflicts the moon—which resembles the face of the Blessed One—as if out of persistent enmity toward the Blessed One," only the *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is implied (*gamyamānā*). However, in the example from the *Kuvalayānanda*, "He who has stolen my beauty and fame on earth," both the causal element and the element of *utprekṣā* are expressed directly (*śābda*). Although this differs from other types of *hetūtprekṣā* (causal fancy), since there is a cognition of the opponent's strength and one's own weakness, [it is distinct].
This does not mean that this [inference] falls outside the scope of the postulation of a cause (*hetūtprekṣā*), for it is invariably concomitant with it;
rather, it is a particular sub-variety of it. Indeed, no one says that because a cloth is distinct from a jar—which is a specific sub-division of earth—it exists outside of earth.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Counter-Argument (*pratyanīka*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Poetic Presumption (*kāvya-arthāpatti*):
where another matter follows by way of the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikā*).
This is considered by those who know the ornaments of poetry to be "poetic presumption" (kāvyārthāpatti).

The policy in which both the stick and the cake are found is called *daṇḍāpūpikā* nītiḥ (the "stick-and-cake" policy). The suffix *ṭhan* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), as in the expression *ahamahamikā* ("I am able, I am able in this action"). Alternatively, the suffix *kan* is added according to the rule *ive pratikṛtau* ("in the sense of 'like' when forming a representation"), resulting in *daṇḍāpūpikā*, meaning "like the stick and the cake. For in this case, by the mouse’s eating of the stick, the eating of the cake—which necessarily accompanies it—is also established as a matter of course. A maxim of this kind is expressed by the word *daṇḍāpūpikā*.

Just as the eating of a cake follows from the eating of a staff [by implication], so too, when a certain matter is established, another matter follows by force of necessity (*sāmarthya*) through the characteristic of a similar logic; that is *arthāpatti* (presumption). The word "poetic" (*kāvya*) is used to exclude the *arthāpatti* favored by the technical logicians (*tāntrika*). This very principle is also called the *kaimutikanyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"). For this reason, the definition was formulated in the *Kuvalayānanda*: "The successful establishment of a meaning by way of *kaimutya* is intended as poetic presumption (*kāvyārthāpatti*)."

If it is argued that this is indeed inference (*anumāna*) because another object is understood through implication (*arthāt*), we say no. This is because the principle of "equal logic" (*samānanyāya*) lacks the nature of a necessary relation (*saṃbandha*). For although the eating of the cake is appropriate when the staff is eaten due to their equal logic, it is not certain; for even when the staff is eaten, there may be no eating of the cakes due to some other cause, such as their being located in a different place. Inference, however, is the certain emergence of one object from another object; therefore, this [implication] is distinct from it.
However, it must be a specific sub-variety of that [earth]. For they do not say that because a cloth is distinct from a jar—which is a specific sub-variety of earth—it exists outside of earth.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Counter-Argument (*pratyanīka*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Poetic Presumption (*kāvyārthāpatti*):
where another matter follows by way of the maxim of "the stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*).
This is considered by those who know the ornaments of poetry to be "poetic presumption" (kāvyārthāpatti).

The policy in which both the stick and the cake are found is called *daṇḍāpūpikā* policy. The suffix *ṭhan* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), as in the expression *ahamahamikā* ("I am capable, I am capable in this action"). Alternatively, it is derived by adding the suffix *kan* according to the rule "in the sense of a likeness" (*ive pratikṛtau*), thus forming *daṇḍāpūpikā*, meaning "like the stick and the cake. For in this case, when the mouse eats the stick, the eating of the cake—which is concomitant with it—is established by implication. A maxim of this kind is expressed by the word *daṇḍāpūpikā*.

Just as the eating of a cake follows from the eating of a stick [as a consequence], so too, when a certain matter is accomplished, another matter follows by implication through the force of a common principle; this is *arthāpatti* (presumption). The term "poetic" (*kāvya*) is used to exclude the *arthāpatti* accepted by the technical logicians (*tāntrika*). This very same thing is also called the *kaimutikanyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"). For this very reason, the definition was formulated in the *Kuvalayānanda*: "The successful establishment of a meaning by way of *kaimutya* is desired as poetic *arthāpatti*."

If it is argued that, since another object is understood through implication (*arthāt*), this is merely inference (*anumāna*), we say no. This is because the principle of "equal logic" (*samānanyāya*) lacks the nature of a necessary relation (*saṃbandha*). For although the eating of a cake is appropriate when a staff is eaten due to their equal logic, it is not certain; for even when a staff is eaten, there may be circumstances such as being situated in a separate place that prevent the cakes from being eaten. Inference, however, is the certain emergence of one object from another by necessity; therefore, this [implication] is distinct from it.

For thus, O All-pervading Lord, when Your splendor shines, neither the sun, nor the moon, nor the stars, nor the flashes of lightning shine; what then can be said of fire? When You shine, all this world shines in accordance with You.

In this context, by means of the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"), it is demonstrated that within the splendor of the Lord’s radiance—as described in the scripture, "The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and stars, nor do these lightnings shine, much less this fire; everything shines only after Him as He shines"—it is difficult even for the thousand-rayed sun and others to manifest their own light. Consequently, it goes without saying that it is impossible for fire, which is far inferior even to them and is extinguished by a mere sprinkling of water, to manifest its own light.
Or rather:
O Lord, if some pearl necklace were to place itself upon your chest, it would not be surprising that your beloved, the daughter of the ocean, has likewise found her place there. (1516)

Here, by means of the placement of the feet upon the chest of the Blessed One as performed by the author of the *Hāralatā*—an irrelevant (aprakṛta) action—the ease with which the relevant (prakṛta) act of placing the feet of Śrī upon the chest of the Blessed One would occur is established through the maxim of "the stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*). Furthermore, this [figure] is blended with *samāsokti*, because the feminine noun *hāralatā* evokes the perception of her being a heroine (*nāyikā*). In the same way, this should be inferred as appropriate in subsequent instances as well.
O Lord, if your foot were to conquer the lotus that possesses a full abundance of luster bestowed by the sun, who among the wise would hesitate to say, "So it is," regarding your face? 1517.

The feet and the face are the agents; the lotus is the object—meaning both the lotus and the moon. The qualifiers beginning with "dinakara" (the sun) apply equally to both. The construction is as follows: who among the wise would doubt that the face likewise conquers the lotus, which possesses a full abundance of luster bestowed by the sun?

Or rather: O Acyuta, if you, fearing the distress of those who seek your aid, take refuge in the fortress of the mountain itself, what wonder is it that Lakṣmī—naturally timid—takes shelter in the fortress of your chest? 1518.

*Arda* means the distressing, the afflicting, or the begging of those who seek [something]. *Cakita* means afraid of that; or rather, *na-ardita-cakita*, meaning not afraid of being asked. This is the sense of "frightened.
Or as it is said:
"By the grace of the Lord, the friend of the world, even the lotus attains poetic expression upon its face. If the entire assembly of poets thereby becomes pure, what is there to wonder at? (1519)

By the grace—that is, the radiance and the favor—of the lotus-like Lord Bāṇa, the friend of the world, and of the Blessed One, whose friendliness toward the world is unconditional as stated in the Vedic verse, "He is our kinsman, our progenitor": by his grace, [the word] *kavitā* (poetry) attains a change of color (*vivarṇatva*) at its beginning—that is, at its face and its first syllable—and thus becomes pure, indeed becomes stainless. According to the Śruti, "The Brahmin is pure, he is a poet" (*vipraśśuciḥ kaviḥ*). The essential point is that the verbal form *vimalam* (stainless) is thereby produced.
O Lord, if one strives for equanimity through Your words, it becomes nectar; otherwise, the claim that anything else could equal it is mere idle talk, O Moon of the Mountain of Serpents.

O Lord! If nectar (*sudhā*) strives for equality—that is, for identity—with Your speech, it becomes *mudhā*, meaning its effort becomes futile; the sense is that because of its lack of essence, it cannot be equal to it. Furthermore, there is a striking word-play: if the phonetic expression *sudhā* strives for *samatā*—wherein the letter *sa* [of *sudhā*] attains the state of the letter *ma* [as in *madhu*]—then it becomes *mudhā*, resulting in the form *mudhā*. As for any other thing attempting to weigh itself against it, even the mention or possibility of such a thing is merely *vārta*—that is, trivial and insignificant; as Amara states: "The word *vārta* is used in three genders to mean 'trifling' (*phalgu*) and 'free from disease' (*aroga*)."
Just as the array of lotuses was conquered by that sun with its sharp radiance, so too, what victory can there be here for this dull circle of kings before your face? (1521)

Here, the genitive case in *vadanasya* is used in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*), whereas in *rājamaṇḍalasya*, it is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). Therefore, it should be understood that this is not a case for the restrictive rule "when both [agent and object] are eligible [for the genitive], it is used for the object" (*ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*). This is because that rule applies only when the suffix *kṛt* is simultaneously applicable to both the agent and the object. Alternatively, since the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) is accepted in the Vārttika "optionally in the residual sense" (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*), the aforementioned rule does not apply—as in examples such as "the instruction of words by the Teacher" (*śabdānām anuśāsanam ācāryeṇa* or *ācāryasya*). Thus, the genitive for both the agent and the object is entirely unimpeded. *Kalya* means free from disease or capable.

"Kalya" means ready at the break of day; "kalyā" means one who speaks auspiciously; it is used in three senses: healthy, dexterous, and [ready]. (Ratnamālā). "Kalya" means ready or free from disease (Amara). It is understood that this refers to a certain such king. That which was the "abjavyūha"—a specific military formation of troops in the shape of a lotus—consisted of heroic men. In reality, however, the meaning is: at "kalyam," meaning at dawn, that which was the "abjavyūha," meaning a cluster of lotuses. "Jaḍaḥ" means stiff or devoid of intellect.

"‘Jaḍa’ refers to one who is dull, stubborn, devoid of intellect, or even frozen by cold, like an object [inanimate matter]," according to the *Ratnamālā*. Thus, it means "of that king, the ruler, whose *maṇḍala* is his kingdom. In the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), however, the meaning is "of that king who is the Moon, which is *jaḍa* (cold), [and] whose *maṇḍala* is his orb. The rest is easy to understand. Here, the victory over the kingdom of the dull king is established as a matter of course (*kaimutika-nyāya*) for the face, which is the conqueror of the array of lotuses; this [figure] is supported by *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *samāsokti* (speech of ellipsis).

Since your face, which is worthy of praise by the Omniscient One, has already conquered the moon—the repository of digits—it is only natural that it should suffer defeat; what doubt, then, can there be regarding its victory over that which is born of dull matter? || 1522 ||

When the moon—praised by the virtuous, the wise, and the excellent; laudable for being the mouth of the Omniscient One; worthy of praise as a jewel among scholars; borne upon the head of Śiva (Dhūrjaṭi); the repository of all arts and sciences; and the abode of all knowledge—has been conquered by you, the wise one, the moon-like mind [of the poet], the dull-witted and obstinate class of beings naturally undergoes defeat and humiliation, and indeed possesses its own waves of agitation. The sense is that those born dull by nature and prone to defeat everywhere are thus overcome.

Regarding the victory over or the overcoming of such a person, what doubt or uncertainty could there be? The sense is that there is none at all. Here too, by means of the *daṇḍāpūpika* (the logic of "when the stick is fetched, the cake is also brought"), the fact that the face of the conqueror of great scholars naturally possesses a victory consisting of the defeat of those born of dull intellect is established.

O Queen of Hari, compared to the pair of your supreme breasts which have conquered the frontal globes of elephants, how insignificant would the victory over Mounts [Girija] be, since this [victory over the mountains] is already renowned throughout the world? 1523.

It is heard from [the lexicon] *Abhidhānacintāmaṇi* that the word *avi* is well-known as meaning "ram"; the term *avi* denotes both a mountain and a ram, according to the rule: "The words *avi*, *śaila*, and *meṣa* mean 'mountain' and 'sun'. The sense is: what is the victory over a ram compared to the victory over the frontal globes (*kumbha*) of an elephant? Here, although the mountain is not inferior to the elephant's frontal globes—such that its conquest would be considered inferior by the logic of "how much more" (*kaimutika-nyāya*)—[the poet implies the opposite].

Nevertheless, it should be noted that there is a deficiency [in the figure] because the two meanings—the mountain and the moon—which are conveyed by the word *eṣa*, are unified through a superimposition of non-difference based on the foundation of *śleṣa* (paronomasia). This same point should be observed in the verse previously cited: "By him, who is sharp-witted, the array of the autumnal lotuses has been conquered."

Just as even heaven (*nāka*) ultimately becomes hell (*naraka*) for one who is other than Your abode, O Acyuta—what wonder is there that the realm of men (*naraloka*), having fallen into the void in its midst, is called hell? 1524.

O Acyuta! Even heaven (*nāka*), though it be a celestial realm, when subjected to thorough investigation, is ultimately nothing other than a hellish state (*nāraka*)—distinct from the well-known hells—belonging to Your divine abode.
[For it is said: "O King, there are delightful palaces that move at will, assembly halls, various pleasure gardens, and lotus-pools of pure water."

The meaning is as stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "O dear one, these indeed are the hells [compared] to the state of the Supreme Self. Amara states: "The words *nāraka* and *naraka* are synonymous. He has reached the middle; that is, he has arrived at or understood that *Ilā*—the earth situated between heaven (*svarga*) and the netherworld (*pātāla*)—is the mortal world (*naraloka*). What wonder is there, then, that the mortal world is a hell?

The sense is: if even the heavenly world (svarloka), which is known from the Purāṇas and other sources to consist of great bliss, becomes like a hell, then what need is there to mention that the mortal world—constantly devoured by thousands of sufferings—is like a hell?

In one sense, even the word *nāka*—analyzed as "that from which the letter *ra* has departed" (*itaḥ raḥ yena saḥ*)—would ultimately result in the very word *nāraka*. Likewise, the word *naraloka*, analyzed as "that from which the syllable *lo* has disappeared in the middle," results in *naraka*. Since the class beginning with *āhitāgni* is an open-ended group (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the past participle suffix is placed at the end of the compound. What wonder is there, then, that the word *naraka* is thus produced?

Or rather, O Śauri, what wonder is there that Mura was quelled by your showers of arrows like fire? Let him [Mura] employ another weapon; even this [fire-like] Mura might be extinguished by you becoming a mere wildfire (murmura).

O Śauri! What wonder is there that the Daitya named Mura, who resembled fire, was quelled by your showers of arrows, showers of shafts, and showers of water? Let that Mura place another Mura—the Asura Mura—who is more powerful than himself, in front for the sake of your victory; [let him] set another Mura before him (using the *loṭ* in the sense of permission, according to the rule *praiṣātisarga*). That other Mura, too, becoming merely a *murmura*—a fire of chaff—shall be extinguished.

"‘Murmura’ means embers," according to the Viśva-kośa. In the alternative sense, let the word *mura* place before itself—that is, at its own front—a different *mura*, namely the word-form *mur*; the meaning is that even this word *mura* results in the form *murmura*. Here, by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*), the pacification of the fire-like demon Mura is established through the pacification of a more powerful other god, who is comparable to a fire of chaff.

O Mother, if that very person whom you behold even once is indeed a treasure-house of a multitude of auspicious virtues, then it is no cause for wonder that he becomes such a constant abode of yours. 1526.
O Goddess, he whom you behold is praiseworthy, virtuous, fortunate, well-born, wise, heroic, and valiant.
The meaning of this has been considered.

Or rather: "O Hari, if even the blue lotus were to attain the status of being the crest-jewel upon the peak of the Vedas, what cause for wonder would there be in your possessing that very same status? (1527)

The intention is that the blue lotus (indīvara) is indeed of the same color as the Blessed One. Its being the crest-jewel of the pinnacle of the Vedas, its being an ear-ornament, and its being knowable through the Vedānta are [the qualities].
If the one who obstructs were immutable, he would be capable of protecting gold; yet, upon the calamity of Prahlāda, having attained a state devoid of boons, he became its destroyer. (1528)

The Blessed Lord is immutable; the sense is that He is devoid of destruction. As the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *avyaya* is not feminine; it refers to a specific type of sound, to Viṣṇu, or in the masculine/feminine/neuter [as an adjective], it means 'unchanging'. If He were merely the ordainer (*vidhāyaka*) for the sake of slaying Hiraṇyakaśipu during the calamity—that is, the occasion of Prahlāda’s misfortune—if He were to maintain a distance (*vyavadhānam*), meaning to remain indifferent due to a lack of immediate involvement (the suffix *ṇvul* being used in the active sense from the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *vi-*), then who would be capable [of protecting the world]?

The meaning is: who else is capable of slaying him? Furthermore, having attained a state of being devoid of boons—this phrase "of Prahlāda" is to be supplied both here and with the word "ka" (who). Having attained a state of being devoid of boons—that is, having become favorable through the granting of a boon—who could be his sustainer and nourisher? Since the Supreme Person alone is renowned for his immutability, as in the passages, "In whom that immortal Person dwells, he whose self is immutable," and "The immutable Person is the witness," if even He remains indifferent toward both the slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu and the nourishing of his son, what other powerful being could possibly effect his destruction? This is the intended sense.

In this context, the word *vyadhāyaka* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). It is called *avyaya* because it does not undergo change (*vyaya*)—that is, it does not lose the collection of phonemes consisting of the form *vya*, *vya*. [This is derived] from the root *yā-* with the prefix *vi-* as an attendant (*upapada*), followed by the suffix *ka* according to the rule *ātonupasarge kaḥ*, and then the elision of the long *ā* according to the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*. The meaning is: "if it were devoid of the letter *va*. [If that were the case], it would become *vadhāyaka*, being formed as *vadhāyaka*.

From the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *ava*, with the suffix *ṇvul*, the vowel *a* belonging to the prefix *ava* is elided according to the rule "Bhāguri admits the elision of the *a* in the prefixes *ava* and *api*. Thus, having attained a state devoid of *ra*—that is, being bereft of the letter *va*—the word *dhāyaka* itself would also become *dhāyaka*.

"O Protector, protect me from the lower realms; even an elephant is a source of evil"—O Lord with eyes like lotus petals, how small is this offense of an elephant compared to You, the Purifier of the World! (1529)

O Blessed One! Even a sinner, even one who has committed evil—here *api* (even) implies contradiction; the sense is "even this person," that is, even me. Here *api* is used as a conjunction of accumulation (*samuccaye*). Regarding the word *dvipa*: since the word *dvirada* (elephant) is composed of two *pa* sounds, and because of the identity between word and meaning (*śabdārtha-tādātmya*), the intended inner meaning is that the object itself also possesses the nature of a *dvipa*. From *apāya*, meaning from calamity (*vipad*). *Gopāya* means protect. For one who purifies the world (*lokapāvana*) and is the protector of all the guardians of the world (*sakalalokapālānām rakṣaka*), how much is the protection of elephants (*dvipāvana*)? That is, the protection of elephants is of little consequence.

One who protects two is a *dvipa* (elephant); thus, for such a protector of two things, the sense that "how much [is his] protection? is also understood. In the compound *dvipāvanam*, there is a compound formed either with the genitive of the residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) or with the accusative case. For one who purifies the world—that is, the purifier of all the universe—the phrase *dvipāvanam* suggests the sense: "How much is this purification of both," namely, of the elephant and of myself? In that case, it should be understood that in the first half of the verse, "protection" takes the form of "purification.
All these examples are provided in accordance with the views of the ancients.
According to the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, however, the definition is as follows:
"When the implication of another matter occurs by virtue of some other matter through a similar logic,
that is called *kāvyārthāpatti* (poetic presumption)."

*Arthāpatti* (Presumption) in poetry is the implication of another matter because it shares the same underlying logic (*nyāya*) with some given matter; and "logic" here refers to the cause. It has four primary divisions: that of one relevant matter implying another relevant matter, one irrelevant matter implying another irrelevant matter, one relevant matter implying an irrelevant matter, and one irrelevant matter implying a relevant matter. Each of these is further divided into twelve types according to whether the implied matter is equal to, greater than, or less than the matter from which it is implied. Thus, there are twenty-four varieties when both presence and absence are taken into account.
The application of the primary subject by means of the primary subject is as follows:

“If, by virtue of your innate splendor, the Kaustubha gem were to attain the state of being dear to your heart, why then should the crest-jewel, possessing innate splendor itself, not likewise attain the state of being dear to your heart? (1530)

"Being dear to the heart" (*hṛdyatvam*) means both residing in the heart and being beloved by the heart. Here, there is a similarity between the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*)—which is being established—and the established subject (*āpādya*), starting from the establishing factor (*āpādaka*). This [figure] is supported by *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

O Lord, by your radiance—which possesses a great splendor like lightning and expands like a full-blown lotus—the dark cloud has been surpassed; yet that it has surpassed the blue lotus is only fitting, for they are equal [in beauty]. (1531)

O Lord! [The term] *sumahācchavidyut* refers to that which possesses lightning (*vidyut*) of exceedingly great and surpassing purity; alternatively, it means that which flashes with a very great luster (*cchavi*), hence *sumahācchavidyut*. [This is derived from] the root *dyut* with the suffix *kvip*. [The word] *puṣkara* refers to both the sky and water. [The adjective] *puṣkalavikāsi* means blooming or expanding in a most beautiful manner, and also fully blossomed. [It is] like a dark cloud (*asitābhra*), a blue water-lily (*asitābja*), or an *indīvara*. [The word] *sthāne* means "fittingly. The rest is easy to understand.
Here, both [the sky and the water-lily] are the subjects (*prakṛta*), and their similarity is established.

O Hari, if that beloved of yours, Rāmā, is intent on protecting you by means of her words of protection, then it is no wonder that even the Earth (Kṣamā) will likewise become subject to her. || 1532 ||

O hare! By the mere utterance of the words "protect" (*rakṣa*) and "save" (*trāyasva*), your beloved Rama—who is renowned as the Lord of the Universe and the divine Queen—is intent upon my protection; if that is so, then Kṣamā (the Earth-goddess) is also under her sway, being obedient to her (*tadadhīnā*). Alternatively, the meaning of *tadadhīnā* is the same as stated before. Or, Kṣamā—the Lord’s forbearance—is also dependent on her, because the forgiveness of offenses committed by devotees by the Lord is brought about by the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) of Lakṣmī; this is the intended sense.

Likewise, it is no wonder that she will become intent on protecting me; for the underlying sense is based on the maxim: "If the king himself is constantly elevated and brought under control, what can his attendants do? What effort is required? In the alternative [poetic] sense, the word *ramā* (Lakṣmī) is expressed through the mention of protection (*rakṣā*).

By the mention of the letter *kṣa* for the letter *ra*, it follows that since [the earth] is subordinate to *kṣa*, she will become *kṣamā* (forgiving); thus, the word *kṣamā* is established, and this meaning—that it is no wonder—surpasses the sense of amazement. Here, however, in comparison with the contextual subject, the beloved of yours who has the form of the Earth (*bhūmi*), the contextual quality of forbearance (*kṣamā*) appears inferior because of its subordination to that [other meaning].

Or rather, O Compassionate One, if you yourself abandon me who has committed an offense against you, then even a lord, heated by the fire of anger, casts away his transgressors to a very great distance. (1533)

Here too, there is a deficiency of the subject under discussion (*prastuta*) compared to that which is being introduced; this is understood from the two qualifiers *karuṇāmayi* ("O you who consist of compassion") and *krodhoṣmala* ("fiery with anger"). For this very reason, this figure is enhanced by *parikara* (poetic elaboration). The distinction, however, is that the former was intermingled with *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
"O Supreme Person (*Puruṣottama*), if you yourself were unable to destroy my sin, how can this not be a cause for wonder? Will even your forgiveness (*kṣamā*) not be able to destroy it? (1534)

"Your forbearance is patience. Here, because the sin is so exceedingly great that it is difficult even for the Blessed One to eradicate, this is the statement of someone who treats it as an established fact; yet, in relation to the Supreme Person, there is a sense of inferiority in treating forbearance as feminine. For this very reason, it is asked: "What is there to wonder at in this? In this case, both the consequence (*āpādya*) and the cause (*āpādaka*) are equally relevant to the context (*prakṛta*).
The introduction of an irrelevant subject by means of another irrelevant subject is as follows:
"O Acyuta, if some creature should desire comparison with you in his heart, then even an atom of Mount Sumeru would carry the weight of the entire earth. (1535)
Here too, there is an excess of the unestablished consequence over the unestablished reason.
The introduction of the irrelevant by means of the relevant is as follows:
"O Omniscient One, if even this lute of mine were present before you, it would surely be surpassed by the singing of a mosquito in an assembly of the finest celestial musicians. (1536)

*Nirajīyata* means "was utterly conquered. It is derived from the root *ji* (to conquer) preceded by the prefix *niḥ*, used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) in the *laṅ* tense. Here, there is an excess (*ādhikya*) consisting in the establishment of a non-contextual meaning—namely, the state of existing as the most preeminent—which is being superimposed upon the contextual meaning, namely, the act of "dwelling" (*varvatīti*).

O Lord of Ramā, if while You are awake for the sake of protecting the world another were to strive [for that task], then the sovereignty over birds would easily fall to a moth in the presence of Garuḍa.

In this case, there is an excellence of the non-contextual matter—the attainment of sovereignty—which is being brought about, over the contextual matter consisting of the act of striving, expressed as "he strives here."

If even the Blessed One himself becomes dwarfed in stature at the time of begging for alms from the earth, what need is there to mention that every other person becomes miserable and shrinks away? || 1538 ||
The phrase "at the time of begging for ground" also applies to the latter half of this verse.
O Lord of Rama, if you yourself were not to grant the desired objects to the multitude of supplicants, would any other beggar give even a clod of earth? (1539)
In this case, there is the reduction of one non-existent thing by another non-existent thing, as well as the inferiority of the non-contextual object being reduced compared to the contextual one.
For example:

"Even in comparison with Patience (Kṣamā), which cannot be fully attained, and with Delight (Rati), who dwells in the heart of Hari—any talk of the other queens is all the more remote from him. (1540)
Here too, there is the production of non-existence by means of non-existence, as well as the inferiority of the non-contextual compared to the contextual.
The establishment of the relevant through the irrelevant is as follows:
