"O Madhusūdana, you lifted up Mount Mandara as it was sinking into the ocean; how great a labor would it be for you to rescue me, who am merely floating in the ocean of worldly existence? (1541)

Here, there is a deficiency because the relevant matter—the rescue of one drifting in the ocean of worldly existence—is inferior to the irrelevant account of the churning of the Mandara mountain by such a person. Furthermore, this figure admits of variety depending on whether another incidental matter (*arthāntara*) that arises is explicitly mentioned or not. Among these, examples have been shown where the incidental matter is explicitly mentioned.

Just as even the jewels found within the waters of the ocean can be counted somewhere, the virtues of the jewel of the Lord of the Serpents (Śrīraṅgam) cannot possibly be counted by that same person. || 1542 ||
"By him alone" means by Śrīnivāsa alone. Here, the unintended further implication—"what need is there to mention others besides Śrīnivāsa?"—is not explicitly stated.

O Lord, even an omniscient one would be as if ignorant regarding the full comprehension of Your majesty; O Hari, even the four-faced Brahmā would be as if not four-faced in attempting to describe You in Your entirety.

In this case as well, the question of what the status of other [figures] might be has not been addressed, as that would lead to a digression; however, the distinction lies in its being mixed with the semblance of contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*).

Just as in the waking state, so too when you, the Lord of the Mountain’s Daughter, are not the sovereign, whatever creature is dependent on anyone else—even if that person were the lord of the daughter of the mountain—he would indeed be a fool. (1544)

O Blessed One! Those who possess *aka*—meaning suffering (*duḥkha*) and evil (*pāpa*)—are called *akinaḥ*. Those who do not become such are *nākinaḥ*; this is the intended meaning of "those gods. Even while You, the Supreme Lord (*adhīśvara*), are awake, [the world suffers]. The locative case here is used in the sense of disregard, according to the rule *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare*; thus, the meaning is "disregarding You. Whatever living being (*jantuḥ*, *prāṇī*) goes under the sway of *aka*—that is, goes under the control of worldly suffering—is so described. From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, all beings situated within the universe are subject to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) produced by their own karma.

In the manner described above, the meaning is that he has taken refuge in those [deities] beginning with Brahmā, who are subject to the suffering of worldly existence. The underlying sense is that even though Śambhu is the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain (Nagabālikādhīśa) and is indeed omniscient, one who—having neglected the Blessed One who consists of bliss and bestows unsurpassed bliss—takes refuge in the four-faced Brahmā and others who are under the sway of karma, would be a fool (bāliśa) indeed, even if he were omniscient; how much more so for others? In the alternative sense (pakṣe), this refers to the word *nagabālikādhīśa*.

The meaning is that if one whose four syllables (*varṇa*) are "a-vidyamānāḥ," "ka-dhī," and "na-gā" [is called] *akādhīnagaḥ*, he results in being a fool (*bāliśa*). Here, the sequence of the elided syllables is not intended to be significant. In this case, the implied alternative meaning—"how much more so others?"—is not explicitly stated.

O Acyuta, for you who possess immeasurable power and simultaneously devour the cosmic eggs along with their coverings, these worlds beginning with heaven are but a trifle; what are they but mere grains of chaff?

In this context, it is established by the logic of *kaimutika-nyāya* (the principle of "how much more so") that the Lord’s swallowing of the various worlds within them—such as heaven (*nāka*) and the rest—is necessarily implied by his simultaneous swallowing of numerous cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*).

Or again: O Janārdana, how much is this sin of mine compared to You, who remove the misfortunes of the entire world? What indeed is a mere puddle for the fierce-rayed sun, which is capable of drying up the ocean at the time of universal dissolution? 1546.

"Who indeed?"—this means "what thing. Here, the *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism) constitutes the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākyārtha*). The two parts—the meaning of the sentence concerning the subject of comparison (*upameya*) and the meaning of the sentence concerning the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—are its components. Among these, when the *arthāpatti* (presumption) pertains to the meaning of the sentence concerning the subject of comparison, both the matter being established and the matter serving as its cause are contextual (*prakṛta*). However, when it pertains to the meaning of the sentence concerning the standard of comparison, both are non-contextual (*aprakṛta*); this alone is the distinction from the previous examples. Other instances may be inferred in this same manner.

Here it is considered: this [figure] does not fall within the category of *arthāpatti* (presumption) as accepted by the experts of grammar (*vākyavid*), because here there is no lack of justification for the establishing factor (*āpādaka*) in the absence of the factor to be established (*āpādya*). Nor does it belong to the figure of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) involving the word *yadi*, because in that case the two terms find their rest in a contrary sense, whereas here that is not so, since the establishing factor is established as a fact and the factor to be established is merely possible.

This is because the two [meanings] rest upon exactly what has been heard. Therefore, this form of *arthāpatti* (presumption) consists in the thought that by whatever reasoning one meaning is established, by that very same reasoning another meaning ought also to be established. In this regard, if an author, through his own creative genius (*pratibhā*), conceives and introduces another meaning—even if it does not exist in the world—it then possesses the status of an *alaṃkāra* (poetic figure), as in the verse beginning with "In the assembly of the best of celestial musicians" (*suravaiṇikavarasaṃsadi*). Otherwise, however, it is merely a case of the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"), as in the verse beginning with "The cosmic eggs with their coverings" (*sāvaraṇān brahmāṇḍān*).

We have cited that according to the ancient method; for this very reason, it was stated there by way of the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"). As for the definition given by the authors of the *Kuvalayānanda*, namely, "the establishment of a matter through the *kaimuti* [logic]," that does not quite appeal to the heart; for since the *kaimutika-nyāya* pertains to matters of inferior significance, it lacks applicability (*avyāpti*) in cases where something superior or greater is implied. For example:

"O Lord of Śrī, if the heat of your [glorious] majesty overcomes even one who has sought refuge at your feet, then the heat born of the summer season will gradually overcome even the moon that sheds nectar. (1547)

In this context, although it is already known that for those who have taken refuge in the Lord, the overpowering of the summer heat by the moon—which emits nectar—is difficult to achieve when compared to the overpowering of the heat of worldly existence (bhavatāpa) by the majesty of His sound, this is nevertheless presented as a logical consequence based on the similarity of the underlying principle; it is not, however, established by way of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument.

Regarding this, Vaidyanātha states: "Arthāpatti is the implication of another matter because it shares the same logical principle (*nyāya*) with some given matter; and here, the 'principle' (*nyāya*) refers to the cause. This definition provided in the *Rasagaṅgādhara* is incorrect, because it fails to apply (*avyāpti*) to an arthāpatti that concerns the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*), as in the example: "What need is there to speak of lotuses? This is because the logic of "how much more so" concerns a lesser matter and thus lacks the status of a "shared principle," and because no actual implication (*āpādana*) is perceived therein.

Nor is it correct to claim that in this case there is merely the logic of *kaimutya* (the "how much more so" principle) and not the status of an *alaṃkāra* (poetic figure), for it is impossible even for a commoner to imagine that the ancient authorities who were experts in the true nature of *alaṃkāras* were devoid of intellect; for even in worldly discourse, the *kaimutya* principle is experienced as possessing aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), and by that very same logic—

"And because its status as an ornament (*alaṃkāratā*) is established. Furthermore, in the example of *arthāpatti* mentioned by you, there occurs the ornament of *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic probability) which will be described later; it is stated [by some] as a hyperbole of the sense of 'if' (*yadyarthātiśaya*), according to the rule: 'When others state the sense of "if," there is a mental construction. In a hyperbole of the sense of 'if,' the resolution lies in the opposite meaning of both the premise (*āpādaka*) and the consequence (*āpādya*). Here, however, there is a distinct charm (*vaicitrya*) in that the premise is established while the consequence is merely probable; this very distinction proves that it is a sub-variety of that [hyperbole], and not something external to it. Thus, there is no need even to suspect a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) there. End of quote.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, the Chapter on Poetic Presumption (Kāvyārthāpatti), in the Alaṃkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Poetical Indication (Kāvyaliṅga):
that which constitutes a justification, being untouched by the relationship of general and particular, [is Kāvyaliṅga].
The poetic figure *kāvyaliṅga* is said to be that which [serves] for the purpose of establishing a meaning that requires justification.
The phrase "not touched by another" (*anālīḍhānta*) is included in order to exclude the figure of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration).
Or rather, O sirs, since there are faults [in me], let other places be sought by you; no room can be found here for you, for someone who washes away the banks of sin dwells within me.

Here, the meaning of the preceding sentence consists in the non-attainment of any opportunity for faults; its support by the meaning of the subsequent sentence—which demonstrates the proximity of Śrī Hari, who is expert at removing every single fault without exception—is the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga*.

"And because its status as an ornament is thus established. Furthermore, in the example of *arthāpatti* (presumption) mentioned by you, there occurs the figure of speech called *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic probability), which will be described later. It is stated [by some] that this is a type of *yadyarthātiśayokti* (hyperbole involving 'if') according to the rule: 'When others state the sense of "if," there is a mental construction. In *yadyarthātiśayokti*, the resolution lies in a contrary meaning between the *āpādya* (the consequence) and the *āpādaka* (the premise). Here, however, there is a distinct charm (*vaicitrya*) in that the *āpādaka* is established while the *āpādya* is merely probable; this very distinction proves that it is an internal variety of that [figure], not something external to it. Therefore, there is no need even to suspect a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in that case. Thus ends the passage.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, the Section on Poetic Presumption (Kāvyārthāpatti), in the Alaṃkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Section on Poetic Indication (Kāvyaliṅga):
that which constitutes a justification, being untouched by the relationship of general and particular, [is Kāvyaliṅga].
The poetic figure called *kāvyaliṅga* is said to be that which serves to support the meaning intended to be established.
The phrase "not touched by another" (*anālīḍhānta*) is included in order to exclude the figure of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration).
Or rather, O sirs, since there are faults [in me], let other places be sought by you; there is no room here for you, for someone who washes away the banks of sin dwells within me. (1548)
Here, the meaning of the preceding sentence consists in the non-attainment of any opportunity for faults;

its support by the meaning of the subsequent sentence—which demonstrates the proximity of Śrī Hari, who is expert at removing every single fault without exception—is the figure of speech known as *kāvyaliṅga*.

O Acyuta, those who say that you are "affectionate toward those who have taken refuge in you" do not possess even a trace of discernment, since by you the acquisition of the entire world’s horses, elephants, and lands was bestowed upon both enemies and friends alike.

By you, the attainment of "viśvāśvagajāvanī" was achieved for both enemy and friend. Regarding the enemy's side, "viśvā" means that the letter *śva* has departed; thus, upon the removal of the letter *śva*, "agajāvanīprāptiḥ" results—meaning the attainment of mountainous terrain (*agaja*) and land (*avanī*). The sense is that their entire possessions were destroyed and they were driven into the depths of the forest.

The term *suhṛtpakṣe* refers to the entire side of friends; *viśvam* means all that consists of horses and elephants; *avanī* means their protector; and *prāptiḥ* means attainment, prosperity, or sovereignty (according to Amara: "attainment" is used for rising or acquisition). This was accomplished. Alternatively, it may mean the acquisition or gain of the *viśvāśvagaja* (the world of horses and elephants) and the *avanī* (the earth). Here, the meaning of the subsequent sentence supports the meaning of the preceding sentence, refined by a specific instance of *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) bolstered by *śleṣa* (paronomasia); this constitutes its distinction from the previous [example].

[Objection: But how can the meaning "attaining land situated on a mountain region" be understood from the word *viśvāśvagajāvanīśa*? For the cognition of a meaning is impossible without the employment of a word that directly denotes it, and the word *viśvāśvagajāvanīśa* lacks the inherent capacity to denote such a meaning. [Response: This is true; however, when another meaning—namely, "one whose color (varṇa) is devoid of horses (*vigata-aśva-varṇa*)"—is presented through the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), it is precisely that [compound] word which is intended here.

The utility of such a word for the subject at hand does not arise from itself; rather, it arises through the assistance of the determination of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*) with the expressed meaning. And because that meaning is the cause for the determination of non-difference, there is the conventional usage of identity (*tādātmya*). This identity has been clearly explained by us in the section on the figure of speech *utprekṣā*, in the verse "vidyunmukhe vikāram," as being evident in works such as the *Mañjūṣā*. Alternatively, according to the established doctrine of the Alaṃkārikas, when the word "agajāvanīśa" is presented through the power of *śleṣa* (punning), its meaning is also presented. Therefore, there is no inconsistency in the cognition of the meaning.

In the *Padavākyaratnākara*, however, it is stated that there is an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) between the suggested meaning in the form of a word and the expressed meaning in the form of an object, just as there is between two expressed meanings conveyed by a single word. This is the passage from that work: "Alaṃkārikas, moreover, hold that words presented through the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) enter into the cognition of syntactic relation (*anvayabuddhi*) either as identical with [the sentence] in some cases, or through the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) in others. For instance: 'Compassion, forbearance, and truth—surely these have been manifested by you; how could they not be the indicators of liberation (*apavarga*), O King? " (Note: The verse cited is from the *Mālatīmādhava* 1.20.)

"In this context, since King Bhīma is the subject under discussion, the identity of the term *bhīmabhūmipa*—which is obtainable through suggestion (*vyañjanā*)—is superimposed [upon him]. It is then demonstrated by the statement: 'How could there be an impossibility of the suggested qualities of liberation (*apavarga*), such as compassion and forbearance—which indicate the proximity of success—being non-different from other vowels and consonants that are not the vowel *a*, which are themselves perceived through resonance (*dhvani*)? And so forth. Further details should be sought in that very source.

Thus, there is no doubt whatsoever that identity (*tādātmya*) is accepted by the Alamkārikas just as it is by the Grammarians (*śābdika*). Following this line of reasoning, the resolution of examples such as "the state of being mute is distinguished" (*mūkībhāvo viśiṣyate*) should also be understood.
O Hari, may the sovereign ocean, which is your support, never depart from you; and may the king of warriors attain invincibility as well as freedom from all enemies. || 1550 ||

O Hari! You are his support—meaning you are his foundation and refuge—and yet the truth is that you yourself have him as your support, your locus; the sense is that this is because you lie upon the ocean. The King of the Ocean, the Lord of the Waters, shall never be *apayāta*—that is, he shall never suffer retreat or defeat in battle. The sense is that one who has taken refuge in you shall not suffer retreat; in reality, however, he is not even *āpayāta*.

*Chedaḥ*: A collection of waters is *āpam*; that from which the *āpam* has departed (*yātam*) or gone is so called, meaning "one from whom the mass of water has vanished. The sense is that it would not [remain] even at all times because it is always full of water. In the alternative sense (the word-play): it would not be *apayātaḥ*—that is, *payātaḥ* (gone with) by means of the letter *pa*, and not *payātaḥ* is *apayātaḥ*. This is because the word *payonidhirāṭ* (the lord of the ocean) contains the letter *pa*. There is an identity between the word and its meaning.

He who is the sovereign of the ocean of milk, having attained invincibility (*aparājitātām*), which is the state of being unvanquished (*aparābhūtatām*), and having attained the state of being free from adversaries (*nirahitatām*), which is the condition of one from whom all enemies have departed (*nirgata-ahitaḥ*), becomes the supreme ruler, the king of kings. How could he possibly retreat? Such is the construction of the verse.

In this alternative interpretation, the word *payonidhirāṭ* (the lord of the ocean) attains "unconquerability" (*aparājitatvam*)—meaning the absence of the brilliance of the letter *pa*—and "devoidness" (*nirahitatvam*)—meaning the absence of the letter *ni*. Thus, it becomes *yodhirāṭ*, resulting in the form *yodhirāḥ*. Here too, the meaning of the sentence in the second half of the verse supports the meaning of the sentence in the first half. This will also serve as an example of that which has the meaning of a word to be mentioned later as its cause.

Just as that which is superior to Indra is yours, while that which is superior to Tandra belongs to another; how could there be identity between these two? Thus they declare the distinction between them here and there.

*Indrādhikaḥ* means one whose glory exceeds even that of Indra; *tandrādhikaḥ* means one with excessive *tandrā* (lassitude), that is, one who is lazy. People—this is the ellipsis—declare the distinction between these two, namely your own [devotee] and the other's [non-devotee], here and there, in various places; or, in the alternative sense, they declare the distinction—that is, the difference—between those two words, *indrādhika* and *tandrādhika*, by means of the letter *i* (*itaḥ*) and the letter *ta* (*tataḥ*). The sense is that the difference between them is only that much and nothing else. Here, the latter sentence-meaning, beginning with "they declare" (*abhidadhati*), supports the former sentence-meaning. [This applies to] the devotees of the Lord and others...

It should be understood that this refers to the intention of regarding the similarity between the two as being in the form of a response to the speaker; otherwise, however, there would be a justification of the sentence-meaning by means of the word-meaning.

Indeed, the greatness of those virtuous ones who serve the Lotus-Eyed Lord is limitless; by virtue of which even Yayāti, though fallen from heaven, became a leader among the virtuous while remaining a leader among the gods.

The greatness of association with virtuous people who serve the lotus-eyed Lord is limitless. By the power of such association with the good, Yayāti—the leader of the gods and dwellers of heaven—though he had fallen from the celestial realm due to some cause, remained one whose leaders were the foremost among the virtuous; that is to say, his own grandsons, Pratardana, Śibi, and others, were his "agranyaḥ" (leaders), meaning they were his deliverers. This refers to the historical account that as Yayāti was falling from heaven, he was rescued by his virtuous grandsons.
Just as Yāyātissa, having fallen into the midst [of the hells], regained his own celestial state,
so too one who has fallen among the virtuous does not become deluded.

Such authoritative proofs as these have been considered here. In the alternative interpretation, the word *dyusadagraṇīḥ* (the leader of the gods) results in *sadagraṇīḥ* (a leader among the virtuous) through the elision of the cluster of syllables *dyu*; thus, another meaning here is also striking. Here too, the meaning of the subsequent sentence serves to support the meaning of the preceding sentence.

Just as [I have sought] refuge in Your feet alone, I choose as my refuge that which is even more excellent than You—this very [refuge] which bestows a happy rebirth upon the worlds, even for You, O Sugata, who grant such a happy rebirth. (1553)
O Blessed One! Thinking that Your very feet are a refuge and protector even superior to Yourself, I choose them as my refuge; I choose them as the means (*upāya*).
For the word "refuge" (*śaraṇa*) is currently used in the sense of a means, as well as for a house or a protector. This term now functions solely as a synonym for the means.

This is according to the statement in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*. He is so called because this very foot of yours bestows upon the worlds a "sugati"—meaning a beautiful path (*upāya*), an accessible place (*sthāna*), or a supreme state (*uttama-daśā*). That such a one as you also grants a "sugati" [to others] has already been stated; however, the actual fact is that it is a "ramanīya-gamana" (a delightful journey). As the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *gati* is feminine and denotes a path, a state, knowledge, a journey, or a means. Here too, the meaning of the subsequent sentence serves to corroborate the meaning of the preceding sentence.

O mind, never fall into the state of darkness by becoming attached to Mādhava; for once that [darkness] has set in, it will not turn back even if you prostrate yourself with your head downward a thousand times.

O Mind! Being truly averse to Mādhava, never fall into equality with the *tāmasa*, that is, do not become equal to those of a *tāmasa* nature. He says "she" (*sā*) and so forth to indicate the undesirable consequence of such a reversal: thereafter, following the attainment of equality with the *tāmasa*, that state of *tāmasa*-equality will not cease even if one falls headlong a thousand times—this is a common worldly saying. Therefore, the sense is: "Do not become *tāmasa*. In the alternative [grammatical] interpretation, "that state of *tāmasa*-equality" refers to the specific manifestation of the word-form itself.

We have stated more than once that the abstract quality of femininity residing in the object is superimposed upon the word. "A thousand times" means even if the opposite state were reached, such as falling headlong; "would not cease" means it would not undergo the distinctness resulting from cessation—the sense being that it remains characterized by its original sequence. Here too, the meaning of the first half-verse is supported by the meaning of the second half-verse. Alternatively, here the negation of attaining the state of a *tāmasa* (one dominated by darkness) is supported by the fact of the engagement with Mādhava.

O Śrī, bestow upon us, who have performed the *saṃprasāraṇa* [substitution], a long-lasting compassion that is full of mercy! O Mother, if you were not to perform this *saṃprasāraṇa*, your compassion would not be manifest at all. (1555)

O Śrī! Make that compassion—whose nature is the long vowel *ā* (the syllable *ā*), and by which the *saṃprasāraṇa* (the substitution of a vowel for a semivowel) has been performed—that is, made to extend very far. The meaning is: "Extend your compassion toward me without interruption. The sense is: "I am one who seeks only the support of your compassion. If you do not perform this extension (*saṃprasaraṇa*), your most excellent compassion would not be manifested, nor would it become renowned.
The underlying sense is that if you do not extend your compassion toward me, who am wretched and have you alone as my refuge, then the very renown of your compassion would fail to manifest.

In the alternative view (*pakṣe*), [the word] has a long vowel *a*, meaning it ends in the vowel *ā* (i.e., it is *ākārāntā*). Make "compassion" (*kṛpām*)—that is, the specific verbal form *kṛpā*—such that it possesses *saṃprasāraṇa*; that is, it has the vowel *ṛ*, which is designated as *saṃprasāraṇa* in place of the semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) *r*. [The word] is thus described. There is a clear pause after *ayi*. The construction is *ayi śrīḥ*.

If the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) were not performed—given that the rule "the *saṃprasāraṇa* of *kṛp* [is applied] in the formation of the *aṅ* suffix" prescribes it as being contingent upon the *aṅ* suffix—the specific verbal form *kṛpā* or *kṛpeti* would certainly not be manifested for you; that is to say, it would not be established. Here, the meaning of the first half-verse, which consists in the necessity of the *saṃprasāraṇa* of *kṛp*, is supported by the meaning of the second half-verse, which consists in the consequence of its non-manifestation if that [vocalization] were not performed. In this case as well, as before, the reason is either the word-meaning consisting in compassionateness (*sadayatva*) itself.
O Maheśa, since we have now obtained fearlessness from taking refuge at Your feet, we look upon the Destroyer (Kīnāśa) with disregard, as if he were a mere monkey (Kīśa). 1556.
O Maheśa! O Blessed One!
That which is declared as the primordial sound at the beginning of the Vedas and established at the conclusion of the Vedas—He who is beyond that which is dissolved in Prakṛti is my Maheśvara.

Thus says the Śruti. For this very reason, the teacher Yamunācārya said: "O Maheśa, [we are unable] to abandon Your lotus feet. *Alapsmamahi* means "we obtained. "Now" (*idānīm*) means "after obtaining such [a boon]. *Kīnāśam* refers to Kṛtānta (the God of Death); it is also understood to mean "mean. Amarasimha states: "The word *kīnāśa* is masculine when meaning Kṛtānta; it is used in three genders when meaning a mean person or a farmer. "On account of being disregarded" (*anādaraṇāt*) means "without regard. *Kīśam iva* means "like a monkey"; we regard him as one who is utterly powerless (*akiṃcitkaram manyāmahe*).

This is the intended meaning. According to Amara, "markaṭaḥ," "vānaraḥ," and "kīśaḥ" all mean "monkey. In the alternative sense, [the word] *kīnāśa* (Yama) is not respected—that is, there is a lack of respect (*anādaraṇa*)—hence a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), meaning "from non-respect," which amounts to saying "from the removal of the letter *nā*. We behold *kīśam*, that is, the word *kīśa*. The meaning is: by expelling the letter *nā* from the word *kīnāśa*, we recognize it as the word *kīśa*. The word *iva* is used as a poetic ornament. The rest is clear.

Here, the latter sentence-meaning beginning with "now" (*idānīm*), which consists in the observation of the lordship of Kīnāśa (Yama), is supported by the former sentence-meaning, which consists in the attainment of fearlessness based on taking refuge at the feet of the Blessed One. This alone is the distinction from the previous examples; for in the previous cases, it was the latter sentence-meaning that supported the former sentence-meaning.

Since we have found you, the foremost one, who possesses tranquility and is worthy of refuge, as our shelter—how could we ever seek another protector before you, who are already endowed with such peace? 1557.

One who is good (sādhu) in providing refuge is "śaraṇya. Its vocative is "he śaraṇya! O Blessed One! [Address Him as] "Agrīyam," meaning supreme, for the sake of others, and unsurpassed. [Address Him as] "Śamavantam," meaning one who possesses happiness (*śam* = *sukham*; *avantam* = *prāpnuvantam*). This is because the root *ava* is taught in the sense of "attainment" (*avāpti*), according to Pāṇini’s rule. The intention is that this is based on the scriptural revelation: "Kaṃ is Brahman, Khaṃ is Brahman," which shows that [Brahman] consists of unsurpassed and vast bliss, and because it has been stated in the Sūtra: "And precisely because of the mention of [the Self] as distinguished by bliss."

We find You—meaning, as previously stated, the foremost one, possessed of peace (*śamavantam*), tranquil (*śāntam*), and the adversary of the six waves beginning with hunger (*aśanāyā*); for the Śruti says, "That which is tranquil and undecaying"—as our refuge (*śaraṇam*), our means, and our protector, in this very birth and even beyond this. [We do not find] another refuge (*śaraṇyāntaram*) who was previously—in the beginning itself—unhappy (*aśam*), devoid of bliss, and therefore unfit (*ayuktam*), unworthy of being resorted to; or rather, one who was unpeaceful (*aśamayuktam*), meaning non-tranquil.

But from where could we resort? The meaning is: "We would certainly not resort [to it]. In the alternative sense: O Refuge-giver (śaraṇya), O you who are excellent in protection! Having obtained you—the foremost, the primary one—who possess the syllable *śa* (*śam*) and protect (*ava*), as our shelter (*śaraṇa*) or home, why indeed from the very beginning (*pura eva*) would we resort to another refuge (*śaraṇyāntaram*)—meaning a forest region (*araṇyāntaram*)—which is "without *śa*" (*aśam*), improper, and substituted for the syllable *śa* with the letter *a*? Why would we resort to such an interior (*antaram*) or middle place?

"Having obtained a home that is excellent for protection, why should one resort to a forest interior which is full of suffering and improper?"—this meaning is truly marvelous. Here, it should be noted that the latter sentence-meaning, consisting of an indifference toward resorting to another such refuge, is established by the former sentence-meaning—the attainment of the feet of the Blessed One who possesses qualities such as being a worthy refuge—and this is further nourished by the charm arising from a *vyatireka* (contrast) rooted in *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
O Mother of the worlds, if you were to look upon them in succession, the Lord of Heaven (Indra) or even the Lord of the World (Brahmā) would truly become as mere locks of hair. (1558)

O Mother of the worlds! If both Indra, the lord of heaven (*nākeśa*), or Brahmā, the lord of the world (*lokeśa*)—according to Amara, "Hiraṇyagarbha is the lord of the world"—should remain unlooked upon, that is, not glanced at with a side-long look (*kaṭākṣita*) by you in due order as before, then they would be merely hair-like (*keśabhūta*), meaning they would be as devoid of essence as hair. In the alternative sense (of word-play), the words *nākeśa* and *lokeśa*, when the letters *na* and *la* are respectively absent from them, become *anāloka* (where the suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā*). Thus, they are rendered without those specific syllables.

The two [words] would become "anālokau" (without light) and "anālokitau" (unobserved) if, respectively, the word *nākeśa* were deprived of the letter *na*, and the word *lokeśa* were deprived of the letter *la*. The meaning is that if they were thus devoid of those letters, they would be established as the words *keśa* (hair). Here, the meaning of the subsequent sentence serves as the reason for the negation of the absence of being marked by the side-glance of Lakṣmī, which was intended to be expressed.
Just as Vāsudeva shines in one way and Vāmadeva spreads forth in another, is he not a fool who, while acknowledging this well-known distinction recognized in the Vedas, asserts their identity? (1559)

The distinction between these two, Vāsudeva and Vāmadeva, is scriptural and well-regarded; the meaning is that it is accepted by all because it is well-known from such Vedic texts as "Rudra is born from Nārāyaṇa. The word *anayoḥ* (of these two) connects with both sides according to the "central gem" (*madhyamaṇi*) maxim. Is not a person who speaks of identity—that is, non-difference—between these two, who are thus established as distinct by scripture, a fool? Indeed, he is a fool.

This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the words *vāsudeva* and *vāmadeva*, there is a difference (*bheda*) between their *su-* and *sukāra* and *ma-* and *makāra* vowels, [expressed] by the suffix *tasi* which functions across all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). To claim non-difference (*abheda*) between these two such words is to be nothing but a fool; this further meaning also produces an extraordinary aesthetic charm (*camatkārātiśaya*). Here, the latter sentence-meaning—“the non-difference of these two,” and so forth—is supported by the former sentence-meaning—“that which appears,” and so forth.
Just as the endless Upanishads here constantly declare Nārāyaṇa to be the Sovereign, if anyone were to say that He is not Śiva, he would surely be one whose vision is perverted. 1560.

The meaning is that the endless Upaniṣads—such as "He is the controller of all; He is the one controller"—constantly proclaim Nārāyaṇa, through such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, indeed, there was only Nārāyaṇa" and "Then the Person, Nārāyaṇa, desired: 'May I create offspring,'" as being the cause of the entire universe. "Vaśin" means one who possesses *vaśa*, which signifies either sovereignty (*prabhutva*) or self-mastery (*āyattatva*); he who possesses this is a *vaśī*.

They call him "Vaśin" (the Subduer), for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *vaśa* denotes dependence and mastery regarding birth, desire, and effort. One should also recall here such passages as "this world exists under his control" (*jagadvaśe vartate*). If anyone were to speak of that very Lord of All, the Vaśin, using the compound *na-śiva*—meaning one who possesses inauspicious qualities—that speaker would surely be "one whose vision is turned away," that is, one who perceives what is contrary to the truth.

The sense is this: if one were to call Him—who is filled with a multitude of auspicious qualities conducive to His status as the Lord of All—inauspicious (*aśiva*), who could possibly have any doubt regarding that person’s perception of a meaning contrary to the Śruti? Alternatively, the Śruti declares that the entire universe is dependent upon Him; thus, for that Controller of all, including Śiva—who is established by the very same Śruti as the cause in the passage "Rudra is born from Nārāyaṇa"—the relationship of being the effect and the cause, and consequently the relationship of being the controlled and the controller, is explicitly stated in the words of the text itself: "Śiva is indeed Nārāyaṇa."

The meaning is this: if one were to say that [the term] is not *śiva* (auspicious) because they do not understand the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based either on the connection of the syllables in reverse order (*yāmakabhāva*) or on the connection of the body as the self (*śarīrātmabhāva*), then what doubt could there be regarding their being one who perceives things in reverse? Alternatively, if one were to say that the word "vaśinam" (the sequence of syllables) is not *śiva*, then such a person is indeed one who sees in reverse; for it is produced in that way by the reversal of the stated sequence of syllables. This is the intended sense.

Here too, there is a corroboration (*samarthana*) of the meaning of the subsequent sentence, "he is the seer of the contrary," by means of the meaning of the preceding sentence, "the master" (*vaśinam*), and so forth. In the previous example, the difference between the Lord and Rudra was stated based on their distinct essential natures (*niṣkṛṣṭarūpa*). Here, however, it should be understood that non-difference (*abheda*) is established by relying upon grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—which is based either on the fact that words denoting the body extend to the embodied being, or on the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakaraṇabhāva*), and so forth.
Just as the sun vies with your foot, which possesses an exceedingly crimson luster like a lotus, they say that even the most brilliant [sun] is preceded by the *visarjanīya* (the final visarga).

O Padmā! The sun (taraṇi) vies with your foot, which possesses an exceedingly ruddy luster (atyaruṇā ruk) that surpasses the dawn. For this very reason, the wise say that this sun, though most radiant and possessed of extreme brilliance, is the foremost among those to be cast out (*visarjanīya*). The word "the wise" (*santaḥ*) is to be supplied as the subject. The sense is: who else indeed could be cast out even when competing with your foot?

In reality, however, they say that this word *taraṇi* has a *visarjanīya* (the *visarga*) preceding it—that is, existing at its final portion—and a *ṇi*, the letter *ṇ*, at its end; for such is the nature of the word *taraṇi*. The meaning is that there is an identity between the word and its referent (*śabdārthayostādātmyam*). Here too, the sense of the second half-verse is supported by the sense of the first half-verse. This is an instance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) with which it is intermingled.

Just as at first the lotus was glorious, but then, becoming its opposite by stealing the beauty of your feet, it attained the state of being "kalama" (a paddy variety) and dwelt in the forest with other non-lotus species. || 1562 ||

The word *he padme* is supplied from the preceding verse. First, it was a lotus (*kamala*) that was auspicious (*saśrīka*), beautiful (*saśobha*), or possessed of majesty (*savaibhava*). Then, however, it became something that steals the beauty of your feet (*tvatpadavasuhāri*)—that is, it robs the splendor of your feet and the luster of your abode—and for that very reason, it is characterized by a "contrary stain" (*vipratīpamala*), meaning a stain of sin (*pāpa*) and impurity (*mālinya*) that has no rival. The sense is: what greater evil could there be than the theft of the excellence of the feet of the Mother of the World?

The analysis of the compound is: "that from which opposition and hostility have departed. He attained, that is, reached, the state of being a *kalama* (a type of rice) and the state of being a thief (*coratva*), as well as the state of being a grain-crop (*vrīhisasyatva*). Immediately thereafter, he resorted to another mark (*anyaliṅga*), meaning another sign; that is to say, his former appearance was concealed by a different dress. He dwelt—lived—in some forest or in the water. In the alternative sense (the word-play), the word *kamala* [is analyzed as]: first, "one who has *ka* (splendor) together with *śrī* (beauty)," meaning its color is manifest.

Now, that [word] in which the two vowels *ma* and *la* are inverted—that is, whose *ma* and *la* have been transposed—is what is meant by that expression. For this very reason, it attained the state of being a *kalama*, meaning the word *kalama*. It is described as having "resorted to another gender" (*anyaliṅga*), meaning that having abandoned its neuter state while remaining in the form of the word *kamala*, it attained the masculine gender. As it is said: "The word *kalamo* refers to a pen, a thief, rice, and a type of grass."

The meaning is that the word *kalama* is taught to be masculine by both the *Viśva* and *Medinī* lexicons, which state: "In the *Medinī*, *kalama* is masculine [and denotes] a rice plant and also a thief. Here too, everything should be understood as in the previous example.
As for instance:

O lotus-eyed one, you distinguish with great clarity between what is beneficial and what is harmful; O Lord of the Mountain whose crest is the serpent-king, how could you not be entirely impartial? (1563)

You perceive the gift (*aṃhati*) of gold—that is, of wealth characterized by gold—to be even more excellent for a person who is beneficial; how then could you not be entirely impartial? The word *aṃhati* means "gift" or "bestowal," as Amara states in his list of synonyms for giving: *apasarjanam aṃhatiḥ*. It is derived from the root *han* with the suffix *ati* according to the rule *hanteḥ aṃhaś ca*, where *han* is replaced by *aṃh*. Etymologically, it is called *aṃhati* because it destroys (*hanti*) evil (*durita*) through this [gift]. How could you not be equal toward all? For the gift of one who is beneficial is exceedingly beautiful, while the gift of gold—representing material prosperity—is likewise a magnificent bestowal. How then could you not be one who is equal to everyone?

But for one who is not beneficial (ahita), there is indeed an indescribable, excessive, and extreme *aṃhati*—that is, harm (*hiṃsā*). [This is derived from] the root *han* with the suffix *ktin*. However, upon examining Hemacandra’s lexicon (*kośa*) which states, "The word *aṃhati* denotes abandonment and disease," even if one were to take the very word *aṃhati* in the sense of "disease" (*roga*) within the context of "one who is not beneficial" (*ahita*), the intended meaning would certainly still be established. Nevertheless, because of the presence of a specific aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) produced by the word-splitting (*padabhaṅga*), the previously stated meaning alone is superior.

Alternatively, since multiplicity of meaning is not a defect in the speech of authoritative persons (*puruṣa*), let there be two meanings even here; the rest is clear. Here, the latter part of the sentence’s meaning—beginning with "equality with all"—is supported by the meaning of the preceding half-verse. It should be understood that this [figure] is assisted by *tulyayogitā* (parallelism), characterized by the equality of the recurrence of both the beneficial and the harmful, which is brought to light by the suggestive power (*pratibhā*) of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Just as there is one friend who is the kinsman of the blue water-lily, while another is the eye of the world; even more than this, let the ocean of compassion be considered the true friend for those who bow in reverence.

Here, there is a specific poetic charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) consisting in the corroboration, by way of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so"), of the meaning of the second half-verse—which consists in determining the Lord's nature as a kinsman to those who have sought refuge—by means of the meaning of the first half-verse, which describes His possessing two eyes that are friends to the world.

Just as there is a distinction between those who partake of the lineage of your sidelong glances and those who do not: the former becomes the sustainer of the world, while the latter becomes the one whose seat is the Lord of the Serpent-Mountain (Śeṣa). 1565.

*Parabhedaḥ* means the preeminent distinction, that is, the great distinction. One may also interpret the meaning as "distinction [arising] from the letters *pa* and *ra*. The first [type of person] is one who partakes in the connection with your sidelong glance; he is a *viṣṭapabhṛt*, meaning a sustainer of the world, a protector of the world (*lokapāla*). The latter is one who does not partake in that; he is a *viṣṭarabhṛt*, meaning a bearer of the seats of others—namely, a servant—or alternatively, one who holds a handful of *darbha* grass, that is, one who performs other sacrificial rites and the like.

‘*Viṣṭara* means a tree, a handful of *darbha* grass, or a seat such as a stool,’ according to Amara. The sense is that there is a great difference between a world-protector (*lokapāla*) and a mere servant (*kiṅkara*). Between the two words *viṣṭapabhṛt* (bearer of the world) and *viṣṭarabhṛt* (bearer of a seat), the difference lies solely in the letters *pa* and *ra*; since the sequence of all other phonemes is identical in both, it is called a "difference of the latter" (*parabheda*).

Here, the unique distinction from previous types [of *arthāntaranyāsa*] is that the single sentence-meaning consisting of the occurrence of the aforementioned "difference of the latter," as presented in the first half, is supported by two distinct sentence-meanings in the second half, which contain a figure of contrast (*vyatireka*).
Or rather: "O Darkness, move far away! The Wielder of the Discus shines eternally within my heart; if you stir even slightly, not even your head shall remain."

"O He-tama!"—this is an address to Rāhu, who is identified through the non-difference of his nature from the quality of darkness (tamas). Here, because of the darkness receding far away, you move about somewhat, as before, even though it does not actually recede.

The two preceding and following sentence-meanings—that even the mere mention of [the Lord] is difficult to obtain, and that the Wielder of the Discus shines within my heart—are supported by the middle sentence-meaning, which acts like a central gem: "The Blessed One, who bears the Sudarśana weapon capable of severing the head of Rāhu, shines in my heart. Thus, the support of two sentence-meanings by a single sentence-meaning possesses a distinct aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) superior to previous examples.
This is also seen in the form of a *mālā* (chain) verse:

"O Mādhava, that man who remains indifferent toward you, though he be of disciplined conduct, would be a *danuja* (demon); but he who constantly worships you, though he be a *danuja*, would be a man of disciplined conduct. (1567)

O Mādhava! One whose conduct (*vṛtti*) is characterized by *mada*—that is, pride—is so described. Even such a human being, though a man, would through intoxication become a *danuja* (demon) due to his indifference; he would possess a demonic nature. In another sense, by substituting the letter *da* for the letter *ma* in the word *manuja*, the form *danuja* is produced. However, one whose conduct is characterized by *dama*—that is, self-restraint—is so described; this means that by substituting the letter *ma* for the letter *da*.

Even that *danuja* (demon), by virtue of his habit of self-restraint (*dama*), becomes exactly like a human (*manuja*); the meaning is that in this case, the word *danuja* would result in being *manuja*. Here, the two intended meanings of the preceding sentence—indifference and the necessity of worship—are supported by the two meanings of the subsequent sentences; thus, it constitutes the figure of speech known as *mālā* (garland). This should be understood accordingly in the following instances as well.
Just as those who are gazed upon by you become bearers of the world-protectors (Lokapālas), O Mother, if they were instead not gazed upon by you, they would surely become bearers of skulls (Kapālas).

"Alokitāḥ" means not seen (*adṛṣṭāḥ*). Those in which the color of the world (*loka-varṇa*) does not exist are "alokāḥ"; the suffix *kap* is applied here according to the rule "śeṣād vibhāṣā. Having been made "aloka," they are "alokitāḥ. Here too, as before, there is the nature of a garland (*mālārūpatva*).
Or rather: "O Śauri, if you constantly increase my fear in this matter, then desire will grow; how then could there be security for me? (1569)

O Śauri! Constantly increase my *śama* (tranquility) and *śānti* (peace). If, in this matter of increasing peace, you should extend doubt or hesitation, then desire—that longing for sense-objects—will become increased and grown. Thereafter, how could there be *kṣema* (well-being)—the welfare consisting of crossing over the cycle of existence and so forth? (As Amara states: "The word *kṣema* is not feminine and means well-being"). The implication is that as long as there is greed for sense-objects, spiritual excellence (*śreyaḥ*) is by no means easily attainable.

In this context, regarding the two words *śaṃ* and *kāṃ*, there is an optional *parasavarṇa* (homogeneous substitution) for the anusvāra in place of the *m* in *śam*, according to the rule *vā padāntasya*. If you expand the *ś* of the word *śama* into *śaṃ* and the *k* into *kāṃ*, then the word *śama* becomes the word *kāma*; thus, because the first vowel (*ā*) is designated as "vṛddha," the word becomes one bearing the technical designation *vṛddha*.

Since the technical designation *vṛddha* is prescribed by the rule “*vṛddhir yasyācām ādis tad vṛddham*,” one must also consider this further implication: after the letter *ka* has been substituted for the letter *śa*, how could there be *kṣema*? If *ka* were substituted, the word would be *kāma* alone, and not *kṣema*. Here, the sentence-meaning consisting of the increase of tranquility and indifference supports the sentence-meaning consisting of the occurrence of the increase of desire; and that [first meaning] in turn supports the sentence-meaning consisting of the doubt regarding the occurrence of welfare (*kṣema*). Thus, because each subsequent element is supported by each preceding one, it possesses the nature of a "garland" (*mālā*).

O Acyuta, just as my consciousness—which, due to the fear of worldly existence, takes on the form of seeking out torments—is characterized by the search for suffering, so too, for one who is fearless, where would there be torment? In that case, it would be consciousness itself. (1570)

O Acyuta! My consciousness—that is, my intellect—is "yātanāmayī," meaning it consists of intense suffering (the suffix *mayaṭ* here denotes abundance). It is "viceyākārā," meaning its very form or nature is such that it must be sought out or investigated; the sense is that due to the abundance of pain born from agitation regarding worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), it has become almost destroyed. Therefore, I entreat you for the sake of making [me] "abhītaḥ"—that is, fearless. The meaning is: I pray to you for the granting of fearlessness.

To the question, "What will be achieved for you by that?", he says: *kva* (where). That is to say, at that time—immediately after granting you fearlessness—where would the *yātanā* (torment), previously described as suffering, be? It would not exist at all; rather, that very *cetana* (consciousness)—that is, the aforementioned intellect (*buddhi*)—would come into being, meaning it would attain existence. The sense is that immediately after the bestowing of your fearlessness, my intellect would become something capable of functioning through linguistic usage (*vyavahāryā*).

In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), *cetana* refers to the verbal expression *cetana*. It is that by which the letter *ce*, which is the form to be sought (*viceya-ākāra*), has been displaced (*vibhraṃśita*). Such is the meaning.

The term *viceḥ* refers to that which has the letter *yā*—that is, the phoneme *ya*—in place of the letter *ci*; thus, having had its *ci* displaced and the letter *ya* substituted in its stead, it becomes *yātanāmayī*. The suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in its own sense (svārthika), according to the rule "the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied after a word denoting the material" (*tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ*), where the word *tat* is separated by a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*). The meaning is that it attains the form *yātanā*. The sense is that there is an absence of fear (*abhītiḥ*), because there is no dread that the form of a word might be distorted through the displacement of existing letters and the insertion of other letters in their place.

The word *yācekṛtau* is a compound (*samasta-pada*). [The question is: "Where would there be the word *yātanā* when the letter *i* is substituted in place of the letter *y*? The sense is that, according to the stated method, by placing the letter *e* in place of the letter *ya*, how could the verbal form *yātanā* exist? This is because its very nature has already been lost. On the contrary, that aforementioned *cetana* itself would become the verbal manifestation *cetanā*. The verbal manifestation *cetana*—having attained the state of *yātanā*—would attain existence as *cetana* alone, because the letter *e* is again placed in place of the adventitious letter *ya*. This is the intended meaning.

In this context, it should be understood that the statement regarding the loss of mental composure rooted in the fear and torment of worldly existence supports the statement regarding the petition for fearlessness from the Blessed One; that in turn supports the statement regarding the cessation of torment; and that finally supports the statement regarding the restoration of mental health.
Just as you leap about in the forest fire, how much further can you go? Behold the vast flood of Hari’s compassion flowing very swiftly toward me; then your pride shall perish.

Here, by the sentence-meaning consisting of the sight of the flood of compassion, the sentence-meaning regarding the destruction of pride is established; by that, the sentence-meaning in the form of the conclusion—the leaping away from the forest fire—is supported. Here, there is the support of a preceding sentence-meaning by a subsequent sentence-meaning whose cause is that very preceding sentence-meaning situated in the middle. This differs from the previous examples in that it takes the form of a "garland" (mālā) and is intermingled with metaphor (rūpaka). An example of the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) where the meaning of a word serves as the reason is as follows:
"When both [the mountains] were engaged in a contest for mutual victory, Meru, the golden mountain, was called 'the mountain of serpents' (pannagagiri) because he was struck [by the other]. (1572)

The Golden Mountain (Kanakagiri), having been pierced—that is, struck—by the horn of the Serpent Mountain (Pannagagiri); the suffix *niṣṭhā* takes the form *na* in the passive sense. Therefore, it "uttered" (*ūce*) that a wound (*aruḥ*) had arisen for it; from the root *brū*, the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is used in the active voice, with the substitution of *vac* according to the rule *bruvo vaciḥ*. In the alternative sense, "Meru" or "Sumeru" was "called" (*ūce*) by people—the ellipsis being "was called"—in the passive voice, using the perfect tense. Here, the sentence-meaning "Meru was so called" is supported by the word-meaning "pierced," which is animated by a metaphorical identification based on the foundation of punning (*śleṣa*), and further reinforced by the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) to be mentioned later.

O Lord of the World, it is as if a creature here, though its conduct is captivating to the heart like that of a king, should become one whose heart is devoid of hope in you; alas, its very conduct would then be like that of a mere animal! 1573.

Though his conduct and disposition were so captivating and pleasing to the heart upon the royal throne, the lion-throne worthy of a king, or even while seated upon it—he whose heart and mind were thus directed toward you—yet, in the event of indifference, apathy, or rejection regarding you, O Lord of the World, he will become one whose livelihood and very mode of existence is that of a *jāṅgamī* (a wandering outcaste).

The meaning is that even the Great King, if neglected by you, would come to lead the life of a *caṇḍāla*, according to the principle stated in the verse: "One should know him who constantly hates Viṣṇu to be one whose semen flows downward. In the word *janaṅgama*, the suffix *khac* is applied by the rule *gamaśca* to form a proper name (*saṃjñā*), and the suffix *mum* is added by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya*. Amara states: "*Caṇḍāla*, *plava*, *mātaṅga*, *divākīrti*, and *janaṅgama* [are synonyms]. The etymological analysis (*vigraha*) is: he goes away (*gacchati*) far from people (*janāt*), hence he is a *janaṅgama*.

The word *jānaṅgamī* here possesses the suffix *ṅīṣ* characterized by the addition of *aṇ*; such is its function (*vṛtti*). There is a masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). In the alternative case, the word *rājāsanahṛdayaṅgamavṛtti* has its phonemes (*varṇāḥ*)—namely those of the form *nigatarāsahṛdaya*—removed from it. For this very reason, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), only the phonemes of the form *jānaṅgamavṛtti* remain, and thus the form *jānaṅgamavṛtti* is produced; this is the meaning.

Here, although the king’s heart is captivating, the sentence-meaning—which consists in its attaining the state of being the heart's resort for Jānakī—is supported by the two words "nirāsa-hṛdaya" (heart devoid of hope) [applied] to you; the specific aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), however, is quite evident.
Or rather,
O Mother, your braid of hair, which by its own color attains a state of being utterly devoid of fine cloth,
alas, becomes like an elephant for the purpose of churning the lotus-pond that is the heart of the Enemy of Madhu.

O Mother! Your braid of hair is exceedingly beautiful by its own color—that is, by its own deep blackness (the suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of all case endings). Attaining a state of friendliness toward the sky (*ambara*), that is, achieving a resemblance to the firmament, it becomes like an elephant for the churning—that is, the agitation—of the lake which is the abode of the lotus named Madhuripu (Viṣṇu), just as a lotus-pond is the dwelling place of the Enemy of Mura. It becomes equal to that; in other words, it acts with such proficiency.

In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), the specific sound-form *kabarī*, *kabarī*—by being "sutarām" (exceedingly) deprived of its own letters (*svavarṇa*) from among the letters present within itself (the suffix *tasi* here takes all case-endings as before)—becomes *karī*. The meaning is that while the word *kabarī* undergoes a state of being devoid of the letter *va* (*vavarṇavidhuratā*), it settles into the form *karī*. Here, the transformation of *kabarī* into *karī*, which would otherwise be impossible, is supported by several constituent meanings such as "sutarām," "varahitatām," and so forth.
It should be observed that this is further nourished by the figures of speech *śleṣa* (punning) and *paraṃparita-rūpaka* (metaphor of a series).
Indeed, O Blessed One, was it not previously from the ocean of milk that you obtained the essence of milk—the Kaustubha jewel—while assuming the form of the Tortoise during its churning? (1575)

O Blessed One! Regarding the compound *agamathanataḥ*: it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the churning (*mathana*) performed by the mountain (*aga*), namely Mandara. Therefore, from *agamathanataḥ*, the sense is "having performed the churning of the mountain" (*agamathanaṃ kṛtvā*). Here, the suffix *tasi* is used in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) with the elision of the gerund suffix *lyap*. As for *kaustubhaḥ* and *ramā* (Lakṣmī): these two are being accepted or taken up. The word *kaustubha* is placed first because, according to the sūtraic indication *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*, this informs us that the rule regarding the priority of placement (*pūrvanipāta*) is not mandatory. Thus, the word *kaustubha* is placed first.

The milk-ocean was "milked" (extracted) by you; that is, its essence—the stable portion—was drained away. The sense is that by taking the Kaustubha jewel, which possesses the most excellent beauty, the entire essence of the milk-ocean was indeed milked. In the alternative sense, the word *dugdhasāgara* (milk-ocean) was "milked" (reduced); that is, when there is a division of the compound as *gamanataḥ* instead of *mathanataḥ*, then due to the removal (*vilopana*) of the letter *ga* (the syllable *ga*), the word *dugdhasāra* (essence of milk) remains. Thus, the word *dugdhasāgara* was reduced to *dugdhasāra*.

The meaning that [the word *kṣīrasāgara*] is thus produced by the removal of the letter *ga* is also striking. Here too, the well-known fact that the milk-ocean is the essence of milk is supported through many constituent elements, such as the act of churning the ocean preceded by the seizing of the Kaustubha gem and Lakṣmī.

Or rather, O Mother, the ray of the sun, having become noble [white] in some places, abandoned its contact with the lowly [darkness]; yet your foot’s luster, never abandoning its primordial supreme color, becomes the sun itself. 1576.

"O Mother! The sun’s ray—the beam of the sun—having become in some way noble (*ārya*), of good lineage (*kulīna*), and righteous (*nyāyya*), or even virtuous (*sādhu*)—according to the *Ratnamālā*: 'The word *āryā* has three meanings: noble, of good lineage, and righteous'—[approaches] the Gaurī. Regarding the term *anuka*, it refers to those who desire; in the sense of "one who desires after" (*anukāmayate*), the suffix *kan* is irregularly applied (*nipātyate*) to the prefix *anu*, as stated in Amara: 'A lover is called *kāmin* or *anuka*. This refers to those who are greedy for the pleasures of the senses (*viṣaya-rasa-lālasa*). He abandons—that is, casts off—his association or connection (*saṅgam*); the augment *nuṭ* is prohibited by the rule *nābhyastāt*."

He is one whose first birth (*ādya-prathamabhava*) has not been abandoned; for that very reason, he is one whose caste (*varṇa*) is supreme (*uttama*) and most excellent (*śreṣṭha*), meaning he has not neglected the Brāhmaṇa caste. By these two terms, the avoidance of what is unfavorable and the adoption of what is favorable are shown; that is to say, his conduct and character are appropriate for the Brāhmaṇa caste. Alternatively, in the phrase "kvacanārya," there is a word division as "kvacana aryaiḥ. Being an *arya*—meaning a Vaiśya—the form is correct due to the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*) "aryaḥ svāmivaiśyayoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.103). As Amarasimha states: "The word *arya* may mean a master or a Vaiśya. Anu...

The meaning has already been stated: "having abandoned the association with *ka*. "One by whom the first and last letters have not been abandoned" means that those two—the first and last—letters, which are respectively prior to and superior to himself (the letter *ka*), namely the *brahma* and *kṣatra* classes (*varṇa*), have followed him; that is to say, he is one who brings about the *brahma* and *kṣatra* classes. Therefore, becoming a sage (*sūrībhavan*)—that is, becoming a wise man (*sūri*) or becoming a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*)—he became one whose delight was fixed upon your feet (*rucirabhirati*). Thus it was.

In this context, the word *sūryakara* (the sun’s rays) is at one point *arya*, meaning its *arya*-vowels (*ṛ* and *ḷ*) are absent; having become so, it "leaves the company of the following" (*anukasaṅgam*), that is, it abandons the conjunction with the immediately following *ka*-vowel (*k*), meaning it discards the cluster of letters *ryaka*. It is described as such because it has not abandoned its first and last letters—the initial and final syllables—which are of the form *sūra*; for the *Ratnamālā* states: "The two 'excellent' ones (*uttama*) are the pre-eminent and the final."

There are also usages such as *uttamaṃ ca naidāgham* (and the supreme summer). For this very reason, the word *sūryakara*—which is becoming a *sūri*, that is, becoming a *sūra*—is derived as *sūra* by the elision of the *rya* sounds; this is the meaning. The factual state of affairs is that [the sun] is so called because its luster (*ruci*) is like the luster of your feet. One should note that, through the identity of word and meaning, the word *sūra* is equal to the venerable feet.

In this instance, the transformation of the sun’s rays into goddesses is unfamiliar and thus requires justification, which is provided by the multiple preceding referents. Furthermore, the aesthetic charm—enhanced by the figure of hyperbole based on identity rooted in paronomasia—is clearly manifest.
Just as gold makes its own [reflected] body of supreme color and itself of inferior color, by making itself the debtor and that [reflection] the creditor, it becomes possessed of debt. || 1577 ||
Gold, the agent, [perceived] the body of Śrī—her divine form—as having a superior color compared to itself, and perceived itself as having an inferior color, a base color. It discerned this.

*Tsat*. In the present participle (*śatṛ*) of the root *iṇ* preceded by *ava*, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs according to the rule "iṇo yaṇ. [The poet] says that he, [the Lord], while making that glorious divine body his own creditor (*uttamarṇa*)—that is, the one who lends the debt in the form of the [four] castes (*varṇa*)—becomes "tsat" (is born/sits), using the present participle according to the rule "lakṣaṇahetvoḥ" (to denote a characteristic or a cause). The meaning is: by means of the cause of acting as a creditor. Consequently, [the body] becomes a debtor (*adhamarṇa*), the receiver of the debt in the form of the castes, and thus remains "with debt" (*sa-ṛṇa*), indeed accompanied by debt. The sense is that it is not capable of returning it to you;
furthermore, by the very name "Svarṇa" (Gold), its state of being in debt is naturally implied.

In this context, the word *svarṇam* (gold) acts as the agent; by making the word *uttamavarṇam* (of the highest caste) devoid of the letter *va*—that is, by turning it into *uttamarṇam* (creditor)—and likewise making the word *adhamavarṇam* (of the lowest caste) [devoid of *va*]—that is, by turning it into *adhamarṇam* (debtor)—and likewise making the word *svarṇam* (gold) [devoid of *va*]—that is, by turning it into *sarṇam* (indebted)—it produces a further meaning that heightens the sense of wonder.

In this context, the fact that gold stands as a debtor and so forth—which is inherently extraordinary—is supported by such phrases as "superior in color to itself," which require justification. It should be understood that this [justification] attains sovereign power through the grace of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), consisting in the description of a relationship between the divine form of Lakṣmī and gold—specifically their roles as creditor and debtor—even though no such relationship actually exists. As Amara states: "The two terms *uttamarṇa* and *adhamarṇa* refer respectively to the lender and the borrower."

Just as the moon, having become sweet-tasting by taking up the nectar of your words, became delicious; how could that same moon, the friend of the night-lotus, ever become delicious again if it were to vomit [that nectar] out? (1578)

"O Blessed One"—this is understood from the context. The moon, the friend of the night-lotus (*kumuda-bāndhava*), having become a "repository of nectar" (*sudhākara*)—that is, a source or place of nectar—precisely because of its "seizing" (*haraṇa*) or taking away of the nectar of your speech; in another sense, *sudhākara* means "one whose rays are nectar. The truth is that it is thus described as having the syllable *su-* as its initial letter, being "to be tasted" (*svādya*), meaning worthy of being relished.

The identity between word and meaning must not be forgotten. "Was born" (*samajani*) means "was produced"; "otherwise" (*itaradhā*) means "in a different manner," that is, by way of the opposite of what was stated. "Vomited" (*vāntaḥ*) means having become the object of vomiting, i.e., ejected. This very friend of the night-lotuses (*kumudabāndhavaḥ*), namely the moon—in the alternative sense, the word *kumudabāndhava* itself—should be understood as being "vomited" because the sound *va* is heard at its end (*tasyānte*). How could it be worthy of being tasted? (*svādyassyāt*)?

The sense is: how could a substance that has been vomited be tasted by others, except after it has attained the status of the moon (sudhākara) caused by its being taken up as the nectar of your words? In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), the word *kumudabāndhava* (the friend of the night-lotus) might be "vomited" [as a discarded term], but it cannot be something to be tasted, because it is to be used with the prefix *kvā* [in the sense of "where"?].

Here, since the tastability of the "vomited" moon is otherwise inexplicable, its nature as the moon [of speech] caused by its being taken up as the nectar of the Lord’s words is postulated; thus, the meaning of the whole sentence is the poetic figure of Presumption (*arthāpatti*) as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

In this regard, there are two intermediate sentence-meanings: (1) the moon’s status as the "nectar-maker" (*sudhākara*), caused by its taking up the nectar of the Lord’s words, which serves to establish its edibility; and (2) its being "vomited," which serves to support the objection regarding its edibility. Thus, these two word-meanings act as causes, and the figure is of the nature of two *kāvyaliṅgas*. The specific charm arises from the fact that it is reinforced by *śleṣa* (paronomasia), just as before. However, in reality, since this is primarily an instance of *arthāpatti* (presumption), it is more appropriate to consider it an example of that alone; this is the correct view.

Or rather: "O Sovereign of All, though this lake water—which desires the excellence of Your complexion—is indeed excellent, yet it has been joined with the dust of wild asses (*kāsaraja*); who indeed would not know this? (1579)

O Sovereign of All! The lotus born of the lake (kāsāraja) is one whose desire is to attain excellence even over your complexion—or rather, one for whom there is a longing (īpsā) for superiority in your color. For this very reason, it has been properly cast down (astaṃ) by you; in another sense, the word *kāsāraja* is "properly destroyed" (*sādhvasta*), meaning its own color has been eclipsed. Nevertheless, even so, it has attained attachment (*saṅgam*)—that is, the obsession (*abhiṣaṅgam*)—toward that very desire for excellence in your complexion.

The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). In that regard, who indeed would not know the word *kāsaraja*—meaning "born from a buffalo" (*mahiṣajāta*)—which has been properly reduced to a short *s* (i.e., *kāsaraja* instead of *kāsarāja*) in place of the destroyed letter *s* with its vowel *ā*? The sense is: having first set out with the desire to obtain a particular rare object, and then being thoroughly defeated, who whose intellect is like that of a buffalo would ever again exert himself for that purpose?

In this instance, the fact that the *kāsaraja* (the dust of the *kāsa* flower) is silver is supported by several preceding words, as it requires justification due to its non-worldly nature; however, another aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) is quite evident.
Just as a family of the learned, when devoted to you and having attained tranquility within itself, becomes truly capable of accomplishing the sovereign empire of the supreme good, O Hari. (1580)

The assembly (*kula*) of the wise who possess discernment (*saṃkhyāvat*), being devoted to you, attains within itself—that is, within its own mind—peace (*śam*), happiness, and bliss; thus, it becomes truly capable of achieving the sovereignty of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa-sāmrājya*). In the alternative sense (the word-play), the meaning is that the word *kula*, having attained the letter *śa* within itself—specifically, between its two constituent syllables—results precisely in the form *kuśala*.

Here, the capacity of the assembly of the discerning to achieve the sovereignty of the supreme good is caused by the fact that they are devoted to you, as expressed in the phrase "being devoted to you" (*tvayi anuraktaṃ*).

O lotus-eyed one, it is only fitting that your heart—though possessing the excellent *prastara* gem, the *kaustubha* jewel, and the *sauvastika* mark—is exceedingly hard toward me, scarred as it is by the arrow-wounds of the hosts of your enemies. 1581.
In this instance, the hardness of Śrīnivāsa’s heart is supported by the meanings of the words "best of stones" (*prastaravara*) and "host of enemies" (*ari-gaṇa*).

Or, as in my own *Stuti of Śrī Hayavadana*: "O Hari, you dwell in the moon (the nectar-rayed one), and you are naturally sweet with the luster of milk; thus, it is entirely fitting that the report 'you are made of rock-salt' (*saindhava*) should reach your throat. (1582)

O Hari! O Śrī Hayavadana! [The moon] is indeed the maker of nectar, the bestower of ambrosia, and the possessor of cooling rays—this is the reality. You dwell [within him]. By this, his sweetness is said to be adventitious. By nature—that is, by his very essence—he is sweet (*madhura*), distinguished by the quality of sweetness, and beloved by the worlds; this is the reality. According to Amara, "the words *svādu* and *priya* mean *madhura*. Therefore, he is one whose luster (*ruci*) is the very relish (*svādimā*) of milk—that is, the sweetness of milk itself.

For one such as you, the statement "Saindhava means salt"—this speech proceeding from above the throat (i.e., uttered without thought)—is truly heartless; that is to say, it is only appropriate that it not be preceded by the heart. The sense is: how could the description of something exceedingly sweet as being "salt" possibly proceed from the mind? In reality, however, the statement "Saindhava means horse" proceeds from above the throat because you have the face of a horse. This is the intended meaning.

According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *saindhava* refers to salt (neuter), a horse (masculine), or one born in Sindh (feminine); in other senses it is used in the three genders. Here, the excellence (*viśeṣa*) lies in the fact that the propriety of the salt-nature—characterized by its fitness for being worn upon the neck—is supported both by the sentence-meaning, "you dwell in the moon," and by the word-meanings, "having a fondness for milk" and "naturally sweet."
In some cases, the meaning of a word and the meaning of a sentence function as causes for one another through mutual dependence. For example:

"May that golden crown which the Lord of the World wears upon His very head be victorious! How could there be a comparison between it and the Golden Mountain (Meru), even if all the gods were to cast it down? (1583)

In this context, both the sentence-meaning—that the Lord of the World bears [the mountain] upon his head precisely because the Golden Mountain lacks similarity to Śiva’s crown—and the word-meaning—that it was held down even by all the gods—combine together to function as the cause.

If it is objected: "Surely the meaning of the word *adhaḥkṛtena* (‘held beneath’) functions as a reason for the absence of similarity between the Lord’s crown and [the mountain], since that [mountain] resides on the Golden Mountain (*Meru*); however, how can the sentence-meaning—'that which the Lord of the World bears'—serve as a reason there, given that it does not reside in that [crown]? [The answer is: Understand that the sentence-meaning, being presented as residing in the crown which is included within the probandum—the absence of similarity to the crown—is a reason by virtue of being the cause for the non-existence of the similarity constituted by such a crown;
thus, both together function as the reason. This is what you must grasp.

Just as I have become weary of ignorance, so too shall there be no trace of happiness for you through me. Abandon me, who am nothing at all, who am the refuge of those with nothing, and who have resorted to that which is not even something.

"I am weary; I have become despondent. The factual state of affairs here is that [the speaker seeks] some person, the Blessed One, as a refuge for those who possess nothing, for the destitute, and for those deprived of other means. In this context, both the meaning of the first half of the verse—the exhaustion of ignorance through its own abandonment—and the meaning of the words beginning with "akiñcanajanānām" (for those who possess nothing) constitute the cause [of the speaker's despondency]. Although there is no mutual dependence between the meaning of the sentence and the meaning of the individual words, they both function as causes; this is the distinction from the previous [type of cause]. Furthermore, another distinction is that this is intermingled with *samāsokti* (synecdoche).

Just as the Blessed One, possessing great serenity, bestows abundant and vast prosperity upon Vinata, how indeed could he— who is ever endowed with the essence of eternal glory— not be a giver of much? (1585)

The Blessed One, being full of grace (*bahuprasāda*), bestows abundant prosperity upon Vinatā. If he is eternally glorious (*nityaśrī*), endowed with essence (*rasānvita*), and possessed of favor (*anugrahānvita*), how could he not be a giver of much? The sense is that, given his eternal splendor, his abundance of wealth, and his possession of grace, it is no wonder that he grants so much to Vinatā. In the alternative (punning) sense, the word *bahuprasāda* is to be split as *nityaśrīḥ*, *asānvitaḥ*. The meaning is that if [the word] is deprived of the syllables *sā*—that is, if the letter *s* is removed—it is heard simply as *bahuprada* ("giver of much").

In this instance, the specific feature is that the sentence-meaning—consisting of the granting of abundant prosperity with Vinatā as the intended object—is supported by the word-meaning "bahuprasādaḥ" (one who bestows much grace) and by the subsequent sentence-meaning "nanu katham iva" (indeed, how [could it be otherwise]?); this constitutes one distinction. Furthermore, within that subsequent sentence-meaning, the quality of being a "bestower of much" is supported by the two word-meanings "nityaśrīḥ" (possessing eternal fortune) and "rasānvitaḥ" (endowed with aesthetic flavor); this is another distinction. The particularity of the aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*), however, is indeed manifest.
In some cases, the meaning of a word serves as the reason for establishing the meaning of a sentence that is to be established.
For example:

"O Lord, he who was previously fickle toward sense objects will now, rendered helpless by your virtues, no longer remember them; submerged in bliss even before, this third instance of his transgression is to be endured. (1586)

In this context, the threefold nature of the cause must be established, as its causal factors are not explicitly stated. This establishment is composed through sentence-meanings (vākyārtha) consisting of the Lord’s being forgotten. In each of those sentence-meanings, there are three causes—such as the instability of the object—which take the form of word-meanings (padārtha). In the phrase *tava* ("of you"), the genitive case is used according to the rule *adhīgartha...* (*Pāṇini 2.3.52*).
