In the phrase *na smartā* ("I shall not remember"), there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of either *ayam* ("this") or *aham* ("I"); and in the phrase *sahyam* ("endurable"), there is an ellipsis of *tvayā* ("by you").
Just as you bound Prahlāda and, being utterly deluded, released Kaṅka, O Acyuta, who can endure the playful arrogance of independence even from You, the Lord?

O Acyuta! You are exceedingly charming, foolish, and gentle—“*mugdha*, *saumya*, *nava*, and *mūḍha*,” according to the *Ratnamālā*. You bound Bali, the descendant of Prahlāda (*prāhlādi*), meaning the offspring of the lineage of Prahlāda, with the nooses of Varuṇa (this is the ellipsis). By the term *prāhlādim*, his being an intimate friend is suggested. You released Kaṅka, that is Jaṭāyu; you liberated him, making him free from the bonds of worldly existence. By the term *kaṅkam*, his extreme indifference due to being a bird is suggested.

Furthermore, the phrase "anyone and anyone" (*kam api kam api*) also suggests the meaning that [the person] is of unknown character and entirely external. Here, the Lord’s playful exercise of His absolute sovereignty (*svātantryadaurlalitya*) requires justification, as its cause is unmanifest. That justification is provided by two sentence-meanings: [His] indifference toward the binding of Bali, who was His own intimate associate (*antaraṅga*), and His liberation of the vulture, who was indifferent [to Him]. In each of those sentence-meanings, the referent of the word *mugdha* ("innocent") serves as the reason.

O Acyuta, just as I previously perceived the Lord as being dependent upon the qualities of the individual soul, so too do I perceive Him now even though I have laid down my burden; please forgive these two offenses of mine.

"Prior to the casting off of the burden"—that is, before [liberation]—I was "bhavya," meaning virtuous (*sādhavaḥ*) in worldly existence (*bhave*), according to the rule *tatra sādhuḥ*. This means those qualities such as passion (*rajas*) and the rest that are conducive to *saṃsāra*; I was dependent upon, or subject to, them. Alternatively, there is a word-break: *bhavī aguṇāyattaḥ*. Being a transmigrating being (*bhavī*), I was subject to the "non-qualities" (*aguṇāyattaḥ*); here, "non-qualities" (*aguṇāḥ*) refers to unwholesome qualities (*apraśastaguṇāḥ*) such as envy, the negative particle (*nañ*) here denoting lack of excellence. Or else, it means being independent of those qualities such as tranquility (*śānti*) and the like which are the means for obtaining the Lord’s glance. [I have now realized] You, the Lord, as none other than my own Self.

"I was ignorant"—I did not know that I am indeed Brahman, non-different from my own true nature; or rather, as it is said, "I am the Lord, I am the enjoyer," meaning I was possessed by the delusion of an independent self. "Even though I had laid down the burden"—even though I had entrusted the burden of protecting myself and my possessions to You—I was nonetheless ignorant in that same way. "Dependent on excellent qualities"—I perceived the Self itself as the Lord. Thus, may You forgive these two offenses, this pair of transgressions of mine, committed before and after the entrusting of the burden.

The true meaning is as follows: after entrusting my burden [to you], I have come to know myself—that is, the Supreme Self—as none other than You, the Lord; for those auspicious qualities such as good character belonging to you, and those such as tranquility belonging to me, I am dependent upon them. Alternatively, I have known the Lord as the Self whose body is the inner self (*pratyagātman*); the sense is that I have known the Self as having become the body of the Lord. By this, the delusion of regarding the self as independent is set aside.

In this instance, two faults must first be justified, as they stem from the lack of clarity regarding the cause. Their justification is effected by two sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*) consisting in the self’s realization of its own divinity—a realization rooted in *śleṣa* (pun/paronomasia) that maintains uniformity between the preceding and succeeding moments of the "entrustment of the burden" (*bharārpaṇa*). In both of these sentences, the cause—whether a single word-meaning or multiple word-meanings—is dependent on a future quality (*bhavyaguṇa*), according to the method already described; the distinction from the previous case lies in the fact that it is animated by an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) based upon *śleṣa*.
In some cases, both [attributes] to be established—which are mutually non-contradictory—assume the status of being reasons in succession. For example:
"O Acyuta, who could possibly describe the majesty and the form of you, for whom they say the goddess Ramā is the most beloved wife and whose name is declared to be the reverse of hers? (1589)

The name of that Ramā is "pratilomā" (reversed), and its meaning—that which is expressed—is Māra; this is the sense. Here, in the context of the unsurpassed nature of both the Lord’s majesty and his form, two things are established as the causes: his having Ramā as his most beloved wife and his having [Māra] as his son, who is the reversed meaning of that very word.
In some cases, two mutually contradictory things successively assume the state of being causes [for a single effect]. For example:
"O Hari, upon hearing the cries of the distressed elephants seized by crocodiles, you, having reflected on their absolute devotion, simultaneously experienced both sorrow and joy. (1590)

"Hare! is an address intended to make known that [the Lord] has assumed an incarnation for the sake of liberating Gajendra. "Aikāntyam" (exclusive devotion) means the state of being one whose final resort (*anta*) is fixed solely upon the Blessed One as his refuge; it is the quality of such a person (*ekāntin*). Alternatively, it refers to the state of one who possesses that which is both "one" (*eka*) and "final" (*anta*), namely *ekānta*. He by whom that has been thoroughly investigated and properly deliberated is described as such.

In this passage, two mutually contradictory states of the Blessed One—simultaneous weariness and joy—are composed as causes, namely: first, hearing the cries of distress from the lordly elephant seized by the crocodile, and second, reflecting upon his [the Buddha's] solitary seclusion.
Sometimes there is a single reason that establishes two mutually contradictory things simultaneously. For example:
"Having at last beheld the Lord of the World, whose appearance was longed for, I experienced both a dejection far greater than any other, and an intense joy. (1591)

For me, who has long beheld Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of all worlds, whose sight was so long desired, it would have been in vain for such an extended period had the contemplation of His divine and auspicious form not occurred; thus arises *nirveda* (world-weariness). Yet, through the attainment of that very vision, there is *ānanda* (bliss). Here, the single cause for both these opposing states—*nirveda* and *ānanda*—is the same: the beholding of the Blessed One.

Regarding this, one might ask: "What is the difference between this *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication) and *parikara* (periphrasis), which consists of the arrangement of word-meanings and sentence-meanings with a specific underlying intention? Listen: in *parikara*, two meanings—implied by the force of the word-meaning or the sentence-meaning—serve as embellishments (*upaskāraka*) for the sentence. In *kāvyaliṅga*, however, the distinction is that the word-meaning and the sentence-meaning themselves assume the state of being the cause (*hetubhāva*).

For instance, in such examples as “*sudhāṃśukalitottaṃsaḥ*,” the presence of cooling nectar-rayed beams—implied by the power of the adjectives—is an embellishment (*upaskāraka*) of the expressed meaning, namely the removal of heat; however, in that case, there is no embellishment of the word-meaning (*padārtha*) or the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Therefore, since the figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) is possible there, *parikara* (the poetic elaboration) alone is appropriate. In *kāvyaliṅga*, however, the causality belongs only to the word-meaning or the sentence-meaning, and there is no dependence on an implied meaning. As in: “*sukhālokocchedini...*” [etc.].

In the example of *kāvyaliṅga* based on the meanings of words and the meaning of a sentence, such as "even at the outset he was free from pride" (*agre 'py anatimān*), they maintain that the two are distinct because they have separate domains; for in both cases, the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is supported by the meanings of words and the meaning of the sentence—respectively, the state of being destroyed by the light of happiness and the subsequent bowing down—without depending on any implied meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*). Thus has *kāvyaliṅga* been demonstrated according to the views of the ancients.

The author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, however, states: "Kāvyaliṅga is an intended meaning that is not characterized as either a means of inference (*anumitikaraṇa*) or by the relation of generality and particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*), but is intended as a support for the contextual subject matter (*prakṛtārtha*). Its status as a 'support' (*upapādakatva*) consists in its being the object of the cognition that produces the ascertainment of that [contextual subject]. The phrase 'not characterized' excludes both inference and *arthāntaranyāsa*. The phrase ending with 'as a support' excludes similes (*upamā*) and the like."

It is intended as a justification for the purpose of excluding only that cause which is explicitly designated as a cause by words such as the ablative (*pañcamī*) and so forth; however, this does not have the effect of meaning that [the cause] must be cognized in that form by the word itself. Consequently, in instances such as "O King, you are to be avoided because of your fierceness, yet you are to be served because you are a refuge of compassion," this is not a figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*).

For the theorists of poetics (alaṃkārikas) accept that *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) belongs specifically to a reason whose causal status is implicit, on account of its aesthetic beauty. This [reason] is first of all twofold, by virtue of being the meaning of either a nominal stem (*subanta*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). The first type is also twofold: its form is either qualified by the meaning of another word or it consists solely of a pure nominal stem. Even here, the first variety is further divided into two types: that which is qualified by the meaning of a sentence, either directly or indirectly, and that which is qualified solely by the meaning of a nominal stem.

He says: "Even that which constitutes the meaning of a finite verb (tiṅanta) is of two kinds—either directly or indirectly qualified by the meaning of a sentence, or qualified solely by the meaning of a nominal stem (subanta). However, a pure distinction [unqualified by anything else] is not possible for the meaning of a finite verb, because an action must necessarily be qualified by its factors of action (kāraka). According to that method, the examples are as follows:

"O Blessed One, you who bestow upon one who merely wishes to fold his hands in salutation a glory far exceeding the world; knowing this, you feel shame when praised as the foremost among the generous. (1592)

For here, in order to establish the seemingly incongruous state of the Lord Śrīnivāsa—who is described as being unique among all—as feeling shame because he is the foremost of the generous, the author, wishing to offer salutation, has presented as the cause a state of insufficiency (paryāptyabhāva) which is co-located with the granting of liberation and sovereignty; this state is characterized by the meaning of a nominal stem alone, and its referent is the meaning of that nominal stem itself.

Now, one might object: "Since the word *jānan* (knowing), formed with the present participle suffix *śatṛ* by the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*, directly expresses the cause (*hetu*), how can there be the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga*? For all theorists agree that when a cause is expressed by a word that explicitly denotes it, this [figure] does not arise. This is not so. The *śatṛ* suffix prescribed by that rule is not a denoter of the cause, such that one could raise such a doubt; rather, it is an indicator (*dyotaka*) of it. Thus says the *Śekhara* commentary on that very rule: "In this [rule], the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth are what are indicated (*dyotya*)."

"But the meaning of the suffixes *śatṛ* and so forth is indeed the agent (*kartṛ*) and so on. This should be understood to apply likewise in cases involving the suffix *śānac*. For this very reason, the author of the *Ekāvalī* has explicitly stated that in such instances, the causality of a word-meaning is not an ornament when a word ending in the third or fifth case is employed—there being merely a statement of cause; rather, it is "poetic indication" (*kāvyaliṅga*), which resides in the word-meaning, when there is a presentation of a cause by means of an adjective. Thus, he has expressly described how causality in such cases is aesthetically inferior when expressed through the third or fifth case endings.

Therefore, the statement by the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*—who provides the example of *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason): "O Mother, you whose heart is overcome with compassion, purifying this very me, you shatter the pride of all who destroy sin"—is consistent with his assertion that purification is capable of supporting the shattering of the pride of others' sins.

And his intention here is this: the figure of *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) does not apply only when the reason is expressed verbally (*śābdatā*). This is because in instances where the suffixes *śatṛ* or *śānac* are prescribed by the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*, the relation between cause and effect (*hetuhetumadbhāva*) functions as a semantic relation (*saṃsarga*), and thus the reason lacks verbal expression, just as it does in cases involving the third or fifth case endings. Although, in the word *punānaḥ*, it might be easy to justify the form using the suffix *cānaś* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) or capacity (*śakti*), since that suffix does not denote the causal relation (*ahetvarthakatvāt*).

Nevertheless, in such instances as "namanmuktaḥ saṃprītaḥ" (being bowed to, he is liberated and well-pleased), since the word *naman*—which ends in a present participle (*śatṛ*) prescribed with a causal sense—is described as the cause for the state of being liberated (*muktatva*), it must be understood that the causality of the *śatṛ* suffix is not directly expressed by the word itself. For unlike the *cānaś* suffix, it is impossible to establish an alternative derivation for this *śatṛ* suffix on the grounds of its denoting habitual action (*tācchīlya*) and so forth, as no such grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) is observed. This should likewise be understood in cases involving the *śānac* suffix prescribed by the aforementioned sūtra; the details of this are found elsewhere.

O Hari, having learned of hardness from embracing the pair of breasts of the Ocean’s Daughter, and maintaining that very hardness in Your heart, how indeed could You be soft-hearted toward the wretched? 1593.

Here, in order to establish the state of the Lord Durghaṭa’s tender heart, the meaning of a nominal stem (subanta) further specified by the meaning of another nominal stem—consisting of the act of holding his [Durghaṭa’s] heart, which is co-located with the study of hardness initiated by the pair of breasts of the Ocean’s daughter—is presented as the cause. In the words *adhīyan* and *dhārayan*, the suffix *śatṛ* is used in the sense of ease (*akṛcchra*) according to the rule *iṅdhāryośśatravṛcchiṇi*.

O Lord, just as you remain untroubled even while bearing the cosmic eggs within your belly, how could you possibly be afraid when this burden of the earth has been placed by me upon you? It is but a trifle compared to that.

Whether it be very small or even greater, here—in order to establish the excellence of the Blessed One, who has been described as being without peer, consisting in his freedom from fear while bearing the burden of protecting himself—a lack of exhaustion is presented as the cause. This lack of exhaustion is co-located with the effortless support of infinite millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), and it is formulated as a nominal meaning not further qualified by any other nominal meaning. In the word *dhārayan*, the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is used in the sense of "without difficulty," just as before.
These three examples are all similar.
Even the gods, such as the four-faced Brahmā and others, tremble at the mere remembrance of Him; yet a certain infant demon, fixing that very Brahman within his heart, put them to shame.

They tremble at the mere thought of him; they fear even to perform remembrance (*smaraṇa*). "A certain child of the Asuras" means Prahlāda. He put those [gods] such as the Four-faced One (Brahmā) to shame. The sense is that by fixing within his own heart the Brahman which is beyond the range of their meditation, he made them filled with embarrassment.

In this context, in order to establish the causality of the shame felt by the Four-faced One (Brahmā) and others toward their own actions, the poet has composed a description of their bondage having as its locus the heart and as its agent the Supreme Brahman. Since that [bondage] alone is easily accomplished and thus incapable of achieving such a specific result, it requires another distinguishing factor; therefore, the sentence-meaning consisting of the fear arising from the recollection of the Supreme Brahman by agents such as the Four-faced One is introduced as a distinguishing factor through the medium of the object, which is the Supreme Brahman itself. And that [sentence-meaning], being thus qualified—
A bond whose locus is such a heart, mounted upon the child of an asura, is a logical reason (hetu), because it is capable of producing the effect consisting in the provocation of such shame.
O Hari, of wondrous power, whose majesty is difficult to fathom even for the peaks of the Vedas, you alone must endure this child who has ventured to speak of all your infinite qualities.

In this context, "childishness" (*ḍimbhatva*)—the meaning of a single pure noun—is the reason for the offense being forgiven. Likewise, "possessing wonderful majesty" (*adbhutavibhavatva*), which consists of the meaning of a noun qualified by another noun (meaning inconceivable sovereignty), [is the reason] for its being difficult to fathom even for the crest-jewels of the Vedas. Thus, in the illustration of a pure nominal meaning, there is also an illustration of a qualified nominal meaning: namely, the description of such qualities and actions of the Lord regarding the offense, and the manifestation of unrestrained boldness in that very description.
O Mother, although he was dear to you, I led him away from his refuge to a state of indifference; now that you abandon him, why should I go to him alone for protection, saying, "Protect him"? (1597)

O Mother! Because of the shelter you provided and the pride of being supported by you, even your beloved Lord was led to indifference—that is, to neglect. The sense is that He neglected even Him who is the refuge of all. Now, at this moment when you yourself are indifferent—this is the sense regarding "me"—if you abandon me; the word "now" connects with both sides according to the *madhyamaṇinyāya* (the maxim of the central gem). Why then should I now go for refuge to that very one, your beloved, whom I previously neglected out of pride? This is a common worldly expression.

The sense is: "Having committed an offense before Him, what favor could I have possibly performed? Let me therefore seek refuge [in Him]. Here, by the words beginning with *imam* ("this"), the meaning of the finite verb (*tiṅanta*)—which consists in bringing about the Lord’s indifference toward the self as the agent—is supported by the meaning of the nominal stem (*subanta*), namely the speaker’s lack of any other resort, which is manifested by the phrase *imam* and so forth, and which has as its cause the turning away from all other refuges. "Alas, O Daughter of the Milk-Ocean, you are utterly naive! To those who do harm to the worlds—even to those who harm your own beloved—you bestow manifold prosperity. (1598)

In this context, regarding the establishment of the Blessed Mother, the progenitor of the world, as being characterized by innocence (*maugdhyopapādane*), the cause is the act of giving (*vitaraṇa*)—which is the meaning of the finite verb (*tiṅanta*)—as qualified by the meaning of the nominal stem (*subanta*), or rather, that very act of giving which consists in the distribution of manifold riches. This is because [the Mother] lacks the capacity for such giving. Furthermore, the act of giving is qualified by the meaning of the preceding sentence, namely, her nature as one who harms the world and so forth. And its status as a qualifier is to be understood indirectly through its status as a qualifier of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

It should be understood that all of this is merely a restatement, by way of a different method, of the divisions into *padārtha* (meaning of words) and *vākyārtha* (meaning of sentences) conceived by ancient rhetoricians; it is intended solely to demonstrate the variety of analytical insights (*vyutpatti*).

Regarding this, the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara* states: "The *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication) is not a true *alaṃkāra* (ornament), because it lacks that specific charm (*vicchitti*) consisting of a particular aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) produced by the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*), since the relation of cause and effect is established in the world [and thus requires no poetic artifice]. As for the charm arising from the blending of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and other figures, that charm belongs to the *śleṣa* itself; it does not constitute an ornament for the *kāvyaliṅga*, because there is no separate charm produced by the latter."

Regarding this, they say: "This is not tenable; for even though it pertains to the worldly realm, it produces aesthetic wonder by being accessible only through the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*), and because the causal relationship expressed in the verse—'O Mother, you whose heart is overcome with compassion, purifying me here, you shatter the pride of all those who destroy sin'—is not established as a fact in the world."

For indeed, in such passages as "In that great delusion called liberation, which cuts off the light of happiness," the fact that the cutting off of the light of happiness and so forth is the cause for [being] identical with great delusion is not established anywhere. Furthermore, even in this way, figures such as simile (*upamā*) would not constitute poetic ornaments, because similarity, being factual, lacks the quality of being fashioned by the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*).

Nor should it be argued that even there, in the aspect of the non-difference of the common attribute (sādhāraṇadharma) which serves as the basis for the simile, that [attribute] is merely imagined; for attributes such as "loveliness" (ramaṇīyatva), which serve as the grounds for comparison, are well-known in the world. Furthermore, there is no obstacle to a worldly aesthetic charm (camatkāra) being considered an ornament (alaṃkāra). Otherwise, it would follow that all ornaments would be abolished.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, the Chapter on Poetic Indication (Kāvyaliṅga), in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Corroboration by a General Truth (Arthāntaranyāsa):
"The establishment of a particular by means of a general, or this [general] by means of that [particular], whether through similarity or otherwise, they call Arthāntaranyāsa."

*Arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different matter) is the support of a particular by means of a general, or of a general by means of a particular. This term is etymologically significant, as it is the "placing" (*nyāsa*) of another matter (*arthāntara*), whether particular or general, for the purpose of corroboration. Corroboration (*samarthana*) is the removal of doubt—namely, the hesitation as to whether "this might be so" or "this might not be so"—by means of a definitive determination that "this is exactly thus," which is to say, certainty. And that [certainty] is of two kinds, based on similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), and each of these is further twofold.

In this regard, it is generally observed that the two primary elements—the general and the particular—function as the objects to be established (samarthyatva), while the two secondary elements—the particular and the general—function as the means of establishment (samarthakatva).

Just as the moon, though it is the brother-in-law of Hari, though childish, dull-witted, and alas, crooked, is borne upon the head by Śiva—indeed, association with the great is the cause of being honored. (1519)
Here, the specific quality stated in the first three quarters is supported by the general quality stated in the fourth quarter through a commonality that is not the subject at hand.
Or rather, how could the deer have been marked with a tilaka of musk when camphor is the [proper] tilaka? Or else, the Lord is independent; whatever He wishes, He does—who can restrain Him? (1600)

"Let the camphor (ghanasāra) be the tilaka"—that is, let it become so—because the Lord Śrīnivāsa, who is present here, is famously known as one whose forehead is marked with a tilaka of that very camphor and musk. Here, the making of a tilaka from camphor, which is worthy of honor by its very name, is entirely appropriate; whereas the making of a tilaka from musk, which is loathsome by its very name, is inappropriate. Having raised this objection, it is resolved in a general sense by the words "or rather" (athavā) and so forth. Thus, the distinction from the previous [example] is its conflation with the figure of speech *ākṣepa* (objection/perspicuity).

Just as the host of enemies, scorched by the blazing flames of his unrestrained prowess and fallen from the surface of the earth, became bereft of glory; for how indeed could there be the arrival of *Ramā* (fortune) for one who has fallen? 1601.

The fires were indeed flames possessing unrestrained power and splendor; by them, the host of enemies—being reduced to the frying pan (bhrāṣṭra), that is, the surface of the earth (Amara states: "the word *ambarīṣa* is neuter, while *bhrāṣṭra* is masculine")—became destitute of fortune (*niśśrīka*), that is, devoid of prosperity. Regarding the word *bhraṣṭa*: it means "subjected to roasting" (*bharjana*), derived from the root *bhrasj* ("to cook") with the suffix *kta* in the passive sense. Alternatively, it may mean "one who has fallen" (*bhraṃśaṃ prāpta*), derived from the root *bhraṃś* ("to fall") with the suffix *kta* in the active sense. In this latter case, the change to *ṣ* is applied by the rule *vraśca*, followed by the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*.

The arrival of *ram* means the attainment of *lakṣmī*. Alternatively, how could there be an augment (*āgama*) consisting of the syllable *ram*? Since the augment *ram* is optional according to the rule *bhrasjoropadhayoramanyatarasyām*, its absence occurs in the form *bhraṣṭasya*; otherwise, the form would be *bharṣṭasya*. This is the intended meaning. The sense of the sūtra is: "In place of the *repha* (the letter *r*) and the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of the root *bhrasj*, the augment *ram* may optionally occur before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; because it is marked with the mute letter *m*, it is placed after the final vowel, and by the mention of the genitive case (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), there is the removal of both the *repha* and the penultimate vowel."

Here too, there is the corroboration of the particularity established by the first three quarters by means of the generality established by the final quarter. The particularity consists in such features as being enlivened by metaphor (*rūpaka*) and paronomasia (*śleṣa*).
O Mother, by obtaining the service of your calves, Kālī has indeed become Kāhalī; for service to the lords who bestow prosperity generally leads even one of dull nature to excellence. (1602)

The *kāhalī* (trumpet) has become *kālī* (Gaurī) due to the attainment of your shanks—such is the sense of this fortune. "Kālī is the sovereign lady of Himavat," according to Amara. "Hā" expresses astonishment. In the alternative reading, the word-division is *kāhalī iti śabdavyaktiḥ, ahā jātā*. Being *ahā* (devoid of the letter *ha*), she has become *kālī*; thus, the word *kālī* has been produced. This is an instance of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration of a particular by a general), aided by a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) based on the identity between the word and its meaning.

Or rather: If a cluster of flowers were to attain the state of being upon her face in order to rival the pair of her jar-like breasts, it would become insignificant here; for the hard indeed brings about the humiliation of the soft. (1603)

If a cluster (guccha)—meaning a bunch of blossoms—were to assume a position facing her (mukhagatatām), for the sake of competing with the pair of her glorious jar-like breasts, then it would be utterly insignificant (tuccha), that is, empty of valor; as Amara states: "śūnya, vaśika, tuccha, and riktaka" all mean empty. In the alternative sense, if the word *guccha* were to assume the state of the letter *ta* (tatām) upon the *ga* residing at its beginning (mukhe), it would become *tuccha*.

In the word *gatā*, the vowel *a* in both syllables is for the sake of easy pronunciation. The meaning is that by removing the letter *ga* and substituting the letter *ta* in its place, the form *tucchā* is produced.
O Mother, if your face were to become turbid due to envy or the like, it would surely turn into a cow; for those who are envious, there must be a loss of their own true nature. (1604)

O Mother! When the moon (*glauḥ*)—out of envy toward your face—reaches an extreme turbidity or cloudiness (*vilatvam*), would it not [become] a beast (*nu*—used here as a particle of deliberation)? In the alternative sense: when the word *glauḥ* has lost its initial *ga-* sound (the suffix *tasi* being used here according to the rule for words beginning with *ādi*), and subsequently experiences or attains *vilatvam*—that is, the state of losing its *la*-sound—then it becomes simply *gauḥ* (a cow). The underlying meaning is that if one’s heart is defiled by envy toward a face possessing such preeminent beauty, that person is indeed nothing but a beast.

The sense is that in the [other] case, if the word *glau* were deprived of its *l*, it would indeed result in *gau*. The sense is that for the envious—those who cannot endure the excellence of others—there would be a loss of their own nature, a mere destruction of their own dignity. In the other case, the sense is that if the word *glau* were to become *gau*, there would be a transformation of its very form.
Or as in this example:
"O Goddess, even an elephant striving to attain the fortune of your gait is defeated; indeed, only those who are dull-witted remain lofty, even when mounted upon a camel. (1605)

Even while striving to attain a destiny equal to yours, a fortune of reaching you, and a status equal to your movement, the elephant has been defeated. Why? To this he says: "The dull-witted" (*mandāḥ*). This means that even those who are lofty, great, and elevated—namely, elephants mounted by the *pecaka* (the owl-like creature at the base of the tail)—are indeed dull-witted and devoid of fortune. As Amarasimha states: "The term *pecaka* refers to the owl, and also to the base of the elephant's tail. Thus, they are merely dull-witted.

Likewise, in this context, the term *manda* carries the sense of "slow" (or dull), as Medinī states: "The word *manda* is used in three genders for 'dull,' 'sharp,' 'foolish,' 'unrestrained,' 'unfortunate,' 'sickly,' and 'small'; in the masculine, it refers to a particular breed of elephant and to Saturn. The implication is that even for those mounted on an owl who strive for the attainment of their desired goals, how could there be the acquisition of great fortune? The specific distinction in these three examples—beginning with "the breasts of Śrī"—is their being a mixture of the figure of speech *viṣama* (incongruity) supported by *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Just as the lotus, O Mother, though cast away by Your foot, rejoices by being Your support; for even a city that was once despised by You becomes auspicious when it takes refuge in You.

O Mother Rāmā! Though the *puṣkara*—the lotus—was driven out from its place by your foot (*pada*) due to your victory over it, and though it was displaced, it remained your city (*pura*), that is, your home, because it was your support, your sole refuge, and your abode (Amara states: "house, city, and town" are synonyms for *pura*). In the alternative sense, the word *puṣkara* was "driven out" (*niṣkāsita*)—meaning it was seated (*āsita*, from the root *ās*) in such a way that the cluster of letters *ṣka* had departed from it—and thus it became *pura*. This is the meaning.
The rest is clear. Here too, there is the support of a particular by means of its similarity to a general.
O Blessed One, if even a conscious being who has been rejected remains full of great regard for you, he will become all the more renowned; for devotion to you indeed bears the fruit of uniqueness.

"O Blessed One!"—the word "by you" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The sense is that even if some conscious being, such as Prahlāda or Bali, has been rejected or overcome by you, [he remains] in you... atyā... (in you).

If one possesses unwavering devotion, then, by virtue of being "utterly incomparable" (*asadr̥śatayā*), he shall become renowned for taking refuge in You; for this results in "unrivaledness" through fame and other qualities—meaning a state of having no equal—or, in another sense, the absence of a second syllable. Alternatively, there is another meaning: if the word *pratyākhyāta* (rejected) does not possess respect for the syllable *tyā*—that is, if it is separated from that [syllable]—then it becomes the word *prakhyāta* (renowned).
Or rather, O Lord, it is like this:
when the great rays of the sun, having encountered your splendor out of enmity, attained the state of stones despite their great speed; for latent impressions are indeed difficult to cast off.

The *mahāraśmayaḥ* (great rays), even upon reaching the state of *aśman*—that is, the condition of being stones—remained indeed *mahārayaḥ* (possessing great speed) and *mahāvidviṣaḥ* (possessing great enmity). In the alternative sense, the word *mahāraśmayaḥ* is one in which the collection of letters *śma* is absent; having thus become *aśmaḥ*, it reached that state. The analysis is: *abhavat mahārayaḥ*. The meaning is that it became established as *mahārayaḥ*. The remainder is clear.

Just as the ocean, despite the waves breaking one after another upon it even when the rivers have approached, does not manifest any internal change nor undergo any transformation through the reversal of its nature; so too [is the Sage]. (1609)

The term "he" (sa) is understood as "Bhagavān," because He alone is the subject under discussion. "Nadīnaḥ" means the Lord of Rivers (*saritpati*). The word "adīnaḥ" (not dejected) should also be supplied [as a predicate]. Due to Your profundity—which serves as the cause—though there is a breaking [of waves] at every step, resulting in self-humiliation; in the alternative sense, although there is breaking [into fragments] higher and higher, in the uppermost parts themselves, [the waves] arise. The singular number is used with reference to the genus (*jāti*). Even when [this state] has arrived...

The meaning is "even when [the situation] had arrived. *Antaḥ* means "in the mind"; in the alternative sense, it means "in the interior region. He did not undergo transformation (*na vyakriyata*), that is to say, he did not manifest weakness of heart. The suffix *yak* is used here in the sense of the reflexive-passive (*karmakartari*). Alternatively, *na vyakriyata* means "he did not abandon his humility" (*nadīnatām nātyākṣīt*). In the alternative sense, it means "he was not agitated."

One whose nature is so profound does not undergo transformation—that is, a change into a state of shallowness which is the opposite of his natural profundity—by way of its reversal. The sense is that even when many causes for the agitation of the heart occur, one of profound nature does not incur a transformation such as shallowness, which is contrary to his own inherent character.

In this context, the word *nadīnaḥ* (the lord of rivers) remains unchanged within its internal form—the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—even though the case endings (*svādivibhakti*), such as the nominative and others, are presented one after another in succession, each distinct from the next. As the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *bhaṅga* [is used] in the sense of defeat, division, disease, and wave. The meaning is that although there exists a mutual difference among the case endings, the base (*prakṛti*) persists in its very state of being unmodified.

It is not only that the word remains unaltered when it is in its original form as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), but rather that it remains unaltered even when that form is reversed; thus he says, "of such a kind" (*īdṛk*). The sense is that it is precisely the word *nadīna*. Even when recited with the order of the syllables of the nominal stem reversed from its original state, it does not undergo modification—that is, it does not possess a different sequence of phonemes compared to the preceding form. Rather, the sense is that it remains exactly as before, namely *nadīna*.

Here, the support of the specific quality (viśeṣa) established by the passage beginning with "even when [the cause] has arrived" and ending with "not in another way" by means of the general quality (sāmānya) expressed as "such as this" and so forth—which is not the subject at hand—is an instance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā*. As for the particular aesthetic charm arising from its commingling with *samāsokti*, it is indeed easy to perceive.
Just as a full-blown white lotus with intense fragrance, once surpassed by your eyes, subsequently attained the beauty of your face; for such indeed is the nature of a son.

O Blessed One! [It is] that white lotus, the *puṇḍarīka*, which is fully blossomed (*vikaca*) and wide-open (*vyākoca*), and whose fragrance is intense—that is what is meant by the term. The sense is that it is proud of its extreme beauty; however, the reality is that it possesses an exceeding sweetness of scent. Now, the construction may be understood as "conquered by your eyes" (*tvannayanajitaṃ*), and for that very reason "diminished" (*apacitaṃ*), meaning it has undergone decay (*apacayaṃ prāptaṃ*); or alternatively, one may join the words as "then, conquered by your eyes, it became diminished."

In one sense, the word *vikacasitāmbujam* was rendered *apacitam*, meaning it was made devoid of the letter *ca*; thus, the sense is that it became *vikasitāmbujam* (a blooming lotus). It obtained your *sarvadāsyalakṣmīm*—the glory of service in every way—or, in the other sense, the beauty of the face (*āsyalakṣmīm*) at all times (*sarvadā*). For indeed, the state (*gati*) or condition of the *sūna*—meaning one who is thoroughly deficient (*suṣṭhu ūna*), entirely lacking in the heroism, fortitude, and so forth necessary for the purification of enmity—is such as this. This is the truth regarding the *prasūna* (flower). Such is its extent.

The sense is that she approaches her own conqueror because she is unable to retaliate; this too is specifically an instance of the general figure of speech known as *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth).
O Mother of All, considering her own delicacy to have been surpassed by yours, she became as humble as butter placed upon the mind; for such indeed is the extent of the path for the delicate.

*Navanītam* means "not remaining" (*na asthitimat*). Regarding *anasi*, which means "on a cart" (*śakaṭe*), the elision of the visarga occurs according to the rule *'śarpare khari vā visargalopaḥ'*. It should be noted that in the word *sthitī* (in the context of *sthitimat*), there is only one *s*-sound, as the non-difference of the word-form is required for the other meaning. The sense is that he has mounted a cart for the purpose of setting out for another country. *Vanītam* means "gone to the forest" (*vanīṃ gatam*); alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "by whom the forest (*vanī*) has been reached" (*itā prāptā*). The meaning is that he has entered the great forest (*araṇyānī*).

In this context, the word *navanīta* (butter) is "possessing the state of *na*" (*nasthitimat*), meaning it possesses the presence of the letter *na*. That which does not possess this is "not possessing the state of *na*" (*anasthitimat*), meaning the *na* has been removed; thus, the sense is that the butter (*vanīta*) [remains] once the *na* has been separated. For indeed, the movement of that which is soft (*mṛdu*) and gentle (*atīkṣṇa*) is of such a nature. Everything else is as before.
O Śauri, just as coral, having undergone disintegration due to its hatred for the luster of Your feet, has become nothing but a common tree— such indeed is the consequence of hatred toward You.

*Vidrumaḥ* means coral (*pravāla*); it is also the word *vidruma*. *Vibhaṅgam* means a complete defeat or humiliation on all sides—so much so that, in another sense, having encountered the destruction of the syllable *vi*, it became merely a tree (*druma*)—in the other sense, the word *druma* itself. Such indeed is the ripening of hatred toward you; for the attainment of birth as a stationary being (a plant) is precisely what results from such enmity.

Just as the young moon, O Goddess beloved of Hari, when struck by the plowshare, becomes pale with its digits fading away; and just as the soft earth, competing with the plowman, goes only to destruction—so too does he [the enemy] perish. 1613.

The young moon, even as it waxes, has its essence (ojas) leaking away in abundance; its brilliance diminishes excessively during the *bahula*—that is, the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*)—such is the actual state of affairs. A *hālika* is one whose weapon is a plow (*hala*); he is a rival who is mild both in body and in valor, that is, gentle. Alternatively, there is a word-break as *hā alika-saṃgharṣī*: "Alas! He is a rival for the forehead (*alika*)," meaning he vies with the forehead. The rest is clear.

Just as one who has taken refuge in the Supreme Person, though afflicted by the arrows of others' words, does not become like before due to his firm conviction—that such a person would not take refuge in supreme wrath—nor indeed would he fall away. (1614)

That person who has taken refuge in the Supreme Person, even if afflicted or wounded by the words and arrows—words that are like arrows—in the case of enemies, shall not, because of his firm resolve and the firmness of his devotion born from the Lord’s grace which strengthens the body, become one who relies on others as he did before; that is, as he was previously when taking refuge in the Lord. He shall not be "paruṣāśritaḥ" (relying on others), for *paruṣa* means a wound (*vraṇa*), according to Amara: "A wound is *vraṇa*, *marma*, or *aruṣ* (neuter)."

The sense is that, just as in the case of Prahlāda and others, by virtue of the Lord’s grace, arrows discharged by enemies are not capable of inflicting even the slightest pain upon him. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), he would not be "resorted to by supreme wrath" (paramayā ruṣā śritaḥ); for, according to the teaching of such texts as "Neither anger nor envy," since anger does not arise in him even when addressed with words that touch his most vulnerable points, the sense is that one who is thus "resorted to by the Great One" (mahadāśritaḥ) shall not perish—that is, he shall not come to ruin.

In one sense, the word *paramapuruṣāśrita* contains no *pu*—that is, the letter *p* (or the syllable *pu*) does not exist [in it]. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the negative particle *na*: "that which lacks the letter *p*" (*napu*). Thus, it becomes *paramaruṣāśrita*, entirely devoid of the letter *p*. Even though such a word has reached a state of being bereft of the letter *p*, the word *paramapuruṣa* would certainly not "perish"—that is, it would not remain meaningless—but rather, the sense is that it would remain awake through its very meaningfulness. As in the following example:

The moon, though it is a source of joy, has reached a certain state of decline as it steals away the wealth of your face; for that which is ill-situated within one's own heart remains ill-situated even in another state of being.

O Blessed One! The moon (*indu*) is understood to be a "stealer of the wealth of your face" (*tvad-mukha-vasu-hārī*), meaning it has the habit of robbing the splendor of your countenance, and it is understood to have the habit of stealing your wealth (*tvat-prabhṛti-dhana-haraṇa-śīlaḥ*). The suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlye*). For this very reason, having reached a certain decline (*kṣayam*)—in the form of the waning of all its digits, like the royal consumption disease (*rājayakṣmā*)—it becomes a "kandu," even though it is already a *kandu*. A *kandu* is a specific object made of iron, flat and circular in shape, serving as a tool for preparing cakes such as *holaka*; it is a neuter noun. (As it is said: "In the neuter, *ambarīṣaṃ*... [referring to a frying pan].

According to Amara, "bhrāṣṭra" is masculine, while "kandu" or "svedanī" are feminine; thus, the meaning of the lexicon is that the word *kandu* is either masculine (*nā*) or neuter (*vā*). The underlying intention is: "even though he partakes in birth from a frying pan (*svedanī*), he remains devoid of luster just like it. In the alternative interpretation, the division is *hārī ikṣayam*. The word *indu* (the moon) undergoes the loss of the letter *i* (*ikṣayam*), and not only that—it undergoes a further change. The particle *api* signifies a conjunction. It means that in place of the letter *i*, the letter *ka* is substituted, resulting in the formation of the word *kandu*.

In this way, even though he has entered the state of being a *kandu* (a tuber), the phrase "he has reached some kind of decay" (*kam api kṣayam yātaḥ*) should be applied by repetition [to both states]. The sense is that, just as in the state of being the moon (*indutva*), he had already contracted consumption (*rājayakṣmāṇam*) even in the state of being a *kandu*, yet he did not abandon it. In reality, however, the meaning is "some kind of decay" (*kṣayam*) refers to the house or the kitchen; for that is the proper place for a *kandu* to reside. As the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *kṣaya* is used in the sense of a disease, a dwelling, the end of an aeon (*kalpānta*), and destruction."

Alternatively, the meaning is that he has undergone depletion due to the excessive scrubbing with sand and other materials performed for the purpose of removing the soot of smoke clinging to him during his stay on the hearth. To the question, "How does his state of decay persist even in another birth? he says: "He who... He who is "ill-situated" (dusthitimān) in his own heart (*svānte*)—the mind (*manas*), as Amara states: "Svānta, hṛt, and mānasa [mean mind]"—is one who constantly possesses evil intentions such as the theft of others' property; the suffix *matup* here denotes a constant connection (*nityayoga*). Furthermore, he becomes afflicted by a corresponding decay and other sufferings.

Even in another state of being—where *bhāva* means existence, essence, intention, action, soul, or birth (according to Amara)—he remains in a state of ill-fortune. The sense is that for those of sinful character who have not performed atonement, the experience of the fruits of their actions in a future birth cannot easily be removed. However, the actual fact is this: the word *indu* (moon), which was situated poorly in its own final part (*svānte*), having acquired a *ka* in place of the elided *i*, nevertheless possesses the eternal presence of the letter *du*. This is the intended meaning.

The word *indu*, even when it undergoes a change of state and attains a different form such as *kandu*, remains in a state of instability; because the harsh-sounding syllable (*du*) was not removed even previously, it remains characterized by that very [syllable]. The sense is that this is because the cluster of syllables ending in *dur* is identical in both the words *indu* and *kandu*. This is an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) in the form of supporting a particular instance by a general one, which is led forward by an identification based on the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) resulting from the manifestation of the identity between word and meaning.
Supporting a general statement by means of a specific instance through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is as follows:
"Venkaṭanātha creates and destroys the world by mere volition alone; he who is incapable in his undertakings requires the assistance of another. (1616)

Here, the specific quality mentioned in the first half-verse, which is the subject at hand, is supported by the general quality mentioned in the second half-verse, which is not the subject at hand, through a contrast of dissimilarity (vaidharmya).
Or as it is said:
"O Mother, you fondle with both hands the lotus that rivals your own hands, feet, and eyes; alas, one of gentle nature does not overcome even an enemy. (1617)
Here, the particularity established by the first three quarters is supported by the generality expressed in the fourth quarter through contrast (*vaidharmya*).

Just as your compassion is equal toward the Lord of the World (Lokeśa), the Lord of Heaven (Nākeśa), the crow (Kāka), and even the monkey (Kīśa), so it is; for one who is truly great and noble does not admit the wretchedness of discriminating between high and low. 1618.

Here too, the specific point stated in the first half of the verse, which is the subject at hand, is supported by the general point stated in the second half, which is not the subject at hand, through the method of dissimilarity (vaidharmya).

Just as gold, having been heated and melted in the midst of fire, becomes radiant in another state, so too, O Acyuta, has your armor arisen for the sake of auspiciousness; for what is unattainable by its own nature?

O Acyuta! Your armor (*varma*), made of gold, having been heated—having undergone penance—in the midst of fire, in the midst of the five fires (*pañcāgni*), and within the fire itself; and thus having become heated, it was therefore quickly (*drutam*) ignited and made radiant (in one sense); and in the other sense, "quickly" means it attained a state of liquefaction, i.e., it melted. It was made beautiful by being refined through *puṭapāka* (smelting in a crucible). In another existence (*bhavāntare*), in another birth, and in another form, this became your armor (*kavaca*).

In one alternative, the word *bharmam*—through the intervention (*antara*) of the letter *va*, that is, through the disappearance (*antardhāna*) of the letter *bha* (the "intervening" [element] being the letter *bha*)—becomes *varmam*. This means that when the letter *va* replaces the letter *bha* (that is, when *va* is pronounced in place of *bha*), the word *bharmam* is transformed into *varmam*. As Amarasimha states: "The word *antara* denotes opportunity, limit, covering, disappearance, difference, and purpose. Thus, the meaning is that the word *bharmam* results in the form *varmam*.

The sense is this: for one who is inherently auspicious (*kalyāṇa*), who performs meritorious deeds (*maṅgalakṛt*), and who is like gold (*suvarṇa*), what is unattainable? Everything is indeed attainable, according to the verse: "O dear one, no one who performs auspicious deeds ever goes to a miserable state. (The *Ratnamālā* states: "Kalyāṇa" means auspiciousness, merit, and gold). Here too, the justification is exactly as before; the distinction lies in its being intermingled with *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and other figures.

Or, for example: "Even a bee, having become attached to Your lotus-feet, attains immortality (*amara*) by becoming free from delusion (*abhrama*). What indeed is unobtainable for one who is devoted to the lotus-feet of You?"
O jewel of the Veṅkaṭa mountain! || 1620 ||

Even a *bhramara*—though it be an animal of the lower realms (*tiryagjantu*) and even though it be lustful (for "bhramara" means both "lustful man" and "bee," according to the *Medinīkośa*)—having become attached to Your lotus-feet, attains *abhramaṃ*, meaning wandering elsewhere or freedom from delusion (*abhrānti*), and thus becomes an *amara*, a god. The word "khalu" is used here for emphasis. In the alternative [grammatical] interpretation, the word *bhramara* is analyzed as *abhraṃ aṃ* in the phrase *abhramaṃ*.

That which has no *bhr* sound—that is, whose *bhr* phoneme has been dropped—is "deprived of *bhr*" (*bhraṃśitabhra*). When it reaches the vowel *a*—meaning it attains the letter *a* in place of the *bhr* sound—it becomes "immortal" (*amara*). In this manner, the word *bhramara* became the word *amara*. Here too, everything should be understood as previously explained.

Just as even a common man who has conceived a longing for Your feet is rendered sinless by You, O Acyuta, and attains immortality—would one who has taken refuge in You not obtain his desired goal? 1621.
"O Acyuta!"—this address primarily signifies the power to remove the specific sins intended to be removed. As it is said:
"Even one who is deeply addicted to great sin, by meditating for a single moment on Acyuta, becomes once more an ascetic, the purifier of those who purify the assembly."

Thus: even a lowly, base person who has conceived devotion at Your feet is rendered sinless by You; having been cleansed of all prior and subsequent sins, he attains immortality—that is, divinity or liberation—in the manner described by the words, "Wherein dwell the ancient Sādhyas, the gods. Alternatively, in this [linguistic] sense: the word *pāmara* (base person) is [first] *pāpaḥ* ("sinful"), derived from the root *pā* (to obtain) with the suffix *aṇ*. By You, it is made *apāpaḥ* ("sinless"), meaning it is deprived of the letter *pa*.
Thus, it attains *amaratvam*—that is, the state of being the word *amara* ("immortal"). This is the meaning.

O Mother, that which has attained victory from beginning to end and remains undefeated even in the middle by even a fraction—victorious is the one who reclines upon the waters; when could there ever be defeat for those who have taken refuge in you? 1622.

The lotus (*kamala*) rests in the water (*jaleśaya*), and the word *jaleśayam* likewise; that which has attained victory—that is, excellence—at its beginning and end, meaning at its initial and final parts, is so described. Alternatively, it is that by which the letters *ja* and *ya* have been attained in the [initial and final] victories. Furthermore, even in the middle—that is, during the intermediate portion—it is not destroyed, nor has it suffered any lapse, even in the slightest degree (*leśataḥ*), meaning even for a mere moment (*lavamātra*). In the other sense (the pun), it means not destroyed by the two syllables *le* and *śa*; the meaning is that the syllables *le* and *śa* have not been corrupted.
"Jayati" means he attains preeminence over all. In the case of the word [referring to] Śiva, the meaning is that the word "jaleśaya" (the one who lies in the water) itself thus triumphs.

Or as it was with Nahuṣa, when he became Indra: O Mother, his own heart laughed out of arrogance; yet when your sidelong glance turned away, he found himself in the very nature of a beast—what indeed might not happen? 1623.

O Mother! That famous Nahuṣa, having become Vāsava—that is, having become Indra—out of *avalepa*, the intoxication of sovereignty over the three worlds, was laughed at within his own heart (*svānta*) alone; "heart, breast, mind, and thought" are synonyms according to Amara. This is an expression of the manifestation of pride, as he laughed thinking, "Who else is my equal? The suffix *kta* is used here in the active sense (*kartari*). He attained the state of a *vāhasa*, that is, the condition of a python; "ajagara, śayu, and vāhasa" are all synonyms according to Amara. He found [this fate].

In this context, the word *vāsava* [is analyzed as follows]: *valepa* means connection with the letter *va*; *avalepa* is the absence of that connection. Thus, "having attained the absence of connection with the letter *va*"—the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used here in the sense of elision (*lyablope*). By the elision of the letter *va*, the form *vāsa* is produced; it was "laughed at" (*hasita*) right within itself—that is, in its own middle portion (*svānte*)—being "bound" (*sita*) by the letter *ha*. The meaning is that it became composed of the letter *ha* in the middle.
It "attained the state of being *vāhasa*" (i.e., the word *vāhasa*), because such a formation results from placing the letter *ha* between the two syllables *vā* and *sa*. The rest is clear.
O Mother, if even a sprout were to strive for equality with the luster of your feet, would your face not show such a broken state by manifesting a pout? (1624)

*Kisalaya* (a sprout) [is so called] because of the bending of the face—that is to say, because of humiliation. *Salayam* means "possessing *laya*" (dissolution or concealment); the sense is that it remains in a state of being invisible to anyone. In the alternative sense, due to the loss of the initial syllable (*mukhavarṇa*), it would be *salayam*; the meaning is that the word-form *kisalaya*, upon the dropping of its first syllable, results in the form *salayam*.

Does anyone who has been thus defeated show a broken face?—the word "of people" is to be supplied as the object. It is a common worldly saying that a proud man, having suffered a loss of face, does not show his face to anyone at all. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), the agent is the word *kisalaya* (sprout), which results from [the combination] *īdṛk* + *salayam*; it shows—that is, indicates by its displacement—the letter *ki*, meaning the syllable situated at the beginning of the word *mukha*.

If the phrase "with its sprouts" were heard as "with its sound," it would suggest that the color has faded from his face; this is the intended meaning. The rest is clear. Here, the general (sāmānya), though not the subject at hand, serves as the supporting argument.

O Mother, how could the sandy bank—which has attained a state of being neuter, having been surpassed by Your hips, and which is shaken by Your feet—ever dare to possess the excellence of a noble dwelling? 1625.

"O Mother! The sandbank (pulina) has attained a state devoid of the male (apuṃbhava), having reached a lack of masculinity by its very nature; for the grammatical rule teaches that 'that which rises from water is called a pulina,' and thus it is neuter—this is the sense. In the alternative [interpretation], the word *lina* remains, meaning it has reached a state (*bhāva*) or condition devoid of the letter *pu*. Therefore, the sense is that they possess masculinity from Your hips (*nitamba*); for the rule prescribes the masculine gender for that word, as in 'the hindquarters are the *nitamba*.'"

Then, having somehow surpassed the house situated directly in front of her hips—that is, being such as it was—or in the alternative sense, being a lotus (*nalina*) whose initial portion (*agra-bhava*) contains the letter *na* (thus becoming *nalinam*), even then it did not abandon its neuter gender; the sense is that it gained masculinity through the foot. It was "shaken off" (*dhuta*), meaning cast aside. The final meaning is that it was eclipsed by the hip in its state as a sandbank (*pulina*) and by the foot in its state as a lotus (*nalina*).
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "What? A *klība* is a neuter. The sense is: "What audacity could it have? How could it attain boldness like a man?"

O Mādhava, although the dwelling of the two *yava* plants was in the same lineage and clan (*gotra-pravara*), there was nevertheless a marriage between them; for where indeed do those who act according to their own will remain subject to injunctions and prohibitions? (1626)

O Mādhava! This address as the Lord of Lakṣmī is intended to support the intended meaning. Regarding the term *lakṣmīśca tvaṃ ca yuvām* (Lakṣmī and you two), there is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) of the masculine word *yuṣmad* according to the rule: "The words beginning with *tyad* [and others] are always [retained] when combined with all [other words]; furthermore, when there is a remainder from among those beginning with *tyad*, the gender and number follow the masculine or neuter. Thus, there is a single-remainder formation of the masculine *yuṣmad*.

"In one"—that is, in a single lineage and ancestral rite (*gotrapravara*), where *gotra* and *pravara* are taken together; the meaning is that it refers to one and the same lineage and ancestral rite well-known in the Smṛtis. Alternatively, "in the lineage and ancestral rite" means on Śeṣādri, the best of mountains. "Becoming" (*bhavana*) means birth or a home. Nevertheless, there is a "marriage-union" (*vivāhayoga*) between you two, a relationship in the form of a wedding. By the phrase "nevertheless," [the author alludes to the following verse]: "I shall declare the expiation for that fool who marries a girl of the same ancestral rite (*pravarā*) or even of the same lineage (*gotra*)."

The contradiction with the statements of Dharmaśāstra authorities such as Śātātapa and Viṣṇu—namely, “one should marry a woman who is not of the same lineage (asagotrā) and not of the same ancestral rite (asamānapravarā)” and so forth—is indicated. The sense is that in one sense, *vi* means a bird (*pakṣin*), namely Garuḍa; he alone is the *vāha*, meaning his vehicle. This is because Lakṣmī is also said to have him as her vehicle in such passages as: “The policy of Ajitākarṣaṇī is Garuḍa, she whose seat is Garuḍa,” and “Her vehicle is the Lord of Birds, whose self is the Vedas. To the question, “Why does she engage in what is thus forbidden by the scriptures? he says: “She is independent” (*svairā*).

The sense is that those who act according to their own will (*svairāḥ*) and follow their own desires—where indeed could they be subject to injunctions and prohibitions? They simply do not become so. The core meaning is that the Lord’s independence (*svairatvam*) is established by the scriptural statement: "He is immeasurable, beyond being enjoined, he goes wherever he wishes, and he is self-controlled."

Just as moss, once conquered by the sun and cast away, attains the state of a mountain here [in the form of Mount Śveta], yet is again conquered by the breasts of Lakṣmī—where indeed could it find the strength to conquer her splendor? (1627)

*Śaivalaḥ* means *śaivālam* (moss). *Avadhvastaḥ* means *avacūrṇitaḥ* (crushed); thus says Amara: “*Avadhvastaḥ* is *avacūrṇitaḥ*. In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), it is *vadhvastaḥ*, meaning either "destroyed by the letter *va*" or "that from which the letter *va* has been destroyed. Having attained the state of a mountain (*śailatām*)—that is, the nature of a hill or the status of the word *śaila*. The rest is clear.
O Queen, the flowers nurtured by you do not wither from heat; yet those growing on trees do wither—where indeed is there no fading for those who possess the nature of blossoms? (1628)

O Mother! "Sumanas" refers both to the wise and to flowers. By "pains" (tāpaiḥ) is meant the afflictions arising from the internal (ādhyātmika) and other such categories, as well as those produced by the rays of the sun and so forth. Those who possess "the state of being a flower" (prasūnatā)—meaning, on one hand, the deficiency (ūnatā) or inferiority of their own mother (prasū), and on the other, the actual nature of a flower—possess that quality; thus they are so described. The rest is easy to understand.

Just as the *makaranda* flower, even when its own petals are being crushed, does not abandon its own purpose, so too do your words; for sweet things do not turn into enemies even toward their own destroyers. 1629.

O Goddess! *Makaranda* means the nectar of flowers, and it is also the word *makaranda*. Because of your words, which serve as the cause [for this realization], even though there is the "crushing of his own"—that is, the crushing of his head (according to common parlance)—in the other sense, even when there is the "crushing" or removal of the letter *ka*, that which has not abandoned its own (*sva*) meaning or purpose (*artha*) is so described; one whose vision is fixed solely on achieving one's own purpose. In the other sense, the word *makaranda*—even upon the removal of the letter *ka*—is *maranda*, having not abandoned its own denotation (*svārtha*).

The sense is that, by virtue of being fully established (*niṣpannatayā*), [the word *makaranda*] does not abandon its own denotation, since the words *makaranda* and *maranda* possess the same meaning. The term "of speech" (*vacasaḥ*) follows the subsequent [words] as well, according to the maxim of the central gem (*madhyamaṇinyāyena*). [The phrase] "attained friendship" (*sakhyaṃ upait*) means it attained intimacy with your speech—that is, with your utterance. To the question, "Why did he not offer resistance even when it was the cause for the splitting of his own head?", [the author] replies: "Sweet" (*madhurāḥ*).

They are sweet by nature, of a pleasing disposition, and of a savory character—according to Amara, "the words *madhura* and *priya* mean both sweet and pleasant. They do not bear enmity even toward their own enemies, that is, they do not harbor hostility toward those who have taken their lives. The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied here according to the rule beginning with "śabdavaira... (Pāṇini 3.1.17). The dative case is used according to the rule beginning with "krudhadruha... (Pāṇini 1.4.37), as in the example: "Who bears enmity toward that first among the proud, that great hero? (Raghuvamśa 2.59).

Just as the netherworld (Pātāla), having attained friendship with the navel of Your Lord, became the companion of His breasts—[the navel] which is free from the wife of Hari (Lakṣmī)—where indeed could that which is the heaviest of all not be a friend to the virtuous? 1630.

O Harimahi! The Creator (kartṛ), having attained friendship with your navel—that is, becoming equal to it—reached its likeness; this is the intended sense. [The compound] *apāra-hita* is to be analyzed as *apāram* (boundless) and *yathā syāt tathā hitam* (attained in such a way that it became limitless). Furthermore, being deprived of the letter *pa* (*pā-varṇa-vidhuram*), it also attained friendship with your breasts—that is, it reached equality with your breasts by becoming a *tāla* (palmyra fruit); such is the meaning. One must not forget the identity between word and meaning (*śabdārtha-tādātmya*).

For indeed, where (kvanu) could that thing which is the teacher of all and worthy of worship by all—the great ones who attain (ayat) the state (sthiti) or boundary (maryādā)—not be a friend? The sense is that such a thing would be a friend to everyone. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), it refers to the word *pātāla*, which is "that in which all syllables are heavy" (*guravaḥ sarve varṇāḥ yasmin tat tathoktam*) and which has "attained the state accompanied by the letter *tā*" (*satāṃ tākārasahitāṃ sthitiṃ avasthānaṃ prāptam*). Thus, the word *pātāla* is described as having all its syllables heavy and being accompanied by the letter *tā*.

Thus, although examples have been presented in their entirety—by means of both similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—without regard for the distinction between what is relevant (*prastuta*) and what is irrelevant (*aprastuta*) in the support of a particular by a general; nevertheless, here, in the first variety, in examples such as "The moon is the brother-in-law of Hari," there is the support of a relevant particular by an irrelevant general; whereas in the two examples beginning with "If he were full of respect for you... and "...due to hatred for the luster of your feet," there is the support of an irrelevant particular by a relevant general.

Regarding the second variety, however, one should understand the distinction as follows: in examples such as "The world [arises] from mere volition," the specific subject under discussion is supported by a general statement that is not the subject; whereas in the four examples beginning with "Even the bee [rests] at your lotus-feet" and in the example beginning with "Defeated and cast down by his hair," it is the specific subject that is not the primary topic which is supported by the general subject under discussion. Thus, the difference between the two should be understood.
Supporting a general statement by means of a particular instance through similarity (*sādharmya*) is as follows:
"O Śrīnātha, may the virtues of those who serve a true Lord like you shine forth; for the dense blackness of the *kṛṣṇasāra* deer, when resting upon the moon, becomes radiant. (1631)

"San" means the praised Lord or Master; and "of the *sat* [beings]" refers to the stars, as well as those who enjoy them. Here, the general statement made in the first half-verse, which is the subject at hand, is supported by its similarity (*sādharmya*) with the specific instance mentioned in the second half-verse, which is not the subject at hand.

For indeed, even among those of unsurpassed prosperity, an insatiable thirst for wealth manifests itself; since even the Abode of Lakṣmī takes away the wealth of those who bow before him in abundance. 1632.

In this case, the distinction from the previous [type] is that there is a substantiation, through similarity (*sādharmya*), of the general subject matter presented in the first half by means of the specific subject matter presented in the second half.
Just as even a mountain that moves crookedly is surely humbled by the Lord of the World, so too has this lord of serpents been surpassed by the Lord of Ramā.
Here too, as before, there is the support of an irrelevant generality by means of a relevant particular; however, the distinction lies in its being interwoven with *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Or as it is said:
"How great indeed was the hope of those possessing supernatural powers, that the Blessed One—though clad in yellow robes—while dwelling in Nanda’s palace, alas, assumed the state of a thief! (1634)

This is *pāṭaccarī*, belonging to a *paṭaccara* (a tattered garment); it took on the state (*daśā*)—meaning the hem or fringe—of that which pertains to a worn-out cloth. Alternatively, the sense is that she assumed the condition (*daśā*) of a *pāṭaccara*, a thief, because her playful act of stealing curds, butter, and so forth has been displayed. Amara states: "A *paṭaccara* is a worn-out garment; *pratirodhin*, *parāṃskandin*, *pāṭaccara*, and *malimluca* [are synonyms for thief]. Ratnamālā states: "'*Daśā* [is used] in the senses of a wick, a state, and the end of a garment."
Supporting a general principle by means of a specific instance through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*):

"O Lord who seeks refuge, one whose nature is compassionate vision would not abandon even the lowly; for the moon, having placed the deer that has sought him upon its own lap, indeed caresses it. (1635)

Here, there is the support of the general subject introduced in the first half-verse by means of a specific instance that is not the subject at hand, through the relation of dissimilarity (vaidharmya).
For indeed, he who is superior by nature attains preeminence in the world of his own accord. Whom do you honor here, O Kṛṣṇa, that you yourself assume the form of a crown? (1636)

"O Kṛṣṇa! Whom do you honor, whom do you place before you, whom do you take as your refuge?—this is the meaning. You are one who 'possesses the form of the head' (mūrdhanyākārabhāk), that is, whose very nature (svarūpa) is to be honored by the heads of all the worlds. The sense is this: it is not by being placed at the forefront of anyone else that you possess the form of the head; rather, you do so by your very nature. In the alternative [grammatical] interpretation, 'O Kṛṣṇa' is simply an address using the word *kṛṣṇa* itself."

Which guttural (*ka-varṇa*) sound do you place at the forefront, [so that] you become one who possesses the cerebrals—the *ṛ*, *ṣ*, and *ṇ* sounds located in the head (the *mūrdhan* position), according to the grammatical rule “*ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣ* are [produced] from the head (*mūrdhā*)” [Pāṇini 1.1.50]? And what is the vowel *a*? You are so called because you possess those cerebrals and the vowel *a*; for the vocative form of the word *Kṛṣṇa* possesses the *ka*, *ṛ*, *ṣ*, *ṇ*, and *a* sounds. Here too, as before, the distinction lies in the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) of the pun (*śleṣa*).
This [type of *parivṛtti*] is also seen when both the capacity (*samarthaka*) and the object of capacity (*samarthya*) are equally relevant to the context. For example:
"O Śrīvallabha, will it be difficult for one favored by you to obtain anything here? By your grace, even a mere serpent has become a most excellent king. (1637)
Darvīkara, Śeṣa, and Sūda; Bhūbhṛdvareṇya, Girirāja, and Rājamukhya. Here, both the subject (samarthya) and the predicate (samarthaka) are contextual (prakṛta). The same applies hereafter.

O Acyuta, just as you have fulfilled the request of those who chose you by saying "I shall protect them," so too do you establish my lineage as preeminent; for one who has taken refuge in you, your devotee, never falls away.

"O Acyuta! 'Protect me'—having been thus chosen by me who made this request, you, acting as my protector, are establishing my lineage and family as preeminent and most excellent. [O Lakṣmaṇa,] listen!

The suffix *tvoḥ* here denotes the sense of cause (*hetvarthe*). You should indeed fashion—that is, make—him who has taken refuge in that lineage as one who practices the means consisting of the bearing and entrusting of burdens. The underlying meaning is: since you are engaged in establishing the preeminence of my own lineage, how could you not protect him who has sought refuge? Your person—that is, a person favored by you—is never lost; this is because of the scriptural declaration: "O son of Kuntī, declare it truly: my devotee perishes not. (Gītā 9.31).

In this regard, there is another meaning: by placing the letter *va* (the first syllable) and the letter *śa* (the second syllable) of the word *varaṇakṛt*—which is "mukhya" because it resides in the mouth (*mukhe bhavam*)—you would fashion the word *śaraṇakṛt* from that word *varaṇakṛt*. This is because, by substituting the letter *śa* in place of the initial letter *va* of the word *varaṇakṛt*, the form *śaraṇakṛt* is produced.
Just as, O Rāma, by your grace even Valīmukha formerly became four-faced; O lotus-petal-eyed one, what cannot your sovereign grace accomplish? (1639)

O Rāma! Even the monkey Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, shall by your grace become four-faced [Brahmā] in the future. Because of the use of the word *purā* (in the sense of "in the future"), the present tense (*laṭ*) is employed according to the rule “*yāvatpurā*” for the meaning of the future. The rest is clear.

O Beloved of Śrī, just as it is with you, so does your Śrīvatsa mark attain the state of being the abode of Śrī; for indeed, he who is dear to your heart becomes possessed of Śrī and attains the status of having auspicious marks.

O Śrīvallabha! That particular mark of yours named Śrīvatsa attains, just like you, the state of being the abode of Śrī—that is, the status of being the dwelling place of Lakṣmī. For it is well known that both you and it are the abode of Śrī, as evidenced by such names as "Śrīda," "Śrīśa," and "Śrīnivāsa," and by the scriptural passage: "In Brahman, the abode of Śrī. Thus says its own mantra-text: "Salutation to Śrīvatsa, the abode of Śrī. Indeed, it is precisely because it is the place where Lakṣmī dwells that it is conventionally designated as "Śrīnivāsa. Furthermore, that object which is dear to your heart—beloved by your mind—and which resides upon your chest; [that too shares this quality].

"Sulakṣaṇatvam" means one who possesses auspicious marks; as it is said, "The marks most dear to Hari are the conch, the discus, the upright sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and so forth. In the alternative sense, he would attain that which is both beautiful and characteristic—that is, the true nature (tattva). He who moves together with [others] is "sadhryaṅ"; thus, he becomes a companion of Śrī, moving in harmony with her.

The established meaning is that the entity which is dear to the heart of the Blessed One, possessed of auspicious marks, and of conscious form, never abandons its abundance of knowledge, sovereignty, and other perfections; and as the entity existing in the form of a mark upon the chest of the Blessed One, it dwells eternally together with Śrī.
This [simile] is also seen even when the two [terms of comparison] are not the primary subjects (*aprakṛta*). For example:

"May the performer of good deeds obtain prosperity, attaining the quality of straightness and essence just like your word; for by performing penance with his head downward, the very sap of the mango tree became the essence of the *sarala* pine. (1641)

One who performs good deeds and acts virtuously shall obtain welfare; this is the sense, based on the saying, "The doer of good attains what is auspicious. The juice of the *rasāla*—whether sugarcane juice or *mākanda* juice—to attain, like your speech, the quality of being straightforward (*sarala*) and the quality of noble flavor (*udārarasa*), performed penance with its head downward and became the very essence of the *sarala* tree. The sense is that by reading the word *rasālarasa* in reverse order, such a form is produced. Here, both the supported and the support are non-contextual (*aprakṛta*).

In this figure of speech (alaṃkāra), both the relation of the supported and the supporter (*samarthyasamarthakabhāva*)—whether implied (*ārtha*) or expressed (*śabda*)—is the determinant of its status as an ornament. However, it is not the case that, as in the figure of poetic cause (*kāvyaliṅga*), the causal relation (*hetuhetumadbhāva*) is determined by the sense alone; for when there is an absence of an explicit indicator such as *hi*, *yat*, or *yasmāt*, it is implied (*ārtha*). This occurs, for example, in the verse: "He who is incapable in his undertakings must depend on the assistance of others. When such indicators are present, it is expressed (*śābda*). An example of this is: "For the truly noble man does not enter..."
