That which was shown in the passage beginning with "by your grace, the serpent... and so forth—here, all other matters that ought to be said have been demonstrated on the occasion of defining the figure of speech *udāharaṇa*, and thus are not elaborated upon here. Furthermore, one should not think that there must be a fixed sequence between the statement of support (*samarthaka*) and the statement supported (*samarthya*), as determined by the order of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), in the manner of the two members of a syllogism, the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*). For there is no rule here that the supporting statement must only be uttered when an expectancy has already arisen due to the apparent impossibility of the statement to be supported.

Even when there is no logical impossibility (*anupapatti*), poets employ it for the sake of clarity in comprehension; the same applies to *kāvyaliṅga*. Thus, there is no fault even if the two are reversed.
O Acyuta, the generosity of one such as you is like the rain poured by a dense cloud upon both the lord of rivers and the mountain peak— indifferent to the distinction between the low and the high.
In this case, the distinction found in the first half of the verse serves as a support for the generality presented in the second half.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, the Chapter on Corroboration by a General Truth (Arthāntaranyāsa), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the *Vikasvara* ornament:
"When the justification of a particular [fact] is made by means of a general [truth]..."
Furthermore, it is specifically described as being "expanding" (vikasvara) for him.

When, having established a particular point by means of a general statement, a poet—unsatisfied with its mere conventional acceptance—proceeds to establish that same point again through a specific instance, either by way of simile (*upamāna*) or as an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different matter), that is the ornament named *vikasvara*.

This has been shown in such passages as "by your grace, that [poisonous] serpent... and so forth. Regarding this, all other matters have been demonstrated on the occasion of defining the *udāharaṇa* (illustrative) figure of speech; therefore, they are not elaborated upon here. Furthermore, one should not think that there is a fixed sequence between the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), or between the corroborating and the corroborated sentences, as determined by the order of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). For there is no rule here that the corroborator must only be expressed once the expectancy—aroused by the impossibility of the corroborated—is present.

Even when [the cause] is not logically established, it is mentioned by poets for the sake of clarity in comprehension; the same applies to *kāvyaliṅga*. Thus, there is no fault even if the two are reversed.

Just as a rain-cloud pours forth water equally upon both the lord of rivers and the mountain peak, O Acyuta, such is the magnanimity of one like you, which disregards the distinction between high and low.
In this case, the distinction found in the first half of the verse serves as a support for the generality presented in the second half.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter on *Arthāntaranyāsa* (Corroboration) in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the chapter on the *Vikasvara* (Expansion) ornament:
"That which is the corroboration of a particular by means of a general [statement]..."
Furthermore, it is specifically described as being in full bloom for him.

When, having established a particular point by means of a general statement, a poet—unsatisfied with its mere conventional acceptance—proceeds to establish that same point again through a specific instance, either by way of simile (*upamāna*) or as an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different matter), that is the ornament named *vikasvara*.
Just as darkness cannot prevail against the sun, so may no task, however small, disturb me here now that my burden has been placed upon you; for fortune cannot afflict one who is blessed.
"Something"—this is the agent; "darkness"—this too is the agent. This is an example of *viśeṣāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a specific instance) in the manner of a simile (*upamā*).
By way of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration), as follows:
"O Śrīvāsa, although there are many mountains, you have taken refuge on Vṛṣaśaila; for not everyone possesses good fortune, since even while the gods looked on, Lakṣmī obtained you."

Or rather, as you out of compassion bestowed the kingdom upon Kapi— for the compassion of the great is indeed unrestrained— even though he was but a cowherd, O Acyuta, the Daughter of the Ocean granted you the status of Lord of the Universe.

This ornament has been presented here in accordance with Dīkṣita, who follows the *Candrāloka*. Jagannātha and others, however, maintain that since there is one *arthāntaranyāsa* consisting of the support of a specific instance by means of a general statement, and another consisting of the support of a general statement by means of a specific instance, these two distinct varieties clearly constitute a single figure; therefore, as the purpose is already served by their coexistence (*saṃsṛṣṭi*), it is not appropriate to accept them as separate ornaments.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on the *Vikasvara* Ornament, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on *Prauḍhokti*:
"The attribution of a cause to that which is not actually the cause of something's excellence."
This is called "bold assertion" (prauḍhokti) by the wise, such as the mouth of Jayadeva.
The poetic figure named *prauḍhokti* (bold assertion) consists in the attribution of causality to an object that is not actually a cause for some degree of excellence.
May the two feet of Hari— red as lotuses blossoming from the interior of the Sarasvatī’s belly, which bestow good fortune upon being remembered and bring joy to his beloveds— be for my welfare.
Here, there is the attribution of causality to the fact of its being produced from the sun within her belly, as the cause for the excessive redness found in the flood of the Sarasvatī.
Just as the floods of the fame of the Enemy of Mura— white as autumnal moonlight, rivers of clouds, and blooming night-lotuses— bestow the appearance of camphor-paste upon the quarters of the sky.

Here too, the cause for the excellence of the whiteness of the night-lotuses is the postulation of a cause such as being drenched by the moonlight of the autumnal moon. However, the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara* states the definition of this ornament as follows: "Proud Assertion (*prauḍhokti*) is the presentation of a connection with something well-known to possess a certain quality, with the intent to convey an excellence produced by that quality in some other object. An example of this is: "O Daughter of the Ocean, I believe that the Lotus-born [Brahmā] created your side-long glances from the essence of the fragrant breezes from the Sandalwood Mountain, intermingled with the rays of the moon. (1648)

Here, in the side-glances, the poet does not intend to convey merely the qualities of the young Malaya breeze, such as coolness and so forth; rather, he intends to convey others as well, such as its power to revive the entire world. Thus, the contact with moonbeams is employed as a qualifying attribute within the essential components of the Malaya breeze for the sake of intensification. Furthermore, the relationship of producer and produced here is not one established by worldly convention, but is rather constructed solely by the poet’s imagination.

And here, if the excellence arising from the connection with a particular attribute of the subject (*dharmī*) and residing in another subject is the object of *vyañjanā* (suggestion), then this is indeed an ornament (*alaṃkāra*). But if it is expressed through the function of denotation (*vācyavṛtti*) as being prompted by those respective [attributes], then it is the province of the ornament of Simile (*samālaṃkāra*) alone.

For example: "O Lotus-eyed One, you were indeed born in a lotus; you hold a lotus in each of your two hands; you reside in the heart of the Lotus-navelled Lord (Viṣṇu); and it is fitting that you possess the fragrance of a lotus. (1649)

In this instance, the excellence of Lakṣmī’s fragrance is described as being caused by her connection with its substratum; thus, the figure of speech is *sama* (Equivalence) alone. And so, according to his view, [the following verse is an example]: "O Blessed One, by means of the nineteen Purāṇas and furthermore by the sixth Veda, those qualities of yours to be abandoned are proclaimed through [beings] born from the wombs of future mothers."

In such cases, one should not claim that the postulation of another unreal object for the sake of establishing the falsity of one [object] constitutes a distinct figure of speech called *mithyādhyavasiti*, because its purpose is already served by *prauḍhokti* (bold assertion) alone—as seen in examples such as: "The hair is dark like the mass of clouds over the Yamunā."

Just as in the examples of bold assertions (prauḍhokti) composed by ancient authors, where the connection with the Kālindī river—the locus of darkness—is brought forward for the sake of intensifying the blackness of the *tamāla* trees, so too can it be easily argued that the connection with the nineteen Purāṇas and others—the loci of falsity—is likewise employed to establish the intensity of falsity in things to be discarded (*heyaguṇa*). Furthermore, the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, Hariścandra, argues that if the determination of falsity (*mithyādhyavasiti*) were indeed a distinct poetic figure, then the determination of truth (*satyādhyavasiti*) would also have to be one; he illustrates this with the verse:
"Those [sacrificial posts] consecrated by Hariścandra and sung of by the Son of Dharma..."
O Mother Gaṅgā, your virtues sport within the lap of the city.
Having cited such examples, here the truthfulness of virtues is perceived through their connection with Hariścandra, Yudhiṣṭhira, and the Vedas (Nigama). Likewise:
"O Lord, your words are worthy of abiding within the interior of a palace made of nectar, situated in the midst of the ocean of ambrosia, upon a seat of the full moon."

In this case as well, since an excess of sweetness (*mādhurya*) is perceived in the expressions due to their connection with the ocean of nectar and so forth, within whose scope would this fall? Therefore, it ought to be a distinct figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*). However, I have already stated that its purpose is fulfilled by *prauḍhokti* (bold assertion) alone.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on Bold Assertion (*prauḍhokti*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Chapter on Poetic Fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*):
"Poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*) is a conjecture that 'if it were thus,' for the sake of establishing something else."
Where there is some conjecture and another means of conjecture, that is "possibility" (saṃbhāvana).

O Hari, if this human lifespan were multiplied ten million times, and if I possessed ten million mouths, I might yet be able to praise even a ten-millionth part of Your singular, infinite abundance of qualities. (1650)

Just as in the examples of bold assertions (prauḍhokti) composed by ancient authors, where the connection with the Kālindī river—the locus of darkness—is brought forward for the sake of intensifying the blackness of the *tamāla* trees, so too can it be easily argued that the connection with the nineteen Purāṇas and other texts—which are the loci of falsity—is brought forward for the sake of establishing the intensity of falsity in those qualities to be abandoned (*heyaguṇa*). Furthermore, by the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, Hariścandra, who argues that if the determination of the false (*mithyādhyavasiti*) were itself a distinct figure of speech, then the determination of the true (*satyādhyavasiti*) would likewise have to be one, he cites:
"The [sacrificial fires] were kindled by Hariścandra and sung by the son of Dharma..."
O Mother Gaṅgā, your virtues play within the lap of the city.
Having cited such examples, it is understood here that the virtues [of the Lord] are true because of their connection with Hariścandra, Yudhiṣṭhira, and the Vedas (Nigama). Likewise:
"O Lord, your words are worthy of dwelling within the interior of a palace made of nectar in the midst of the ocean of nectar, upon a seat of the full moon."

In this case as well, since an excellence of sweetness (*mādhuryātiśaya*) is perceived in the expressions due to their connection with the ocean of nectar and so forth, within whose scope would that [sweetness] fall? Therefore, it would constitute a distinct figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*). However, I have already stated that its purpose is achieved through *prauḍhokti* (bold assertion) alone.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on Bold Assertion (prauḍhokti), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra. Now begins the Chapter on Poetic Fancy (saṃbhāvanā):
"Poetic fancy (saṃbhāvanā) is a conjecture that 'if it were thus,' made for the sake of establishing something else."
Where there is some conjecture and another means of conjecture, that is *saṃbhāvana* (poetic probability).

O Hari, if this human lifespan were multiplied ten million times, and if I possessed ten million faces, I might perhaps be able to praise even a ten-millionth part of Your singular, infinite abundance of qualities. (1650)

O Lord, if Mount Kailāsa, melted by the mass of rays from the white-rayed moon and made smooth as the essence of camphor, were to be weighed against the essence of Your compassion; [it would not equal it]. 1651.

In the first [verse], the reasoning regarding the hymnist having ten million faces and so forth serves as the means for inferring that even a mere ten-millionth part of the greatness of a single attribute of the Blessed One is beyond such calculation. In the second, however, the reasoning regarding the mountain of snow being melted by the rays of the moon serves as the means for inferring that it is unfit to be compared to the essence of the Blessed One’s grace.

O Mother, if there were not this toil of yours in complying with the Lord—who bestows fruits according to one's karma—this world would be merely "Śrīmat" (the prosperous), far removed from any talk of the distinction between the wealthy and the wretched. (1652)
Or rather: O Hari, if by Your grace I were ever to become the Creator myself, I would surely not compose speech that falters upon falling into the dense thicket of the wicked's mouths. (1653)

Or rather: O Acyuta, if such a state of being a subordinate [to Your qualities] were established for me, then I might somehow be able to speak of, hear, or even behold the abundance of Your loveliness. (1654)

"Such subordination (*tādṛśaśeṣatvam*). The intention behind qualifying subordination as "such" is this: although even now he possesses his natural subordination to none other than the Lord, nevertheless, he lacks that subordination characterized by having a thousand faces which is so exceedingly skillful in describing the Lord's beauty and so forth. The sense is that [he cannot] speak because he has only two thousand tongues; the sense is that he cannot hear or see because he has only two thousand eyes. For he is indeed *cakṣuśśravas* (the one with eyes on his ears).

Or rather: "O bunch of flowers, if you were to abandon the behavior of a crane, become a knower of reality, and remain only in the presence of the virtuous, then you would surely attain the state of being the breasts of Lakṣmī. (1655)

*Stabaka* means a cluster or bunch; the word *stabaka* itself refers to the "crane's conduct" (*bakavṛtti*)—described as "looking downward, deceitful, intent on achieving one's own ends," and so forth—as well as the presence of the two syllables *ba* and *ka*. Having abandoned or cast off this crane-like behavior, and being a refined person (*śiṣṭa*) of virtuous conduct and a knower of reality (*tattvavit*), [the name] remains. In the alternative sense, "refined" (*śiṣṭa*) means remaining; that which has the collection of syllables *sta*, *sta* remaining after the removal of the syllables *sna*, *ba*, and *ka*—that is, only the letter *sta* remains.

The meaning is as follows: he whose dwelling or presence is before virtuous, pure-natured (sāttvika), or beautiful objects is so described. Alternatively, if he were such that the letter *na*—which is heard last (*agramavaḥ*)—is properly (*sādhu*) placed at the end, then he would attain the state of being the breast of Lakṣmī; that is, he would undergo birth as a breast. The sense is that by the elision of the letters *ba* and *ka* from the word *stabaka*, and by the addition of the letter *na* at the conclusion, the word *stana* (breast) is produced.

In this instance, the conjecture that the cluster [of blossoms] will first become the abode of a virtuous woman—preceded by its abandonment of the behavior of a crane—is the means for the conjecture that it will attain the status of being Lakṣmī’s breast. The use of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and other figures, however, constitutes its distinction from previous examples.
O Mother, if by my praise you were to expand even slightly the fragrance within [your heart], then the state of Dāmodara would be attained by me; of this there is not even a trace of doubt.

O Mother! If, by means of my praise—that is, by the hymn composed by me—you should grant even a slight (*daram*) gladdening joy (*āmodam*) within the mind, then and there alone would the supreme state of Dāmodara be attained by me. In the alternative sense: *daram* is a compound of *da* and *ra*; [the word *antara* takes the accusative case when joined with *antara* or *antareṇa*, according to the rule *antarāntareṇayukte*]. Thus, the meaning is "between the letter *da* and the letter *ra*" (*dakārarephayormadhye*).

If one should produce the word "āmoda" from the sound "āmoda," then the term "Dāmodara" would be established; this is the meaning. Here, the worshiper’s slight conjecture regarding the arising of the fragrance of Śrī’s heart is a means for the conjecture regarding the establishment of the term "Dāmodara," which is interwoven with *śleṣa* (paronomasia). The same applies in what follows.

Just as the arrival of the gods, shaken by Your noble hand, becomes truly free from passion (vītarāga), so too, O Acyuta, if it were to transform through excellent understanding, it would indeed be equal to Your fingernail. || 1657 ||

O Acyuta! The celestial Kalpavṛkṣa (wish-fulfilling tree), shaken by your noble hand, would—being thus shaken and consequently overcome by an excess of dejection—become detached from passion (*vītarāga*) and, as it were, become an ascetic (*tapasvin*). If, by its "good-mindedness" (*sumatā*)—meaning by its being endowed with beautiful splendor (*suma*, where *su* means beautiful and *matā* means state)—it were to "transform" (*pariṇamet*), that is, if it were to turn into a flower; [in the other sense, if it were to attain liberation].

In that case, however, it would be like your nail. Here, the word *surāgama* (the arrival of the gods) could also be interpreted as *vītarāga* (one free from passion) or *vigatarāva-varṇa* (devoid of the sound of lamentation); thus, the meaning "only through a wise mind (*sumati*)" will be transformed [into these other senses], which is a source of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*). In this context, the conjecture regarding the transformation of *surāgama* into *sumati* serves as the means for the conjecture regarding its similarity to a nail.
Or rather: If one were ever to truly recognize your magnanimity, O Śrījāna, then even the celestial tree would at that moment cease to be falsely called "Devadāru" (the divine wood). 1658.

The sense is that the celestial tree (*devataru*) is insentient. If, at any time (*jātu*), it were to produce your magnanimity—using "if" (*yadi*) as a supposition because a conscious action is impossible in an insentient thing—that celestial tree would, at that very moment (*tadātve*), become a *devadāru* tree, a specific type of minor tree called *bhadradāru*. The meaning is that it would exist, shrunken and far removed from even the scent of the renown for magnanimity, like a *devadāru* tree in some forest.

In this context, the word *devataru* (the celestial tree) would, at that moment, undergo the substitution of the letter *ta* with the letter *da*; that is to say, having removed the *ta*, it is read as *dā*. The sense is that it would attain the state of *devadāru* (deodar), becoming the word *devadāru*. Here, the possibility of the celestial tree possessing the Lord’s magnanimity and knowledge serves as the means for establishing the impossibility of its being deodar.
O beloved of the Bull-bannered Lord, if Indra were ever to seek to harm you in reality, he would surely lose his luster and, in the end, become a mere cat among trees.

O Beloved of Vṛṣācala! Even Indra (Biḍaujāḥ), though designated as your brother—let alone anyone else—is the sense intended. If, by any chance (jātu), he were to truly (tattvena) and in reality (vastutaḥ)—and not through a superimposed anger—hate you, then at that time Biḍaujā, having lost his vigor (gataujāḥ) and being rendered lusterless by the power of hating the Lord, would become a *sāla* tree; that is to say, he would obtain birth as a stationary being (sthāvara). Ultimately, in the final outcome, even a cat (biḍāla) might become one.

The sense is that even one born as an animal may have some of his sins removed by birth as a stationary being (a plant). The intention is that such is the fruit of hatred toward the Blessed One. In the alternative [punning] sense, the word *biḍaujāḥ* is so called because its *o* and *jā* sounds have departed. That is to say, when the sounds *o* and *jā* are removed from the end—that is, from the final portion—what remains is the sound *biḍ*. When this is joined with the collection of sounds *āla*, it results in the form *biḍāla*. Here, regarding *viḍaujaḥ* (Indra) and the Blessed One...

The apprehension of two forms of hatred serves as the means for the apprehension of the state of being a *sāla* tree and a cat; however, the specific excellence of the poetic figure (*vicchitti*) is indeed manifest.
Or rather:
O Acyuta, if a dark cloud, having stolen your splendor and settled upon some stone, were to display its own beauty, then that [stone] would be reduced to ashes by the wise.

O Acyuta! Having stolen your splendor from the dark cloud—the blue rain-cloud—it has dissolved somewhere upon a stone or a mountain (Amara states: *grāvāṇau* means both a mountain and a rock). In this alternative sense, its "state of having the letter *ka* as its final" (*kāntimat-tva*)—that is, its luminosity; in the other sense, its state of having the letter *ka* as its final syllable. In this latter case, there is doubling of the letter *ta* in the word *antimat-tva* according to the rule *anaci ca*.

The meaning is this: if, then, that *abhraka* were to be reduced to ash by the wise—those born of the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*) and those learned in Āyurveda—it would be subjected to the final expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of being turned into ash, as a means to remove the sin incurred by stealing an object praised by the Lord of the Universe. In the alternative sense (the *pakṣa*), it would be "reduced to ashes" (*bhasitaṃ kriyeta*). This is because, regarding the production of ash, the superiority of black *abhraka* alone is traditionally remembered.

Here, the reasoning that the dark cloud possesses luster upon some stone serves as the means for the reasoning regarding its reduction to ash. The excellence of the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), however, remains just as before.

O Hero of the Raghus, if Mahādeva were ever to become a great battle against you, it would truly be a transformation brought about by the breaking of his body, for you are the one who shattered that bow.
O Raghuvīra! Should Mahādeva, the conqueror of death, at any time engage in a great battle—a powerful conflict—against you, that Mahādeva [would do so] by means of the dissolution of his own body.

"It is true that he would be disfigured by the tearing apart caused by your arrow; there is no doubt in this matter. He states the reason for this: "For you are one by whom the bow (dhanu) of Śambhu was shattered (dalita). Therefore, the sense is that even though Mahādeva has been struck by a great weapon (mahāraṇa) by you, he would certainly be disfigured by the tearing of his body (dehavidāraṇa). In the alternative sense (pakṣe), [the word] *mahādeva* would be disfigured by the splitting of its body—that is, by the replacement of the letter *da* with the letter *ha*. The meaning is that the word *mahādeva* would become disfigured into the word *mahāhava* ("great battle").

Here, the poet's imaginative conceit (*saṃbhāvanā*) that Mahādeva was engaged in a great battle concerning the heroic scion of Raghu, which serves as the proof for the conceit that he possesses the transformation resulting from the shattering of that [scion's] body, is composed by means of a supporting reason (*hetūpaṣṭambha*).

Or rather, O Blessed One, if a mirror were to desire to rival the orb of Your cheeks through some crooked means, it would surely shatter into pieces; for it did not know that You are indeed the crusher of Mura.

O Blessed One! A "mukura" (mirror) is a "kusṛti" (crooked path); "kusṛti" refers to a wicked course or a devious way, as Amara states in his list of synonyms for deceit: "kusṛtir nikṛtiḥ śāṭhyam. In this context, the word is derived from the root *sṛ* (to go) with the suffix *ktin*, preceded by the syllable *ku*, implying a departure from the [proper] path (*sṛti*). Thus, the sense is that the word "mukura" is actually "mura" [when stripped of its deceptive form]. There is an identity between the word and its meaning: if [the moon] were to desire to conquer the orb of your cheek, it would surely shatter into fragments; there is no doubt about this. This is the intended meaning.

Now, one might ask: even though he had thus attained the state of Mura, how did the mirror (mukura) proceed with the desire to conquer you, the slayer of Mura (murabhit)? To this, he says "tvam" (you). That mirror, it is said, did not know you to be the "crusher of Mura" (muradalana). The sense is that I imagine it did not know [this].

Just as when the entire assembly of poets is seen here to be flawless by the preeminent protector of all, then that [assembly] truly becomes the "Assembly of Poets" (Kavikula); let this be properly reflected upon. 1663.

The term *avi* here refers to a flock of sheep; however, the word *avi* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for that which resembles a sheep. Thus, the meaning is: even a multitude of those who are exceedingly foolish. When they are beheld—that is, when they become the object of the side-glance (*kaṭākṣa*)—in their entirety by the Lord, the Supreme Sovereign and Protector of all, who is primary (*mukhya*) and not secondary (*agauṇa*), then the "flock of poets" (*kavikula*)—the assembly of learned men who compose poetry—will truly come into being; there is no doubt in this. If there is doubt, then let it be thoroughly investigated.

The intention is that when the power of the Blessed One is contemplated, the meaning stated is indeed understood correctly. In this context, the word *avikulam*—being "deficient" (*vikalam*) by the letter *a* (i.e., lacking the initial *a*), as will be explained by the term "principal" (*mukhyena*)—is understood to mean "by the first letter. O Protector of All, O Lord of All, O Blessed One: if it is seen with the principal, i.e., the first letter *ka*, that is, if it is seen formed with the initial letter *ka* having displaced the original letter *a*, then its meaning would simply be *kavikulam*.

In this context, it should be understood that the consideration of whether a member of the flock of sheep has come within the range of the Blessed One’s sidelong glance serves as the means for considering whether he belongs to the flock of poets.
Or, for example:
"O Mother, if a cuckoo were to consider itself a match for your speech, what would be lost to him? Knowing him to be a boar, would a wise person call him such? (1664)

O Mother! If the cuckoo should consider itself sufficiently capable—that is, competent—to rival or equal your speech, by means of expressions such as "namas" or "svasti" (using the dative case), then what would be lost, or what deficiency would there be, in this highly audible and manifest speech of yours? This is said even if the cuckoo were to presume itself so capable at its own will.

The sense is: "Knowing that what loss could there be to the incomparable beauty of your speech? What intelligent person would say of that cuckoo, "He is equal to your speech"? Furthermore, it also means one might say of that boar, "He is equal to your speech. The implication is: if someone, being unskilled in discerning the relative degree of merit between himself and others, should consider himself superior to one who is actually inferior, a person of refined intellect would regard him as having a mind as gross as a pig's.

The meaning is: "knowing that the syllable *ki*—which is the color of the fame (*kīrti*)—of this cuckoo (*kokila*) has been cut off or discarded. There is an identity between the word and its meaning. An intelligent person would call that cuckoo a "kola," because when the syllable *ki* is dropped from the word *kokila*, it results in the form *kola*; this is the intended sense. Here, the conjecture beginning with "if indeed" (*yadināma*) serves as the means for the conjecture beginning with "he would know him to be a *kola*. The excellence of the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), however, is quite evident.
O Mother, if even the sun’s rays, having stolen the crimson beauty of Your feet, consider themselves noble, then they would surely become boars; what doubt can there be in this? (1665)

The term *ārya* means "to be honored. In this context, it signifies one who lacks the quality (*varṇa*) of being noble (*arya*). Here, the attribution of nobility to Sūryakara—even though he is a thief—serves as the means for establishing his true nature as a pig (*sūkara*); thus, there is conformity with the definition [of poetic suggestion].
Or rather:

O Mādhava, if the honey—which is devoid of taste and possesses the nature of being tasteless—should desire to attain the excellence of flavor, let it not be perceived first; let it instead attain the state of a mango tree and thus achieve its fruitfulness.

O Mādhava! This [term] serves as an embellishment for the meaning about to be stated. "Devoid of sweetness" means lacking in tastiness; therein, the cause is the state of being "without flavor" (*arasatvabhāk*). That which has no *rasa*—that is, no excellent flavor such as sweet and so forth—is described as such. The sense is that its very nature (*tattva*) is something unenjoyable due to its discordance with any praiseworthy quality.
The word *rasa* refers to taste, water, potency, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others, poison, liquid,
enjoyment, disease, the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), the bitter and other [six] tastes, and also mercury (*pārada*).

Thus says Hemacandra. By the power of the specific epithet *makaranda*, it is understood as "the juice of some very insignificant flower. If [a bee] should desire the *rasa*—the flavor—of your speech, then at a later time (*agre*), having become the object of Lakṣmī’s sidelong glance through the ripening of accidental merit and the like, he shall attain the state of a *mākanda*, that is, the state of being a mango fruit; for Hemacandra and Medinī both state, "The word *mākanda* also refers to the mango (*sahakāra*). It is called *mākanda* because it "calls out" (*kandati*) to me, Lakṣmī, for the sake of its own protection.

And it is understood that this refers to the childhood of Lakṣmī. The suffix *aṇ* is applied to the root *kadi*, meaning "to call," in the sense of its object (*karmani*). [The phrase] "may he obtain" (*vindatu*) means: at that time, may he possess fruitfulness—that is, the state of being endowed with the fruit consisting of the essence of your speech, which is his own desired object. [The phrase] "he might go" (*iyāt*) means: only when such a birth from the *ākanda* (the mango tree) is accepted will Mādhava obtain the essence of your speech; the sense is that he would not obtain it by himself in the form of the previously mentioned *makaranda* (nectar). In the alternative interpretation (*pakṣe*), it is devoid of that initial *ma*—the first letter, namely the syllable *ma*.

The state of being (*bhāva*) is existence (*sattva*). The existence of *rasa* is *rasattva*. That which possesses this is *rasattvabhāk*. One who does not possess it is *arasasattvabhāk*. This is the intended meaning of the two qualifiers "devoid of the letter *m* and the letter *r*" (*makārarephaśūnya*). *Makaranda*: the word *makaranda*, when established as *kanda*, is the sense. At the beginning (*agre*), that is, at the start, by means of *māḥ*—the letter *m*—it is characterized (*lakṣya*) or seen; thus it is established as *mākanda*. The analysis of the phrase is: "that [becomes] the state of being fruit" (*saḥ phalatvam*).

That word "mākanda" should attain the state of being a fruit—that is to say, the status of denoting a fruit. Here, the attribution of the nature of a mango (*mākanda*) to nectar (*makaranda*) serves as the means for attributing the possession of the fruit consisting in the attainment of the essence of the Lord’s speech. It should be understood that this is enlivened by an identification based on a pun rooted in the identity between the word and its meaning.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on Poetic Fancy (saṃbhāvana), in the Alaṃkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on False Determination (mithyādhyavasiti):
"If another false object is conceived for the sake of establishing a certain falsity..."
That is declared to be the poetic figure named *mithyādhyavasiti* (false attribution).
The poetic figure named *mithyādhyavasiti* (false attribution) consists in the postulation of another false object for the purpose of establishing the falsity of some given object.

O Murāri, just as the thirteenth sun—the friend of the lotus and possessor of rays exceeding all calculation—dispels the darkness from within the hearts of those devoted to the pure [Vedas], so too has the darkness within the hearts of Your devotees been dispelled by You. 1667.

O Murāri! By that [sun] who possesses rays exceeding all calculation—namely, by the thirteenth friend of the lotus (the sun), meaning by a sun distinct from the one renowned for having exactly a thousand rays and for being twelve-fold in nature—for those who resort to you...

For those who have attained the meditative states corresponding to you, or for those serving you through the science of *nyāsa*—the suffix *kvip* being used here from the root *juṣ* in the sense of "pleasure" or "service"—and for those who are pure, meaning those possessing all forms of purity as described in such passages as "The purification of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) through the knowledge of the Lord is considered supreme," [for them] the word *agnīnām* (of fires) should also be supplied. The great darkness within the heart—the internal darkness consisting of the quality of *tamas*—is dispelled, that is, it is cast away.

Here, for the sake of accomplishing the complete removal of the darkness from the heart of one who has taken refuge in the Blessed One—a feat utterly impossible [for anyone else]—an elimination performed by thirteen suns, which is likewise utterly impossible, is described. This is an instance mixed with *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Just as the linseed plant, having been surpassed by your brilliance, burns in the forests with its head cast down, so too might Sītā, at the end of the alliance, come to favor you, O moon of the Raghu dynasty.

O Lord of the Raghu dynasty! This [comparison] is intended to embellish the meaning sought to be expressed. *Atasī* is the flower of the linseed plant; the elision [of the suffix] occurs according to the rule “*puṣpamūleṣu bahulam*” (Pāṇini 4.3.166). Having been surpassed by the splendor of your radiance, it remains in the forests with its head bowed down—that is to say, standing in a contrary position. In the end, at the conclusion, having made a *saṃdhi*—meaning that since a conflict with a powerful force is improper, one makes peace; in the other sense, this refers to the intention to express the state of being a *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination).

If Sītā were to attain the state of being Jānakī, she would acquire your liking, your splendor, and her devotion to you; otherwise, it is implied that her liking for you would not be easily obtained. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), if the phonetic expression of the word *atasī* were to exist in reverse order, it would become *sīta a*; then, if a *saṃdhi* consisting of a long vowel of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) were to occur between the letter *t* and the vowel *a*, the form *sītā* would be produced. That very [result] is difficult to achieve, because when the single-substitute rule (*ekādeśa*) characterized as "substitution by the following vowel" (*ato guṇe*) applies, the *savarṇadīrgha* does not take effect.

Thus, the word would be *sīta* ending in a short vowel (*it*), and not *sītā* ending in a long vowel (*dīrgha*); this is the intended meaning. Here, for the sake of fulfilling that which was excessively improbable—the attainment of the favor of Śrī Raghunandana—there is the conceptualization of her being excessively improbable in the form of attaining the state of being Sītā. Other elements, such as the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) of the pun (*śleṣa*), are quite evident.
Or for example:
"O Jewel of the Bull Mountain, the Creator speaks with his sixth mouth, saying that even you are more generous than the sixth tree born from the eighth ocean. (1669)

This is a pure example. Likewise, in the context of defining the figure of speech *prauḍhokti*, the verse beginning with “from the nineteenth Purāṇa” (*ekonaviṃśasaṃkhyakapurāṇataḥ*), which was presented incidentally, is also a pure example of this [figure].

In the third chapter, the *Mayūkha* on the definition of poetry (*kāvyalakṣaṇa*), of the *Candrāloka*, ten figures were defined as being the very nature of poetic definition: *akṣarasaṃhatiśobhā*, *abhimāna*, *hetu*, *pratiṣedha*, *nirukti*, *mithyādhyavasāya*, *siddhi*, *yukti*, *kāraṇamālā*, and *kārya*. These were subsequently assigned by Appayya Dīkṣita to the category of *alaṃkāras* (poetic ornaments) in his *Kuvalayānanda* due to their capacity to produce aesthetic charm (*camatkāritva*). Among these, it should be understood that this present figure is *mithyādhyavasiti*. Regarding this, the definition and the illustrative example are seen as follows:
"It would be *mithyādhyavasāya* (false attribution) if there were an unreal relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*)."
Wear this garland of celestial flowers, strung upon a thread of moonbeams.
Thus; other points to be stated will become clear at their respective occasions.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, the Lake of False Attributions, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Lake of the *Lalita* Ornament:
[It consists in] the description of the subject matter to be portrayed, without mentioning the actual event, while the substratum is already introduced.
In that context, the description of its reflection is considered *lalita* (graceful).

The figure *lalitā* consists in the description of a connection with the contextual activity (*prakṛtavyavahāra*) upon that very same subject (*dharmī*), without mentioning the contextual designation (*vyavahāra*) of that subject. The mention of "the third case ending" is for the purpose of excluding illustrations such as "They praised the ocean of virtues, desiring to cross the sea with their two arms," which is an instance of *nidarśanā*. The phrase "upon the contextual subject" is for the purpose of excluding *aprastutapraśaṃsā*.

This is a pure example. Likewise, in the context of defining the figure of speech *prauḍhokti*, the verse "From the nineteenth Purāṇa" (*ekonaviṃśasaṃkhyakapurāṇataḥ*), which was presented incidentally, is also a pure example of this [figure].

In the third moonlight-ray (*mayūkha*) of the *Candrāloka*, titled "The Characteristics of Poetry" (*Kāvyalakṣaṇa*), ten figures were defined as characteristics of poetry: Akṣarasaṃhati, Śobhā, Abhimāna, Hetu, Pratiṣedha, Nirukti, Mithyādhyavasāya, Siddhi, Yukti, and Kārya. These were subsequently assigned by Appayya Dīkṣita to the category of *alaṃkāra* (poetic ornaments) in his *Kuvalayānanda* on account of their aesthetic charm (*camatkāritva*). It should be understood that among these, the present one is *Mithyādhyavasiti*. Regarding this, the definition and the illustrative example are seen as follows:
"If there should be a false attribution (*mithyādhyavasāya*) wherein the means and the end are unreal..."
Wear this garland of celestial flowers, strung upon a thread of moonbeams.
Thus; other points to be stated will become clear at their respective occasions.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, the Lake of False Attributions (mithyādhyavasiti), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Lake of the *Lalita* Ornament:
[It consists in] the description of the subject matter to be depicted, without mentioning the actual facts, while the subject itself is introduced.
In that context, the description of its reflection is considered *lalita* (graceful).

The *lalitā* ornament consists in the depiction of a connection with the subject matter at hand (*prakṛta*) upon that very same substratum (*dharmī*), without mentioning the conventional designation (*vyavahāra*) pertaining to that subject matter. The mention of the third case ending (*tṛtīyāntam*) is for the purpose of excluding instances such as the *nidarśanā* (illustrative simile) in the verse beginning, "Desiring to cross the ocean with their two arms, they praised the ocean of virtues.
The phrase "upon the substratum of the subject matter at hand" (*prastutadharmiṇi*) is for the purpose of excluding the figure of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).

How great the distance between me, a wanderer on the desert path of worldly existence, and Your eternal empire of union! Yet, O Acyuta, from this very spot, I have suddenly become desirous of ascending to the summit of Mount Sumeru.

Here, without explicitly stating the subject matter of the context—that "I, being merely a traveler on the desert path of worldly existence, desire to attain Your unassailable eternal sovereignty"—the poet has instead presented its reflection: "I wish to ascend the difficult-to-climb peak of Mount Sumeru from here in a single leap. For if the actual subject matter had been directly stated, it would have been nothing more than a *nidarśanā* (illustrative simile).

Or rather: Where is one like me, whose speech is limited, and where are you, whose excellent qualities are beyond counting even by the Vedas? Standing on the very ground, I wish to gather the entire collection of the Kalpa-tree's flowers.

Here too, though my intellect is limited, I desire to speak of the infinite auspicious qualities of the Lord, which cannot be fully delimited even by the Vedas; thus, without even mentioning the object [of my discourse], I have fixed myself upon the subject itself, as if standing on the ground and wishing to pluck all the flowers from the celestial wish-fulfilling trees.
Or as it is said:
"O Hari, although I am not a worthy recipient of Your most heart-felt compassion, who could restrain the boundless ocean if it were to overflow its shores? (1672)
In this case as well, since you possess an unrestrained flow of compassion even toward me, who am lowly, who indeed could restrain you whose sovereign power of independence is beyond questioning?

Thus, by not explicitly stating the primary meaning of the sentence (*bimbabhūta-vākyārtha*), only the reflected meaning (*pratibimbavākyārtha*)—namely, "unrestrained" (*unmaryāda*) and so forth—is presented.
O Śauri, you have shown compassion toward me by giving birth to me in the family of the great and virtuous, just as grain is winnowed of its husks when a dense wind blows.

The sense is that, just as grain is highly esteemed when the wind is dense and thick, blowing favorably, so too [the opportunity] must be utilized while free from the chaff (*tuṣa*). Regarding *nibusīkāryam*, it means "to be made free from chaff. As Amara states: "The word *kaḍaṅgara* is neuter for chaff; *busa* is also neuter; and *tuṣa* is masculine for the husk of grain. That from which the chaff has departed is *nibusam*.

Here, without explicitly stating the meaning of the subject sentence—that the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*) must be accomplished precisely at the moment of birth in a noble family by the power of accidental merit and the like—only the meaning of a sentence reflecting that [subject] has been illustrated.
Whether it be recited in the Śruti or recited in the Smṛti, he who does not find Hari— there is indeed no difference between the barking of a dog and the crowing of a cock.

He who does not find Hari may be one who has studied the *Śruti* or one who has studied the *Smṛti*; in both cases, the suffix *ini* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *iṣṭādibhyaśca*. Due to that connection, the word *śruti* and *smṛti* take the locative case in the sense of the object, according to the rule *ktasyenviṣayasya karmaṇyupasaṃkhyānam*. Thus, it is a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*), meaning "one who has studied the three Vedas (*trayī*) or the Dharmaśāstra."

The meaning is "it might be. There would indeed be no difference between the barking of a dog (*śvān*) and the crowing of a cock (*kukkuṭa*), for the sense is that both are equally devoid of purpose. In the alternative interpretation, the word division is: "between the words 'dog' and 'cock,' there is no difference in their being [mere] sounds."

The meaning is that there is no non-difference between the two sounds, but rather a difference itself. Here, instead of describing how the study of the Śrutis and Smṛtis is useless for one devoid of devotion to the Lord, the author has merely composed its reflection (a parallel instance).
Or as it is said:
"Some worship another than You, while others, O God, worship You alone. For crows remain crows even when their heads are lowered; could they ever become swans? (1675)

"Crows" (kākāḥ) refers to ravens; even with their heads bowed down (*adharita-śiras*), the word "crows" (*kākāḥ*) is reversed [in meaning]—this is the sense. Here, without demonstrating the meaning of the original statement—that those who worship other deities cannot attain similarity with the devotees of the Lord even through great effort—the meaning of a reflected statement has been described instead. Furthermore, the other aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) is evident in both examples.

Nor should it be argued that the purpose of this [figure] is fulfilled by *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), on the grounds that even where there is difference everywhere, there is non-difference. For in that case, there is the determination of non-difference between one thing (*padārtha*) and another thing (*padārtha*), as seen in examples such as "The moon shines upon the golden creeper"; however, here it is not a matter of one linguistic usage being identified with another linguistic usage, so this is not the province of *atiśayokti*. Nor can it be explained by *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description) based on similarity, because the subject (*dharmin*) lacks the quality of being the "matter at hand" (*prastutatva*).

Nor is it an illustration (*nidarśanā*), for that [figure] is intended only when two usages pertaining to a single subject are employed; however, in the present case, the usage relevant to the subject at hand is not so employed, and thus it is indeed a different poetic figure. And so:
"Where is the lineage originating from the Sun, and where is my intellect of such limited scope?
Out of delusion, I desire to cross the ocean, which is difficult to traverse, by means of a mere raft."

In this regard, the example cited by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśikā* is entirely inconsistent, because *lalita* must necessarily be admitted [as a distinct figure] and because *nidarśanā* does not apply here. Such is the intention of those who accept that *lalita* is a separate figure of speech.

Others, however, maintain that *lalita* is not a separate figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*), as its meaning is already encompassed by *nidarśanā*. If it be asked: "How can *nidarśanā*, whose life consists in the presentation of two modes of behavior—one pertaining to the subject and one to the non-subject—rest upon the presentation of the behavior of the non-subject alone?", listen, O long-lived one: here, for the most part, figures of speech occur both verbally (*śrauta*) and through implication (*ārtha*). Among these, those based on implication are not enumerated as distinct figures of speech from the verbal ones, but rather as distinct varieties, because they are subsumed under the general definition of that figure.

Furthermore, this nature of the illustration of the sentence-meaning consists in the non-difference of the two modes of discourse, which is implied by the demonstration of the non-difference of the substratum (dharmin) that possesses those two modes of discourse. In this regard, there is no rule that the demonstration of the non-difference of the substratum possessing the two modes of discourse must be based solely on the literal sense (śrauta); rather, it is sufficient that it be merely demonstrated.

Therefore, just as in the verse "A mortal seizing another's wealth undoubtedly eats poison," where the non-difference between the two substrates (dharmins)—the one characterized by the two transactions—is established by the direct statement (*śruti*), so too in the verse "Fie upon another's property! Yet this evil-minded man eats poison," although the non-difference between the substrate of the contextual transaction (implied by sense) and the substrate of the non-contextual transaction (stated directly) is established through implication (*ārtha*), the status of *vākyārthanidarśanā* remains intact.

The distinction that in one case there is a literal (śrauti) nature and in the other a figurative (ārthī) nature is not denied; however, the essential nature of *padārthanidarśanā*—namely, a connection between the attribute of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) based on the identification (*adhyavasāya*) of those two attributes as non-different—is indeed distinct [from simile]. Furthermore, being either of these two is the general definition according to the method of the ancients. If, however, *lalita* were a separate ornament, then *luptopamā* and the like would also have to be separate from *upamā* and the like, for the reasoning you have provided applies equally to them.

But if this were the case, would not *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) simply be absorbed into *rūpaka* (metaphor)? For it could equally be argued that when both the object (*viṣaya*) and the correlate (*viṣayin*) are expressed, it is a verbal (*śrauta*) metaphor, whereas when only the object is expressed, it is an implied (*ārtha*) one. True; however, where the body of the figure (*alaṃkāra-śarīra*) is identical in both cases, it is proper to designate it by that specific figure alone. Just as similarity (*sādṛśya*), which constitutes the body of the *upamā* (simile), remains identical even in cases like the *luptopamā* (elliptical simile), it is therefore right to designate those too by the term "simile."

It is not [distinguished] by another figure of speech; rather, since properties such as elision or completeness are not integral to its very body, even though they themselves are excluded, they do not exclude the nature of simile (*upamā*).

Thus, it is established that the same applies elsewhere as well. And so, since the identity—constituting the body of the *rūpaka* (metaphor)—which is delimited by the *viṣayitāvacchedaka* (the delimiting property of the subject), with respect to an object appearing under the form of the *viṣayatāvacchedaka* (the delimiting property of the object), is distinct from the nature of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) which consists of an object appearing under the form of the *viṣayatāvacchedaka*, it is not logical for these two to be considered a single figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*). However, they say that since the lack of distinction in the essential nature of *nidarśanā* (illustration) and *lalita* (the charming) has already been demonstrated, they must indeed be considered a single figure of speech.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter on the *Lalita* ornament in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the chapter on the *Praharṣaṇa* ornament:
"If the accomplishment of a desired object occurs without effort, it is *Praharṣaṇa*."
The accomplishment of a desired object without effort toward the means for its attainment is the ornament named *praharṣaṇa*.
Or for example:
While a cowherd girl was preoccupied with household chores, meditating on the elixir of the embrace of Kṛṣṇa, she was hurriedly and accidentally pulled up by him and forcibly embraced. (1676)

The cowherd girl—meditating with longing and expectation, preoccupied with household chores and therefore moving quickly and hurriedly, and consequently stumbling with faltering steps—was suddenly and forcibly embraced by Kṛṣṇa as he lifted her up. Herein lies the attainment of the desired goal for the cowherd girl, even though she was devoid of any deliberate effort.
And *praharṣaṇa* (the "delighting") is the obtaining of even more than the desired object.

Thus, it is established that this also applies elsewhere. And so, since the identity—constituting the body of the *rūpaka* (metaphor)—which is delimited by the *viṣayitāvacchedaka* (the delimiter of the superimposed object), exists within the object appearing as delimited by the *viṣayatāvacchedaka* (the delimiter of the actual object), it is distinct from the nature of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), which consists of an object appearing as delimited by the *viṣayatāvacchedaka*. Therefore, it is not proper for these two to be considered a single figure of speech. However, they argue that since the lack of distinction between the natures of *nidarśanā* (illustration) and *lalita* (graceful) has already been demonstrated, they constitute a single figure of speech.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter on the *Lalita* ornament in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the chapter on the *Praharṣaṇa* ornament:
"If the accomplishment of a desired object occurs without effort, it is *Praharṣaṇa*."
The accomplishment of a desired object without effort toward the means for its attainment is the poetic figure named *praharṣaṇa*.
Or as it was:
while a cowherd girl, preoccupied with household chores, was meditating on the elixir of the embrace of Kṛṣṇa, she was suddenly and forcefully embraced by Him as He rescued her from stumbling. (1676)

The cowherd girl—meditating with longing and hope, distracted by household chores and therefore moving quickly and hurriedly, and consequently stumbling with faltering steps—was suddenly and forcibly embraced by Kṛṣṇa as he lifted her up. Herein lies the attainment of the desired goal for the cowherd girl, even though she was devoid of any deliberate effort.
And *praharṣaṇa* (the "gladdening" figure) is the obtaining of something even greater than the desired object.
The second *praharṣaṇa* is the accomplishment of an object exceeding that which was the scope of one's desire, occurring without any effort directed toward that [exceeding] object.
Longing for a long time, thinking, "If she were seen by Nanda’s son, I would be joyful," the cowherd girl obtained in secret the entirety of the treasure of his embrace.

In this context, for the young cowherd girl who imagines her own joy merely by the sight of the Lord acting as the agent and herself as the object, there arises the acquisition of an even greater benefit: the attainment of the sovereign empire of the entire essence of an exceedingly intense embrace.
O Śrīnātha, those who perceive you as one capable of destroying the helplessness born from wandering through saṃsāra have indeed been granted four hands by you. (1678)

*Vihastatām* means the state of being bewildered or agitated; as Amara states: "The words *vihasta* and *vyākula* are synonyms. In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), one whose hands have departed is *vihasta*; the state of such a person is *vihastatā*. The distinction from the previous [example] is that the attainment of the "extraordinary benefit" (the acquisition of four hands) by those people who were worshipping the Lord in order to somehow regain their possession of hands is accomplished through a pun (*śleṣa*) inherent in the word *vihasta*.

O Śauri, having approached you with the thought, "May I become even more slender in beauty through your grace," alas, your friend has instead become possessed of the great beauty of refined gold, for he was honored by you.

O Śauri! The sense is that your friend is "kucela" (ill-clad). By your grace, may I possess even the slightest fortune, or—according to the manner expressed in such sayings as "as much as fills the belly"—may I have exceedingly meager wealth; the sense is that I am not one who desires an excess of it. Having approached you with this thought, and thereafter being honored (*apacita*) by you—"pūjā, namasyā, apacitiḥ" according to Amara—the one whose golden splendor (*tapanīya-śrī*), meaning his wealth of gold, became abundant, became so described.

The word *bateti* is used to express either wonder or joy. Furthermore, the sense that "even one possessing very little splendor might become [one with] great splendor," desiring this, should be supplemented by the meaning: "he became possessed of a splendor exceeding even that related to the sun (*bhānu*), having a wealth of refined gold (*tapanīya*). In the alternative interpretation (the pun), the word *tanīyaśśrīḥ* is to be analyzed as follows: it is to be read as *tvayā tataḥ*, meaning "by you, after the letter *ta*" (*tataḥ*); and it is to be divided as *pacitaḥ*. Thus, being joined or composed (*citaḥ*) with the letter *pa* (*pakāreṇa*), the word becomes *bahu* as a separate term.

The sense is that "in such a way as to be abundant" means by having one additional syllable compared to the syllables previously existing. Thus, the word *tapanīyaśrīḥ* came into being. Here, the attainment of a benefit greater than what was expected by Kucela is described.
O Lord of Kosala, you granted the status of Indra to your enemy who desired the status of a Vasu on earth through his defeat by you; how can we describe such great magnanimity in you?

The state of being a Vāsava on earth is the status of a lord among the gods of the earth; and in heaven, the state of being a Vāsava is the status of Mahendra. [The term] *vāsava* means "one who has dwelling (*vāsa*)"; the state of such a one is *vāsavatvam*. The factual reality is that you have destroyed all enemies. Here, too, it is exactly as before.

O Mother of the worlds, a single dark cloud, desiring to attain equality with you in the beauty of its hair, performed penance with its head cast downward and somehow attained the state of shimmering hair.

O Mother of the worlds! The dark blue-black *mecaka*—whether it be the moonspot, darkness, or the dark-blue color of a peacock's eye (as Hemacandra states: "*mecaka* refers to the dark-blue, the black, darkness, or a peacock's eye")—seeks equality with the splendor of Your hair, that is, the luster of Your locks. For this very reason, having performed penance alone with its head cast down in solitude—according to the saying, "One should perform penances alone"—it has somehow managed to attain the state of being Your hair.

In this context, the word *mecaka* (dark-blue) is to be analyzed as *ka-ca-śriyā amekaḥ*. Desiring equality with the beauty of your hair (*kaca-śrī*), it is "one from which the syllable *me* is absent" (*amekaḥ*)—the suffix *kap* being applied according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*. The sense is that, once deprived of the syllable *me*, the remainder is *caka*; thereafter, having undergone inversion (*vilomatām*), it attains the state of the word *kaca* (hair). Here, the attainment of the status of "hair" (*kaca-tva*) by the *mecaka*, which is superior to the desired beauty of the hair, is described. The specific charm of the pun (*śleṣa*) and other figures remains as before. For example:
Just as the traveler in the desert searches for some shade to soothe his exhaustion, suddenly the fierce orb of the summer sun is concealed by a cloud.

By the phrase "a traveler in the desert," the perpetual scarcity of shade is indicated. By the phrase "some shade whatsoever," it is meant that the shade of extremely small trees such as the *śākoṭaka* is sparse.

Here, the praise of the sudden appearance of a great cloud—which conceals the orb of the fierce-rayed sun during summer—on the part of a desert traveler seeking any shade whatsoever, serves to illustrate how, while a conscious being reflects upon some refuge for the sake of alleviating the exhaustion of coming and going on the path of worldly existence (*bhava*), the Blessed One, having become manifest through the power of some accidental or incidental merit, [appears].

In this sentence, which takes the form of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), the sense culminates in the matter at hand—that "the alleviation of that heat has been accomplished"—and thus the acquisition of a meaning exceeding the intended one is quite evident. Indeed, this alone is the distinction from previous [types of *aprastutapraśaṃsā*], namely, its being intermingled with *aprastutapraśaṃsā*.
When an effort is being made for the accomplishment of a means,
the fortuitous attainment of the actual result itself is called *praharṣaṇa* (the delightful).

In the world, it is well known that effort directed toward a means is undertaken for the sake of attaining a fruit that has not yet been obtained. When the acquisition of that very fruit occurs unexpectedly from such effort, that too is *praharṣaṇa* (the "unexpected gain"); this is the third variety.
O Lord, just as a man desiring prosperity through service to you gazes toward your mountain peak, he beholds the courtyard of his own home as beautiful as the ocean.

"O Lord!"—this is the address. Here, because he has set out toward Śeṣācala for the purpose of accomplishing service to the Blessed One, which is the means to attaining sovereignty ending with the mastery over elephants, he attains such sovereignty right there on the veranda of his own palace; this is the third instance of *praharṣaṇa* (the production of joy). And this is reinforced by the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (poetic exaggeration) consisting in the reversal of the temporal sequence between cause and effect.
Or, for example:

A cowherd maiden, desiring to seek out the root of Kṛṣṇa’s power to subjugate others while he was in a bower on the bank of the Yamunā, forcibly encountered him there and brought him under her control. (1684)

In this instance, by going to a bower on the bank of the Yamunā for the purpose of obtaining roots and other items as means to subjugate the Blessed One, the subjugation of the Blessed One is achieved right there. Thus, it should be understood that the general definition common to all three types of *praharṣaṇa* is: the attainment of a desired object even without an effort directly aimed at that end.
In the *Candrāloka*, however, only the second variety is defined as "the effortless attainment of more than the desired object" (*praharṣaṇa*); the first and third varieties are not.

Others, however, maintain that in the first example of *praharṣaṇa*, the ornament of *praharṣaṇa* should not be admitted because of the description of attaining a desired object even in the absence of an effort directed toward that desired end; for since effort is a cause only with respect to an effect in general, when the desired end is accomplished despite the absence of effort directed toward that end or its means, the case falls under *vibhāvanā* (the manifestation of an effect without its cause). Therefore, they say that *praharṣaṇa* has only two varieties;
the distinction between them being that in the former the absence of the cause is expressed by words (*śābda*), whereas here it is implied (*ārtha*).
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, the Section on *Praharṣaṇa*, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Section on the *Viṣādana* ornament:
when there is the attainment of an object contrary to what was desired, that is *viṣādana*.

This is the distinct category [of *kāvyasaṃkara*]: where, for the sake of attaining a desired object, no causal effort is made and only a mere wish is formed, yet a contrary result is obtained; and where, even though a cause has been employed for a desired object, no contrary result arises from it, but rather [the result occurs] by the power of its own cause.

However, where the attainment of a contrary result arises precisely from the very cause employed for a desired purpose, there is *viṣama* (the Uneven), because the relationship characterized as the state of producer and produced between such a cause and the contrary result is discordant. Furthermore, because of the attainment of a result contrary to what was intended, it is indeed a case of *viṣādana* (despair). Thus, this [figure] is not subsumed under the varieties of *viṣama*. It should be understood that the general definition common to the three types of *praharṣaṇa* (Joy) is: "the attainment of the desired object even through a [seemingly] adverse means."

In the *Candrāloka*, however, only the second variety is defined as "the effortless attainment of more than the desired object" (*vāñchitārthādhikaprāptir ayatnena praharṣaṇam*); the first and third varieties are not.

Others, however, maintain that in the first example of *praharṣaṇa*, the ornament of *praharṣaṇa* should not be admitted because of the description of the attainment of a desired object even in the absence of an effort directed toward that desired end; for since effort is a cause only with respect to an effect in general, when there is the accomplishment of a desired end despite the absence of effort directed toward that end or its means, it falls within the scope of *vibhāvanā* (the manifestation of an effect without its cause). Therefore, they say that *praharṣaṇa* has only two varieties;
the distinction being that in the former case the absence of the cause is expressed by words (*śābda*), whereas here it is implied (*ārtha*).
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, the Section on Praharṣaṇa, in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra. Now begins the Section on Viṣādana:
Viṣādana occurs when there is the attainment of an object contrary to what was desired.

This is the distinct category [of *kāvyasaṃkara*] where, for the sake of attaining a desired object, no causal effort is made and only a mere wish is formed, yet the attainment of a contrary object occurs; and where, even though a cause has been employed for a desired object, there is no attainment of a contrary object from it, but rather [the result arises] by the power of its own cause.

However, where the attainment of a contrary result arises precisely from a cause employed for a desired purpose, there is the figure *viṣama* (the Uneven), because the relationship characterized by the status of producer and produced between such a cause and the contrary result is discordant. Furthermore, because of the attainment of a result contrary to what was intended, this is indeed a blend with *viṣādana* (despair). Thus, it should be understood that this [figure] is not already included within the varieties of *viṣama*, since its distinct domain, untouched by *viṣama*, will be demonstrated immediately hereafter.
"Just as the sun shines, so may I find the happiness of a wife"— thinking thus at evening, alas, the sun sank into the ocean.

For here there is no scope for "incongruity" (*viṣama*), because there is an absence of the application of a cause toward a desired end; for the very nature of incongruity consists in the incompatibility between a desired end and its intended cause, characterized by a relationship of producer and produced with respect to a contrary result. Therefore, it is "the giving of poison" itself that stands here as the constituent element of the *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).

For here, the irrelevant narrative of the cakravāka bird—who passes his time neglecting the means to attain the empire of eternal supreme bliss, while perceiving the excessive and transient worldly prosperity as something most permanent—concludes precisely when that same person, having lost such prosperity, becomes some unfortunate individual; thus, this is an instance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
"Thus has this been done; this task remains to be done; this will lead to our happiness"—while reflecting in this manner, alas, a person who is averse to you is carried away by death. (1686)

In this case, there is the attainment of an object in the form of removing death, which is contrary to the desired happiness. While one thinks, "This has been done, this is ready, and this other thing is half-finished," Death seizes such a person, who is thus occupied with worldly striving, and departs.
Thus, the meaning of the statement from the Mahābhārata has been considered.
The second type is as follows:
When she embraced the son of Nanda, the cowherd woman, though her face was covered with shame, had her bodice loosened because her two breasts were swollen with joy. (1687)

In this case, the contrary of the desired non-covering of the face is the loosening of the bodice; this occurs because it is the opposite of the shame that served as the cause [for covering], and it arises precisely from its own cause—the swelling of the two breasts due to joy—not from an effort conducive to covering. Nor is there here a failure to produce the desired result from a cause employed for the sake of achieving that desire, since the desired object in the form of covering the face has indeed arisen. Therefore, this is merely *viṣādana* (frustration), not *viṣama* (the incongruous). This ornament, too, is an invention of Dīkṣita alone.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, the Viṣādana-saras, in the Alaṅkāra-maṇihāra.
Now begins the Ullāsa-saras:
when, through the virtues or vices of one person, the virtues or vices of another [are manifested].
They say that *ādhāna* is described as the ornament of *ullāsa*.
And that [mutual relation] is fourfold: of a quality by a quality, of a defect by a defect, of a defect by a quality, and of a quality by a defect. The examples in order are as follows:
"May even my sidelong glance fall [upon him] out of compassion—O lotus-eyed one! May I too become blessed; even the Grandfather (Brahmā) desires this, so what need be said of others? (1688)

Here, through the quality of being a *bhāgavata*—characterized by devotion to Śrīnivāsa—the Pitāmaha and others are endowed with the quality of blessedness (*dhanyatva*) due to contact with his sidelong glance; and "endowment" (*ādhāna*) here means the cognition of possessing that quality.
The cowherd’s wife, her bodice loosened by the swelling of her two breasts from joy, remained thus. || 1687 ||

Here, the meaning contrary to the desired non-covering of the face is the loosening of the bodice; this occurs because it is the opposite of the shame that serves as the cause for covering, and it arises from its own cause—namely, the swelling of the two breasts due to joy—not from an effort conducive to covering. Nor is there here a failure to produce the desired result from a cause employed as a means to achieve that desire, since the desired object, which consists of the covering of the face, has indeed arisen. Therefore, this is merely *viṣādana* (frustration), not *viṣama* (the figure of discordance). This *alaṃkāra* is also an invention of Dīkṣita alone.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, the Lake of Despondency, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Lake of the Ornament of Exaltation (*ullāsālaṅkāra*):
when, through the qualities or defects of one thing, the qualities or defects of another [thing] arise...
They say that *ādhāna* is described as the ornament of *ullāsa*.
And that [type of *parivṛtti*] is fourfold: merit for merit, defect for defect, merit for defect, and defect for merit. Examples in order:
"May even my side-glance fall [upon me] out of compassion, O lotus-eyed one; 'I too might become blessed,' even the Grandfather (Brahmā) desires this—what need to mention anyone else? (1688)

In this context, through the quality of being a *bhāgavata*—which consists of devotion to Śrīnivāsa—the Pitāmaha and others are endowed with the quality of blessedness by virtue of contact with His sidelong glance; and "endowment" (*ādhāna*) here means the cognition that they possess that quality.
O Blessed One, by Your grace, one who has taken refuge at Your feet exists as something inconceivable to the world, yet manifest in a form exalted before all; he stands above everything. 1689.

He whose form is praised as foremost and made magnificent, being thus "udārita" and "udārīkṛta," and who is described as one whose letter 'a' (akāra) has been split or pierced by the letter 'u' (uvarṇa)—he exists as one who is to be honored above all the world, being esteemed for his excellence. In the alternative sense, the word *aparibhāvya* is transformed into *uparibhāvya* by first removing the initial vowel 'a' (avarṇa) and then placing the vowel 'u' (uvarṇa) in its place; such is the meaning.

Here, by means of the quality consisting of the Lord’s grace, there is the bestowal of qualities such as being beyond comprehension upon one who has taken refuge at His feet. The distinction is that while the former was pure, this one is intermingled with *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

O Hari, just as one born among the species of aquatic creatures—if by some chance they should ever be seen by you—alas, even a crab would surely become a man of noble lineage; indeed, O Lord, he would be truly well-born.

O Leader! O Lord of All! Even a crab (*kulīra*), born into the lineage of aquatic creatures and dull-witted beings, if ever by chance—and not as a matter of course—he were seen by You; that is to say, if he were glanced upon by You through the power of the ripening of accidental or other merits, then he would become a man of noble birth (*kulīna*). (The word *kulīna* means one of good lineage. As Amarasimha states: "The words *mahākula*, *kulīna*, *ārya*, *sabhyasajjana*, and *sādhu* [are synonyms for one of noble family]. The suffix *kha* is applied here according to the rule "from *kula*, *kha*."

"Could he not indeed be a human being?"—the word "hanta" expresses the joy born from reflecting upon the power of the Lord’s sidelong glance. In another sense, the word *kulīra* (crab), when deprived of its *ra* (*nara*) and joined with that very *na* (*ita*), becomes *kulīna* (well-born); this secondary meaning is also striking. Here too, by means of the quality consisting of the power of the Lord’s sidelong glance, even the crab is endowed with the quality of being a well-born man.
The blending of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and the specific charm are as before; however, the distinction here is that it is infused with the element of *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic fancy).

O Mother, just as a man who possesses great grace and is free from essencelessness, being himself a giver of much and possessing self-restraint, becomes worthy of praise by the four castes; [so too is he]. 1691.

O Mother! He who attains the state of being "dāntimat" (possessing self-restraint)—that is, becoming self-disciplined; in the alternative sense, a person whose final letter is the letter *da*—this being an epithet for the one who is "bahuprasāda" (one who has received great favor). From you—that is, through your grace—he becomes "bahuprasāda," meaning one who is the recipient of great favor bestowed by your mercy.

"Sārahitatvam" means the state of being both essential (*sāra*) and beneficial (*hita*). The meaning is: "having attained the state of being the supreme benefit for those who seek [it]. The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used here due to the elision of the suffix *-lyap* (as in *prāpya*). Alternatively, "from you" means "from your glance. He is so described because he possesses abundant grace (*prasāda*), that is, serenity. For this is said to be a great quality of a donor: "That which is the mildness of the giver is the very spotlessness of the full moon. Therefore, the aforementioned meaning follows precisely from his being "essential and beneficial."

Having become one who bestows much (*bahuprada*) and is *sthūlalakṣa* (liberal), in the alternative sense, the word *bahuprasāda*—having attained the state of being devoid of *sā* (the vowel *ā*) and thus lacking its *varṇa* (letter)—is formed as *bahuprada*; this is the meaning. For this very reason, he would be praiseworthy (*ślāghya*) by the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), namely the four classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. In the alternative sense, the word *bahuprasāda*, which consists of five letters (*pañcavarṇa*), would be praiseworthy only by virtue of having four letters (*caturvarṇatva*) when deprived of the letter *sā*. This is the meaning.

In the first sense, the analysis (*vigraha*) is *cāturvarṇyam* as "the four castes" (*catvāro varṇāḥ*), with the suffix *ṣyañ* added in its own sense (*svārthe*) according to the rule *catuvarṇādīnāṃ svārthe*. In the second sense, however, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has four castes.

From that, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) according to the rule *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaśca*. Here, by means of the quality of the power of the Lord’s grace, there is the bestowal of qualities such as freedom from sorrow upon His devotee; or else, by the power of the Lord’s sidelong glance, there is the bestowal of great grace and so forth.

O Daughter of the Jar-Ocean, even a man who, due to the power of an evil destiny, is full of great negligence, if he becomes an object of your gaze and attains honor, shall indeed become a giver of much.

O Daughter of the Ocean of Milk! One who, due to misfortune or poverty, is full of negligence and faces many calamities—such a person, if he becomes the object of your glances (your sidelong looks), will surely become a "bahuprada" (one who bestows much). In the alternative sense, the word *bahupramādaḥ* (one full of great negligence) is a masculine noun (*puruṣaḥ*). If such a man becomes the object of your glances, he shall attain *mānitatām* (the state of being honored by the world); in the alternative sense, by the removal of the letter *ma*, he attains *anitatām* (the state of being joined with the letter *ma*). Thus, he indeed becomes a *bahupradaḥ* (one who gives much), a liberal donor; in the alternative sense, the word *bahupramādaḥ* is transformed into *bahupradaḥ*.
