Here, by virtue of the spreading glance of Lakṣmī, even poverty (durgati) is endowed with qualities such as great generosity; the distinction lies in its being infused with the figure of speech *paryāya*, which consists in describing multiple attributes—such as being highly negligent and being highly generous—within a single substratum. As for its intermingling with *śleṣa* and other figures, it is exactly as before.
Just as a certain eminent man, though initially accompanied by others, is seen by you to gradually become a Vaiśvānara himself by his very nature—what doubt can there be? (1693)

O Blessed One! It is well known that the foremost of men (*agrya-nara*), the first-born (*agrajanmā*), the human being (*manuja*), is indeed a *brāhmaṇa*. Even if someone—initially followed by dogs (*śvānugata*)—meaning one who possesses the prohibited conduct described in such passages as "the one who plays with dogs and lives by hawks," becomes through Your sequence—that is, by the power of the ripening of his own merits acquired through chance and so forth—if he beholds Vaiśvānara, the Fire, he becomes pure and radiant like Him. Alternatively, [in the case of the name], he is one who is initially followed by the two syllables "vaiśvā" (*vaiśvā-anugata*), and whose "foremost men" (*agryau narau*) consist of the letters *na* and *ra*; thus he is so called.

The meaning is that if any sound whatsoever is perceived through the sequential order of the phonemes as previously described, it becomes Vaiśvānara alone and no other sound. Here too, by virtue of the excellence of the Lord’s majesty, the quality of purity is imparted even to the impure through the power of that perception. The distinction lies in the mixture of the *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic conceit) and the *paryāya* (succession), which consists in describing multiple substrata—namely impurity and purity—within a single locus.
Just as, O Lord, by virtue of residing within Your abode, even a bird does not abandon its own nature; what then need be said of one who shall become a lotus-eyed woman? 1694.

"O Master! Even while not abandoning his own nature (prakṛti)—that is, his own inherent disposition—and even while acting solely in accordance with that nature, rather than performing acts such as meditation (upāsanā), this is the sense. By virtue of the fortune (bhāgya) consisting of the status of dwelling within the divine abode (sadman) of the Blessed One—that is, by the good luck of residing inside His temple—even a bird (pakṣin), that is, even a winged creature belonging to the animal kingdom."

The Lord Padmākṣa, though not yet Padmākṣa, will become Padmākṣa; he will attain the state of Padmākṣa. [The suffix] *cvi* [is used here]. Even one who is as far removed as a mere bird from the fragrance of being oriented toward the means (upāya), by virtue of the fortune of dwelling in Your divine abode, will—according to the principle stated in "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"—become fit for the same form as the Lord (sārūpya) like a knower of Brahman. This is the sense. Therefore, what more remains to be said regarding His majesty? There is nothing further left to be told beyond that; such is the meaning.

The analysis of the compound is: *pakṣe svām in-prakṛtim*. It means "not abandoning its own *in*-base," that is, its own base (*prakṛti*) joined with the possessive suffix *in*. The sense is that it possesses a base ending in the suffix *in*. The analysis of the phrase is: *pakṣī pakṣīti-śabdaḥ sadmāntasthānabhāk yataḥ*. This means: "because the word *pakṣī* (bird) occupies the position of a semivowel (*antasthāna*) along with the letter *d*. That is to say, because it coexists with the letter *d*, it is called *sadmam*; it occupies (*bhajati*) the intermediate place (*antasthānam*), which is the middle portion; thus it is so described.

Therefore, for that reason, she shall become Padmākṣī; she will be established as Padmākṣī. Here, the sense is that everything to be said has been stated through this method of exposition, and nothing else remains. In this context, by virtue of the greatness and qualities of the Lord’s temple and by residing therein, even birds acquire the quality of attaining the same form as the Lord (sārūpya). Everything else is exactly as before.

Just as, for instance, the emerald (marataka) shines by virtue of its similarity to that [emerald] which, though it has attained the state of being the first jewel (*ādya-maratva*) and yet has also reached the state of being the ultimate destroyer (*atitarāntakatva*), does so through the abundance of its greenness and its nature as a gem. 1695.

*Marataka* refers to the *gārutmata* (emerald) and the term *marataka*; there is identity between these two. "The state of being the first *amara*" means the state of being a former deity, that is, the state of being a *daitya* (demon); the sense is that even though [that status] had passed away, it returned by the power of karma, as in the case of Vṛtra and others. Furthermore, immediately thereafter, there was the state of being an "excessive end-maker" (*atitarāntakatva*), meaning an extreme destroyer of the world, which is consistent with the nature of a *daitya*. This too was attained.

In the [first] half-verse, that which has attained the state (*tattva*) of being "preceded by *m* and *r*"—meaning that whose first two syllables are the phonemes *ma* and *ra*—and furthermore, after the phoneme *ma*, there are the phonemes *ta* and *ka* in great measure (*atitarām*).

The meaning is that it has attained the state of that which is exceedingly dark (*atitarāntaka*). The intention is that the word *marataka* consists of these four syllables. It shines by virtue of its abundance—that is, through its similarity—to the state of being a knower of the reality of Hari (the Blessed One), or rather, a knower of the supreme reality whose form is Hari; thus he is a "knower of the reality of Hari" (*haritattvavid*). Regarding his state as a knower of the reality of Hari, [it is said]: "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer. (Gītā 14.2)
The meaning is that, having attained equality with the Blessed One according to the manner described above, it shines forth.

"Haritatvavit" means that which finds (vindati) greenness (haritatva), that is, the quality of being yellowish-green; [the suffix] *kvip* is added to the root *vid*. It "shines" by virtue of an abundance of that, meaning through its similarity to that. This expression is used because the emerald (*marataka-maṇi*), due to its green color, possesses a resemblance to the Blessed One.

The non-difference between the colors blue and green is established by poetic convention (*kavisamaya*). Here, the presence of phonemes such as *ma* and *ra* residing in the word "emerald" (*marataka*) and the possession of the quality of greenness residing in its referent are determined as non-different due to the sovereign power of the identity between word and meaning; this is the secret. Through the quality of greatness inherent in the Blessed One, the quality of possessing that similarity is imparted to the emerald by one who knows that reality.

It should be noted that this [verse] is embellished by the figure of speech *paryāya* (succession), according to the method previously stated, as well as by the specific figure of *vibhāvanā* (poetic causation) characterized by the production of an effect despite the presence of an obstacle established through the determination of non-difference between two meanings subsumed under words such as "knower of the green reality" (*haritatattvavit*).

Just as the state of being an immovable deity was previously attained by one who later underwent a contrary color and gait, even though it became emerald, it did not deviate from its own nature due to the brilliance of Hari.

By which emerald (*marakata*)—that is, by the *gārutmata* gem and the word "emerald" (*marakatapada*)—at first, the station of the immovable gods (*acalāmarasthiti*) was attained; that is, the station, the boundary, of the "immovable god" (*acalāmara*), meaning a Brahmin (*bhūdeva*), was reached, signifying that Brahminhood was obtained. In the alternative sense (the word-play), the "station of the immovable" (*acalāmarasthiti*) refers to the fixed position of the letter *m* and the letter *r*; for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *sthiti* is used in the feminine sense of 'abiding,' 'boundary,' and 'limit. Thus, it refers both to that emerald and to that [specific] word.

"At the time of his end, having a 'contrary color' (*pratīpavarṇa*)—meaning a color contrary to that of a Brāhmaṇa, namely the color of a Śūdra—his 'course' (*gati*), that is, his connection [to rebirth], was described as such; it was defiled by association with a low-born man (*vṛṣala*), like that of Ajāmila and others."

Having become "bhāvaḥ" (an existent); in the alternative sense, having become that which possesses a "pratīpā varṇagatiḥ"—that is, a reverse order of syllables at its end in its final portion, specifically the position of the two syllables *ka* and *ta*—meaning the word *marakatam* has become *maratakaṃ*; [it is] characterized by *rucyā* (delight) toward Hari, the Blessed Lord, according to the scriptural teaching "whomever He chooses," or by the love directed toward Himself by the Lord; in the alternative sense, it is characterized by a luster equal to that of the Blessed Lord. This is the ellipsis to be supplied.

The sense is that it has not fallen away from, nor deviated from, its own meaning—namely, the unsurpassed human goal (puruṣārtha) in the form of the ultimate liberation (niḥśreyasa) desired by itself; rather, it remains as if it were fully accomplished. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), the meaning is that it has not deviated from its own denotation, namely the emerald (gārutmatamaṇi); for since the capacity of the word *marataka* to convey a particular meaning is well-established, there is no deviation from its own meaning even when the word *marakatapada* is used.
Here too, everything should be understood in the same manner as in the previous example.

O Blessed One, just as a rain-cloud (*vārivāhaka*), though deprived of its first three syllables and having moved to another position [in the word *vāhaka*], does not abandon its own meaning due to its strength, so too [the Buddha], though devoid of the first three syllables [of his name] by the power of Your grace, does not abandon His own purpose even when situated among other [worldly] qualities. 1697.

O Blessed One! Although Vārivāhaka (the cloud) and the word *vārivāhaka* have abandoned the first three syllables—the first three castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇa (in the case of the word, the three syllables *vāri-vā*)—nevertheless, it remains so because of its affection for You, that is, due to the existence of love for You.

Or, because of the existence of your grace. By "being rich in strength" (*balāḍhyatayā*), the meaning is by possessing mental strength characterized by non-despondency, which is included among the seven means such as discrimination (*viveka*); for if such strength were absent, the attainment of the desired human goal would be impossible. This is the sense of what is heard in scripture: "This Self is not to be attained by one who is devoid of strength. In the alternative [poetic] sense: the meaning is "because of the existence of a luster equal to yours" (*tvadruceḥ*). Or else, the meaning is "in accordance with your intention" (*tvadabhiprāyānurodhāt*).

By "rich in strength" (*balāḍhyatayā*), it refers to being endowed with the two syllables *ba-la*; thus, in accordance with your will, according to the maxim "not with every word [should one respond with every word]," [the word] is *vārivā*.

Thus, by the prohibition of the three [other] vowels, the two syllables *balā* which are prescribed in their place—meaning that even when situated among other vowels, or even when reaching a lower vowel (*avaravarṇa*), or even when connected to another vowel identical in form to *valā* (such as *balāhaka*)—the intention is that it is established as such. Indeed, in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the word *vārivāhaka* itself is read as *balāhaka*. He did not abandon his own purpose, his desired supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*).

The sense is that, regarding the attainment of the human goal (puruṣārtha) when the true essence of devotion to the Blessed One is present, even a connection with a low caste is not an obstacle. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), the word *vārivāhaka* does not abandon its own denotation, because it retains the same meaning even when it is the word *balāhaka*; this is the sense. Here too, there is the attribution of a quality to the cloud (*balāhaka*) by means of a quality of the Blessed One. The rest is as before.
Attributing the fault of one thing to another is as follows:
even though they strive in many ways, those who never attain the state of your abode blame the Creator for creating them here as mere mosquitoes. (1698)

In this context, there is the imposition of the fault of censure upon the Creator (Vidhi), who—due to the defect of not allowing devotees of the Lord to dwell in the abode of Śrīnivāsa—created them as mosquitoes even within that divine temple.
O Blessed One, wishing to praise you and your infinite and most wonderful majesty, I instead censure the Creator for having fashioned only a single tongue to perceive such flavor.

Here, by means of the defect of [the Creator's] lack of knowledge regarding the excellence of the various flavors, the defect of censurability is attributed to the Ordainer (Vidhi) for having fashioned [the world] with many tastes.

Though it has slipped from the feet of Acyuta, my heart runs after unsubstantial objects of sense without restraint; though unknown to me, I have been deceived in vain by the Creator who fashioned it thus.

This is the speech of a certain person who has taken refuge [in the Lord], becoming despondent because the restraint of the mind is exceedingly difficult even with great effort. For instance: "Even though my foot—meaning the foot of the Blessed One Acyuta—is bound, that is, fixed immovably; or in another sense, even though it is shackled by a chain in a specific place that is difficult to release (durmocaka)—may it remain 'unknown to me,' that is, entirely unnoticed by me, while wandering among worthless objects and lands" (*viṣaya* means "sphere of perception," "place," or "country," according to the *Medinī* lexicon).

The sense is that [the mind] runs about, tasting the very flavors of the objects of sense through various inclinations (*rucibheda*). In the alternative sense (of the metaphor), the meaning is that it runs freely from place to place, unrestrained from the prison-house. My heart—my mind—is "unsubdued," meaning untrained by nature; by this, it is suggested that even though it is by its very nature a nourisher [of the self], it has been rendered so. "I have been led astray in vain" means I have been deceived for no purpose at all.

The sense is this: even upon reflection, I do not perceive any purpose for him [the Creator] in creating such a mind that is so utterly difficult to subdue and fickle, especially since he does not deceive it himself. Here, by means of the defect of fickleness in the mind of one who has sought refuge (the devotee), the defect of being a deceiver is attributed to the Creator, its maker. In the present instance, regarding the mental state of the seeker of refuge, this is embellished by *samāsokti* (synecdoche/metaphorical identification), wherein the mental state of one who has escaped at will from an uncontrolled prison is perceived. However, the distinction is that in the previous example, both [the subject and the object of comparison] were pure (*śuddha*).
Or rather:

O Lord, if you should turn away even slightly, surely the Ordainer (Fate) would become our protector; for, O Blessed One, no one at all would remain without a protector—of this there is no doubt. (1701)

"O Lord, O Blessed One! Is there not some overlord—some person possessing sovereign power—who might be the Creator, or even Brahmā himself? This is a common worldly saying. The sense is: 'What of it? [The answer is: if you are even slightly *parācīna* (turned away or indifferent), one will remain truly without a protector (*anātha*). The sense is: when you are indifferent, who else could be the protector? In the alternative sense, the word *adhinātha*, if the syllable *dhi* were removed, would result in the word *anātha*."

Here, by the slight fault of being averse to the Blessed One, even the Lord Brahmā is made to incur the defect of being masterless; however, the charm of the pun (śleṣa) demonstrated here is the distinction from previous examples.
The attribution of a fault to one thing by means of the quality of another is, for example:
"Your inner disposition is indeed vast, capable of enduring excess"; thus people repeatedly and at will heap upon it the burden of their sins. (1702)

In this context, by means of the Blessed One’s quality of absolute forbearance, there is the imposition of the fault—namely, the burdening of those who are difficult to tame—with their own arbitrary misdeeds.

O Lord of Ramā, O All-pervading One, you who are the most affectionate friend to all—just as there is enmity between the first and last letters [of the alphabet], who on earth does not know that even Vaiśvānara (the Fire-god) is internally a dog? 1703.

O All-pervading Lord of Lakṣmī! O Friend of all, whose universal friendship is proclaimed by the Vedic declaration, "The Friend is the refuge of all"—in You, who pervade from beginning to end (meaning throughout the duration until the fall of the body), who indeed on this earth would not harbor within his mind an imperishable enmity—that is, hostility—even toward one such as Vaiśvānara, meaning even toward one equal to fire, the sense being that even toward one who is exceedingly pure? (Who would not harbor such enmity toward a dog-like person? No one at all.

He knows. The sense is that even if one is unable to speak out openly like a dog due to courtesy, one should nevertheless know it thus in one's heart. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), it refers to that which has the syllables *vai* at the beginning and *ra* at the end—meaning it is joined with the syllable *vai* at the start and the syllable *ra* at the conclusion. Thus, *vaiśvānaram* refers to the word "Vaiśvānara," which, when taken as a single compound word, means "one who has a dog (*śvāna*) within."

Who indeed does not know that [the word] *vaiśvānara* has two syllables, *śvā-na*, situated between the two syllables *vai-ra*? The sense is that everyone knows that the word *vaiśvānara* is of such a nature. Here, by means of the Lord’s qualities such as being a friend to all, the fault of enmity toward Him is described.

Or rather, O Mother, it is as if Nahuṣa, though he was of great majesty while in heaven due to the reversal of Your sidelong glance, fell at the end and became Mahāśayu (the Great Serpent), despite having attained such power.

O Mother! Nahuṣa—though he was "mahāśaya," meaning one of great aspirations (as Amara states: "one of great aspirations is called mahāśaya"), which implies that even while enjoying the sovereignty of the three worlds; though his desires were unimpeded; and though he had attained "ūrjitata," or strength in every respect—even so, due to the averted glance of your eye, at the end, having fallen from heaven, he became a "mahāśayu," that is, a great serpent (an ajagara).

Regarding the phrase "ajagare śayurvāhasa ityubhau," Amara states that both [words] are used for a python (*ajagara*). Elsewhere, the word *mahāśaya*—at its end, the syllable *acyuta* (the letter *a*) having fallen away (*cyutākāraḥ*)—attains the state of being *ūrjita* (strengthened) by means of the letter *u* (*ukāreṇa*), that is to say, it attains the state of being composed of the letter *u*. The particle *api* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). The meaning is: not only does it attain the state of the letter *a* falling away at the end, but it also attains a connection with the letter *u* in that very same place. The intended sense is that it results in the form *mahāśayu*.
Here, by means of the quality of great magnanimity residing in Śrī’s sidelong glance, the defect of Nahuṣa’s possession of a great mind caused by its opposite is depicted.
The attribution of another's qualities through the fault of someone else is as follows:

"O Hari, you are the wielder of the staff," while the fierce-rayed sun and others perform their respective duties; when the Lord sleeps indolently, people rest at their ease for the welfare of the worlds. (1705)

The construction is as follows: when the Lord is indolent, people sleep at their own will. Here, by means of the defect of cruelty suggested by the Lord’s role as the wielder of the staff (the rod of punishment), there is the attribution of a quality—namely, the accomplishment of the world’s security rooted in the fulfillment of the respective duties of Caṇḍakara (the Sun) and others. And this [quality] is supported by a corroboration (*arthāntaranyāsa*) located in the fourth quarter of the verse, which functions through the method of contrast (*vyatireka*). In this context, the meaning of such Vedic passages as “From fear of Him the wind blows, from fear of Him the sun rises” should be kept in mind.

This wielding of the staff by the Blessed One is described as cruelty from the perspective of worldly view; however, in reality, it is indeed a virtue, as stated by the commentators on the Bhagavad Gītā. This being so, this will serve as an illustration of how the qualities of one [being] are imparted through the qualities of another.
O lotus-eyed one, just as you severed the neck of the King of Cedi with your discus, was anything truly severed for him? For he attained nothing less than union with you, the Supreme.

In this instance, by means of the defect of cruelty—which was the cause for the Lord cutting off the neck of the King of Cedi—there is the bestowal of the quality consisting in his attainment of union (*sāyujya*) with Him; this is the pure type.
Just as a living being, radiant as the earth, may become the object of your grace, O Acyuta, so too may one devoid of wealth become merely a burden to the earth through your displeasure. 1707.

Whether on the earth or in the world, even if one were radiant and powerful, becoming a lord, yet being destitute and fallen into misfortune, he would merely become a burden to the earth—a burden to the world. The implication is that there would be no purpose whatsoever served by him. In the alternative sense (pakṣa), the word *dharaṇibhāsvara*—being "nissva," meaning deprived of its own vowel (*s*)—becomes *dharaṇibhāra*; such is the meaning, which is a source of poetic charm.

In this instance, the favor shown by the Blessed One is a merit (*guṇa*), by which there is the bestowal of qualities such as bodily sustenance, the power to illuminate the earth, and beauty upon [the subject] in the first half-verse; whereas his displeasure (*nigraha*) is a defect (*doṣa*), by which there is the infliction of defects such as the loss of one's own wealth followed by becoming a burden to the earth in the second half-verse. Thus, both modes have been demonstrated, and this constitutes a specific distinction from previous examples. This same principle applies to the examples that will be presented hereafter.
Although Śarva was originally Sthāṇu, he became omniscient through the power of your compassion; otherwise, that Lord of Beasts would have remained a mere beast, falling even with his head downward.

In this regard, by means of the quality of the majesty of the Blessed One’s compassion, even Sthāṇu is endowed with the quality of omniscience; conversely, by means of the defect [of his lack of compassion], Paśupati is endowed with the defect of being a "Lord of Beasts" (paśupati). Thus, both cases are established.

Just as even a person who is unfit may indeed become a member of the assembly if he is looked upon by you with compassion, so too this "essence of the assembly" (sabhāsāra), when its nature is inverted, becomes a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa).

O Blessed One! If even one who is uncivilized (*asabhya*) is looked upon with favor by you, he indeed becomes civilized (*sabhya*), worthy of the assembly; even one who is ignoble (*anārya*) becomes a member of the assembly (*sabhāstāra*). As Amara states: "Noble-born, well-bred, noble, civilized, virtuous, and good—these are synonyms for *sādhu*. Therefore, for this very reason, it follows that he is the essence of the assembly (*sabhāsāra*), being preeminent within the assembly.

The meaning is that it "becomes. According to Amara: *sāra* is used in the sense of strength (*bala*), the solid core (*sthirāṃśa*), and what is right (*nyāyya*); as a neuter noun it means "excellent" (*vara*), and in the three genders it means "best. In this context, the word *sabhāstāra* (courtier), being devoid of the letter *ta*, results in the form *sabhāsāra*. However, in the case of the opposite—that is, when your glance is adverse or when it is recited in reverse order—there would be a semblance of aesthetic flavor (*rasābhāsa*). That which lacks *bhāsa* (splendor or manifestation) is *abhāsa*; thus, *rasābhāsa* means a semblance of flavor, i.e., tasteless (*nīrasa*).

Alternatively, "rasāyām" means on the earth, and "abhāsaḥ" means lack of luster (aprakāśa). Or, "āsaḥ" is derived from the root *as* meaning "to be cast out" (nirasyate), with the suffix *ghañ* in the passive sense; thus, "rasābhe" means that which is cast out by both "rasa" and "ābhā. In this context, the word "sabhāsāraḥ" transforms into "rasābhāsaḥ. Here, through the quality of being moistened by grace (*kṛpārdratā*), even one who is unfit for the assembly (*asabhyah*) is endowed with qualities such as being a courtier (*sabhāstāratā*); conversely, through the opposite of that, even a courtier (*sabhāsāraḥ*) is endowed with the defect of being a mere semblance of aesthetic flavor (*rasābhāsatva*).

Or rather, O Mother, even that lord of heaven (Indra), if seen by you first, would instantly become a lord of the earth; for even a lord of heaven, if neglected at the outset, would surely become a lord of the earth.

O Mother! He whose lord has departed is *vīśvaraḥ*, meaning one who is without a protector (*anātha*). If that man were looked upon by you first—*agre* meaning "in front"—then at that very moment (*sadyaḥ*), he would become a lord (*īśvaraḥ*) in heaven (*dyavi*); *dyavi* is the locative singular of the word *div*. Because of the connection with the word *īśvara* according to the rule "the [locative] case ending follows *svāmī*, *īśvara*, *adhipati*, etc.," the word *div* takes the seventh case. The meaning is that he would become Indra. Alternatively, there is a word-division in *sadyaḥ* as *sat yaḥ*.

The construction is: "He who was looked upon by you in such a way that he was truly praised. The rest is the same. Alternatively, in the sky (dyavi), according to the Śruti, "His immortal part is in heaven," the Lord is in the supreme ether (parame vyoman) in the manner stated: "He becomes his own ruler" (sa svarāḍ bhavati).

The meaning is that one becomes independent of karma and possesses the sovereignty of liberation. Furthermore, even though he was formerly the lord of heaven (dyavīśvara) and Indra himself, if he were neglected by you today, he would now be a mere lord of the earth (vīśvara) or truly helpless. The point is that the presence or absence of your glance alone is the cause of sovereignty or poverty. Regarding the word *syāt*, the doubling of the letter *s* is optional according to the rule *anaci ca*.

In one sense, if the word *vīśvara* is preceded by the syllable *dy*, that is, joined with the syllable *dy* at the beginning, it results in *dyavīśvara*. But this is not all; there is also a marvelous implication: even though it begins as *dyavīśvara*, if it is deprived of the syllable *dy* (*adyaḥ*), it becomes *vīśvara*. Herein lies both [the contrast]: through the quality of Lakṣmī’s glance being gracious, the quality of sovereign power (*svārājyaiśvarya*) arises for the one she gazes upon; yet, due to the defect of her neglect, even Indra incurs the defect of being lordless (*anāthatva*).

O Lord, just as Vyāsa, Vibhīṣaṇa, and Bali did upon approaching you, a person’s lifespan increases; yet, alas, even one with a full lifespan is destroyed here like a woolen thread (*ūrṇāyu*) when [the thread] is exhausted. 1711.

One is called *Nātha* because people seek from him all human goals, such as long life, health, and so forth; thus, *Nātha* is the vocative address "O Lord! When one has approached you—that is, when one has taken refuge in you—one increases with a full lifespan, like Vyāsa, Vibhīṣaṇa, and Bali. As it is said: "Aśvatthāman, Bali, Vyāsa, Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa, Kṛpa, and Paraśurāma—these seven are the long-lived ones."

The meaning is that their long life was spoken of as being due solely to the greatness of taking refuge in the Blessed One. Even one whose full lifespan has been reached—though his full lifespan has been reached—is "ūrṇāyuḥ," like a ram, and is slain or killed by people who offer oblations at Durgā and the like, by those seeking meat, or by enemies; this is the ellipsis. Thus, turning away from You is the cause for the destruction of even Brahmā’s lifespan.

The state [of devotion] is such that, as it is said: "Hatred directed toward Mukunda consumes one's lifespan and accumulates all defects, being equal to the loss of sense objects. The summarized meaning is this: one who has approached the Lord increases his full lifespan, whereas one who has departed from Him is destroyed like a short-lived spider. In the alternative (allegorical) sense, the word *pūrṇāyuḥ* (full-lifespan) refers to the attainment (*gati*) of the letter *pa*; *na pagatiḥ* means non-attainment, that is, in the absence of the letter *pa*.

"Being like a spider, he is bound"—because *ba* and *va* are not distinct, "is bound" means he is tied within the collection of words. The word *iva* is used as an ornament for the sentence. Here, by virtue of the Lord’s qualities such as being the bestower of all fruits, the bestowal of the quality of full lifespan upon one who has taken refuge in Him is established; and by the absence of those [qualities], the imposition of the defect of being bound like a spider upon another is likewise established. The specific distinction here is its intermingling with the figure of simile (*upamā*).
O Hari, just as the multitude clinging to your feet appears full in every respect, so too, even if that which is full were to fall away, it would undoubtedly appear as a mere tuft of wool. (1712)

O Hare! the multitude of people clinging to you—attached to your feet—is seen by all as being complete in every respect; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. But the multitude fallen from your path—fallen from your feet—even if naturally complete, would become *ūrṇālakṣyā*: like wool (*ūrṇā*), such as the fleece of sheep and so forth, *alakṣyā* means unworthy of regard. Or else, *ūrṇālakṣyā* means visible (*lakṣyā*) as being primarily composed of that [wool]. Amara states: "The word *ūrṇā* refers to the wool of sheep and the like."

In this alternative, although the word *pūrṇā* (Full) is [actually] *pūrṇā*, it is "deprived of the letter *pa*" (*pac-cyutā*), meaning that the *pa*—the letter *pa*—has fallen away from it. Thus, being devoid of the letter *pa*, it becomes observable and visible as *ūrṇā*, possessing the phonetic sequence of *ūrṇā*. Here, by means of the Lord’s quality of majesty, there is the bestowal of the quality of fullness of life upon the people clinging to His feet. Such possession of greatness is a quality of the Lord; yet, because of that [majesty], there arises the defect of being characterized by wool (*ūrṇā-lakṣyatva*) caused by falling at His feet. Both of these [the quality and the defect] possess a striking charm (*vicchitti*) superior to previous examples.

O Mother, previously, due to your smile which was like camphor, I was indeed devoid of essence and light; then, somehow, having become heavy and devoid of essence, I have now descended to the earth and am entirely transformed.

O Mother! Camphor (ghanasāra), prior to obtaining the state of being your servant—that is, before attaining the status of your gentle smile—was "aghavan," meaning possessed of the suffering caused by not having obtained servitude; for Amara states, "agha means sin, suffering, or calamity. Therefore, it was indeed *asāra* (essence-less); the compound is formed with the negative particle *na*, which carries the sense of *nañ*. Furthermore, it is *anaḥ*; "to breathe" (*ana*) takes the suffix *ac* (in the *pacādi* class), thus *anaḥ* means "living" (*jīvan*), implying that it somehow continues to exist through great effort.

Then, immediately after obtaining a smiling countenance, having become the opposite of everything—having reached a state where all previously mentioned qualities such as being burdened by sin were reversed—he became "rasānagha," meaning sinless on the earth (rasā) and sinless (anagha) through his essence (rasa). Being thus, he was "sāraḥ"—excellent or powerful—and he "āsa," which means he shone. This is derived from the root *as* belonging to the *divādi* class in the sense of shining, in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). By the reversal of both "being burdened by sin" (*aghavat*) and "not being excellent" (*anasāra*), there is the mention of the two opposites: "being excellent" (*sāratva*) and "being sinless" (*rasānaghatva*).

In this context, the word *ghanasāra* first does not possess the letter *gha*, thus being *aghavan*. Being devoid of the letter *gha*, it becomes *nasāra*. Then, when deprived of the letter *na*, it results in *sāra*. Thus, the nature of the word based on the deficiency of its constituent letters has been stated. Now, he describes the nature of the word through the reversal of all its letters in their entirety, beginning with "atha."

The meaning is as follows: "sakalaviparītaḥ" (the complete opposite) results in the word "rasānaghaḥ" (O sinless one), because all its syllables are read in reverse order due to the absence of any deficiency in its phonemes. Here, the excellence of camphor (*ghanasāra*)—consisting of qualities such as its white luster and its power to remove heat—is contrasted with the defect of being "worthless" (*aghavatva*), which arises from the failure to obtain it; furthermore, the excellence of being "essential" (*sāratva*), which results from obtaining its service, is presented. Both of these are composed with a distinctiveness that sets them apart from previous examples. The aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*) arising from the identity between word and meaning is indeed manifest.
Just as,

O Mother, previously even the assembly of immortals was abandoned by the world when they were unseen by you, so now that [world], though possessing infinite prosperity, has perished and been abandoned by your compassionate glance.

O Mother! Previously—even the assembly of immortals, let alone the assembly of mortals—[was abandoned]. This is the sense. Because of the non-attainment of your glance (tvadadṛṣṭeḥ), that which was abandoned by the world (viṣṭapena tyaktam)—meaning it had its residence in its own respective worlds relinquished—is what is described as such. That is to say, it was cast out from its own abode; "destroyed" (naṣṭam) means it reached invisibility somewhere, having vanished. But now, by your compassionate glance (dayādṛśā), it has been abandoned by calamity—that is, it has been released from misfortune.

It is not merely that there is the removal of the undesirable; rather, there is also the attainment of excessive desirable things. Thus he says: "It possesses infinite arising—that is, it becomes characterized by an unlimited prosperity of every kind.
"In this regard, O Goddess, the entire three worlds were abandoned by you;
they had become almost destroyed, but now they have been restored to fullness by you."

Thus, the venerable Yāmuna Ārya’s sublime verse—“By the kindling of the nectar of even a slight compassionate glance, the three worlds, which were lost due to the absence of that [grace] in the past, are now protected with infinite prosperity”—is here kept in mind in accordance with the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa*.

In this context, the word *viṣṭapatyaktam* is such that the syllable *ṣṭa* does not exist—that is, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound preceded by the negative particle *na*. When the syllable *ṣṭa* is removed (*bhraṣṭa*), the resulting word is *vipatyaktam*. This means that from which there is the "arising" (*udaya*) or manifestation of Patañjali, the final incarnation of the Residue (*śeṣāvatāra*). The sense is that all words are produced by him.

In this regard, there is one *ullāsa* (manifestation) wherein, by virtue of the quality of the power of Śrī’s sidelong glance, the host of gods—who are not its objects—possess the defect of abandoning the world; and there is another *ullāsa*, as before, wherein, by virtue of that same quality of the power of her glance, he who is its object possesses the quality of abandoning his calamity and so forth.
Or rather,

O moon of the solar dynasty, may the king of monkeys and the king of the night-stalkers, along with their two younger brothers, find peace— alas!— having attained the king's respect for his kingdom through his wrath and compassion respectively.

O moon of the Raghu dynasty! By your wrath, O King, Vālin and Rāvaṇa—the lords of the monkeys and the night-stalkers—having reached *daram* (fear), were extinguished; that is, they attained extinction (*nirvāṇam*) and went to their end. Their younger brothers, Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa—[addressing the King] with the vocative "O King," which serves as an epithet for "O moon of the Raghu dynasty"—[attained peace]. (Note: *Āji*, *yuddha*, *samiti*, *āji*, *samid*, and *yudh* are synonyms for battle, according to Amara.)

"Attaining regard for the kingdom" (*rājyādaram rājye ādaram etya*) means having acquired excessive regard for it due to the acquisition of the kingdom through hereditary succession; this is the sense. "They both attained tranquility" (*nirvavatuḥ*) means they obtained the bliss of *nirvāṇa*. This is because the root *vā* preceded by the prefix *ni-* is seen to convey both meanings (cessation and bliss). Thus, the *Medinīkośa* states: "Nirvāṇa [is used] in the sense of setting, in bliss, in the bathing of an elephant, in union, and also in liberation."

Here, through the anger and compassion residing in the illustrious Raghunandana—which function as fault and virtue respectively—Vālin and Daśānana, on one hand, and Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa, on the other, first attain the loss of their kingdom and the gain of their kingdom, and subsequently undergo the imposition of the faults and virtues characterized by destruction and happiness. Thus, this combination of both [faults and virtues] is a unique distinction from previous examples, being a confluence of *yathāsaṃkhya*, *śleṣa*, and *tulyayogitā*.

In this regard, the *ullāsa* (manifestation) of the first and fourth [verses] is literal (*anvartha*), while that of the two middle ones is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) due to the "umbrella-bearing" analogy (*chatrinyāya*). Some maintain that, being fully realized through the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason), this does not occupy the ground of a separate ornament (*alaṃkārāntara*). Others hold that, because it consists of worldly meaning (*laukikārtha*), it is not an ornament at all.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of Splendor (*ullāsasara*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of Disdain (*avajñālaṅkārasara*):
"If those two [the cause and the effect] were not present, that would be the ornament of disdain (*avajñālaṅkṛti*) by means of them."

If, by means of those two qualities and defects, there were no imposition of another's quality or defect—namely, the imposition of a quality upon someone through [another's] quality, or the imposition of a defect through a defect—it would constitute the figure of speech known as *avajñā* (disregard).

Just as one might say, "I have taken refuge in you, the ocean of compassion," yet not even a drop of compassion has been shown toward me; let the sinner go to the ocean, or even to the soles of its feet, yet it shall remain no more moist for him.

Here, there is the non-establishment (*anādhāna*) of two qualities—namely, the Lord’s affection for those who have taken refuge in Him, which is like the abundance of water residing in an ocean, and His moistness with the soles of His feet toward the sinner who has sought refuge—in relation to the two qualities [of the other]. Here, the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākyārtha*), being in the form of a simile (*dṛṣṭānta*), is intermingled with two meanings of the individual sentences (*vākyārtha*) in the form of reflections (*pratibimba*) that constitute the original objects (*bimba*).

O Hari, just as a person who turns away from the moon remains forever stained like a blemish upon the lunar orb, so too a person who is averse to you does not attain purity, even while dwelling among a multitude of flowers that are filled with nectar.

Here, by means of the quality characterized as being composed of nectar shared by the assembly of the wise and the orb of the moon, there is no imposition of the quality of brightness upon the Lord and the blemish (kalaṅka)—both of whom are turned away from Him; thus, this is distinguished from the previous example by its association with a simile based on a common attribute established through *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Or rather, O Lotus-eyed One, how can one who disputes with you find your foot—even if he goes to Gayā, performs the *viloma* rite, or even utters your name? (1718)

Alternatively, "vilomatannāmavācya" refers to a sacrifice denoted by the word *pratilomaga*; that is to say, a sacrifice. Whether he be one who has gone to Gayā or one who performs the sacrifice—such a man, O lotus-eyed one! while contending with you—that is, engaging in dispute according to the manner expressed as "Thine is mine" and "Mine is thine"—how could he attain your state?
For Yama, the son of Vivasvat, who is this king residing in your heart, [is the judge].
If you have no dispute with that, do not go to the Ganges, nor to the Kurus.

The sense is that it is stated that the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) belongs only to one who possesses non-contention (*avivāda*), which consists in the offering of the burden of one's own station to Him. All points to be discussed here have been explained in detail in the section on *samāsokti* (condensed expression). In this instance, the qualities such as the sanctity of Gayā and Ayodhyā serve to establish the qualities of attaining the state of the Blessed One.
The non-imparting of a fault by means of a fault:

"O Blessed One, what loss is there for you if some unfortunate person turns his face away from you? If the friend of the lotus should close its petals because of an eye ailment, would that cause any harm to it? (1719)

The instrumental case in "nayanarujā" (by eye-disease) is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*upalakṣaṇa*). Here, through the two defects of being turned away and being closed [respectively], the eye-diseased person and the unfortunate one fail to inflict any defect—specifically the defect of loss—upon the Lord and the lotus, who are friends to each other. This too, like the first example, is mixed with a simile (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Just as he who is known on earth as Śrīnivāsa shines resplendent upon the Hill of Serpents (Ahgiri), even if some should at any time speak of him contrarily, could he ever become devoid of Śrī? (1720)

The Lord who shines upon the Hill of Serpents (Ahigiri), renowned on earth as Śrīnivāsa—there is a word-split here: *saḥ vā niśrīḥ* ("He is indeed devoid of Śrī"). The sense is that even though he has been addressed in a contrary or hostile manner by certain Śaivas who cannot tolerate the supremacy of the Lord, saying "This is not Śrīnivāsa, but rather Kumāra," he remains at all times—or whenever it may be—even if called *niśrīḥ*, meaning "devoid of Śrī"; for this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the prefix *nis-* (as in the expression *nivātapadma*).

The construction "bhavitā vā" (or "it shall become") implies the sense of "what?"—meaning that because Śrī resides only upon His chest, He never at any time abandons His state of being eternally possessed by Śrī. As it is said in the *Śrīmadrāmāyaṇa*: "He who has the Śrīvatsa on His chest is eternally endowed with Śrī. In this alternative sense, even if the word "Śrīnivāsa" were ever uttered in reverse order—that is, read backwards as "savāniśrīḥ"—the resulting meaning "he shall become one devoid of Śrī" is also striking.

Here, the attribution of the defect of being "devoid of Śrī" to the Lord does not actually occur, despite the objection raised by the Śaivas that "He is not Śrīnivāsa. Indeed, the particular aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*) is quite evident.
O Hari, just as we know you to be the Lord of All through the unanimous testimony of the Vedas, what loss is there if some old cow were to call you the lord of a mere mountain? (1721)

Because many scriptural passages (śrutis) are unanimous in propounding a single meaning, [the opponent’s objection] is like the "bellowing of an old cow" (*sthaviragavī*), that is, the prattle of an aged person. By the word *sthavira* ("old"), his mental derangement is indicated; or alternatively, it means "an old cow. In reality, however, the *sthaviragavī* refers to the scriptural passage: "Viṣṇu is the lord of the mountains. By the phrase "some [passage]" (*kāpi*), its lack of unanimity with other scriptural passages is indicated. Here, by describing the defect of inferiority—consisting in the Lord Śrīnivāsa being the lord of only the mountains—through the cited scripture, there is a description of the imposition of a defect characterized as a loss (*hāni*).

Or rather, let people call him "one whose victory is unstable" and "one who does not protect"; yet, why should he—whose eyes are like fresh water-lilies—not be one who conquers here and protects the forest? 1722.

"Janaḥ" means a common person (*pāmara*). According to the *Viśva* and *Medinī* lexicons: "The word *janaḥ* is used for the world, for the world beyond Maharloka, and also for a common person. "Sthirajayaḥ" refers to one whose victory is firm and eternal; he who is not so is "asthirajayaḥ" (one of unstable victory). "Anavanaḥ" means one who does not protect. Through these two epithets, his incapacity to ward off the undesirable and to bestow the desirable is indicated. Thus, let him speak—that is, let him say—what is "vipratīpam," which is directly contrary to the nature of the Blessed One; this is an expression of disregard.

May the Blessed One—who has eyes like fresh water-lilies, whose lotus-eyes are ever-new, who is victorious, and who is immovable (acala), meaning he possesses unwavering victory—be our protector (avana); would he not indeed be so? By these two aforementioned attributes, which stand in contrast to their opposites, it is indicated that he is preeminent in the removal of the undesirable and the attainment of the desirable.

The sense is this: if some vulgar person were to say, "This is Anavana (one who does not protect)," then by that very fact, how could he not be Sthirajaya (the conqueror of the steady) and a protector? In the alternative sense, if the word *navatoyajalocana* (having eyes like fresh water) were uttered in reverse order, it would become *vanajayato naca* (the forest-conqueror, not moving); for such is its formation. Here, through the defect of a vulgar person's inverted description, the absence of such a defect in the Blessed Lord is established, adorned with the resulting aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).
Or rather, O Hari, if a fool censures you, what does that matter to you? Let it be so. And if you do not pay him any heed, alas, he too shall gain nothing at all. (1723)

"What is *chātam*? What is *chinnam*?"—the root *chid* (meaning "to cut") takes the suffix *kta*. By the rule *adecaḥ*, there is the substitution of *āt*. According to Amara: *chinnaṃ chātaṃ lūnam* ("cut, torn, severed"). If you do not respect that censurer, the fool, then it is a marvel that for him too nothing has been *chātam* or *chinnam*. However, the resolution (*parihāra*) is as follows: the word division in the second half-verse is *kim api śātam*. Nothing at all is *śātam*; that is, no happiness (*sukha*) exists. According to Amara: *śarma-śāta-sukhāni ca* ("bliss, ease, and happiness"). [The form *śātam* is derived from] the root *śo* (meaning "to thin" or "to diminish"), belonging to the *divādi* class; the suffix *tan* is applied by way of general rule (*bāhulaka*).

The term *ādecaḥ* implies the substitution of *āt*. The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is "that which makes the inauspicious auspicious. Here, there is the non-occurrence of the fault of being a fool, which is caused by the act of censuring [the Lord]; that is, the non-occurrence of the fault of foolishness, which is prompted by the fault of the Lord’s disregard. Thus, there are two varieties of the figure *Avajñā* (Disregard). The distinction is that the first is pure (*śuddha*), while the second is enlivened by paronomasia (*śleṣa*).

Regarding this, some maintain that in examples of "disregard" (avajñā), such as "A pitcher receives very little water even upon reaching the ocean; if the lotuses close, what loss is there for the moon of nectar? and so forth, one need not accept a separate figure of speech called avajñā. For in those cases, since the description consists in the non-production of a quality or defect in one thing despite the presence of a quality or defect in another—both of which are capable of producing such effects—it is more appropriate to speak of it simply as *viśeṣokti* (the description of a specific distinction).

They say that this is because the definition [of *viśeṣokti*] remains intact, as it is described through the absence of that abundance in a mountain pass despite the abundance of the waters of the ocean, and the absence of defects in the moon despite the closing of the lotuses; however, in reality, the figure of speech *viśeṣokti* is not easily applicable here.

They say that in such examples as "The waning of the oil in the heart did not occur even while the lamp of love was burning," there is an absence of the defining characteristic of *viśeṣokti* (the figure of speech characterized by a specific cause), because the well-known causal relationship between the proximity of the ocean's waters and the departure from the mountain, and between the abundance of water and its lack, does not exist here—just as there is no such relationship between the flame of a lamp and the waning of its oil.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, the "Chapter on Disregard" (Avajñāsara), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the "Chapter on Permission" (Anujñāsara):
Permission (*anujñā*) is the seeking even of a fault out of eagerness for its virtues, if such exists.
The figure of speech *anujñā* (permission) consists in the solicitation of even an object renowned for its defects, due to a longing for some particularly intense quality.

O Bhavahara, O Lord of the mountain whose peaks are like the hoods of serpents, let there be only distance between you and me; for that is the cause of my respect, whereas proximity leads only to neglect.

In this case, the distance from the Lord of Śrī Veṅkaṭagiri is the defect; the acceptance of that [distance] is the cause, and being a reason for respect is the excellence (*guṇa*). And this is shown by a general *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by another matter) in the form of supporting a particular instance.

O Acyuta, whether I remain as a stationary mountain belonging to you, or even if I possess mobility, does it matter? For were you not, in the past, the bestower of liberation upon all things—both moving and unmoving—in the Kosala kingdom?

In this context, the fault lies in praying for birth as an immobile being such as a tree or creeper, or as a lower animal such as a serpent, bird, or deer; however, the merit lies in the fact that even abiding on Veṅkaṭādri in such a form becomes a cause for liberation. And this merit is demonstrated by the example of the bestowal of ultimate bliss upon all beings, both moving and stationary, within the Kosalā region.

Or rather, let there be neither attachment to you in me, as there was in the King of Cedi, nor enmity; but let there be an uninterrupted continuity of remembrance toward You, O Acyuta, which may endure.

In this context, it should be understood that the speaker’s longing for the defect of enmity toward the Blessed One—exemplified by Caidya and others—is due to a craving for the quality characterized by being the cause of an uninterrupted stream of remembrance of Him. Here, the verse "From hatred, kings such as Caidya [attained perfection]" should be kept in mind.
Or rather, let this self be cast away anywhere whatsoever in Your sacred ford; O Acyuta, what loss could there be from that, since it proceeds by Your power? (1727)

O Acyuta! Let this conscious self become a *nihākā*—a specific type of aquatic creature known as a lizard (*godhikā*)—in any of Your holy places, such as Svāmipuṣkariṇī; for according to Amara, "the words *nihākā* and *godhikā* are synonymous. Even upon attaining the state of a *nihākā*, through Your yoga—that is, through meditation on You or by association with Your devotees—it is by Your majesty that [it may attain] a favorable and virtuous course of existence.

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *prasavya* is of common gender (*vācyaliṅga*) and denotes that which is adverse or favorable. Here, "of oneself" (*ātmanaḥ*) is the ellipsis. The sense is: "What loss would there be? No loss at all; rather, it would surely lead to welfare. The intended meaning is that such is the power of your association. In the alternative interpretation, the word *nihākā*—by means of your connection (*tāvakena yogena*), that is, by way or through skillful means (*upāyena*, *yuktyā*)—is *prasavyā*, meaning adverse or contrary; [the phrase] "of that" (*tasyāḥ*) is in the ablative case. That is to say, because of reciting [it] in reverse order through skillful means or strategy.

The repetition "kāhāni kāhāni" would possess a sequential order. In this view, regarding the word "syāt," there is doubling [of the syllable] according to the rule "anaci ca. Here too, the figure of speech is *anujñā* (consent/approbation), just as before.
O enemy of Kaṃsa, if you wish to grant us nothing but saṃsāra itself, then let it be so; yet could that very saṃsāra ever truly be "substantial" (sāra) if it were not devoid of divine fortune? 1728

"O enemy of Kaṃsa! The meaning is that this very saṃsāra has been experienced by us since beginningless time. If you wish to give [it] even beyond this—that is, if you desire to grant it further—let it be so; for the command of the ruler is indeed not to be transgressed by those subject to his rule. Even then, nothing undesirable occurs, as he says: 'even at any time. That very same saṃsāra, through divine prosperity (*devasaṃpad*), [becomes auspicious].
As it is said: 'In this world there are two types of created beings: the divine and the demonic;
that which is devoted to Viṣṇu is divine, while the opposite is demonic.'"

Such is the divine endowment (*daivī saṃpat*) described by the aforementioned manner—that which was proclaimed in the passage beginning with "Fearlessness, purity of being" and concluding with "The divine endowment leads to liberation. One who is not separated from that, but rather joined with it, might at some time become essential (*sāra*), or the construction may be "might even at some time become essential"; the particle *api* is used here in the sense of possibility.
As we are driven here and there by our karmas according to the will of the Lord,
may our minds be fixed upon Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, through auspicious practices and acts of charity.

The meaning is this: according to the manner described above, at any time or in any place, through the ripening of such fortuitous merit (yādṛcchika-sukṛta) and other factors, devotion may indeed arise toward You; thus, its essential value is certainly possible. For that [devotion] is said to be of a status equal to liberation (apavarga).
O Lord of Kariśaila, if You are gracious, if I am near You, and if there is faultless devotion toward You—[then all is attained].
O Blessed One, if even your servant is thus united [with you], then this very cycle of existence is itself liberation.

Thus [it is said]. In this context, "O God" (*he deva*) is an address. The meaning—that the very word *saṃsāra* (transmigration), when separated from the syllable *saṃ* by means of the word-form *saṃ*, would become the word *sāra* (essence)—also enhances the aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*). Here, one should understand that the prayer for *saṃsāra* in its form as a defect is based on the possibility of the emergence of qualities such as being born into a divine fortune (*daiva-sampat*) at some point or other. This ornament (*alaṃkāra*) is likewise the original invention of Dīkṣita.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of Permission (anujñālaṅkāra), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra. Now begins the Chapter on Disparagement (tiraskārasara):
"If there is aversion toward a quality due to its association with a defect, that is tiraskṛti."
If there is hatred even toward that which is well-known as a quality due to its being accompanied by a specific defect, that is the figure of speech called *tiraskāra* (disparagement).
O Madhusūdana, may I never possess even the riches of Indra, for if one is immersed in them, one does not—whether by chance or otherwise—attain remembrance of You. (1729)

In this case, because of the connection with the fault of forgetting the Blessed One, there is aversion even toward the riches of Mahendra, which—though established as virtues—are [actually] defects. This figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) is the invention of Paṇḍitarāja; for he, having defined this [figure] according to the stated method beginning with "due to the persistence of a specific fault," and having not defined this [other] "disparagement" (*tiraskāra*), finds his only refuge in the forgetfulness of the author of the *Kuvalayānanda*, who nonetheless defines "consent" (*anujñā*). Otherwise, why would we, O Lord of the Pramathas, having returned to our natural state, not seek the riches of the immortals, while you remain near us in the form of a Piśāca?

It should be understood that this may also arise from the expectation of the presence of qualities such as being born into a lineage endowed with divine fortune (*daivasaṃpad*). This ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is likewise the original invention of Dīkṣita.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of Permission (anujñālaṅkāra), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra. Now begins the Chapter on Disparagement (tiraskārasara):
"If there is aversion toward a quality due to its association with a defect, that is tiraskṛti."
If there is hatred toward that which is well-known as a quality because of its association with a particular defect, that is the figure of speech called *tiraskāra* (disparagement).
O Madhusūdana, may I never possess even the riches of Indra, for if one is immersed in them, one does not attain spontaneous remembrance of You, even by chance. (1729)

In this case, because of the connection with the fault of forgetting the Blessed One, there is aversion even toward the riches of Indra—which, though established as virtues, are [here regarded as such] due to that very fault. This poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) is the discovery of Paṇḍitarāja; for he, having defined it according to the stated method beginning with "due to the persistence of a specific fault," and having not defined this [other] figure, *tiraskāra*, while defining *anujñā* (permission), has only his own forgetfulness to fall back upon. Otherwise, why would we—having returned to our natural state—pray to you, O Lord of the Pramathas, for the celestial riches of the immortals, saying, "May we enjoy them"? If it were otherwise, we would have said: "Why do we pray for the riches of the immortals, O Lord of the Pramathas? [implying they are undesirable]. Thus, the definition of *anujñā* by the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* is merely a lapse of memory. Otherwise, how could one say: "Why do we, having returned to our natural state, pray to you, O Lord of the Pramathas, for the riches of the immortals, saying 'May we enjoy them'? [since they are undesirable]. Therefore, the definition of *anujñā* by the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* is nothing but a lapse of memory. Otherwise, we would have to say: "Why do we, having returned to our natural state, pray to you, O Lord of the Pramathas, for the riches of the immortals, saying 'May we enjoy them'? [since they are undesirable]. Thus, the definition of *anujñā* by the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* is merely a lapse of memory. [since they are undesirable]. Thus, the definition of *anujñā* by the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* is nothing but a lapse of memory. Otherwise, we would have to say: "Why do we, having returned to our natural state, pray to you, O Lord of the Pramathas, for the riches of the immortals, saying 'May we enjoy them'? [since they are undesirable]. Thus, the definition of *anujñā* by the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* is merely a lapse of memory. Otherwise, we would have to say: "Why do we, having returned to our natural state, pray to you, O Lord of the Pramathas, for the riches of the immortals, saying 'May we enjoy them'? [since they are undesirable]. Thus, the definition of *anujñā* by the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* is nothing but a lapse of memory. [since they are undesirable]. Thus, the definition of *anujñā* by the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* is merely a lapse of memory. Indra and the other gods exist with the tips of their crowns shattered by the blows of the heavy pestles of grain-beating upon the thresholds of your palaces.
Thus he stated that since contempt would not manifest in the verse cited there, [the definition] would fail to apply.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, the Chapter on Disparagement (*tiraskāra*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of the Slight (*leśa*):
"If a quality is treated as a defect, or a defect as a quality,"
The wise call that ornament *leśa*, which is described as follows:

Where a quality is described as a defect because it is a means to an undesirable end, and a defect is described as a quality because it is a means to a desired end, that is the poetic figure named *leśa* (the slight).
Just as when many mountains shine upon the surface of the earth, O Mountain, this is the fruit of your bearing Indra— that all [the gods] rest upon your summit free from fear.

Here, in the first half-verse, the defect of the other mountains being unable to support the Lord is conceived as a virtue because it is conducive to the manifestation of fearlessness. In the second half-verse, the virtue of Śrīnivāsa’s supporting [the earth] is conceived as a defect because it is the cause of being borne upon the heads by all people.

And this [verse] constitutes praise by means of *samāsokti* (poetic suggestion), wherein there flashes forth the conduct of an irrelevant subject: that while many kings devoid of merit remain in a state of ease, a king endowed with supreme virtues such as magnanimity will experience the distress of being crowded by supplicants.
Indra and the other gods exist with the tips of their crowns shattered by the blows of the heavy pestles of rice used for pounding at the thresholds of your palaces.
Thus he stated: "Because, in the verse cited therein, there would be no occurrence of the manifestation of contempt."
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, the Chapter on Disparagement (tiraskāra), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of Leśa (leśālaṅkāra):
"If a quality is treated as a defect, or a defect as a quality..."
The wise call that ornament *leśa* (a slight hint).

That figure of speech in which a quality (guṇa) is described as a defect (doṣa) because it is a means to an undesirable end, and a defect is described as a quality because it is a means to a desirable end, is called the ornament (alaṃkāra) named Leśa.

O Mountain, just as you remain free from fear upon the surface of the earth despite the many other kings rising up, this is the fruit of your support of Indra: that all [the gods] rest their heads upon you.

In the first half of this verse, the defect of the other mountains being unable to support the Lord is conceived as a merit, since it is conducive to the manifestation of fearlessness. In the second half, the merit of Śrīnivāsa’s supporting [the earth] is conceived as a defect, because it serves as the cause for the crowns of all people to be placed upon him. And this is a praise by means of *samāsokti* (synecdoche), wherein there is the manifestation of an unmentioned worldly situation: that while many kings devoid of virtues remain in a state of ease, a king endowed with supreme virtues such as generosity will experience the distress of the thronging of supplicants.

It is combined with censure in the form of the manifestation of censure and with "disguised praise" (*vyājastuti*) in the form of the manifestation of praise, occurring respectively in the first and second halves [of the verse].
Intolerance alone is superior; fie upon the power of forbearance! O Rame, others may be happy, but your friend is made to suffer because she endures everything from everyone.

Here too, there is a description of faults and virtues as being virtues and faults respectively; however, the distinction lies in its being embellished by the figure of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth).
O daughter of the ocean, do not harbor the pride that you are a treasury of all virtues; for it was by those very virtues that you became the cause of the churning of your own most pure father.

In this instance, the description of a quality as a defect is "pure" (śuddha). Nor should it be suspected that this figure is already accounted for by the two forms of *vyājastuti* (ironical praise), because here there is no final resolution through a reversal of the meaning presented on the surface in every case. For in the verse beginning "A treasury of all virtues," the intention is not to praise Fortune (*śrī*) in the form of a reproach against her qualities on the part of someone distressed by poverty; rather, it is precisely a censure [of the person] on account of being the cause of his father's ruin.

Thus, in the verse beginning "Asahanam eva jyāyaḥ," the intention is not to censure others who possess the quality of forbearance (*bhūmi*), but rather to describe one’s own state of ease; for in this statement of one who is distressed by seeing the exhaustion of those who endure everything, it is improper to censure others, as it would be more appropriate to offer praise instead. Even if there were *vyājastuti* (ironic praise) in the verse beginning "bhūyassu samullāsiṣu," let it be so, for since that figure has its own scope, it cannot override this [intended meaning].
O Mother, while your own beloved—the mendicant of the three worlds and friend to the ragged—remains, how can you be proud because of the relief from the world’s poverty? (1733)

In this instance, because the quality perceived at the conclusion—which consists in the removal of the poverty of the entire world other than the Blessed One—is not described as a defect, and because the defect of the Blessed One being described as a defect—namely, the failure to dispel His state of being a mendicant for the three worlds and His friendship with the poorly clothed—is not conceived as a quality, there is *vyājastuti* (ironical praise) entirely untouched by even a trace of *leśa* (the figure of speech involving the attribution of a defect to a quality or vice versa), since quality and defect reside in different subjects; thus, its scope is clearly established.

Therefore, even a slight trace of *vyājastuti* (concealed praise) does not constitute a sublation [of the primary figure]; thus, it should be noted that in the previously cited verse beginning with "bhūyassu samullāsiṣu," there is a coexistence of both figures.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, the Section on Leśa (Hinting), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra. Now begins the Section on Mudrā (Seal):
Mudrā is the indication of a meaning through words intended for another primary subject.

The ornament *mudrā* (the seal) consists in the indication of a meaning intended to be indicated by means of words primarily devoted to conveying another intended meaning. This too is indeed an innovation of Dīkṣita. The distilled meaning is this: *mudrā* is the communication of a specific meaning that is to be made known—by a word devoted to the primary subject matter, or by a part of such a word, or by a collection of words, or by a collection of parts of words, or by a collection of both—in whatever manner possible. As for the part of a word, it may be meaningful or meaningless in the context;
and the meaning to be indicated may be relevant to the context or irrelevant; one should not be overly fastidious about these details.
Indra and the other gods exist with the tips of their crowns shattered by the blows of the heavy pestles of grain upon the thresholds of your palaces.
Thus he stated: "Because, in the verse cited therein, there would be the consequence that the suggestion of contempt (*tiraskāra*) does not arise."
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, the Chapter on Disparagement (*tiraskāra*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of the Slight (*leśa*):
"If a quality is treated as a defect, or a defect as a quality,"
The wise call that ornament *leśa* (a slight indication).

That figure of speech in which a quality is described as a defect because it is a means to an undesirable end, and a defect is described as a quality because it is a means to a desired end, is called *leśa*.

Just as when many mountains shine resplendent upon the surface of the earth, O mountain, this is the fruit of your steadfastness toward Indra— that all [the gods] rest their heads upon you without fear.

Here, in the first half [of the verse], the defect of the other mountains being unable to support the Lord is conceived as a merit by virtue of its favoring the unimpeded manifestation [of His power]. In the second half, the merit of Śrīnivāsa’s supporting [the earth] is conceived as a defect by virtue of being the cause for the crowns of all people to be placed upon Him. And this is a praise through *samāsokti* (poetic suggestion), wherein there arises the manifestation of an unstated worldly situation: that while many kings devoid of merit remain in a state of ease, a king endowed with supreme virtues such as generosity will suffer the distress of the thronging of supplicants.

It is combined with censure in the form of an expression of blame and with "disguised praise" (*vyājastuti*) in the form of an expression of praise, occurring respectively in the first and second halves [of the verse].
"Intolerance alone is superior; fie upon the glory of forbearance! O Rame, others are happy, but you, my friend, who endure everything with all, are held in contempt by everyone. (1731)

Here too, there is the description of faults and virtues as being virtues and faults respectively; however, the distinction lies in its being embellished by the figure of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle).

O daughter of the ocean, do not harbor pride, thinking yourself a treasury of all virtues; for it was by those very same qualities that you became the cause of the churning of even your most pure father.

In this case, the description of a quality as a defect is "pure" (śuddha). Nor should it be suspected that this figure is already accounted for by "disguised praise" (vyājastuti) in its two forms, because here there is no final resolution in the opposite of the meaning directly expressed on the surface. Indeed, in the verse beginning with "A treasury of all virtues," the intention is not to praise Fortune through a reproach of her qualities on the part of someone distressed by poverty; rather, it is precisely a censure [of her] because she is the cause of his father's destruction.

Thus, in the verse beginning with "asahanameva jyāyaḥ," the intention is not to censure others who possess the quality of forbearance (bhūmi), but rather to express one’s own state of ease; for in this statement of one who is pained by observing the exhaustion of those who endure everything, it is improper to censure others, and on the contrary, it is more appropriate to offer praise. Even if there were *vyājastuti* (ironical praise) in the verse beginning with "bhūyassu samullāsiṣu," let it be so, since that figure has its own scope and cannot override this [intended meaning].
O Mother, while your own beloved—the mendicant of the three worlds and friend of the ragged-clad one—remains, how can you be proud because of the relief from the world’s poverty?

In this instance, since the quality perceived at the conclusion—consisting in the removal of the poverty of the entire world other than the Blessed One—is not described as a defect, and since the defect of the Blessed One being described as such—namely, the defect of not dispelling His state of being a mendicant for the three worlds and His friendship with the poorly clothed—is not conceived as a quality, there exists a *vyājastuti* (disguised praise) entirely untouched by even a trace of the *leśa* (slight) figure, because the quality and the defect reside in different objects; thus, its scope is clearly established.

Therefore, even a trace of *vyājastuti* (artful praise) does not constitute a sublation [of the primary figure]; thus, it should be noted that in the previously cited verse beginning with "bhūyassu samullāsiṣu," there is a coexistence (*samāveśa*) of both figures.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, the Section on Leśa (Glimmer), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra. Now begins the Section on Mudrā (Seal):
Mudrā is the indication of a meaning by means of words intended for a different subject, serving as a pointer to a hidden sense.

The ornament *mudrā* consists in the indication of a meaning intended to be suggested by means of words primarily devoted to conveying a different (explicit) meaning. This too is indeed an innovation of Dīkṣita. The distilled definition is as follows: *mudrā* is the communication of a particular meaning that is to be made known—by means of a word, a part of a word, a collection of words, a collection of parts of words, or a collection of both—in any manner whatsoever, through a word or phrase primarily devoted to the contextual subject matter. As for the "part of a word," it may be meaningful or meaningless in the present context; and as for the "meaning to be indicated," it may be either contextual (*prakṛta*) or non-contextual (*aprakṛta*). One should not be overly insistent on these distinctions.

Those groups of sages, endowed with minds devoted as they truly are, worship her at her feet—this Sugīti, born from the *bhṛgu* and *jagaṇa* meters, praised by the disciplined, possessing unequalled victory, and a true knowledge. (1734)

In this verse, which is primarily intended to describe Lakṣmī, another meaning is also intended by virtue of its being composed in the *gīti* meter. Regarding that, if the primary sense is directed toward Lakṣmī, the meaning is as follows: "The groups of sages (*ṛṣigaṇāḥ*) who are constant" means those whose senses are restrained—that is, whose minds are one-pointed—or alternatively, those who are "exclusive devotees" (*ekāntinaḥ*). These groups of sages, being "devoid of sin" (*āgo'petāḥ*)—meaning being free from transgression (*āgas*), i.e., faultless—worship and serve that Fortune (*śrī*) at her feet (*padoḥ*, i.e., her two feet). The compound *apetāpoḍha* is a genitive (fifth-case) compound.

Bhṛgu’s daughter was born from the lineage of Bhṛgu—the group consisting of the sons and grandsons of the sage named Bhṛgu, headed by Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ; within that lineage, the two gods Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ were manifested. And Khyāti gave birth to Śrī, who became the wife of Nārāyaṇa, the God of gods.

Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*. [I bow] to her who is to be praised (*īḍyām*) by ascetics (*yatibhiḥ*), that is, by wandering mendicants (*maskaribhiḥ*); who possesses unequalled victory (*aviṣamajayām*), meaning whose victory is "unequalled" in the sense that it is just and universally acknowledged; who is thus of beautiful song (*sugītim*), for "song" (*gītiḥ*) means singing, and she is one whose song is "beautiful," meaning whose fame is praiseworthy. This "knowledge" (*vidyām*) refers to the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyām*), which is to say, Śrī. As it is said: "O Goddess, you are the knowledge of the Self, the means for attaining the fruit of liberation."

Because wealth (*śrī*) is denoted by the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*) in such passages as "me, who am accompanied by knowledge," there is here a metaphorical identification of cause and effect. "Worship with the mind; meditate upon"—this is the instruction of a certain teacher to a certain disciple.

In the case of the *gītivṛtta* (lyrical meter), however, those *gaṇas* which are "endowed with *ga*"—meaning endowed or joined with a *guru* (heavy syllable) designated by the term *ga*—and which are "endowed at the end" (*asyānte*)—meaning they are joined with a *guru* at their conclusion—are to be understood here as having four *mātrās* (*catuṣkalāḥ*), provided that all [syllables] beginning, middle, and end are *gurus*. Furthermore, those *gaṇas* consisting of four *laghus* (light syllables) are established in the *āryā* and other such meters. These are "unrestricted," meaning they are devoid of a fixed order and are employed according to the requirements of each specific case. Regarding the verse: *jñeyāssarvādimadhyāntaguravo'tra catuṣkalāḥ | gaṇāścaturlaghūpetāḥ pañcāryādiṣu saṃsthitāḥ* || It means: In this context, the *gaṇas* should be known as having four *mātrās*, being either heavy in every position (beginning, middle, and end), or otherwise; while those *gaṇas* composed of four *laghus* are situated in the *āryā* and similar meters.

Thus, because the rule for the application of syllable-groups (gaṇas) in Āryā meters is taught as being unrestricted—consisting of those heavy at the beginning, middle, or end, accompanied by four light syllables, and interspersed with other groups of four light syllables—in this context, there is one group heavy at both ends; three groups heavy at the beginning, middle, and end, namely the *bhagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, and *sagaṇa*; and one group consisting of four light syllables. These five groups are to be employed in the *Āryā* and other such meters as the occasion requires.
