This is the meaning of the *kārikā*. To the question "And how many are they?", he says: "The seers" (*ṛṣi*). The meaning is that there are seven groups (*gaṇa*) corresponding to the number of seers. The term "gopetāḥ" (accompanied by *go*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "those [groups] accompanied by [the syllable] *go*, which are groups of seers not fixed [to specific meters]. To the question "And who are they?", he says: "Those beginning with *bha*" (*bhajamanasā*). This means those whose designations begin with the letter *bha*. To the question "And where are they to be employed?", he says: "In the feet" (*padoriti*). This means in the two feet consisting of the first and second halves of a verse-quarter (*śloka-caturthāṃśa*), i.e., the preceding and following halves. The word *pada* is substituted for the word *pāda* according to the rule "*paddan*."

They resort to and take refuge in [these rules]. Now, regarding the groups (*gaṇas*) of four syllables, which might otherwise occur without restriction, he establishes a rule with the words "born of Bhṛgu" (*bhṛguja*). "Born of Bhṛgu" refers to Paraśurāma; he is counted as the sixth among the incarnations of the Lord, such as the Fish (*Matsya*) and others. From this, the term *praṣṭha* (the foremost/sixth) is obtained. Thus, "born of the group of Bhṛgu's son" (*bhṛgujagaṇajā*) means that the sixth group is the *ja*-named group (*jagaṇa*); the meaning is that the sixth group must consist of a *jagaṇa*. By this, the rule is stated that the sixth [group] must be a *jagaṇa*.

"Aviṣamajayām" means that in the odd parts (viṣame), specifically in the positions of the odd-numbered gaṇas, there is no *jagaṇa*—thus "aviṣamajayā. The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *yā* (to go) to form *jayā*. That which does not possess this [jagaṇa] is "aviṣamajayā"; the meaning is that it is devoid of a *jagaṇa* in the first, third, and other odd positions. By this, the rule is stated that a *jagaṇa* should not be employed in the odd positions. It is "īḍyām," meaning worthy of praise, by means of *yatibhiḥ*, i.e., pauses (*vicchedaiḥ*), according to the grammatical injunction: "The term *yati* denotes a pause."

The meaning is "endowed with a charming division. This is because its definition will be stated later as "possessing the beauty of a pause" (*kṛtayatiśobhām*). "This *sugīti*" means this beautiful song, that is, the *āryā* known by the name *gīti*. "May I know [this] science"—this is the first person singular of the optative (*liṅ*) from the root *vid*. Herein is the characteristic: "In the first half of the *āryā*, there are invariably seven gaṇas followed by a *ga* (a short syllable); there is no *ja* (a heavy syllable) here in the odd positions; and the sixth [syllable] is not light. *lakṣmaitatsaptagaṇā gopetā bhavati neha viṣame jaḥ | ṣaṣṭhoyaṃ na laghū vā prathame'rdhe niyatamāryāyāḥ ||* [This is the definition: In the first half of the *āryā*, there are invariably seven gaṇas followed by a *ga* (a short syllable); there is no *ja* (a heavy syllable) here in the odd positions; and the sixth [syllable] is not light. The second half is free from these restrictions. The *āryā* has two halves; the first half consists of seven and a half feet, while the second half consists of six and a half feet. The first half is divided into three feet: the first foot consists of three *ma-gaṇas* (a heavy syllable between two light syllables), the second foot consists of a *ra-gaṇa* (a light syllable between two heavy syllables) and a *ta-gaṇa* (a heavy syllable between two light syllables), and the third foot consists of a *na-gaṇa* (three light syllables) and a *ga* (a short syllable). The second half is divided into two and a half feet: the first foot consists of a *bha-gaṇa* (a light syllable between two heavy syllables) and a *sa-gaṇa* (a heavy syllable between two light syllables), and the second foot consists of a *ya-gaṇa* (a light syllable between two light syllables) and a *ta-gaṇa* (a heavy syllable between two light syllables). Thus, the first half consists of seven and a half feet, and the second half consists of six and a half feet. The first half is called the *pūrvārdha* (first half) and the second half is called the *aparārdha* (second half). The *āryā* is so named because it is derived from the *āryā-gīti*. It is said: "The *āryā* is the mother of all meters; she is the source of all poetic compositions. Therefore, one should strive to compose verses in the *āryā* meter. The *āryā* is of two kinds: the *pathyā-āryā* and the *vipulā-āryā*. The *pathyā-āryā* is that in which the seventh syllable of the first half is short, and the fifth syllable of the second half is long. The *vipulā-āryā* is that in which the seventh syllable of the first half is long, and the fifth syllable of the second half is short. There are four types of *vipulā*: the *pathyā-vipulā*, the *prathamā-vipulā*, the *dvitīyā-vipulā*, and the *tṛtīyā-vipulā*. The *pathyā-vipulā* is that in which the seventh syllable of the first half is long, and the fifth syllable of the second half is short. The *prathamā-vipulā* is that in which the seventh syllable of the first half is short, and the fifth syllable of the second half is short. The *dvitīyā-vipulā* is that in which the seventh syllable of the first half is short, and the fifth syllable of the second half is long. The *tṛtīyā-vipulā* is that in which the seventh syllable of the first half is long, and the fifth syll
Since the characteristics stated in the first half of the Āryā exist in the second half as well,

the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa) sang that Gīti, which possesses the beauty of the caesura in both halves, provided that the characteristics mentioned in the first quarter of the Āryā somehow occur in both halves.
Thus, the entire definition of song has been stated very clearly.

Here, by means of the phrase *sugītim* (a beautiful song), which is intent upon describing Śrī Lakṣmī, the fact that this meter is named *gīti* is indicated; and by the words *bhajamanasā* and so forth, the specific rules regarding its gaṇas and other such matters are indicated. Thus, there is the figure of speech *mudrā* (the seal), enlivened by a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the relevant (*prakṛta*) and the irrelevant (*aprakṛta*). Nor should it be argued that there is only *śleṣa* here and not *mudrā*; for even when *śleṣa* is present, since the indication of the matter to be indicated (*sūcyārtha-sūcana*) is also clearly manifest, the figure *mudrā* remains unrestrictedly applicable.

Nor should one entertain the misconception that, because of this pun (*śleṣa*), a distinct object is difficult to find; for a distinct object will be demonstrated immediately hereafter. Therefore, in this case, there is indeed a commixture (*saṃkara*) of the figures of speech *śleṣa* and *mudrā*; such is the direction [of the argument].

Although in this treatise on poetics (*alaṃkāra-grantha*) there is no necessity to indicate the name of the meter (*vṛtta*), nevertheless, since this verse is included within the science of prosody (*chandaśśāstra*) as an illustration (*lakṣya*) that does not deviate from its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), it is possible to indicate it; thus, one must apply the definition. For this very reason: "The *mudrā* [figure] is the indication of a suggested meaning by means of words directed toward the subject at hand: 'She is eternally heavy, young, and broad-eyed. (This verse serves as an illustration of the meter *vipulā*.)

In this context, within the description of the heroine (*nāyikā*), the *mudrā* (a figure of speech) consists in the indication of the subject matter by means of the presentation of the *yugmavipulā* [meter] in the *anuṣṭubh* [verse], which serves as the very nature of its name. Although in this work there is no need to indicate the names of the meters (*vṛtta*), nevertheless, since this second half-verse falls within the body of the *Chandaḥśāstra*—which deals with both definitions and examples—it possesses the quality of being indicative; it is with this intention that the definition should be applied, so that the text of the *Kuvalayānanda* may be consistent.

In this context, the reading found in some recent manuscripts—"by being included within the treatise on prosody" (*chandaśśāstramadhyapātitvena*)—expressed with an instrumental ending, is not clear; for in the majority of ancient manuscripts, the reading with a locative ending—"in being included within" (*madhyapātitve*)—is observed, and it has been explained accordingly in the commentary *Rasikarañjanī*. Thus, that text states: "Now, one might object: 'Since the meter (*vṛtta*) is not to be defined here in the context of describing the conduct of a young woman, its name need not be indicated, and therefore the figure of speech *mudrā* does not occur here'—to this he replies with the words 'even though' (*yadyapi*)."

True; although there is no need to indicate the name of the meter here, nevertheless, if the latter half of the definition of *vipulā*—namely, "that in which the seventh syllable is light in both even feet is considered *yugmavipulā*"—were illustrated by the example "nitambagurvī taruṇī," then there would be a need to indicate the meter. With this in mind, he offers the following rebuttal with the words "tathāpi" (nevertheless), stating that this is an illustration of the figure of speech *mudrā*.

By this [statement], those who—highly favoring the reading ending in the instrumental case (*chandaśśāstramadhyapātitvena*)—grasp that the figure *mudrā* belongs only to that which indicates an unstated (aprastuta) suggested meaning, provided it occurs within a work belonging to the *chandaśśāstra* (treatise on prosody) characterized by both definition and illustration, such as the second half of the verse beginning with "nitambagurvī," and not to anything else within poetry that indicates an unstated suggested meaning, are refuted.

Furthermore, if the text were read with the third case ending (*tṛtīyāntatayā*), it would result in the aforementioned situation where the commentary and the subject of the commentary fail to look toward one another. As for those [works] in whose *Candrāloka* examples and definitions are found, they are mostly those very same ones; for others, new ones are composed.

Thus, since the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* has himself promised to compose verses containing both definitions and illustrations for the figures of speech seen in the *Candrāloka* composed by Jayadeva, [it follows that] here...

This is because the method of constructing verses found in other texts is untenable, and because a metrical work characterized by such definitions and illustrations is unknown. In reality, however, the firm conviction is that *mudrā* as an ornament consists precisely in the indication of the subject matter at hand (*prakṛtārtha*). It should be understood that *mudrā* is the indication of a matter to be indicated, whether it be the subject matter at hand or not; for its formal definition is: "The indication of a matter to be indicated (*sūcyārtha*) by means of words intended for the subject matter at hand."

And thus, although such a figure does not fall within the scope of compositions characterized by those specific definitions due to the exigencies of a poet’s creative impulse, this ornament remains entirely intact in other poems wherever there is an indication of irrelevant episodes, figures of speech, and so forth—as in the verse beginning: "Having turned the deer of the Tāṭakya [Rāvaṇa] into gold, I playfully sport with the tiger [Śiva], while my finger-ring alternates between the two jar-like breasts."

Otherwise, for the great poets who are the foremost among the assembly of bards, the composition of the life-stories of Rāma and others with such great effort would result in the futility of employing the variety of words indicative of *vṛtti*, *alaṃkāra*, and so forth, wherever they might appear. Regarding this, Veṅkaṭārya of Bukkapattana, the author of the *Alaṃkārakaustubha*, has stated: "When the non-contextual is indicated by the poet through words intended for the contextual meaning, that which is thus indicated is declared to be the *mudrā* ornament."
Thus defining this ornament called *mudrā* as the indication of an irrelevant matter that is to be indicated, [the author] says:

"The beauty of the sapphire in her tresses, the weight of the conch on her neck, the makara-design on her breast, and the luster of jasmine in her teeth which are lovely with the nectar of her smile..."
May that Mahāpadmā, who delights in Mukunda, whose feet are adorned with tortoises and whose pair of hands holds lotuses— the beloved of Mukunda— be instantly propitious toward me.

Having thus cited [the verse], [the commentator] indicated the nine treasures (*navanidhi*)—which were not the subject at hand—by stating: "Here, by the words *nīla* and so forth, there is an indication of the nine treasures. Indeed, in the context of a description of Lakṣmī, the indication of the nine treasures was not the relevant topic. All other details have been elaborated by us in the commentary on the verse beginning with *paryāyeṇa stanakalaśayoḥ* in our *Haṃsasaṃdeśarasāsvādinī*.
Just as a serpent adorned with a necklace [is formidable], so too this period of Rāhu among the foremost planets remains constantly inauspicious during the days of the celestial wanderers.

Endowed with the Vaijayantī garland, he is a possessor of unsurpassed enjoyment (*bhogī*), where the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) denotes abundance, praise, or excellence. He is the enemy who is Time (*kāla*) for Rāhu; he is the Blessed One among the foremost of luminaries, such as the Ādityas; and he dwells within the *vāras*—the assemblies of sky-traveling deities (*diviṣad*), the planets (*graha*), and the days (*vāsara*). He is "internal" (*antara*), situated within, according to such scriptural passages as: "He who is within the sun," "He who, dwelling in the sun, is internal to the sun," and "He who is the internal of all. Thus he abides.

Although He exists as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all, He is *ariṣṭa*—meaning "one for whom there is no *riṣṭa*" (misfortune or impurity); that is to say, He is one whose sins have been destroyed (*apahatapāpman*). The sense is that even while being the inner controller of all, He remains untouched by even a scent of the defects inherent in those [beings]. In this context, during the days of the Sun and other planets, Rāhu, as the "seizer of time" (*kālahāra*), occupies specific portions of the day-measures according to the sequence of numbers indicated by the consonants *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, and so forth. Specifically, he resides for a duration of the eighth, second, and subsequent half-yāmas. For example, on Sunday, the eighth half-yāma is the time of Rāhu.

"One should observe that the second half-yāma of the Induvāra [Monday] is likewise [inauspicious]," and so forth. This indicates the established principle of the science of astrology (jyotiśśāstra) regarding the continuous inauspiciousness of certain times for undertaking undertakings.

I take refuge in that certain auspicious, noble, and wholesome seal of compassion—which is vast, sleepless like a fresh lotus, dwelling in the heart of the lotus-eyed Lord, and which is beneficial. 1736.
In this context, by the two meaningful words *pathyā* and *āryā*,
it is designated as *pathyā* by those learned in prosody: that [meter] in which a foot is seen in the first two quarters among its three parts.
Thus, there is an indication of the meaning of the needle—namely, the nature of the noble ones (*ārya*) who are on the path characterized by the aforementioned qualities.

Thus, in the phrase "some seal of compassion" (*kāmapi karuṇāmudrām*), the fact that the ornament (alaṃkāra) presented in this verse is named *mudrā* according to the definition previously stated is indicated by a single constituent part of a meaningful word (*arthavatpadaikadeśena*). This is another type of *mudrā*.

Just as, alas, the lightning-streak whose radiance was dispelled by your brilliance, though hidden somewhere within a cloud, became restless out of a weight of fear toward the daughter of the ocean (the submarine fire). 1737.

The word *jīmūta* occurs in the sense of both "cloud" (*jalada*) and "mountain," according to Amara’s lexicon which states: "*jīmūtau meghaparvatau*" (the two *jīmūtas* are the cloud and the mountain). Here, by means of the meaningful and punning term *capalā*, the name of this meter has been proclaimed by the King of Nāgas: that [meter] in which there are two *ja*s in the second and fourth positions, situated between *ga*s in both halves of the verse, is called *capalā*.

Thus, this indicates the meaning of the definition of the *āryā* named *capalā*, which possesses both [the first and second] meanings, characterized by having a *gaṇa* consisting of a "guru" (heavy syllable) in the second and fourth positions, as previously defined.

O Lord of Vṛṣācala, for one who possesses not even a trace of compassion, there is infinite happiness; yet you, overcome by mercy and desiring to dispel the suffering of others, undergo affliction. (1738)

In this passage, there is the figure of speech known as *leśa* (the "slight"), characterized by the definitions mentioned immediately above: namely, the attribution of the quality of possessing infinite bliss to the defect consisting in the lack of even a trace of compassion, and the attribution of the defect of possessing afflictions caused by the desire to dispel the suffering of others to the quality consisting in being overwhelmed by pity. Furthermore, this *leśa* is indicated by the word *leśa* itself—which is a part of a meaningless compound—thereby making known that which is to be named after it.

May that Lord of Lakṣmī, whose eyes are like fresh lotuses, who by nature delights in dwelling in the fortress of the serpent-hill (Śrīparvata), and whose beautiful form triumphs over the dark clouds, be victorious for a long time. 1739.
Here, by means of the meaningful words formed from the pairs of initial syllables of the four quarters combined,
there is an indication of the name of the author of the work, which is to be indicated as "the composition of Kṛṣṇa, the Nine Durgās."

In this context, I shall cite a hymn composed by myself called the *Alaṅkaraṇamālikā*, which—like a hymn to the garland of constellations (*nakṣatramālā*) and other such works—is a unique composition never before attempted by anyone, concerning the divine queen of the god Śrī Hayagrīva; it indicates the names of the *karana*s, such as *Bava* and *Bālava*. Its first two verses are as follows: "May that indescribable fortune of the horse-faced one (Hayānana), which is the auspiciousness of the king of the ocean of milk and is to be enjoyed by the rows of lotus forests, make me fit for the composition of hymns praising his own virtues. (1740)
Having restrained all eleven organs for the removal of every calamity, I praise the Sovereign of the World with these eleven verses; may she be gracious.

The *karaṇas* are eleven in number, namely the sense organs (*indriyas*). Alternatively, the *karaṇas* known as *bava*, *bālava*, and so forth—classified as movable (*cara*) and fixed (*sthira*)—are likewise eleven in number. Having restrained them by withdrawing them from their objects, and having bound them within certain parts of the verses; here, by the words "having restrained all eleven *karaṇas*," it is indicated that through these punning and meaningful terms, the names of the *karaṇas* will be sequentially suggested within the forthcoming verses of praise.

O Mother, O jewel among daughters-in-law, even the lotus-eyed Lord bears you upon his chest; what more need be said? You are highly honored by all the worlds, O daughter of the ocean of nectar. (1742)
In this case, by means of two meaningless parts of the word *ambavadhū*, there is the indication of a meaning that suggests the name and form of the act of making a bangle.

I take refuge in you, the youthful daughter of the horse-faced one, whose lotus-like eyes are fresh, and who serves as the protective trench for the multitude of sprouts of incomparable, supreme, and auspicious virtues. 1743.
Here, by means of two meaningless parts of the words *nikurumba* and *ālavāla*, the names of the child’s ears are indicated.

O Mother, may your two feet—the bestowers of auspiciousness, the source of sweetness, those whose majesty is well-known, which grant joy and bestow fortune—be the heirs to the Lotus-born (Brahmā) for me. (1744)

*Lavaṇimā* means *lāvaṇya* (beauty), as seen in the usage from the *Śṛṅgārataraṅgiṇī*: "The stream of the ocean of the quality of *lavaṇima*, which is even more minute. Here, the two givers are indicated by the meaningless partial words *lavaṇima* and *itya* [from *iti ya*], which suggest the names of the *kaula* and *karaṇa* [astrological] systems.

May she who is the beloved of the horse-faced one, the refuge of all, and possessed of exquisite loveliness, come to me—she who causes the lotus of my heart to blossom at the sight of Hari, who is captivating, fragrant, and radiant with the humming of bees. 1745.

By the sight of Lord Hari and the Sun, it is blossoming (*savikasana*), awakened (*unnidra*), and radiant (*ullāsi*). It is captivating (*hāri*), enchanting (*manohara*), fragrant (*āmodi*), and full of joy (*pramodavat*), as well as sweet-smelling (*surabhi*). "Ulāsana" means that in which things shine forth; it refers to the shining forth of the mantra of refuge for the six-footed one (*ṣaṭpada*)—that is, the bees (*bhramara*). The rest is easy to understand. Here, by means of a collection of parts of words that are both meaningful (such as *dayita* and *lalita*) and meaningless, the name *Taitula* is indicated.
May that indescribable Abode, the younger brother of the moon, the subduer of Hayagrīva, born from the ocean of nectar—may it lead us to the end of the heat of the burden of worldly existence. 1746.

The grammatical construction (*anvaya*) is as follows: "May those [two] who possess a younger brother with cool rays (the Moon) bring about the destruction of the heat of worldly existence. Here, by the meaningless phrase "born of the ocean" (*sāgaraja*), which is a part of a compound, the name of the maker of the *Garaja* [poem] is indicated.
O Mother, beholding your innocence, a certain person—like a merchant with deposited wealth—having sold his own supreme self to you, O wonder, obtains great glory from you.

"Possessing the wealth of deposits" means one who possesses the wealth of entrusted goods and the wealth in the form of deposits. A "deposit" (*nyāsa*) is an object placed in the custody of another for protection; as Amara states: "A deposit is a man [entrusted] for safekeeping. It is derived from the root *ni-as* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). "Excessive beauty and folly" refers to that which is most minute—having an exceedingly subtle nature—and also very small. "Self" refers to the soul, and "wealth" refers to riches.

By selling [the materials] and having [the temple] constructed, one attains great majesty as Śrīnivāsa and immense prosperity. Here, the term "vaṇigja" indicates the name of the architect (vaṇigjakaraṇa) by means of a meaningless portion of a word.

May that certain auspicious mudrā, which bestows welfare, protect you from the heat of worldly existence; she who is ever awake for the protection of the world, whose heart is moist with compassion for those who offer praise to the Lord of the three daily libations, and who grants the state of being fit for liberation.
Here, by the meaningful word *bhadrā*, there is an indication of the name *Bhadrakaraṇa*; the distinction is that by the word *mudrā*, there is also an indication of the poetic figure *mudrā*.
His entire empire, including even the birds upon his banner, was indivisible; he bestowed such abundant wealth as is honored by all the gods.
Here, by the meaningful word-part "bird" (*śakunī*), there is an indication of the name of the *Śakunikaraṇa* [meter].
Even one of most clever intellect who never bows at your two lotus-feet is indeed a donkey, lacking four legs; there is no doubt in this matter—what is the use of a multitude of words? (1750)
Here, by means of the meaningful word-part "catuṣpāt" (four-footed), there is an indication of the name of the rite, namely "Catuṣpātkaraṇa."

May the Blessed One, whose arms possess the coils of the best of serpents and who is the sovereign of speech, swiftly grant us—who are filled with intense agitation regarding existence—a certain torrent of compassion. 1751.
Here, by the three syllables "nāga-ve," which constitute a portion of the compound word "nāgavara," there is an indication of the name of the instrument called "nāgava."
These intense torments of worldly existence do not long remain haughty; for the peacocks of the mind, with the glances of Kamalā and wide smiles, destroy them.

O peacock of the mind! O peacock of the heart—this is the address. Those oppressive heats of the summer season, the torments of the monsoon of worldly existence (bhava), which for so long were haughty and arrogant, no longer remain. Why is this? To this he says: "by the lotus" (kamala). They are "thickly smiling," meaning as beautiful as the clouds of the rainy season. This epithet contains the intention that they possess the skill to destroy both the heat and the arrogance.

The side-glances (apāṅga) of Kamalā, that is, Śrī, destroy these torments. The word *tu* is used for emphasis; as Amara states: "Words such as *evaṃ*, *tu*, *punar*, and *vai* are expressive of emphasis. Thus, the meaning is "they certainly destroy them. The implication is that therefore they will not remain for long. Here, by the sequence of syllables in the word *kiṃstughnanti*, there is an indication of the name of a medicinal plant (*kiṃstughna*), which consists of meaningful words, meaningless word-parts, and the combination of both.
May this garland of ornaments, the Mother of the worlds—stitched with auspicious virtues, perpetually embraced by splendor, expansive, slender, and heart-pleasing—attain fullness. 1753.

This garland of ornaments, which is the Mother of the worlds—Śrī herself—sewn together with the threads of her auspicious qualities (in one sense) and with the auspicious qualities of Śrī such as good character and affection (in the other sense), and further woven by the embrace of beauty (in one sense) and by the poetic excellence known as *śleṣa* (in the other sense)—as defined by the statement, "In poetry, beauty is held to be the extreme brilliance of the composition," and the definition, "The mutual interlocking of words is called *śleṣa"—this garland, which serves as the cause of the poem's excellence.

May she extend that heart-pleasing praise—which is determined to be a garland of ornaments—residing upon her chest; for here, by the phrase "garland of ornaments" (*alaṅkāraṇamālikā*), there is an indication of the suggested meaning (*sūcyārtha*) that this praise is not composed of the sequence of *bava*, *bālava*, and other such *karana* periods.
This is the final verse of this hymn:
May this work, composed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa Brahma-tantra-parakāla, the preceptor of the jewel-like lineage of King Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Mahīśūra, be victorious. (1754)

Just as there may be a conjunction at the beginning of a foot for some syllable, O Lord of the Serpent-Mountain, this sequence is appropriate here; however, what follows may be both heavy and light. (1755)

O Lord of the Mountain! (Ahigiriśvara! According to Amara, *agrya* means "foremost," "supreme," or "excellent" (*agre parārthe 'parārthyāgraprāgraharaprāgryāgryāgrīyamagriyam*). For anyone whatsoever—of whatever caste, such as a Brāhmaṇa or other—and for Your feet, whatever connection there may be consisting of taking refuge (*prapatti*), this is the proper, fitting sequence (*krama*) in this world, a praiseworthy order. As the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *krama* [is used] in the sense of power, the stepping of feet, and also in the sense of a sequence (*paripāṭī*)."

Alternatively, the construction may be: "this sequence is appropriate. But as for another [deity] besides you, even a guru—though great—would become light and insignificant due to the excessive labor involved in establishing a connection; the word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis, meaning that such a connection would indeed be unworthy of praise.

If, in a *pakṣa*, a *pāda*, or the fourth part of a verse (*padya*), at the beginning (*agre*)—that is, at the start—there occurs a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of any letter whatsoever, such as the letter *ka* or others, characterized by the definition stated in the rule "consonants without intervening [vowels] are a *saṃyoga*" (*halo'nantarāssaṃyogaḥ*), then this conjunction, being joined (*yukta*) or conjoined (*saṃyukta*), is called *krama*. It bears the designation *krama*.

In this context, when this [consonant] designated as *krama* occurs subsequently—that is, when it exists later—the preceding syllable, even if it possesses the status of being "heavy" due to the cause of being followed by a conjunct consonant as defined by the rule "a syllable is heavy when followed by a *saṃyoga*," may also be "light," possessing the lightness defined by the rule "a short vowel is light. By the phrase "and light," it is indicated that this occurs only in certain instances. As it has been stated: "At the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pāda*), a *saṃyoga* of a syllable here is designated as *krama*;
because of that which stands later, there is sometimes lightness even for a heavy [syllable]."

Thus, as in this very verse, even though there exists a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) at the beginning of the fourth quarter, the lightness (*laghutva*) of the preceding syllable must necessarily be accepted—just as in the expression, "O beautiful one, with little expense the village folk eat delicacies"—for otherwise, there would be a violation of the meter (*chanda-bhaṅga*).

This should be observed. Here, by the word "krama" occurring at the beginning of the fourth quarter, the intended meaning is indicated: that the conjunction of the letters *ka* and *ra*, which are the initial sounds of their respective groups (*svādi*), and which is characterized by the definition presented in this verse, is designated by the term "krama. This is suggested along with an example not distinct from itself and the purpose for employing such a designation. Furthermore, the distinction here is that this [figure] is blended with the previously mentioned *ullāsa* (expansion) and with a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) concerning both the relevant and the irrelevant subjects.

It should be noted that even when the first syllable of the fourth foot is pronounced with a lighter effort, no irregularity in the verse is observed. Likewise, in the *Navaratnamālā* composition, the specific types of gems are indicated by the inclusion of their respective names; similarly, in the *Nakṣatramālā* composition, the names of the lunar mansions are indicated by the names of deities such as Agni and others. This very same figure of speech applies in such cases, as well as in the indication of future events within dramas, according to Dīkṣita.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of Mudrās, in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on the Garland of Jewels (Ratnāvalī):
"If there is the placement of meanings that are traditionally recited together..."
That is renowned as the Ratnāvalī, distinguished by the division of sequential and non-sequential [methods].

The ornament named *ratnāvalī* (the jewel-garland) is the placement of meanings that are well-known in common worldly usage, the Vedas, and so forth, as being recited together. It is of two kinds: sequential (*sakrama*) and non-sequential (*akrama*). Sequentiality consists of the placement of meanings known to be recited together in their proper order. Non-sequentiality consists of the mention of some of those meanings—despite their being known to be recited together—in a deficient manner, in reverse order, or lacking the established sequence even though they are known to be recited together.
In both types [of *śleṣa*], there is a twofold division for each based on whether the sequential meanings are connected with the subject matter (*prakṛta*) or not. Connection with the subject matter—

This should be observed. Here, by the word "krama" occurring at the beginning of the fourth quarter, the intended meaning is indicated: that the conjunction of the letters *ka* and *ra*, which are the initial sounds of their respective groups (*svādi*), and which is characterized by the definition presented in this verse, is designated by the term "krama. This is shown together with an example not distinct from itself and the purpose for employing such a designation. Furthermore, the distinction here is that this [figure] is blended with the previously mentioned *ullāsa* (flourish) and with a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) concerning both the subject at hand and the subject not at hand.

It should be noted that even when the first syllable of the fourth foot is pronounced with a lighter effort, no irregularity in the verse is observed. Similarly, in the *Navaratnamālā* composition, the specific types of gems are indicated by the inclusion of their respective names; likewise, in the *Nakṣatramālā* composition, the names of the lunar mansions are indicated by the names of deities such as Agni, and so forth—this is precisely this same figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*). The same applies to the indication of future events in dramas, according to the Dīkṣitas.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of Mudrās, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Garland of Jewels (*Ratnāvalīsara*):
"If there is the arrangement of meanings that are traditionally recited together..."
That is renowned as the Ratnāvalī, distinguished by the methods of both sequential and non-sequential practice.

The ornament named *ratnāvalī* (the jewel-garland) is the arrangement of meanings that are well-known in common usage, the Vedas, and so forth, as being recited together. It is of two kinds: sequential and non-sequential. Sequentiality consists in the arrangement of meanings known to be recited together in their established order. Non-sequentiality, however, consists in the mention of some of those meanings either out of order, in reverse order, or even when they are recited together, lacking the established sequence.

In both types [of *mudrā*], there are two varieties each, depending on whether the sequential meanings are connected to the subject at hand (*prakṛta*) or not. Connection with the subject occurs in some manner, such as by serving as an embellishment (*uparañjaka*) for the subject of comparison (*upamāna*). Non-connection with it occurs through the sequential placement of those respective names in some fashion, either by means of a pun (*śleṣa*) or by way of the *mudrā* ornament itself. All of this will become clear in the examples; this too is indeed the discovery of Dīkṣita.
Among these, an example of the *prakṛtānvayavatī* (type where the connection belongs to the subject) with sequential order (*sakramā*) is as follows:

Like Brahmā, he possesses all the scriptures; like Hari, he shines intensely, clothed in yellow garments; and like Śiva, the mountain Mahendra bears upon its head the river that flows from the feet of the lotus-eyed one. (1756)

All the *agamās* are the trees and the *āgamās* are the Vedas; he who possesses these is so described. He by whom the garment was drunk—that is, by whom the sky was swallowed—is called "one who has drunk the sky," in the sense that the sky was encompassed by his natural expansion, as in the phrase: "Having forcibly drunk the sky with his naturally lofty chest. He is the lotus-eyed Hari. [He drinks] the river born from his feet—the celestial Gaṅgā (Ākāśagaṅgā)—and the [earthly] Gaṅgā. The rest is clear.

Here, there is a sequential placement of the three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—who are well-known in the Purāṇas and other texts for their roles as the agents of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and who are established as the objects of comparison (*upamāna*) connected to the subject at hand.
O Śauri, you are like the earth in forbearance, like water in providing nourishment, like fire in brilliance, like the wind in pervasiveness, and like the sky in stainless purity.

Here, according to the method of comparison (*upamāna*), there is a sequential placement of the five great elements (*mahābhūta*)—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—which are mentioned together in the Purāṇas and other texts as being involved in the present context.
That very [devotion] is connected to the subject matter by way of being colored [by it], as follows:

"O King, my devotion has sprouted through the power of my past merits, put forth shoots from hearing of your virtues, grown into leaves from reflecting upon them, and now bears fruit through the sight of you. (1758)

"Sumitā" means blossomed. "By sight" means by the act of seeing. Here, there is a superimposition of the nature of a creeper upon devotion. In this verse, the four stages—sprout, leaf, flower, and fruit—which follow the order established in the world, are arranged as embellishing attributes through the words "aṅkuritā" (sprouted) and so forth.

You are the Lord, the illustrious minister, the friend of all, and the one who dwells within the heart-treasury of everyone; yet, O Wielder of the Discus, Your state remains exceedingly difficult to attain for those bereft of the power of Your grace. (1759)

O Cakradhara! By the word *cakra*, the kingdom is also understood, according to Amara’s lexicon: “*cakraṃ rāṣṭre’pi*” (the wheel is also [used for] the kingdom). You are the Lord, the Sovereign of All, as stated in such Vedic texts as “*eṣa sarveśvaraḥ*” (He is the Lord of All); by this, His transcendence is expressed. In the alternative sense, the meaning is a certain king. He is one whose *śrī*—that is, Lakṣmī—is his *saciva*—his companion or assistant—as Amara states: “*mantrī sahāyasacivau*” (minister, companion, and assistant). Or, it may mean the assistant (*saciva*) of Lakṣmī. In the alternative sense, he is one whose minister (*saciva*) is endowed with *śrī* (prosperity).

By this presence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), supreme compassion is indicated. He is the "friend of all" (*sakalasuhṛt*). According to the Śruti, "Nārāyaṇa is the abode, the refuge, the friend, and the goal. By this, his accessibility (*saulabhya*) is expressed. In the alternative sense, "all" means those endowed with all arts, that is, experts in royal policy; he is one who has such friends as allies.

"Beloved by all" means he dwells within the treasure-chest (kośa) situated in the heart; thus it is said, based on the Śruti passage beginning with "resembling the interior of a lotus bud" and concluding with "in that, everything is established. By this, his affection (vātsalya) is manifested. This very quality called affection is stated in the Kaṭhavallī:
"The Person the size of a thumb dwells in the middle of the self;
as the ruler of the past and the future, one does not shrink away from him."

Thus, the meaning of this scripture is made recognized by the aforementioned qualifications. "Vātsalya" (parental affection) means a love that overcomes all faults; in another sense, it means residing within the treasury of gold and other riches that are dear to the hearts of all people. Having thus stated that you reside in the hearts of all sentient beings yet remain difficult to perceive, he says "tadapi" (even that), and so forth.

Even so, Your state—Your essential nature—is difficult to attain for those people who are destitute of the power of Your grace; for according to such scriptural passages as, "Him who is difficult to see, hidden and entered into," and "Just as those ignorant of the field (akṣetrajña), though walking over and over above a buried treasure of gold, do not find it," [Your nature is inaccessible]. In the other sense, even Your well-known station (pada) is a fortress (durga) impossible to reach by those destitute of Your grace, strength, and an army.

Here, there is a sequential placement of the seven well-known elements—sovereign, minister, ally, treasury, territory, fort, and army—which are traditionally recited together and which, as embellishing factors, are connected to the subject at hand.

Just as this Hari is the radiant one, the dharma, the protector of those who take refuge, and the lord of the worlds; so too does Śiva—the life-breath of the universe, praised by the Puṇyajanas—protect those like me.

This Lord Hari is Indra and the Blessed One; he is the pure fire, free from sin, and Dharma-Yama. In the alternative sense, according to the expression "the eternal black Dharma," he is the very embodiment of Dharma. He is called *naiṛta* because the prosperity (*śrī*) of the *rakṣasas* has resorted to him; in the alternative sense, he is *śritarakṣī*, one who protects those who have sought refuge. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the root *rakṣ* with the object [ending in the second case], and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*. He is thus described as one whose *śrī* (prosperity) is such [a protector]. Since the word does not have the designation of a river name, the suffix *kap* is not applied.

Alternatively, in the case of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), *dharmaśritarakṣaśrīḥ* is a single compound word. He is one whose glory (*śrī*) is such that it protects those who have taken refuge in Dharma—that is, in the form of a trust (*nyāsa*). In this interpretation, there is an optional doubling of the letter *ś* in *dharmaśrita* according to the rule *anaci ca*. The Lord of the worlds (*bhuvanānām patiḥ*) is Varuṇa; in another sense, he is the sovereign of the worlds (*lokānām adhināthaḥ*). The Life-breath of the universe (*jagatprāṇaḥ*) is the Wind (*samīraṇaḥ*), the reviver of the world.
For no mortal lives by means of either the out-breath (*prāṇa*) or the in-breath (*apāna*).
But by the other they live, upon which both of these depend.

Thus it is stated in the Śruti. Kubera is "worshipped by the Puṇyajanas" and "praised by those who perform meritorious deeds. Śiva is "Śarva" and the "embodiment of auspiciousness," according to the Śruti: "The eternal, auspicious, and infallible [Brahman]. Here, there is a sequential arrangement of the eight well-known world-protectors (lokapālas), beginning with Indra, who serve as coloring agents (*uparañjaka*) for the subject at hand; their status as coloring agents consists in being superimposed (*āropyamāṇatā*). As it has been said: "When the object [of comparison] becomes a coloring agent, that is Metaphor (*rūpaka*). For here, Śrīnivāsa is colored by the nature of Indra and the others.

O Blessed One, this king Bhāsvat, who is like the sun, is wise, a lord of speech, renowned for his poetry, called Maitri, most excellent, and one whose banner of victory is raised high; he has taken refuge in you.

*Pārthiva*: known on the earth. Under the rule "known therein," by the sūtra *sarvabhūmipṛthivībhyāmaṇañau*, the suffix *añ* is applied. Alternatively, one born on the earth (*pṛthivyām*) is a *pārthiva*; the meaning is "belonging to the earth" (*bhauma*). *Kāvya-prathita*: famous for his own poetic compositions; that is, one whose fame is renowned through works concerning himself. Or, in another sense, he is famous as a *kāvya* (poet) because he is celebrated through the poetry composed by himself. *Maitrī-khyāta*: renowned for friendliness, that is, for being a well-wisher toward all living beings.

Elsewhere, "Mitra's son" (mitrasya bhānoḥ apatyam) refers to one called Maitri; the meaning is that Saturn (śani), the son of the Sun (ravi). "Uttama" means best or most excellent; in the alternative sense (pakṣe), it means "high darkness" (unnataṃ tamaḥ), which is Rāhu—according to Amara, "tamastu rāhuḥ. He is one whose banner of victory (jayaketu) is raised high; in the alternative sense, he is both one who has achieved high victory and a comet (ketu). The rest is clear. Here, by means of words such as "bhāsvat" (the radiant one), the subject of description [is characterized].

Since the nature of the Sun and the other [planets] is perceived as being inherent in the Blessed One, there is an arrangement of the nine well-known planets—Sun and the rest—in their sequential order, as they are connected to the subject at hand.
Just as it is said:
"Abandon desire, conquer anger, cast off greed, and abandon delusion; renounce pride and even envy—surely you shall become the recipient of Hari’s sidelong glance. (1762)

Here, there is a sequential arrangement of the six factors—desire and so forth—which are well-known to be recited together and which, by way of the figure of speech *samuccaya* (accumulation), are connected with the subject at hand.
An example of a sequenceless [verse] possessing the connection of the original context (*prakṛtānvayaśālinī akramā*):

"O friend, conquer the senses, observe the restraints, master your posture, and you shall attain Brahman; practicing breath control and withdrawal of the senses, meditate with concentration and absorption. (1763)

Here, there is an arrangement of the restraints (yama), observances (niyama), postures (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi)—which are the eight limbs mentioned in the sequence of Patañjali’s Sūtras—by way of their collective application to the subject at hand, albeit with a slight reversal of their order.
O Hari, your earth-like abundance, your boundless splendor, your fame that faces every direction, your auspicious touch, and your multitude of virtues shine forth as truly infinite.

*Pṛthvī*: the great earth; by the rule *oto guṇavacanāt*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. In the alternative sense, it means *bhūḥ* (the ground). *Tejaḥ*: power or majesty; in the alternative sense, fire. *Sarvatomukham*: spreading in all directions; in the alternative sense, water. *Śubhasparśanatā*: the state of being one whose touch (*sparśana*)—that is, whose giving—is auspicious (*śubha*). In the other sense, it refers to the wind (*sparśana*), which is auspicious (*śubha*).

Its state is "infinite," meaning unbounded; elsewhere, this refers to space (*ākāśa*). Here, there is a presentation of the five great elements, beginning with earth, with a slight alteration of their order, serving as a coloring factor (*uparañjaka*) that connects them to the subject at hand.

O Acyuta, by your word they have declared Dhṛṣṭi to be victorious, Jayanta to be triumphant, Siddhārtha to be the achiever of his purpose, Aśoka to have attained [his goal], and Sumantra to be the protector of counsel.

O Acyuta! [He is so called] because, at the commencement of the battle, seeing his own kinsmen standing ready to fight and observing that they had lost their fortitude through grief—this being evident from such passages as "My limbs fail me"—[Acyuta] made Vijaya (Arjuna) free from sorrow (*aśokam*) by means of Your speech in the form of the Gītā, beginning with "Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these lords of men," and ending with "I shall deliver them; do not grieve."

He is so called because he protects the excellent counsel—that is, the final verse—whose deliberation is beautiful; thus, as it is said, "to the guardian of the treasure who is vigilant," he is the protector of the mantra. People say that he has attained the status of being a means for achieving the purpose, which consists in victory over the enemy; therefore, his purpose (artha) is accomplished.
The implied sense is that by following the duty of a Kṣatriya correctly through the abandonment of delusion via the instruction of the Gītā, he obtained victory. In this regard:
Dhṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Siddhārtha, Arthasādhaka,
Aśoka, Mantrapāla, and Sumantra was the eighth.

Thus, it should be understood that this description of the eight ministers of the Raghu dynasty—Dhr̥ṣṭi and the others—who are traditionally recited together in the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa* and are relevant to the present context, serves as a poetic embellishment (*uparañjaka*), despite their somewhat altered order.

Like Indra, you are protected and possess the nature of well-being; like Yama, you are followed by the sacrificial fee (or: you follow the path of justice); like Kubera, the king of kings, you are the lord of wealth; and like Varuṇa, you are the master of the essence of clouds (or: the lord of profound sentiment). || 1766 ||

Pālitaḥ means one who possesses well-being, the stability of heaven, and the stability of his own wealth. Dakṣiṇā refers to the southern direction; he is "followed by" that, meaning he is its lord. Alternatively, he is followed by *dakṣiṇa* (generous) people. Rājarāja refers to one named Rājarāja and a sovereign king of kings (*rājādhirāja*). He is the lord of *ghanarasa*, which is water. The compound *ghana-raseśa* is analyzed as: the lord of the earth (*rasā*) is a king (*bhūpati*), and he is both "dense" (*ghana*) and the "lord of fluids" (*raseśa*). The rest is clear.

In this instance, there is a partial transposition in the order of the four world-protectors beginning with Indra, and they are connected to the subject matter by way of being objects of comparison. This very example also serves as an illustration of a deficiency in sequence, because only four out of the eight world-protectors have been included.

The Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), who is beloved by the elephant-faced being (Gaṇeśa) and adorned with ornaments called serpents on earth, shines wondrously; and [the Lord] wearing a forest garland (Viṣṇu), whose rising glory is meditated upon as arising from the lotus-born (Brahmā), likewise shines. 1767.

By "dviradamukhaiḥ" is meant by creatures such as elephants and other beings; elsewhere, it refers to Dviradamukha, the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnarāja), who is dear due to his presence as a being (*sattva*). "Bhujaga" is his name, which serves as his ornament; elsewhere, he is so called because his ornaments are named after serpents, taking the form of hooded snakes. "Girīśa" refers to the king of mountains as well as Śiva. And "vanamālī" refers to one possessing a forest-grove, as does the Blessed One (the Lord).

"By whom [the world] was brought forth by a multitude of lotus-born ones"—in another sense, "by whom prosperity, height, and manifestation were brought about in a lotus-born one (Brahmā). Here, there is a description of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, whose well-known order is entirely reversed; furthermore, through the method of poetic coloring (*uparañjana*), they are connected to the subject at hand.

May we behold the lotus-foot of the Lord of Śrī, which is served by the essence of the *gārutmata* gem, adorned with a pendant of pearls, as delicate as coral, red as a ruby (*padmarāga*), and praised by the wielder of the thunderbolt.

In this case, although they are mentioned together, since the five jewels—such as the emerald and others—which lack established sequential order, are described by way of their coloring and so forth in some manner connected to the subject at hand, this *ratnāvalī* (string of jewels) is likewise of a non-sequential nature.

Just as the regions of the Lord of Serpents' mountain possess limbs joined with massive peaks, agile Kaliṅgas, broad Vaṅgas, abundant and great Darbhas, and excellent settlements; (so too does this city). 1769.

[They are] those possessing dense peaks; in another sense, those whose limbs (*aṅga*) are joined with a "dense peak" (*ghana-śṛṅga*), meaning preeminence (*prādhānya*). In the other sense, they are those in whom the regions called Aṅgas—joined with dense peaks—are present. According to Amara, "peak" (*śṛṅga*) refers to both preeminence and a mountain summit. Preeminence is attributed to Aṅga because it is enumerated first among the regions. [The mountains] possess restless Kaliṅgas, which are either specific birds or the Kaliṅga country; and they possess large *lavaṅga* trees. *Amarakośa*: "Peak" (*śṛṅga*) is used for preeminence and a mountain summit. Preeminence belongs to Aṅga because it is reckoned first among the countries. The Kaliṅgas are either a species of bird or the Kaliṅga country; they are restless. The *lavaṅgas* are large *lavaṅga* trees.

"Pṛthulāḥ" means broad; "viśālāḥ" means extensive; and "vaṅgāḥ" refers to those specific regions bearing that name. The rest is clear. Here, the identity of the regions of Aṅga and others with the region of Phaṇigiri is perceived; thus, the mention of the regions of Aṅga and so forth—which are not established in their conventional order—is relevant to the subject at hand.
The *ratnāvalī* (string of jewels) with sequential order but lacking connection to the subject matter is as follows:

"O bestower of boons, you who possess the power of the sun-jewel, you have appeared on Mount Hari (the mountain of Hari) at will to protect the worlds from their torments; whereupon the snows shine forth like elephants. (1770)

O Hastivarada! On that mountain Veṅkaṭādri—also called Haribhūbhṛt—which possesses the luster of gems with thick, dense rays (ghṛṇayaḥ) or which has the radiance of jewels with the hue of a cloud—you have manifested in order to protect the worlds at will from their afflictions. On that mountain where cool, refreshing springs (utsāḥ)—as Amara states, "utsaḥ" means a spring or fountain—"shine," the manifestation of the Lord there is described as being a means for the cessation of suffering.

Here, there is a sequential placement of three elements—power (*prabhāva*), mantra, and energy (*utsāha*)—which are traditionally recited together, yet which do not cohere with the subject matter by way of being ornaments of the *mudrā*. The same applies to the subsequent examples as well.
Or again,
O lotus-eyed one, he who has his impurities destroyed by the dust of your lotus feet, O Ananta, while residing on the summit of the king of serpents— he indeed is worthy of dwelling in that land.
*Nīvṛt* is a country (*janapada*). Herein, the arrangement (*nyāsa*) of decline, stability, and growth follows the sequence previously described.

Just as this lotus-born Brahmā was honored by the mind that partakes in discipline through the Vedic collection, may that Blessed One— the divine Saindhava, whose nature is auspicious and who consists of the Vedas and other scriptures— protect you.

*Sāmnāya* means "with the traditional transmission" (*saṃpradāya*), according to Amara’s lexicon: *athāmnāyassaṃpradāye*. It consists of the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman* [Vedas], as indicated by the mantra-verse: *ṛgyajussāmarūpāya*. Here, the term *divyasaindhava* refers to Śrī Hayagrīva; for there is a specific poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) called *mudrā*, characterized by the fact that the sequential arrangement of the *Ṛk*, *Yajuḥ*, and *Sāman*—which are mentioned together in scriptures such as *ṛco yajūṃṣi sāmāni yo'dhīte sakṛdañjasā*—is suggested by the phrase "consisting of the form of the *Ṛk* and so forth. This sequential binding is what is indicated here. This is the specific distinction.

Just as even enemies were led toward Your supreme abode during the sacrifice for the subduing of Aridamana, so too am I [led] here to the Gārhapatya fire; O Lord, for how long must I remain here before You come to me? (1773)

O Lord, conqueror of the unsubdued, you who possess a clever and skillful engagement in battle—O Protector! even your enemies, such as the King of Cedi and others, have been led by You to Your supreme abode. I alone am one who has sought refuge in You with my whole being. In this worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), characterized by the duties of a householder (*gārhapatya*)—the analysis of the compound *gārhapatya* being "the duty of a householder" (*gṛhapati*)—and in the various ritual acts of the respective stages of life (*āśrama*), [I remain devoted]. (The suffix *yak* is applied here in the sense of "action," according to the rule: *patyantapurohitādibhyo yak*).
The sense is: "I do not know up to what extent you will come to me, or how much I shall trouble you. In this regard, there is a sequential order among the Dakṣiṇa, Āhavanīya, and Gārhapatya fires.

O Acyuta, whatever has been accomplished by the multitudes of sacred fords, and whatever has been done by us through the service of the three Vedas— even that may be surpassed here by another who has undertaken the initiation for crossing the ocean of worldly existence under you.
Enough! The distinction here is that the four ages, beginning with Kṛta, are placed in sequence as ornaments of style (alaṃkārarīti), even though they are not connected to the subject at hand.
Just as the Lord,

whose chest bears the auspicious mark of the *āmalaka* fruit, descended upon the Mountain of Serpents for the protection of the worlds, so too does Hari manifest there, burdened by compassion and eternally slaying the enemies of those who bow before him.

"Abhirāma" means delightful. "Lakṣmaṇa" means one in whom there is beauty (*lakṣmī*); the suffix *na* is added in the sense of possession according to the rule for words beginning with *pāman*, and by the rule "the vowel of *lakṣmī* becomes *a*," the *ī* of *lakṣmī* is changed to *a*, followed by the substitution of *ṇ*. He whose chest is of such a nature is described as such. "Kṛpābharataḥ" means from the weight of compassion (*dayā*). The suffix *tasi* is used here in place of all case endings. "Vinatanityaśatrughnaḥ" means he who slays the eternal enemies of those who are bowed down—namely, desire (*kāma*) and the rest; the suffix *ka* is added to the root *han* because it belongs to the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*.

Here, there is the sequential placement of the four characters beginning with Rāma, who are not relevant to the primary subject, by way of the poetic style (*rīti*) of the *mudrā* ornament (*alaṃkāra*) supported by paronomasia (*śleṣa*).

Just as the lake of Urmiṇī shines with the lotus of Sītā’s laughter stirred by the breeze, so does the form of the Lord of the Bull Mountain shine, his fame renowned and his head-pervading the entire universe.
Here, Sītā, Ūrmilā, Māṇḍavī, and Śrutakīrti—who are well-known in the traditional texts—are to be arranged in the same manner as before.
Or for example:

"Śauri, the subduer of gods, asuras, and men, who bestows Pradyumna upon those who bow to him, sports amidst the eternal, expansive mountains adorned with serpents, while his command remains unobstructed. (1777)

He who draws forth the gods, asuras, and humans by the abundance of his qualities; who bestows Pradyumna—that is, the gift of supreme majesty—upon those who bow before him; whose command is unimpeded, being Aniruddha;
Śauri sports upon the lands of the Serpent Hill (Ahicchatra), which possess eternal splendor. Herein lies the symbolic placement of Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.

Or rather, blessed is he who follows the nature of the cātaka bird, performing actions solely for the sake of pleasing him; he meditates on that lotus-eyed one at his will, shedding tears of joy. (1778)

He whose dharma is of the nature of single-minded devotion, like the dharma of the *cātaka* bird, is so described. The meaning is that such a person follows the conduct of the *cātaka*; for it is remembered in scripture: "Just as the *cātaka* has surrendered [to the rain-cloud]... He is blessed. The rest is easy to understand. Here too, as before, there is a presentation of the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*)—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—in sequence across the four quarters of the verse.

O Lord, bestower of boons upon the leaders of the assembly, you who are skilled in dividing the Danavas and have wielded the rod of punishment against the sons of Diti—may you yourself become the means for my attainment; may you do so with earnest care.

Here too, there is the sequential placement of conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force, even without their direct connection to the subject matter at hand. Since the names of these means are recorded in this verse by the word "upāyabhūtaḥ" (being a means), which is devoted to the primary sense, it is also an indication of the suggested meaning (*sūcyārtha*); thus, because of the presence of the figure of speech *mudrā*, this *Ratnāvalī* is distinguished as being "crowned" by that [figure].

O Lotus-eyed One, just as the white mountain, possessing the crystal-like luster that removes the fear of those who chant the Veda, quickly melts away their sins, so too does Your mountain-like form spread throughout the four castes.

O lotus-eyed one! You are praised by the four-faced Brahmā; you are the remover of terror, the dispeller of fear. You are white with the luster of crystal—of which Amara says: "śukla, śubhra, śuci, śveta, viśada, śyeta, and pāṇḍura [are synonyms for white].

You are that by whom evil has been swiftly driven away—"pradrāvi, drāva, and sandrāva" mean fleeing, according to Amara—and you are the burner of that which is called *veṃ*, namely sin (*pāpa*). *Kaṭa* refers to that [sin], and you are its consumer.
Indeed, because it burns away all evils, it is called Veṅkaṭādri.

Thus, because it is well known that [the word *dharādhara*] removes sin; "those two" refers to you and the mountain Śeṣādri, which is the "upholder of the earth" (*dharādhara*). The meaning is that the fourfold nature (*cāturvarṇya*)—that is, the state of having four syllables—belongs to the word *dharādhara*, as it is composed of such [syllables]. It spreads [this meaning]. Here, there is a sequential placement of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. Because the mention of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and so forth is established by the term *cāturvarṇya*, this is also a *mudrā* figure, just as before.

O Blessed One, just as that wise man, describing Your divine deeds, has grasped You through the practice of *nyāsa* and, established in the contemplation of You, has reached the supreme abode while still remaining within the stages of life (*āśrama*). 1781.

O Blessed One! He is so called because he describes that divine life. By "having grasped you through *nyāsa*," that is, by the entrusting of the burden (*bhara-nyasana*), he has brought you under his control. By the word "grasped" (*gṛhīta*), there is a recognition of the term "grasped" found in the mantra for performing the *nyāsa*: "You are taken with a marriage-rite (*upayāma*); I take you for the Brahman, for the Greatness; Om—thus one should yoke the Self."

Established in your meditation, the wise man attains—that is, reaches—the supreme abode by means of the *āśrama* alone, that is, without the exertion involved in performing other means. In the word "ayati," the root *i* (from *idhā*) is elided as per the rule "iṭ-kiṭa-kaṭi. Here, the sequential placement of the stages of life (*āśramas*)—the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the ascetic—who are mentioned together in the *Smṛtis* and other texts, is indicated; thus, everything is as explained previously. By the words *varṇin* and *gṛhin*, the student and the householder are understood respectively.

Just as one desiring the fruit of auspicious means resorts to the four chapters [of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*] to avoid the contradiction between existence and non-existence, so do I, O Kamalā, take refuge in Hari, who possesses abundant internal consistency within You.

O Kamalā! I take refuge in you, being one who meditates skillfully—that is, with great proficiency—in order to avoid and pacify the obstruction caused by existence (bhava), which consists of worldly life or birth; for I am desirous of attaining Hari, who maintains a vast lineage and connection with you, and who is the means for achieving auspiciousness, the fruit of which is the ultimate goal consisting of liberation (niḥśreyasa).

Herein is a sequential indication of the four topics—reconciliation, non-contradiction, means, and fruit—which are expounded in the four chapters of the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*. By indicating these meanings through its four chapters, this work is also a "seal" (*mudrā*). This *Ratnāvalī* is headed by that [seal], just as before.

Furthermore, one should discern the specific distinction here: by the phrase "Hara" (the Destroyer), the nature of the Brahman to be attained is described; by "I take refuge," the nature of the individual self (pratyagātman) who attains is described; by "the four chapters," the means of attainment is described; by "the auspicious means and fruit," the nature of the fruit is described; and by "the opposition between worldly existence and liberation," the nature of the obstacles to attaining that nature, means, and fruit are described—though these have been presented somewhat out of their sequential order.
That Bhīmasena, victorious in battle, finds truth and righteousness; he attains a most excellent lineage and, together with Lakṣmī, serves you, O God. (1783)

Here, by means of the manner of the *mudrā* ornament conjoined with *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is the presentation of the five Pāṇḍavas, beginning with Yudhiṣṭhira, according to their well-known order; this constitutes a specific distinction in aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) compared to the previous examples.

Just as you, O Haricandana, provide for one who enjoys his wife and others, who is free from the *pārijāta* tree, who possesses the happiness of progeny, and who is full of fragrance—you are the bestower of beautiful fortune upon the gods. 1784.

O Haricandana! [The term] *haricandana* means that Hari himself is the sandalwood; this is his vocative address. You are "delightful" (*rucirā*), meaning beautiful even to the gods, implying that you are praised by them as well. Being so described as one who "gives" (*dadāti*) that *śrī*—be it prosperity or splendor—you are thus addressed. By the word *haricandana*, a specific celestial tree is also understood; in that case, the phrase may be supplemented to mean "one who gives the delightful *śrī* (splendor) of the gods."

He is so described because he enjoys his own dependents—who have taken refuge in him—as well as his wife and others, to whatever extent is appropriate; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), kinsmen and the like are included. He is "apārijāta," meaning one by whom the host of enemies (arijāta) has been cast away. He is "sasantānasukha," existing together with the happiness of progeny; for that very reason, he is "sāmoda," which means both full of joy and possessing fragrance. The sense is that because Hari is metaphorically represented as sandalwood, [the term implies both]. Thus, you fashion or create [him].

The sense is that you cause your own worshiper to attain all forms of prosperity. Here, there is a sequential placement of the five divine trees, beginning with Mandāra and Pārijāta. Since the term "divine tree" (*daivataru*)—even as a single word-part—indicates the intended meaning (the *sūcyārtha*) embodied by the verse, it should be understood, as before, that this [verse] is adorned with the *mudrā* ornament.

May that Person protect us—he who, like a blue lotus, is radiant with the beauty of a mango tree, who dispelled the grief of the *caraṇāravinda* (the lotus-feet) by his own final words, and who was rendered useless (*apārtha*) [by the cessation of worldly purpose]. 1785.

May that Man, resplendent like a blue lotus, protect me—[the word "me" being understood]. He is he whose charioteering sport consists of the glorious Līlā, who accompanied Pārtha (Arjuna) when he had taken refuge at his lotus-feet, and who, by his own final words—"I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve"—removed his sorrow and thus acted as his assistant. Herein lies the arrangement of the five arrows of the God of Love according to their well-known sequence, beginning with "the lotus, the aśoka," and so forth.
Or rather, may I joyfully perceive the infinite one, the sustainer of life, who provides the drink of his own teachings and is clad in saffron robes, as I draw him into the lotus of my heart. (1786)

The construction is as follows: while bringing—that is, leading—to the heart-lotus that Lord Ananta, who is renowned throughout all the worlds and the Vedas, who dispels those people who obstruct His own discourse, who is the bestower of affection, and who is clad in saffron-colored garments with a yellow upper cloth (the Amarakośa states: *saṃvyāna* and *uttarīya* mean an upper garment), one should contemplate Him with joy. Herein lies the sequential placement (*nyāsa*) of the vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—as established in the Śrutis and other scriptures.

O lotus-eyed one, by means of dharma, may I make you—the sole object of verbal expression, untouched by defects, possessing excellences beyond description, and most fortunate—a subject for my mind. 1787.

O lotus-eyed one! [I bow to Him] whose excellent qualities—beyond the reach of definition, inaccessible to speech and mind, and untouched by any defect—are such that the Śruti declares, "From whence words turn back. By these three words, [the Lord's] divine and auspicious form is indicated, as described in the *Antarāditya-vidyā*: "Just as a lotus is golden-hued, so are His eyes; He has risen above all evils; He rules over the worlds beyond this, and over the desires of the gods."

Thus, the state of having lotus-eyes (*puṇḍarīkākṣatva*), the quality of being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), and the state of being a mine of attributes such as lordship over all worlds and desires are indicated. In this context, the scriptural passages beginning with "free from sin" (*apahatapāpmā*) and ending with "whose resolve is true" (*satyasaṃkalpaḥ*), as well as those beginning with "He who is omniscient" (*yassarvajñaḥ*), are also to be considered. For this very reason, He is "subhaga," meaning one whose *bhaga* (fortune) is beautiful; for it is said: "Sovereignty, heroism, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion—these six are declared to be *bhaga*."

Thus, he who possesses these six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya) is so described; that is to say, He who is denoted by the word "Bhagavat. He is accessible through scripture alone, according to the Śruti, "That person is known from the Upaniṣads," and the Sūtra, "Because He has the scriptures as His source. The meaning is that His form and other attributes, as demonstrated here, are to be understood solely through the scriptures. Such as You are, I worship with *dharma*—the Vaiṣṇava injunction being the highest of all dharmas:
"Of all dharmas, this dharma is considered by Me to be the most superior."
Whatever merit a man may gain by always worshipping the lotus-eyed Lord with hymns of praise through devotion;

By means of this aforementioned supreme dharma—worship, salutation, praise, and so forth—I shall diminish the range of the mind and grasp it with a purified intellect, according to the Vedic revelation: "But with a purified mind. Here, there is a sequential presentation of the five objects of the senses—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—which are well-known in both worldly experience and the Vedas, though they do not directly connect to the subject at hand. By the word "viṣayam" (the object), there is also the figure of speech known as *mudrā* (the seal), because it indicates the intended meaning through the suggestion that these objects have been arranged in sequence. It should be understood that this is like a *ratnāvalī* (jewel-necklace) strung together by that [sequence].

O Acyuta, just as a word-forming suffix (*taddhita*) bestowing auspiciousness might leave me—the performer of good deeds—as the sole remainder of a thousand compounds, so do You regard me; for You are the very form of the eternal root that exists without beginning or end.

"O Acyuta! [He is] so called because He bestows that which is auspicious, brings about welfare, is well-known in the scriptures, and is beneficial in the form of a means—namely, the means for attaining You, consisting of devotion and surrender, which is the locus of all auspiciousness. This is according to the Gītā: 'I give that yoga of discernment by which they come unto Me. He is *nādyantaḥ* (without beginning or end), a compound with the negative particle *na-*, meaning that for Him neither a beginning nor an end exists."

The term *dhātu* is devoid of origination and destruction; it is derived from the root *dhā* with the *uṇādi* suffix *tun*, according to the rule "from the roots *asita-nigami-masi-saci-vidhāñ-kruśi*, [the suffix] *tun* [is added]. This word ends in a long vowel (*udanta*). This is made clear in the *Śrutaprakāśikā* and the *Upaniṣadbhāṣya* during the commentary on the Vedic passage: "By the grace of the *dhātu*, [I shall attain] greatness. Its nature is such that, being free from the modifications of existence characterized by birth and destruction, it is the sustainer and nourisher of the entire universe.

Therefore, for a thousand years—that is, for a long duration of time—consider me as one whose very existence remains solely for you; the sense is that I am destined to be your servant until the end of my life. Regard me as such, one whose auspicious and beneficial mode of conduct consists of service (*kaiṅkarya*). Herein, the essential nature (*svarūpa*), the means (*upāya*), and the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) are to be understood according to their respective places.

Herein is the sequential enumeration of the five types of *vṛtti* (grammatical formations) renowned in the circles of grammarians, namely: *kṛt*, *taddhita*, *samāsa*, *ekaśeṣa*, and *sanādyanta*. Furthermore, as before, the meaning of the needle is indicated by the term *kalyāṇavṛtti*, signifying that those who have attained their respective *vṛttis* (modes of life or livelihoods) are composed here. It should be noted that because the expression *sanādyanta* and so forth is a restatement of a technical rule from Pāṇini’s Sūtras, the suffix *ṅmuṭ* does not apply. For this very reason, it is said: "These twelve [suffixes] beginning with *san*..."
In this treatise, such usages involving the augment *ṅamuṭ* as "etac-chāstram-uṇādiṣu" and "dhātu-sūtra-gaṇa-uṇādi-vākya-liṅgānuśāsanam" are thus rendered consistent.
O lotus-eyed one, that wealth which does not attend upon your lotus feet—even if it belongs to men in numbers beyond counting—cannot bring joy to the wise. (1789)

O lotus-eyed one! That wealth which, though existing solely for the sake of men's own interests, does not embrace Your lotus feet—that is to say, that wealth which is not offered at Your lotus feet—though it be beyond counting and immeasurable, shall not bring joy to the wise, those who know Brahman; the sense is that such wealth is utterly useless. Herein, the sequence of the nominal stem meanings—possessive suffix (*svārtha*), object (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṃkhyā*), and case-role (*kāraka*)—follows the established convention of the grammatical community (*śābdika-goṣṭhī*).

O Blessed One, I take refuge in You, the locus of the worlds, who bestows supramundane fruits, and who—though beyond the scope even of the words of the scriptures—is here the subject of dispute for those shrouded in darkness. (1790)

O Blessed One! I take refuge in You—who are beyond the scope of the words of scripture, who are beyond the range of darknesses (tamas), that is, of ignorances (ajñāna) which are like cataracts (timira), and who are the uprooter of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa)—the very white fortnight (śuklapakṣa) [of ignorance]—and who bestow that supramundane fruit which is liberation (niḥśreyasa). I take refuge in You, the substratum (adhikaraṇa) or support of the worlds, with absolute certainty (aviśaya), free from all doubt. In this context, the ancients know an *adhikaraṇa* (a formal section of inquiry) to consist of five elements: the subject matter (*viṣaya*), the doubt (*viśaya*), the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final conclusion (*uttara*), and the purpose (*prayojana*).

Thus is the sequential arrangement of the five factors of a topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) as established in the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā; and by the term *adhikaraṇa*, there is also the indication of the meaning that is to be indicated.

Just as one who has conquered Indra through his wealth and power is capable of removing fear at will, O lotus-eyed one, so too may you, when beheld by you, become radiant with the splendor of your rays. 1791.

*Sukalaḥ* means one who is both a giver and an enjoyer; as Amara states: *sukalo dātṛbhoktari*. *Bhaya-haraḥ* means capable or able to remove fear—the terror of oneself and those dependent on one—the sense being "the giver of fearlessness to the frightened. *Bhānumadaṃśubhiḥ śrīmat sarasijam iva locanam yasya tasya sambuddhiḥ*: an address to him whose eye is like a glorious, radiant lotus by the rays of the sun. Here, there is a sequential placement (*nyāsa*) of the six—lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy—and thus this [verse] possesses a distinct charm (*vicchitti*) compared to the previous ones.

O Blessed One, just as one who is straightforward through the teachings may become stainless and free from the great darkness of delusion, so too, O Lord born from the lotus that bows through self-restraint and subduing of the senses, may your devotee conquer the group of six internal enemies.

The term *śramadamanaḥ* refers to the Perfectly Awakened One (*saṃbuddhi*) who brings liberation from the exhaustion of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). The term *naman-sarasijabhavaḥ* refers to Him to whom Brahmā, born from the lotus, bows; O Blessed One! Your devotee may indeed be straightforward (*avakra*), meaning one whose character is not crooked. He is pure (*vimala*) and stainless through both general and specific virtues (*dharma*), for the Veda declares, "By dharma one casts off evil. Therefore, he is so called because his character (*śīla*) is directed toward the destruction (*hati*) or removal of darkness (*tamaḥ*), that is, the quality of ignorance (*tamoguṇa*). Furthermore, he is one by whom the group of six enemies (*ariṣaḍvarga*), such as desire and the rest, has been conquered.
Neither anger, nor envy, nor greed, nor an unwholesome mind arises in those devoted to the Supreme Person who have performed meritorious deeds.

The intended meaning is that this is because of such a statement. Here too, there is a sequential arrangement of precisely desire, anger, and so forth, by means of another method. Furthermore, the distinction is that this is a *mudrā*, because the specific thematic meaning indicated by this particular form is suggested by the phrase "one who has conquered the group of six enemies."

Just as the sages, beholding Rāma— who possessed well-knit peace and war strategies, who was like a lordly elephant in his gait, and who was equipped with a bow— sought refuge in him without hesitation, desiring to attain their goal through him.

One whose body has joints and articulations that are perfectly well-knit—by this, his extraordinary beauty, which captivates the minds of the sages who will be described hereafter, is indicated. As it is said:
"The arrangement of the major and minor limbs in their proper proportions, with joints and articulations that are very smooth and supple—that is called beauty."

Thus [it is said].
