Having beheld Rāma—who possessed a vehicle like that of the lord of elephants (Airāvata) and was equipped with a bow—the sages, desiring to attain non-duality with him through a firm embrace, took refuge in him. One should here recall the narrative from the Padma Purāṇa: that the sages, infatuated by the beauty of the Blessed Lord, the son of Daśaratha, who had entered the Daṇḍaka forest, became as eager to embrace him as women are.

Alternatively, the meaning is that they took refuge [in Him] desiring non-duality—that is, freedom from dispute—with Him; for, according to the stated principle, "Non-dispute, however, is the surrendering of one's own self at His very feet," they took refuge desiring to entrust the burden of their self-protection to His lotus-feet. Here, there is an arrangement of the six well-known political expedients—peace (*sandhi*), war (*vigraha*), marching (*yāna*), halting (*āsana*), duplicity (*dvaidha*), and seeking protection (*āśraya*)—presented in their traditional order.

I bow my head in every direction to that son of Daśaratha, whose arm-heat dispels the fear of the Surabhi cow, who quenched the forest fire of autumn with a downpour of arrows, and who is like a supreme mass of snow.

I bow my head in every direction to that son of Daśaratha—he whose heat of the arm is the dispeller of fear, whose downpour of arrows is itself a torrential rain, by whom the night-stalkers (niśicara) were laid low as if by a forest fire, whose army is supreme cold, and who possesses a host of supreme snow-masses (paramahimānīka). [The suffix *kap* is applied here according to the rule *na-dṛ-śat-śca*. I pay homage.

The meaning is that I bow down in every direction according to the procedure stated in the verse: "First in front, then behind, salutations, salutations from all sides, O All. Here, there is a description of the six seasons beginning with spring, in their proper order, through the partial application of words such as *surabhi* and others, and by means of word-play (*śleṣa*) on terms such as *ūṣma*.

O Acyuta, who else besides you could be the performer of acts such as creation, the controller of the instruments [of action], the bestower of all auspicious things, and the one who strikes down those who take refuge at your feet? (1795)

O Acyuta! You are the agent of the acts of creation and so forth—the creation of the universe and its like; by this, the Śruti passage, "O Bālāka, he who is the maker of these persons and whose work this is, he indeed is to be known," is recognized. Furthermore, you are the controller of the instruments, that is, the senses, according to the Śruti, "The hearer of the hearing," and so forth.

The "affliction" (*ādhi*) refers to mental anguish; the "agents" (*karaṇāḥ*) are those who cause it, or its instruments and means. "Destruction" (*hatim*) refers to its injury or removal. "The bestowing of all auspiciousness" (*sakalaśubhasaṃpradānam*) refers to the granting of every kind of welfare to them alone. By these two terms, the removal of the undesirable and the attainment of the desired are expressed. The construction is: "Who else but You performs this? In this regard, they say there are six grammatical factors (*kārakas*): the object (*karman*), the agent (*kartṛ*), the instrument (*karaṇam*), the recipient (*sampradānam*), likewise the point of departure (*apādānam*), and the locus (*adhikaraṇam*).
Thus is the sequential arrangement of the six grammatical factors (kārakas) as stated by the grammarians.

May the lotus-eyed one, the treasure-house of the seven worlds, be victorious—his staff-like arms are the lords of the ocean of the kingdom of the agitated asuras, and his heart is adorned by the lotus-eyed Lakṣmī. 1796.

The word *lavaṇā* is feminine by its very nature and denotes beauty (*lāvaṇya*), as Mallinātha and others have explained in various places, such as in the passages "beauty is indeed *lavaṇā*" and "of her whose remaining connection was like the beauty of *lāvaṇya*. According to the *Viśva-kośa*: "The word *lavaṇa* [denotes] taste, a Rākṣasa, and a particular ocean; *lavaṇā*, however, [denotes] splendor. One who shines with that [splendor] is *lavaṇāśālī*. The lord of the oceans is the kingdom itself of the lords of the Asuras, such as Hiraṇyakaśipu, Naraka, and others, which has been agitated.

May the lotus-eyed one be victorious—he whose arm is like the King of Oceans and who holds that very ocean as his churning-staff; he whose chest, adorned with the lotus-eyed Śrī, is the repository of the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr; and he who is the lotus-eyed one. Herein lies the distinction from previous examples: there is a sequential presentation of the seven oceans—Salt, Sugarcane, Wine, Clarified Butter, Curd, Milk, and Water—as established by their traditional recitation together in the Purāṇas and other texts.
Furthermore, through the phrase "repository of the seven worlds," there is the figure of speech *mudrā* (seal), as it indicates the ocean by means of a needle-like hint.

May our utterances declare the truth concerning that Lord, who is as vast as the ocean, who is beloved by the earth, who possesses a golden luster, who resides within the orb of the sun, and who is accessible through the fierce austerities of the virtuous.

Our utterances—our words—are directed toward Him who possesses boundless compassion; the reason for this is that He is the beloved of the Earth, the daughter of the Ocean. In this regard, the verse of the venerable Ācārya, "The eternal Śrī resides in the orb of the Sun," should be remembered. For this very reason, the phrase "having a golden luster, situated in the orb of the Lord of Day" serves as a descriptive qualification. Here, one should keep in mind the form of the divine spiritual body described in the Antarāditya-vidyā: "This golden person who is within the sun."

May they speak of—that is, describe—the divine Nārāyaṇa, who is attainable and accessible through the fierce and intense austerity of virtuous and noble people; who is Truth, endowed with absolute existence, according to the Vedic revelation, "Truth is knowledge"; or who is the controller of both the liberated and the unliberated, as heard in the Dahara-vidyā: "Now that which is Sat is immortal, and that which is Ti is mortal; and by means of Ya, he holds both together."

The sense is this: let them constantly discern my words as referring solely to Śrīnivāsa—the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣottama, whose form is eternally divine and auspicious—and let them compose literary works concerning Him alone. Here, there is a sequential arrangement of the seven *vyāhṛtis*, beginning with *bhūḥ* and so forth, which are traditionally recited together in the Vedas. By the term *vyāhṛtayaḥ*, there is an indication of the intended subject matter (*sūcyārtha-sūcana*), and thus, as before, the verse is characterized by the presence of a *mudrā*.

O dark-eyed Mother, people in this world call you one whose smile is illuminated by the gentle and auspicious face of Aṅgiras, which has the color of a red lotus, and who is peerless and irresistible.

"Padmavarṇām" means one whose complexion is like the color of a reddish lotus, according to the Śruti. Likewise, "maṅgalam" means gentle and beautiful; as Amara states: "The word *saumya* refers to what is beautiful or has the Moon as its deity. She is "one whose limbs (*aṅga*) are such," and her vocative case form is "O lady of such limbs," with the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* applied according to the rule "aṅgagātra."

"O you whose gentle smile (tanuhasita) is radiant with rasa—either the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa) or the sentiment of compassion (dayā-rasa)—and not deceptive like [the conduct of] a king who 'strikes while smiling'! By this it is suggested that her gentle smile is more virtuous even than the gentle smile of the Blessed One; for, according to the saying "That smile is indeed a form of illusion (māyā) that causes the madness of people," his smile is of the nature of an illusion that intoxicates the world. Thus is her address: "O you whose gentle smile is radiant with rasa."

"O dark-eyed one!"—this is because it has been said, "And she, this one with dark eyes. O Mother! You are incomparable (*atulyā*), peerless (*asadṛkṣā*), and unrestrained (*anavagrahā*)—meaning omnipresent (*sarvavyāpinī*). According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *avagraha* [is used] in the sense of obstruction of rain, an impediment, and the forehead of an elephant. Alternatively, *anavagrahā* means possessing unbridled sovereignty (*niraṅkuśasvātantryā*), since even the sovereignty of the Lord, which is beyond questioning, is dependent upon her. As it is said: "Beholding whose face, He (the Lord) performs everything, being entirely subject to her will," and so forth.
"Thus the virtuous say"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Here, there is a sequential placement (nyāsa) of the nine planets, beginning with the Sun, without their connection to the subject at hand; this constitutes a "seal" (mudrā) because it indicates a meaning suggested by the term "nine planets. In contrast, the verse previously cited, beginning with "The Sun is the King," is connected to the subject at hand and concerns the Lord; thus, there is a distinction between the two.

How indeed could this hero—who is adorned with mountain peaks of serpents, who possesses the sentiments of the heroic, the compassionate, and the marvelous, and who shines with a great smile—not bring others under his sway? For he is peaceful, having made his enemies utterly loathsome and fierce through his own fearlessness. (1799)

"By compassion" means by wonderful, marvelous mercy. He whose great facial luster—the radiance of his face—is such that he has rendered his enemies loathsome, deformed, wicked, and cruel. "Peaceful," he is the adversary of the six waves [of worldly existence]; whom indeed would he not bring under control by his own fearlessness and his own splendor? The meaning is that he would subjugate everything by his very majesty alone. Herein, the nine aesthetic sentiments (rasas) are traditionally remembered as: the erotic (śṛṅgāra), the heroic (vīra), the pathetic (karuṇa), the marvelous (adbhuta), the comic (hāsya), the terrifying (bhayānaka), the loathsome (bībhatsa), the furious (raudra), and the peaceful (śānta).
Thus is the sequential placement of the nine well-known aesthetic sentiments (rasas). However, in some places they are listed as follows:
the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, and the terrifying.
The sentiments of disgust, the marvelous, and the peaceful have also been declared by the ancients.
Thus the sequence is recited; however, in accordance with that, there will be examples of the reversal of the sequence to be described hereafter.

O Madhuhara, O Mādhava, may you— who possess the strength of the months of Bhādra, Āśvina, and Kārttika, and who have subdued the month of Māgha— surely grant me that pure luster of Śukra which is honored even by the dwellers of heaven.

This is the speech of a certain devotee who seeks both worldly and transcendent human goals: "O Madhuhara (slayer of Madhu), O Madhuvairin (enemy of Madhu), O Mādhava! O Śrīnivāsa! You—[being] that very one—unto me, whose intense ascetic practice (*tapas-caryā*) is like a cloud (*ghana*), [grant] *bhādra* (a collection of *bhadra* elephants) and *āśvayuja* (a collection of horses); for both terms, the suffix *aṇ* denotes a collective group. [The compound *bhādrāśvayuja* is formed with] the suffix *ka* according to the rule for words ending in *ig*."

"One who has a companion that is *ūrjasvala* (vigorous) and *baliṣṭha* (most powerful)" is what is meant by that [compound]. The state of being such is *tattātā*; "he desires (*iṣyate*) to go (*gacchati*) toward that" is *bhādrāśvayujorjasvalasahāyataiṣaḥ*. [The root] *iṣ* meaning "to go" belongs to the *divādi* class; from it, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). The meaning is: "one who possesses great assistance consisting of an army equipped with four divisions. By this, prosperity in this world (*aihika-samṛddhi*) is sought. Regarding *śukra*: "The word *śukra* may refer to Bhārgava, the month of Jyeṣṭha, or Vaiśvānara [fire]; it is masculine," according to the *Medinī* lexicon. *Śukra* means fire. *Vahni*... [the rest of the sentence is cut off].

Like that [sky], you should make yourself pure and stainless; by this, his possession of every kind of purity required for the means to liberation (apavarga) is indicated. According to the Viśvakośa: "The word *śuci* refers to that which is pure, unblemished, the spring season (*śṛṅgāra*), the month of Āṣāḍha, and the bright fortnight. You should also make yourself worthy of honor by the sky-dwellers—the deities of the *ātivāhika* path beginning with *arciḥ*—and ultimately served by them as well.

The sense is that, according to the statement, "Having enjoyed all pleasures, one shall at last go to the abode of Hari," you should likewise cause [the devotee] to experience the sovereignty of this world first, and finally to be endowed with the experience of the sovereignty of the supreme liberation (niḥśreyasa). Herein, the sequence of the twelve months—Madhu, Mādhava, Śukra, Śuci, and so forth—is established as recited in the Vedas, Smṛtis, and other texts.
Or rather, it may be like this:

I behold this pair situated upon Mount Vṛṣādri, praised by the beloveds born from the limbs of the Crab (Cancer), possessing an incomparable forehead, free from fickleness, with unequalled hands, and having caused all the Śamīna fish to bow down. 1801.

Here follows a sequential description, by way of symbolic ornaments (*mudrālaṅkāra*), of the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*)—beginning with Aries and Taurus and ending with Pisces—as they are well-known in astrology and other sciences.

[He beholds Him] whose forehead (*alika*) is incomparable (*atula*), peerless (*asadṛśa*), and worthy of praise (*īḍya*) by Gaurī, the beloved of the Enemy of Kāma (Śiva); [the forehead] which is free from fickleness (*vicāpala*), meaning its nature is unwavering. This is either an adjective for the act of beholding, or it describes Him whose hands (*karau*) are unequalled (*asamau*). He is one whose followers are *śaminaḥ*—those possessing tranquility—and their lords (*ināḥ*), meaning the foremost among the peaceful ones.

"Vinatāḥ sakalāḥ śamināḥ" means those who have bowed down and are entirely self-controlled; "yasya yasmin vā tat tathoktam" refers to that which is situated on the mountain of Dharma (Vṛṣādri), namely the couple in the form of Śrī and Śrīnivāsa, a dyad consisting of female and male. Having seen or meditated upon this with the eyes, [the word] "karkam"—where *ka* and *la* are interchangeable—means sin (*pāpa*), according to Amara’s lexicon: "Kalka is not feminine and denotes impurity or sin. One who possesses such [sin] is "karkī"; one who does not possess it is "akarkī. The construction is: "May I become such a person," meaning "may I be one whose former and subsequent sins have been destroyed and dissolved. This is the intended sense.
The example of a sequenceless [verse] lacking connection with the subject at hand (*prakṛtānanvayavatī*) is as follows:

"May he who is compassionate, who has conquered Kashi, and who bestows sweet nectar upon those [who seek it], be meditated upon—he who bears within his heart the Goddess Lakshmi, who is bowed down by the virtuous and who dwells in Dvaraka. (1802)

He shall give grief—the sorrow caused by widowhood—to some of those women who were the wives of the demon named Madhu; [the suffix] *tṛn* is used here after the root *dadāti*. The sense is that he is the destroyer of the Daitya Madhu. He is "radiant with victory" (*vijitakāśī*), where the suffix *kta* denotes the state of being victorious, and the suffix *ṇini* is added to the root *kāśati*; this is similar to the expression, "the monkeys are radiant with victory" (*jitakāśinaḥ*).

May that Supreme Person, Śrīnivāsa—the meaning being that he is the compassionate Being who bears within his heart Lakṣmī, the protectress of all worlds, known as Avantī because she possesses multitudes of gates (vārāḥ) through which the virtuous bow (natāḥ)—be meditated upon by me. (The word "may" is understood from the context). Herein it is said:
"Ayodhyā, Madhurā, Māyā, Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā, and Dvāravatī—these seven cities are the bestowers of liberation."
Thus is the placement [of mantras] by deviating from the sequence of those whose order of recitation is well-established.

Just as [the world consists of] Puṣkara, Śālmali, Jambū, Plakṣa, Krauñca, Kuśa, Medura, and Phaṇiśaila, so this one alone—possessing great branches and surpassing the seven continents—is victorious. 1803.

"Abundant" (*puṣkalāḥ*) means exceedingly beautiful; as Amara states: "Puṣkala may mean excellent or exceedingly beautiful. It is that [mountain] in which there are specific trees such as the *śālmali*, *jambū*, and *plakṣa*. It is so described because it has filled the great quarters (*mahatyaḥ āśāḥ*)—the directions—with its own expanse, making them lush with *krauñca* birds, *kuśa* grass, or water. The suffix *ka* is applied here according to the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā*; although the rule *ke ṇaḥ* would normally require the shortening of the vowel, the word *āśā* does not undergo this shortening because the rule *āpo'nyatarasyām* makes such shortening optional.

This very Phaṇiśaila alone, surpassing the seven continents, is victorious. Here, there is a placement of the seven continents—which are enumerated together in the Purāṇas and other texts as "Jambū, Plakṣa, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, Śālmali, and Puṣkala"—by transposing their order; furthermore, the term "seven continents" (saptadvīpa) serves as an indication of the intended meaning through a needle-like hint.

O Mother, your pair of eyes always brings joy to Aṅgiras as he praises you, bestows radiance upon Marīci, and grants delight to Atri, Yajña, Pulaha, and Kratu; it provides vastness to Vasiṣṭha and bestows happiness upon Bhṛgu. 1804.

O Mother! [He is] the radiant Marīcimān, the sun-like one who brings forth great joy (*sapulaha-rṣakara*) to the Blessed One of the Three Ages, producing horripilation and delight (*sapulaka-pramodāvaha*). Regarding *pulaka*, the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *pulasa* [is used] in the masculine for horripilation (*pulaka*), and as an adjective for that which is vast (*vipula*). *Vipula* means extensive. Regarding *styāna*, the *Medinī* states: "*Styāna* [is used] for the unctuous (*snigdha*), for an echo, and also for density and laziness. [He is] the *vasiṣṭha*—the most excellent (*vasīyāṃsaḥ*), the best—among the *kratubhujaḥ* (sacrifice-eaters), meaning among those who are world-protectors (*lokapāla*). The word *vasu* denotes excellence. From that, by applying the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*, the form *vasiṣṭha* is derived.

And this is clear from the *Kaumudī* commentary on the sūtra “*śvaso vasīyaśśreyasaḥ*”. It is "granting happiness" because of the statement: "The sight [of Him] is the cause of the power of the lords of the world. And it is "vast" and "granting happiness to Vasiṣṭha, who had stilled his sacrificial rites"; thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of two adjectival members.

Or rather, let my words always praise your pair of eyes—which grant happiness to that Indra (the consumer of sacrifices), who is called Kratubhuj because he possessed a vast and excessive *styāna* (sloth), namely the incapacity resulting from the loss of his sovereignty caused by the curse of Durvāsas. In this context:
"The one of great splendor created seven mind-born sons: Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and Vasiṣṭha."
Thus is the placement of the great sages mentioned in the Purāṇas, with a slight deviation from their sequential order.

Just as this world has been whitened by you—possessing the splendor of Airāvata, Kumuda, Puṣpadanta, Añjananāyaka, Supratīka, Vāmana, and Supuṇḍarīkākṣa—so too is it whitened by your fame, O Sārvabhauma. (1805)

O Vāmana! O You who assumed the incarnation of a dwarf by Your own will! O Supratīka! O You whose divine, auspicious form is such that "He is entirely golden, down to His very fingernails"—as described in the scriptures! O Supuṇḍarīkākṣa! This is an address to Him whose eyes are like a beautiful lotus (*puṇḍarīka*). By the word *su* (beautiful/excellent), all the connotations of the term *kapyāsa* found in the Śruti—"Just as the interior of a monkey's mouth" (*tasya yathā kapyāsam*)—are fully expressed: namely, [the lotus] having arisen from deep water, possessing a perfectly polished stalk, and being blossomed by the rays of the sun.

[The verse] is thus summarized: O Leader of Añjana, O Lord of the mountain named Añjana! [Your fame is white and bright, like the luster (ruk) of Airāvata, Kumudapuṣpa, and the elephant’s tusk (danta)—that is, the radiance of those things—so says the construction. By your world-renowned fame, known throughout all lands (sārvabhauma), the entire universe has been made white and radiant. Here, there is a transgression of the proper order regarding the directional elephants (diggajas) mentioned in the statement, "Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka," and so forth.

O Lord of the Serpent Hill, in ancient times, while reclining upon a banyan leaf at the Sarasvatī of the dissolution, You revealed Your own majesty to the sage Mārkaṇḍeya; this [account] is as pleasing to the ears as the Gaṅgā. 1806.

This narrative is well known from the Araṇyaparvan. Herein, the specific distinction from previous instances lies in the complete inversion of the order of Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī—whom one hears recited in the Śruti in sequence with vocative endings as "imaṃ me Gaṅge Yamune Sarasvati"—and their subsequent placement.

Just as the river of the Bull Mountain (Gaṅgā) is hospitable toward those on its banks—its waters glowing within the lotus-buds that blossom at the touch of the sun's rays, and its bees buzzing loudly [with joy]—so too is she eager to remove the misfortunes of others. 1807.

The "touch" (marśa) of the sun refers to its contact—that is, the touch of its rays. Regarding those situated on the bank (*taṭagān*), the term *sausnātikī* means "one who inquires about a good bath"; it is formed with the suffix *ṭhak* according to the rule *'pṛcchatau susnātādibhyaḥ'*. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "she who asks those who have well-bathed. Here, there is a complete inversion of the five dramatic junctures (*sandhi*)—the Opening (*mukha*), the Epiphany (*pratimukha*), the Development (*garbha*), the Pause (*avamarśa*), and the Conclusion (*upasaṃhṛti*)—which are established by their conventional order of recitation.
Furthermore, this is characterized as being interwoven with a suggested poetic fancy (*gamyotprekṣā*).
O Hari, the attendants of yours—restraint, observance, posture, and mastery over breath—rescue even one seized by the messengers of Death merely through the retention of Your name.
O hare!
Because he forcibly seizes Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Yama, and Varuṇa as well, he is therefore called Hari.

By the manner stated thus, the possession of the power to withdraw Yama is illuminated as an embellishment for the subject at hand; likewise, the capacity to eliminate sins, as expressed in the phrase "Hari removes all evils," is also shown. Your attendants are Sunanda, Nanda, and others who serve in your assembly. He describes them with the words beginning with "Yama," and so forth.

The *niyama* (restriction) of *Samavartin* Yama—the command that "sinners must be brought into my presence"—is the *āsana* (dismissal or rejection). Those who possess the *āyāma* (length or extent) of such [rejection] are those whose vast prowess (*parākrama*) is preeminent in setting aside the commands issued by Kṛtānta (Yama); this is the meaning. For this very reason, even a man seized by the servants of Yama—such as Ajāmila—is [rescued]; this is the underlying sense. (Note: Regarding the gloss on *prāṇa*: "Prowess (*śakti*) is valor; *prāṇa* is vigor," according to Amara.)

By the mere holding—that is, the mere grasping—of your name; by the word "mere" (*eva*), even the slightest touch of any other means is excluded, as well as the necessity of deliberate intention (*buddhipūrvakatva*) regarding that [name]. The sense is that they "bring back"—snatching [the soul] from the hands of Yama’s messengers and leading it under their own control. In this regard: "For he who, even though helpless, has uttered the auspicious name of Hari, has indeed performed expiation for the sins of ten million births."

A hundred such scriptural authorities are to be recalled here. This is the sequential arrangement of the restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and concentration (dhāraṇā)—which are well-known through their traditional recitation in the Yogaśāstra—though they are here devoid of meditation (dhyāna) and absorption (samādhi).

Just as you once heard some sweet words of Ramā, so now, O Lord, you who are composed of excellent qualities, pacify the intense fire of worldly existence for me, your meditator, with your glance that is as cooling as Kālī.

"Sweet"—meaning exceedingly charming in the manner described by the words "Who in this world is thus free from fault? and so forth; the sense is that it need not be many such verses. The meaning is that by that much alone, the clarity of your mind, which is intent upon her, will be easily attained. "Of Ramā"—the sense is, of her who has become the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) for your attainment. "Hearing the speech"—that is, while hearing it.

Immediately thereafter: O Lord! You, who are composed of excellent qualities and abound in virtues such as compassion and parental affection, with that gaze which is as cooling as a streak of dark clouds (kālikā), extinguish the intense and fierce forest fire of worldly existence for me, the meditator. Or, one may construe it as "the intense fever. Herein is a description of the seven famous cities—beginning with Ayodhyā and Mathurā—with certain omissions and a deviation from their conventional order.

May she who is the essence of auspiciousness, the mother of the Lord of Love, born from the ocean, whose abode is the forest of lotuses, who wears rags due to the power of her wrath, and who destroyed the sovereignty of Indra by her curse—may she be victorious! (1810)
Here, in the Purāṇas and other such texts, there is the placement of Bhāratī, Bhavānī, and Śacī, who are mentioned together, yet without any established traditional order.

May the two feet of the Daughter of the Ocean— feet which are as beautiful as those of Vidhi and Vāmadeva’s wife, and which are skillful in conquering darkness— rest upon my head, being exceedingly delicate.
Here were Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, and Kāśyapa;
as well as Kātyāyana, Gautama, Suyajña, and Vijaya.
Thus concludes the description of the four—Vāmadeva, Gautama, Vijaya, and Jābālī—who, despite being traditionally recited together, lack a fixed order of succession.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, the Ratnāvalī-sara, in the Alaṅkāra-maṇi-hāra.
Now begins the Tadguṇa-sara:
"Tadguṇa" is the assumption of another's quality through the relinquishing of one's own quality.

*Tadguṇa* (the quality of that) is the grasping of a quality belonging to another object situated nearby, preceded by the relinquishing of one’s own quality. This is an etymologically meaningful designation, based on the fact that "this [object] possesses the quality of that."
Just as it is,

this Vṛṣagiri here, colored by the luster of Your limbs which is skillful at dulling the beauty of the finest blue lotuses, shines forth in accordance with its name, "Añjana" (the Collyrium Mountain).

Just as people, failing to recognize Hari, might mistake him for a Garuda perched upon a parrot in order to conquer the entire world—a Garuda whose plumage is overspread with the luster of emeralds—so too [they fail to recognize him]. (1813)
O Mother, this pearl of your nose appears like a *guñjā* berry: it darkens the darkness below with the luster of your lower lip, while above, it acts as a star with the radiance of its own light.

Just as when the golden-hued Sarasvatī enters a lake for her aquatic sport, the waters themselves proclaim their own "golden-colored" nature, as described in the Vedas, so too do they proclaim it in you. 1815.

The meaning is that the quality of being golden-hued (*hiraṇyavarṇatva*), as stated in the Vedic scripture beginning with "Golden-hued, pure... and so forth [is attributed]. In these examples, the relinquishing of one's own qualities followed by the assumption of the qualities of another is quite evident. It should be understood that there is a mutual distinction among them: this [figure] is embellished by *samā* (simile) in the first, by *bhrāntimad* (error) in the second, by *upamā* (simile) in the third, and by suggested *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) in the fourth.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, the "Chapter on Similitude" (Tadguṇasara), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the "Chapter on Original Form" (Pūrvarūpasara): the restoration of one's own former quality is called *pūrvarūpa*.
The poetic figure named *pūrvarūpa* consists in the recovery of one's own original quality by one who had previously abandoned that quality and assumed another.

Just as Hari, seeing that the heart of Śrī— who had ascended the ocean and was possessed of great luster— was filled with embarrassment because of her own dark-blue hue, restored her to her former state by means of the radiance of his own jewel.

There was a particular sense of shame on the part of Hiraṇyavarṇā, thinking that an unsurpassed darkness had arisen upon her due to the agitation of the embrace of my beloved’s heart; [the Lord], however, by the radiance of his own jewel, the Kaustubha, restored this Śrī to her former state as Hiraṇyavarṇā, just as she was before.

Nor should it be argued that, because the Goddess Śrī described here as golden-hued is distinct from the yellow color [of the body] and the reddish glow of the Kaustubha gem, how can there be a recovery of her former form? For the description of yellow and reddish colors as being one and the same is established by poetic convention (*kavisamaya*). Thus it has been said in the *Alaṃkāraśekhara*:

The meaning is that the quality of being golden-hued (*hiraṇyavarṇatva*), as stated in the Vedic scripture beginning with "Golden-hued, pure... and so forth [is attributed]. In these examples, the relinquishing of one's own qualities in order to assume the qualities of another is quite evident. It should be understood that there is a mutual distinction among them: this [figure] is embellished by *samā* (similitude) in the first, by *bhrāntimad* (illusion) in the second, by *upamā* (simile) in the third, and by suggested *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) in the fourth.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, the "Chapter on the Quality of That" (tadguṇasara), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the "Chapter on Original Form" (pūrvarūpasara): the re-acquisition of one's own former quality is called *pūrvarūpa* (original form).
The poetic figure named *pūrvarūpa* consists in the recovery of one's own original qualities by one who had previously abandoned them to assume the qualities of another.

Just as Hari, seeing that the heart of Śrī— who had ascended the ocean and was possessed of a deep blue hue by her own radiance— was filled with embarrassment, restored her to her former state by means of the luster of his own jewel.

There was a sense of embarrassment, a particular kind of shame, that even for Hiraṇyavarṇā, an unsurpassed blackness had arisen due to the agitation of her beloved’s embrace. With the luster of his own jewel, the Kaustubha, he made this Śrī golden-hued once again, just as before; and herein there is no...

It might be argued that since Śrī is described as golden-hued (*hiraṇyavarṇā*) while [the Goddess] is yellow, and the luster of the Kaustubha is reddish, how can there be a recovery of the former form? This objection must be set aside, for the description of yellow and reddish hues as one is established by poetic convention (*kavisamaya*). Thus it is stated in the sixteenth chapter of the *Alaṃkāraśekhara*, the jewel of the tradition of poets, beginning with "Of Kamalā and Saṃpat," and continuing through "In the cases of Nīlalohita, golden dust, flames of fire, and so forth," ending with "Unity alone is intended."

O Lord of the Mountain of Serpents, may she whose eyes are like lotuses, who whitens with her smiles the pearl ornament upon your chest—which has been turned blue by her own luster—bring you well-being. 1817.

In both examples, the recovery of one's own quality (svaguṇa), which was previously abandoned, is quite evident. Some have designated this very phenomenon as *tadguṇa* (the "quality of that"); however, that is not tenable, because there is no scope for *tadguṇa* here. For the operation of *tadguṇa* occurs only when, through the abandonment of one's own quality, another's quality is assumed.

And this [transfer] is not possible here, because although for the Goddess of Fortune (*śrī*) and for pearl ornaments there may initially be the taking up of another's qualities after abandoning one's own qualities, subsequently there is an absence of both the abandonment of one's own qualities and the taking up of another's qualities. For this very reason, in the definition of that [type of] quality-transfer (*tadguṇa*), the phrase "one's own qualities" (*svaguṇa*) is intended to signify merely the relationship between a quality and its possessor as obscured by the compound, common to both adventitious and non-adventitious qualities.

Furthermore, in cases such as "vibhinnavarṇā garuḍāgrajena" (of different colors by the elder brother of Garuḍa), the objection that this is indeed *tadguṇa* (the quality of another) because the previously apprehended reddish color (*aruṇavarṇa*) is abandoned in favor of adopting the quality of another due to its being [merely] one's own quality, is refuted. For even so, since only one's own quality is actually attained and there is an absence of another's quality, it is impossible to describe it as *tadguṇa*.

Furthermore, if it were said that "this alone is the *tadguṇa* [figure]," then in well-known examples of the *tadguṇa* ornament such as "Your nose-pearl acts like a ruby by the luster of your lower lip," there would be no *tadguṇa* ornament at all. Nor is this a desirable consequence, for it would result in the aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*) established by experience being left without any basis. This is the general direction of the argument.
Furthermore, those experts in poetic ornamentation state that even when an object has undergone transformation, the persistence of its former state is also called *pūrvarūpa*.
Even when an object has attained a state of dissimilarity in comparison to its previous condition, the persistence of that previous condition is also the figure of speech known as *pūrvarūpa*.
Just as this painting, O lotus-eyed one, through your grace has attained liberation from its bonds, so too does this self attain release from the qualities of its own pure primordial nature. (1818)

This self, the individual soul (*jīva*), although having attained liberation from bondage—that is, from the connection with *prakṛti*—by Your grace, nevertheless undergoes bondage through the qualities of *prakṛti*, such as *tamas* and the rest, which are "extremely pure" yet "exceedingly impure"; this is a marvel. But the truth is this: the "extremely pure" qualities of *prakṛti* refer to the natural qualities, the inherent attributes such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth; that is to say, they are innate qualities.

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The term *prakṛti* may refer to the equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇasāmya*), as well as to the inherent nature of ministers and the like. Through these [qualities], one attains non-release—that is, inseparability (*avinābhāva*)—or release, which is connection; the meaning is that the eightfold group of natural qualities becomes manifest. Here, by means of the power of paronomasia (*śleṣa*), the continuity of the prior state—in the form of not being released from the qualities of the Great Pure Nature (*mahāśuddhaprakṛti*)—is indicated for the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is distinct from its previous state through bondage and liberation.
O Sun of the worlds, although darkness has dissolved away by the light of your divine radiance, the fortune of the virtuous returns once more; this is indeed marvelous! 1819.

O Creator of the worlds, O progenitor of the universe! (Alternatively, "of the worlds" is to be construed as qualifying "of those who worship": O Creator [Savitar] of those who worship! By means of Your divine light—whether that be vision or splendor—even when darkness, meaning ignorance or the primordial nature characterized by it, has been dispelled; or elsewhere, even when physical gloom has vanished, for those who worship You once again, there arises a state of supreme darkness.

O most excellent ones (*sattama*), the glory (*śrī*)—meaning wealth, power, or the excellence of knowledge and so forth, or even liberated sovereignty—is present elsewhere; for Amara states that *sattama* means "most excellent" or "extremely beautiful. Here too, by the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), it is shown that even when darkness has vanished, that glory persists.
Just as before, O Mother, those whose necks once bore trembling necklaces due to your sidelong glance—even now, alas, those same necks still bear trembling necklaces. (1820)

O Mother! Before the spreading of Your side-long glances—that is, prior to their emission—those people whose throats (the openings of their gullets) possessed *satarala* meals (where *tarala* means *yavāgū*, thus meaning meals accompanied by thin gruel; the sense is that their food was of inferior quality); even after [the spreading of Your glances], through the attainment of the excellence of prosperity following the diffusion of Your side-long glances, those same *satarala* meals remained in their throats. In the alternative sense (of the metaphorical interpretation): in their necks there were *satarala* necklaces—that is, strings of pearls (*muktāvalyaḥ*) accompanied by a central gem (*madhyamaṇi*).

The word *hanta* expresses wonder (*āścarya*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The term *atarala*—meaning 'unsteady,' 'fickle,' 'trembling,' or 'brilliant'—is of three genders; it is masculine when referring to the central gem of a necklace (*hāramadhyamaṇi*), and feminine when referring to gruel (*yavāgū*) or wine (*surā*). Here too, by means of the pun (*śleṣa*) on the phrase *sataralāhārāḥ*, the persistence of their former state is demonstrated.

Just as when the three worlds were shaken by the subduing of the Ten-faced one, even though the disturbance was quelled by the son of Daśaratha, the heavens were nonetheless agitated by the unrestrained, intoxicated, and formidable sports of Rāvaṇa. (1821)

The heaven (*dyauḥ*), which is the celestial realm (*svargaḥ*), was crowded and oppressed by the unrestrained and unimpeded (*viśṛṅkhalaiḥ nirargalaiḥ*) bold displays of Rāvaṇa, the ten-faced one (*dāśānanasya*). In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*): [the heaven] was crowded by the bold displays of Airāvaṇa, who was unrestrained by intoxication (*madena viśṛṅkhalaḥ*)—that is, whose fetters had fallen away (*vigalitanigalaḥ*). At the time of the ten-faced one’s presence, Airāvata remained with his rut dried up by the majesty of that [Rāvaṇa’s] staff-like arms; now that he has passed away, Airāvata has become one whose rut has fully returned, and thus his movement has become unimpeded. Here, even upon the subduing of the ten-faced one, the persistence of the heaven’s former state is brought to life through *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Just as one was previously without *samādhi* while existing [in the world], O Murāri, so too a person who now desires to reach Your feet—even while intensely practicing *samādhi*—alas, remains without *samādhi*. (1822)

"One whose mental concentration (*samādhi*) is non-existent" (*asama-ādhika*), meaning one for whom there is no equal concentration; or "one who is indeed without concentration" (*asamādhi-ka*), meaning one who is joined with a dissimilar concentration; or "one devoid of concentration" (*samādhi-rahitaka*); or "one who is indeed without equal or superior" (*niḥsamābhyadhika*). Here too, there is an inclusion of *śleṣa* (punning) based on the persistence of the prior state characterized by the absence of concentration.

O Mother, just as a person of good character bestows food upon whomever your sidelong glance reaches, alas, even when that person is deficient, he still bestows food because of his own goodness of character.
O Mother! When your sidelong glance falls upon a man, he becomes virtuous;
he is praiseworthy, he is possessed of merit, he is blessed, he is of noble birth, and he is wise. O Goddess, he whom you look upon is a hero and is valiant.

In the manner thus described, being possessed of auspicious qualities, he bestows—that is, distributes—food; [this is derived from the root] *śraṇa* (meaning "to give") belonging to the *caurādika* class, with the suffix *ṇya* added for the sake of the base meaning itself, followed by the present tense marker (*laṭ*). This man, even though that glance of yours has turned away from him and is thus defective toward him, remains [steadfast] due to his own excellent virtues.

"He distributes food. The word "batā" expresses wonder. The resolution [of the pun] is as follows: *guṇatā* is the state of being a *guṇa*; *suguṇatā* is excellence of quality (*suṣṭhu guṇatā*). The meaning is the status of a cook trained in culinary arts. Regarding this, the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *guṇa* is used for a bowstring, a subordinate element, beauty and so forth, a cook, a sense organ, renunciation, heroism, the *sattva* quality and so forth, the junctions of the day (dawn, noon, and sunset), and ropes."

The meaning is that he distributes food; *visrāvitā* refers to *śrāṇā*, which is gruel (*yavāgū*), and thus he is so described—he becomes a cook who distributes food in the houses of others. According to Amara, "gruel is *uṣṇikā* and *śrāṇā*. Here too, the persistence of his former state is described through a pun (*śleṣa*).

Or, for example: "O Śauri, it is indeed a marvel how a certain preeminent among the twice-born, having attained human status and even greater glory, became a possessor of abundant happiness through Your glance. (1824)

The reality is that Kucela was the most eminent among the twice-born, the best of birds, and the leader of the Brahmins. By means of human attributes—the characteristics of a man—he became superior even to Kubera; such is the actual state of affairs. Furthermore, he was a "su-khaga"—a beautiful bird—or rather, one who attains (*gacchati*) abundant (*bhūri*) happiness (*sukham*); this is the literal meaning. He became so. The word *kila* indicates tradition. The rest is clear. Here too, the persistence of his former state is demonstrated.

Alas, though Laṅkā had fallen under the power of Vibhīṣaṇa and its glory was destroyed by the Ten-faced one, it came to possess increased splendor through many gates by the majesty of you, O Hero of the Raghus. || 1825 ||
The glory of the ten-faced one has increased manifold; the truth is that his prosperity is of various kinds. Everything else is as before.

Just as even in a state of reversal, the letters of your words remain identical; O daughter of the ocean of nectar, they do not abandon their own sequence of phonemes, remaining full of aesthetic essence.

O daughter of the nectar-ocean! This is intended to illustrate the excellence of the sweetness of your speech. "Brāhmaṇavarṇāḥ" means those whose *varṇa* (color/complexion) is distinguished or preeminent; however, the true meaning is "those with excellent syllables. For this very reason, they are "equal to your words," that is to say, accompanied by the mind, or rather, highly esteemed by your speech. The true sense is that they are equal to your words in their sweetness. "Sārasarasāḥ" refers to the five-fold nectars (*makaranda*) which are both essential (*sāra*) and flavorful (*sarasa*); it should also be understood as "the most excellent (*sāra*) and delightful (*sarasa*)."

Therefore, even in an adverse state, at a time of the reversal of dharma, they do not abandon the sequence of their own colors—the order appropriate for the Brāhmaṇa caste; the sense is that they remain exactly as before. In reality, however, even when recited in reverse order (prātilomyena), they do not abandon the sequence or succession of their own colors—their own syllables—because the serial order remains identical in both the direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) readings of the word *sārasarasā*.
The distinction here is that the persistence of the prior state is enlivened by a pun (*śleṣa*) based on the identity between the word and its meaning.

Just as one who has become a constant servant here of Śauri, the Lord of the entire universe, can never attain identity with Him— even when released from his physical body— he remains exactly as he was.

Now, at this present time— that is, during the state of being connected with this body— the person who remains a constant servant of Śauri, the Lord of the entire universe, thinking "All individual selves are by nature the servants of the Supreme Self;
therefore, I too am Your servant," bows down in reverence.

The sense is: "from such scriptural authority as this. *Pratīkena* means by a part, that is, by the body. Or, it may mean "even though liberated from the *pratīka*"; that is to say, even though he has attained the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) preceded by the casting off of this body. He shall never attain—nor reach—*aikya*, which is non-difference from that Blessed Lord. Rather, he shall remain exactly like Him, similar to Him; for there is the scriptural teaching of "supreme equality" in the passage: "Stainless, he attains the highest equality" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 3.1.3).
By this [scripture], it is shown that just as pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like it.
Thus, O Gautama, the self of the sage who understands becomes [liberated].

Thus the meaning of the scripture has been described. The meaning of this scriptural passage is as follows: when pure water is poured into pure water, it becomes exactly like that [water] and not even slightly different. In the same way, for one whose nature is reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), the self (*ātman*) also becomes similar to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); however, it does not attain identity (*abheda*), because of the hearing of the word "like that" (*tādṛk*). The word *tādṛk* denotes similarity (*sādṛśya*), and similarity is necessarily constituted by difference (*bheda*).

Furthermore, the sense is that he would remain exactly as he was—a perpetual slave—and not himself become the sovereign of all. In this context, the word *sadādāsa* (perpetual slave) is a *pratīka* (a syllable-by-syllable reversal), being read in reverse order; according to Amara, "the term *pratīka* applies to that which is contrary. The sense is that even when recited [in reverse], it remains exactly as it was—a perpetual slave—and does not possess a different sequence of syllables. Here too, the persistence of the previous state is just as before. Both of these varieties of *pūrvarūpa* (reversion to the original form) are the invention of Jayadeva.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, the Chapter on Pūrvarūpa, in the Alaṃkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Atadguṇa:
they know *atadguṇa* to be the non-acceptance of the qualities of another with which one has come into contact.
The figure of speech *atadguṇa* consists in the non-acceptance of another's qualities even when in close proximity to one who possesses them.

The sense is: "on account of such scriptural authority" (*ityādipramāṇāt*). "By the *pratīka*" means by a limb, that is to say, by the body; or alternatively, "even though liberated from the *pratīka*. That is to say, even though he has attained the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) preceded by the casting off of this body, he would never attain—nor ever reach—identity (*aikyam*), which is non-difference (*abheda*) with that Blessed Lord. Rather, he would remain just like Him, similar to Him. This is because of the scriptural teaching of "supreme equality" (*paramasāmya*): "The stainless one attains supreme equality" (*nirañjanaḥ paramaṃ sāmyamupaiti*).
By this [scripture], it is shown that just as pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like it.
Thus, O Gautama, does the self come to belong to the sage who possesses such knowledge.

Thus the meaning of the scriptural passage has been described. This is the meaning of the scripture: when pure water is poured into pure water, it becomes exactly like that [water] and not even slightly dissimilar. Likewise, for one whose practice consists of reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), the self (*ātman*) also becomes similar to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), yet it does not attain identity (*abheda*); this is because of the hearing of the word "like" (*tādṛk*). The word "like" denotes similarity, and similarity is necessarily constituted by difference (*bheda*).

Furthermore, the sense is that he would remain exactly as he was—a perpetual slave—and not himself become the sovereign of all. In this context, the word *sadādāsa* (perpetual slave) is a *pratīka* (a syllable or part of a word), according to Amara’s definition: "A *pratīka* occurs in a contrary [or reverse] order. The meaning is that even when recited in reverse, it remains exactly as it was—a perpetual slave—and its phonetic sequence (*anupūrvī*) does not change. Here too, the persistence of the previous state is just as before. Both of these varieties of *pūrvarūpa* (the figure of speech where a preceding form is maintained) are the invention of Jayadeva.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, the Chapter on Pūrvarūpa, in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Atadguṇa:
they know *atadguṇa* to be the non-acceptance of the qualities of another with whom one has come into contact.
The figure of speech *atadguṇa* consists in the non-acceptance of another's qualities even when in close proximity to one who possesses them.

O Mother, though you dwell constantly within the heart of the Lord of the Serpent Mountain—which possesses the exquisite luster of the finest sapphire that shatters the enemy Vala—why is it that you do not acquire even the slightest bit of blueness? 1828.
Or as it is said:

O You who recline upon the serpent, although Your splendor is completely obscured by the mass of rays from the clusters of gems on the hoods—reddened by the weight of the exceedingly pure luster of the excellent serpent—You do not at all abandon Your own state of being "An-Asita" (the Un-darkened). 1829.
O lotus-eyed one, although this yellow garment has been worn by you incessantly, it does not abandon its own yellowness; yet even while wearing it, you do not abandon your own whiteness.
O Hari, abode of Kamalā, when your luster and the luster of Kamalā meet with one another, they shine forth intensely as if perfectly distinct, resembling respectively the Yamunā and the Sarasvatī.

In the first example here, the non-apprehension of another's qualities is expressed by the words (śābda), while the non-abandonment of one's own qualities is implied (ārtha). In the two subsequent examples, the non-abandonment of one's own qualities is expressed by the words, whereas the non-apprehension of another's qualities is implied. Furthermore, between these two, it should be noted that in the second example, the distinction lies in the fact that the Lord and Pītāmbara are mutually related. In the fourth example, however, both [the non-apprehension of another's qualities and the non-abandonment of one's own] are implied.

Nor should it be argued that the figures *tadguṇa* (the excellence of one) and *atadguṇa* (the lack of excellence of one) are already encompassed by the figures *ullāsa* (exaltation) and *avajñā* (disdain), which consist respectively in the manifestation and non-manifestation of excellence in one thing due to the excellence of another. For the word "excellence" (*guṇa*) as a constituent of the definitions of *ullāsa* and *avajñā* denotes that which is the opposite of a defect; furthermore, the manifestation or non-manifestation of excellence in one thing due to the excellence of another does not constitute the transfer or non-transfer of that very same excellence.

However, just as the arising or non-arising of awakening occurs for good and bad students through the instruction of a true teacher, so too do the arising or non-arising of two other qualities occur here, produced by those [original] qualities. In this context, the word *guṇa* (quality) refers to attributes such as color, taste, smell, and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the perception or non-perception of another's quality, what is intended is the coloring or lack of coloring by another's quality—according to the analogy of a red crystal or the staining of a garment—and it is precisely in this sense that the examples have been shown.
Thus, in the example about to be presented, there is no figure of speech called *atadguṇa*; rather, it is simply the figure of *avajñā* (disregard).

O Lord, though you dwell here perpetually upon the summit of the King of Serpents—a mountain as hard as a hundred times a hundred crores more than a hundred crores—you never exhibit any harshness whatsoever.
In this case, because the quality (guṇa) consisting of harshness does not serve as an embellisher (anuparañjaka), its non-acceptance does not constitute the figure of speech *atadguṇa*.

For even when placed under proper discipline, a fickle mind does not attain such purity by force; nor does a female buffalo, though grown old, ever adopt the behavior of a cow through mere similarity.

Even when the mind is fixed upon the moon—the Lord of Rites—it does not indeed attain such purity, clarity, and freedom from heterogeneous impressions (that is, a state free from conflicting notions); in the other sense, whiteness. Why is this? He says: "Because of fickleness. The meaning is: precisely because of its instability. Even though it has increased equally [with the moon], it remains solar...

The female buffalo (*sairibhī*), though increased by her own kind, does not adopt the conduct or status of the *saurabhī*. [The word *sairibhī* takes the suffix *ṅīṣ* due to its being a genus name. A *saurabhī* is a *surabhi*—a cow or a divine cow; as Amara states, "the word *surabhi* refers to a cow and, in the feminine, to a fragrant substance. This [female buffalo] belongs to that [lineage], hence *saurabhī*, taking the suffix *ṅīṣ* because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*. She does not adopt the conduct or condition of even a young heifer (*vatsatarī*) related to her; the sense is: she does not even adopt the conduct of a heifer, much less that of a direct *surabhi*.

In this case, although [the word *sairibhī*] is equal to the word *saurabhī* and has thus attained the designation of "vṛddha" (vowel-lengthening) by virtue of being similar to it—according to the grammatical rule: "That whose first vowel among its vowels is a *vṛddhi* is called *vṛddha*"—nevertheless, the word *sairibhī* does not share the same status as the word *saurabhī*. This is because, despite both words being *vṛddha*, they are mutually distinct in their nature. The superimposition of the feminine gender residing in the object onto the word is merely figurative; the function of the word *sairibhī* does not conform to the status of the word *saurabhī*. The sense is that even though both words possess the quality of being *vṛddha*, they remain heterogeneous to one another.

Furthermore, the word *sairibhī* does not share the same grammatical derivation (*vṛtti*) as the word *saurabhī*. The point is that while *saurabhī* possesses a secondary derivative derivation (*taddhita-vṛtti*)—meaning "this belongs to Surabhi"—the word *sairibhī*, being purely conventional (*rūḍha*), lacks such a derivative derivation. In this context, the meaning of the entire sentence serves as an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), because it stands in the relationship of a prototype and its reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*).

In this context, the meaning of the illustrative sentence (*dārṣṭāntika-vākyārtha*) consists precisely of the figure of speech *atadguṇa* (the "non-attaining of qualities"), which is animated by an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) based on the punning coalescence (*śleṣa*) of two meanings—such as the Lord and the moon—conveyed by words like "Vidhu" and so forth. However, the meaning of the exemplifying sentence (*dṛṣṭānta-vākyārtha*) takes the form of the figure of speech *avajñā* (disregard) according to the method previously stated; thus, there is a specific distinction in aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) from the previous examples.

Regarding this, the author of the *Sarvasva* maintains that there are two varieties based on whether the possessor of the quality (*guṇavat*) situated near the perceiver of qualities is superior or equal. His intention is as follows: since the non-perception of a quality related to an inferior object is inherent and thus fails to produce aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*), it does not constitute an ornament at all; therefore, a third variety based on inferiority is impossible. Others, however, assert that there are not even these two varieties, because they lack any specific intermediate aesthetic appeal (*camatkāra*).
Although these two—

*avajñā* (disregard) and *tadguṇa* (assuming another's quality)— are not distinct from *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation), since they are encompassed by its general definition— "the non-arising of an effect despite the presence of a complete cause"— nevertheless, they are enumerated as separate figures of speech because they possess specific forms that stand in opposition to *ullāsa* (manifestation) and *tadguṇa* [respectively]. Thus they say.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, the "Chapter on Tadguṇa," in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the "Chapter on Anuguṇa":
if [an object] acquires the quality of another due to the proximity of something else possessing a quality of its own kind...
For that [practice] is indeed conducive to the enhancement of a quality already established previously.

The ornament *anuguṇa* consists in the description of the excellence of one's own qualities, which were previously present, due to the proximity of another possessing similar qualities; this begins with Jayadeva.

O Mother, your eye, possessing a luster perfected by the blooming blue lotus and as if anointed with collyrium, appears like a threefold application of kohl when gazing upon your lover, owing to its own radiance. 1834.

"Saṃsiddhi" means "by nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*), according to Amara’s lexicon which states, "saṃsiddhi and prakṛti are synonyms. A "saṃsat" is an assembly or a multitude; thus, "beneficial to the saṃsat of blue lotuses" means that which resembles them. Here, the natural blackness of Lakṣmī’s eyes is further enhanced by the application of collyrium and other ointments.

O Mother of the World, your divine body shines with an intense saffron hue, as it is overspread by the luster produced by your golden garment, which is softened by the glow of a girdle of fresh rubies. 1835.
Thus, in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra, the eighty-first section is the *Anuguṇa* (Conformity).

As for *Janiviśeṣokti* (Particularity of Birth), since it is covered by the general definition—"the description of an effect despite the presence of abundant causes"—nevertheless, they say that because it possesses a distinct form that stands in opposition to *Ullāsa* and *Tadguṇa*, it is enumerated as a separate figure of speech.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, the "Chapter on Similitude" (Tadguṇasara), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the "Chapter on Consequence" (Anuguṇasara):
If [an object], by virtue of the proximity of another possessing a quality of its own kind...
For that [practice] is indeed conducive to the further enhancement of a quality already established.

The ornament *anuguṇa* (the concordant) consists in the description of the excellence of one's own qualities, which were previously existing, due to the proximity of another possessing similar qualities; and this begins with Jayadeva.
O Mother, your eye, possessing a luster perfected by the blooming blue lotus and as if smeared with collyrium, appears like the three-fold collyrium when gazing upon your beloved. 1834.

"Saṃsiddhi" means by nature; according to Amarasimha, "saṃsiddhi and prakṛti are synonyms. A "saṃsat" is an assembly or a multitude; "beneficial to that" (tasyā hitaṃ) means resembling it. Here, the natural blackness of Lakṣmī’s eyes is further enhanced by the application of collyrium and the like.

O Mother of the World, your divine body shines with an intense orange hue, as it is overspread by the luster produced by your golden garment, which is made smooth by the glow of a girdle of fresh rubies. 1835.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, the *Anuguṇasara*, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the *Mīlitasa-ra*:
if no distinction whatsoever is perceived due to similarity, it is *mīlita* (the "blended").
The poetic figure named *mīlita* occurs when the distinction between two similar objects is not manifested due to their resemblance.
O Lotus-eyed one, you laugh at your husband as he repeatedly applies golden ointment to your gold-hued cheek; distressed by not seeing [the reflection], he becomes perspiring. (1836)

"O Padmā! [The word] *kāñcanī* refers to turmeric (*haridrā*), as Amara states: "Turmeric is called *kāñcanī*, *aniśā*, and *pītā*. It means its powder; the sense is that it is used as an ointment on festive occasions such as a wedding. You laugh at your husband—who is distressed because he cannot distinguish the ointment from your own complexion due to their similarity of color as he repeatedly applies it to your cheeks, which are as fair as gold—and who is therefore perspiring, thinking, "My effort has been in vain"—for he is thus filled with regret.
Here, there is a non-determination of the difference between the golden quality of the lotus-like surface of the cheek and the application of the turmeric powder.
O Slayer of Mura, upon your forehead—which possesses the tender form of a blooming dark-blue water-lily and is naturally fragrant—who indeed could recognize this musk tilaka? (1837)
Here, due to the similarity between the dark hue and fragrance [of the bee] and the musk-tilaka on the forehead of Śrīnivāsa, there is an uncertainty regarding their distinction.
According to the opinion of the Easterners (Prācām), however, the definition is as follows:
"When an object is concealed by another object—whether by a mark that is natural or adventitious—that is illustrated as *mīlita*."

Where another object is concealed or hidden by some other object—whether innate or adventitious, common to itself and other objects, inherent, or similar—by means of a mark (*liṅga*) or characteristic (*cihna*), in both such cases there is the figure of speech named *mīlita*. The essential point is that *mīlita* is the concealment of the true nature of one of two things by a stronger one, due to the similarity of their characteristics.

Nor should it be argued that there is no distinction here from the *sāmānya* (commonality) which will be discussed later in the verse beginning with “*tāṭaṅkavajrarucibhara*,” because there is a clear difference between them: where two objects possess identical characteristics (*liṅga*) and one of them, being more powerful, causes the very nature of the other to be concealed, there is *mīlita*; whereas where the individual natures are perceived despite the concealment of their difference due to the similarity of qualities (*guṇa*), there is *sāmānya*. Thus they are distinct.

Just as the lord of rivers did not long endure the rising of anger in the corners of the eyes of the descendant of Kakutstha— which were naturally lovely with their reddish glow— he remained paralyzed for a time.
Or as it is said:
"The anger that arose from love on the naturally fair cheek-surface of Lakṣmī, who is golden-hued—even by the Bull-born One (Brahmā) himself, it was reportedly not recognized. (1839)

Just as your face, charming with its smile, has its lotus-eyes naturally blossomed, O Mother, how could I know from where your grace comes upon those who bow before you, even though it has already taken its place within you? 1840.

Therefore, the meaning is that he remains "stunned," not revealing his own self. Here, in the first case, the adventitious arising of anger is concealed by the mark of the glance of the descendant of Kakutstha—his own natural, inherent redness—which is common to both the concealment of his own self and the rising of anger. In the second case, however, the adventitious rage is concealed by the mark of the redness on the surface of Śrī’s cheek—her own naturally established quality—which is common to both her own concealment and the rising of wrath.

In the third case, however, the distinction is that the natural grace is concealed by means of the face of Śrī herself—by such signs as her naturally charming smile, which is common to her own innate disposition for concealing her grace.
Or as it is said:

"Just as at dawn, when the sun is upon the bow [of the sky], devotion—though it has taken root in the hearts of those who gaze toward Hari from the peak of Mount Vṛṣabha with their hair standing on end—does not manifest clearly in those who are trembling. (1841)

Here, devotion itself is concealed by the mark of the "sign" (*liṅga*), which takes the form of a common attribute—namely, the trembling of horripilation produced by the onset of the adventitious winter season.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Mīlita (Hidden) Ornament, in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra. Now begins the Chapter on the Sāmānya (General) Ornament:
"When a particular [object] is not perceived due to its similarity [to another], it is called Sāmānya."
The figure of speech called *sāmānya* consists in the non-perception of distinguishing attributes due to the similarity of multiple objects.
O Mother, whose eyes are like the red lotus, how could I know that you would show favor even to those who have merely set foot before you, let alone to those who bow down? 1840.

Therefore, the meaning is that he remains "stunned," not revealing his own self. Here, in the first case, the adventitious arising of anger is concealed by the glance of the descendant of Kakutstha through the sign of its natural redness—a quality common to both his own innate state and the rising of anger. In the second case, however, the adventitious rage is concealed by the sign of redness on the surface of Śrī’s cheek—his own naturally established quality, which is common to both his own concealment and the manifestation of wrath.

In the third [instance], however, the distinction is that the natural favor is concealed by means of Śrī’s own face—specifically through signs such as the charm of her smile—which are natural to her and common to her acts of concealment and grace.
Or, for example:

"Just as at dawn, when the sun is upon its bow, devotion—though it has taken root in the hearts of those trembling with horripilation as they gaze upon Hari atop the bull-peak mountain—does not manifest clearly. (1841)

Here, devotion itself is concealed by the mark of the physical signs—such as horripilation and trembling produced by the onset of the adventitious winter season—which serve to hide its common characteristics.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*, titled "The Chapter on Mīlita" (Hidden). Now begins the chapter on the figure of speech "Sāmānya" (Commonality):
When a particular is not perceived due to similarity, it is called "Sāmānya."
The figure of speech called *sāmānya* consists in the non-perception of distinguishing attributes due to the similarity of multiple objects.

Or rather, O Lord of Vṛṣagiri, during your pastime in the forest during the rainy season, neither the Daughter of the Ocean nor you could distinguish her golden-hued form from the lightning amidst the circle of clouds.

In the figure of speech *mīlita*, there is a total non-perception of difference—both that based on common attributes and that based on specificities such as individuality; whereas in *sāmānya*, although the mutual differences between individuals are perceived, only the non-perception of their mutually distinguishing attributes is presented due to similarity. This is the distinction.

For in the illustration of the figure *mīlita* (the concealed), the adventitious whiteness of the turmeric ointment and so forth does not appear as a distinct entity from the naturally white surface of Lakṣmī’s cheeks and the like. However, in the illustration of *sāmānya* (the common), there is indeed a manifestation of the Lord and Lakṣmī, and of the cloud and lightning, as distinct individuals; yet, their specific qualities—such as "this is the Lord" and "this is the cloud," or "this is Lakṣmī" and "this is the lightning"—are not perceived.

Therefore, because the distinction is concealed, it is called *mīlita* (the hidden); even when it is not concealed, if the distinguishing features do not appear due to similarity, it is called *sāmānya* (the general). Thus, both terms are etymologically appropriate.
Or, for example:

"O Slayer of Madhu, even though your locks of hair and your forehead-mark on the forehead are loosened and separated, people do not perceive them as such immediately, because of the great similarity in their many colors. (1843)

O Blessed One! A person does not perceive the difference on Your forehead between the *alaka* (curling hair), the *tilaka* (mark), and the *mṛgamada-tilaka* (sandalwood mark)—even though there is an extreme disparity (*atimātra-bhidā*), even though there is an excessive distinction (*ativeela-bheda*), and even though there is a distinction between the two sides by way of their respective colors (*avarṇa-tivarṇābhyām*)—because of the great similarity of color (*varṇa-sāmya*) with the dark blue (*nīla-varṇa*). In this context, the meaning is that although the *alaka* and the *tilaka* are indeed distinct, they are not perceived as such due to the similarity of their color; however, the other [sandalwood] mark is distinguished from the former because it possesses a different aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).

Just as there is blueness in a cloud, O Mādhava, so too is there a resemblance to Your form in it; these two are not known to possess distinct qualities, for they are therefore recognized as having similar colors.

This is the speech of someone regarding the Blessed One, Śrīnivāsa, as he dwells in the forest at the onset of the rainy season: "O Mādhava! There is a dark blue hue (*nailyam*) in the cloud (*ghana*), and therefore the likeness of that cloud exists in your body (*vigraha*); thus, these two—the cloud and the form of the Blessed One—possess identical colors (*sadṛśavarṇau*). Ultimately, that is to say, upon close examination..."

The meaning is that these two do not fail to possess distinction—that is, they do not lack difference—because both consist of the letter *nī* (in *nīlatva* and *taulya*). In this context, the reference to "these two" (*etāv etau*) as masculine is intended to point toward the substantive nouns. Ultimately, at the end (*antataḥ*), they are those whose phonemes (*varṇa*) are similar, namely the phoneme *ly*. The sense is that they are known to possess distinction—that is, to be endowed with difference—by means of the two phonemes *nai* and *tau*.
This meaning—that a distinction is perceived between the words *nailya* and *taulya* precisely by those [phonemes]—is also striking. Here too, the principle is the same as before.
According to the opinion of the Easterners (Prācāḥ), however, the definition is as follows:

"When, through the desire to express equality of qualities, the identity of another [object] with the subject at hand is expressed by means of a connection (yoga), that is declared to be the figure of speech called Sāmānya."

Where that which is actually distinct from the subject at hand is described as not being perceived separately from the subject due to the intended expression of equality of qualities, there the figure of speech named *sāmānya* (commonality) arises from "conjunction," which consists in the connection with common qualities. The essential definition is that *sāmānya* occurs when, despite the two things being perceived as having distinct intrinsic natures, their difference is concealed by the equality of their qualities. The distinction between this and *mīlita* (the hidden) has been explained in that very same place. [This applies] in the case of *tadguṇa*.

However, [in that case] there is the acquisition of another's qualities preceded by the abandonment of one's own qualities; here, on the other hand, it is the state of being indistinguishable from another who possesses equal qualities, without having abandoned one's own qualities at all—therefore, there is a difference between the two.
Just as a row of emeralds, beautiful with peacock feathers and inlaid in a pair of armlets, was not perceived separately once it had attained non-duality with the luster of his divine golden body.
O Mother, your row of teeth, its form swallowed by the mass of radiance from the jewels in your earrings, was not perceived as distinct even by people skilled in careful observation. (1846)

In the first example, with reference to the delight in the divine form of the Lord under discussion, it is stated that the rows of emerald gems—which are not under discussion—are indistinguishable from it due to the similarity of their green quality. In the second, however, because of the similarity of their white quality, the row of teeth of Lakṣmī, who is under discussion, is described as being perceived as non-different from the mass of brilliance of the diamonds in her ear-ornaments, which are not under discussion; such is the distinction between the two.

And thus, according to this view, in the verse by another, "The faces of the fair-browed women who had entered the lotus-pool were not perceived," as well as in our own verse, "During the wandering in the forest during the rains," although there is an appearance of difference between the face and the lotus, another poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) must be recognized because the differentiating characteristics do not manifest; for *mīlita* (concealment) is impossible through the concealment of essential nature, but rather through the concealment of difference.

This is because even a "universal" (sāmānya) is impossible [in this context]. Alternatively, the general definition of the figure of speech *Sāmānya* (Universalization) is: "the non-perception of distinction due to the equality of qualities. And since this non-perception of distinction occurs sometimes when a difference is being perceived and sometimes when it is not being perceived, one must postulate its internal subdivisions. Regarding the first type, according to the view that "if no difference at all is seen due to similarity, it is *Mīlita* (Blending)," consider the following: "Her eyes are tremulous at the corners; her words are of tremulous and charming syllables; her gait is slow with the weight of grace; and her face is exceedingly lovely."

Thus, the throbbing of the limbs of the deer-eyed women occurs spontaneously through their own natural grace; therefore, even though the onset of passion has taken hold there, it is not perceived as such.

Thus, in the aforementioned verse cited as an example of *mīlita*, and in our own verse beginning with "Upon the bow, at dawn, [he saw] Hari," since both entities are known by their essential nature (*svarūpa*) in a situation where that nature is concealed, one must admit that *mīlita* consists in the non-apprehension of difference due to similarity. If the definition of *mīlita* were accepted merely as "non-apprehension of difference due to similarity," then it should be understood that there ought to be internal subdivisions of *mīlita*.
All of this is clear in the *Kuvalayānanda*.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter on Generalities in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the chapter on *Unmīlita*:
they know *unmīlita* to be the manifestation of the distinction between two things that possess identical qualities.

When a distinction has been reached through the equality of qualities such that no determination of difference occurs, yet a distinction becomes manifest due to some cause, this is *unmīlita*, the antithesis of *mīlita*.

O Śauri, when Your body’s radiance flows upon the flood that sports along the bank, the cowherd women recognize the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā) as having merged with it, as if by her very coldness.
Eyes tremulous at the corners, voices with faltering and curved syllables, a gait slow with the weight of grace, and a face exceedingly lovely—
thus does playfulness naturally manifest upon the limbs of the fawn-eyed women.
Therefore, in this case, no manifestation of the rising of intoxication is perceived, even though it has taken root.

Thus, in the aforementioned verse cited as an example of *mīlita* (the hidden), and in our own verse beginning with "at dawn, upon the bow [of Indra], [he saw] Hari," if one accepts the definition of *mīlita* as "the non-apprehension of difference due to similarity between two things whose essential natures are known" in a context where their essential natures are concealed, then another poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) must necessarily exist. It should be noted that if one accepts the definition of *mīlita* merely as "non-apprehension of difference due to similarity," then there must be internal subdivisions of *mīlita*.
All of this is clear in the *Kuvalayānanda*.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, the "General" section, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the "Unfolding" (*unmīlita*) section:
they know *unmīlita* to be the manifestation of the distinction between two things possessing identical qualities.

When a distinction has been reached through the equality of qualities such that no determination of difference occurs, yet a distinction becomes manifest due to some cause, there arises *unmīlita*, which is the opposite of *mīlita*.

Just as the cowherd women recognize the daughter of the Sun (Yamunā) when she has joined with the bodily luster of Śauri as he sports on her bank during the flood, they perceive it through that very coolness.

Here, when an uncertainty has arisen regarding the distinction between the flood of luster from the Lord’s divine form and [the Yamunā] due to the similarity of their blue quality (*nīlaguṇa*), the distinction of the Yamunā from that [form] is revealed by the cause of its coldness (*śaiśiryena*).
Even when a distinction cannot be determined due to the similarity of their qualities, this [confusion] is observed, as in the following example:
