"During the Rāsa-sport, while the entire world of moving and non-moving beings was illuminated by the moonbeams of the Lord of Śvetadvīpa, the deer-eyed women perceived Mādhava as playing the flute. (1848)

Here, through the occasion of the sound of the flute, there arises a flash of the Lord’s distinctness from that [sound], brought about by the figure of speech *tadguṇa* (the quality of another), which consists in the Lord’s relinquishing His own dark luster (*nīliman*) and assuming the quality of the moonlight’s brilliance; this occurs because the non-determination of difference has been presented. In the word *anvabudhan*, the suffix *laṅ* is applied to the root *budh* (meaning "to perceive") belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*; due to its being marked with the *it* augment, the substitution of *aṅ* for *cli* occurs, as in the usage: "And he, O descendant of Kakutstha, did not perceive."
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, the Unmīlita-sara, in the Alaṅkāra-maṇi-hāra.
Now begins the Viśeṣaka-sara:
When two similar things are perceived as distinct due to their difference in properties, that is Viśeṣaka (the Distinguisher).

Even when there is no concealment of difference, if the specific distinction fails to manifest due to similarity, then upon the manifestation of that distinction by some cause, it becomes a "distinguisher" (viśeṣaka) as the counter-correlative to the universal.

Just as, by Your grace, although the marks such as the four-armed form are identical for those who have been liberated, the recently liberated ones indeed distinguish You by means of Lakṣmī residing upon Your chest. (1849)

Here, when an uncertainty arises regarding the distinction between the flood of luster from the Lord’s divine form and [the river], due to the similarity of their blue quality, the distinction of the Yamunā from that [form] is manifested by the cause of its wintry coldness.
Even when a distinction cannot be determined due to the similarity of their qualities, the following is observed: Or as in this example:
"In the entire world of mobile and immobile beings, which was whitened by the radiance of the cool-rayed moon, the deer-eyed women perceived Mādhava playing his flute during the Rāsa-sport. (1848)

In this passage, there arises a non-apprehension of difference (*bhedānadhyavasāya*) brought about by the *tadguṇa* ornament—characterized by the Lord’s relinquishing His own dark luster and assuming the quality of the moonlight’s brilliance—whereupon, through the instrumental cause of the sound of the flute, the manifestation of the Lord’s difference from that [moonlight] occurs. In the word *anvabudhan*, the suffix *laṅ* is applied to the root *budh* (meaning "to perceive") belonging to the Bhvādi class; because it is marked with the indicatory letter *it*, the substitution of *aṅ* for *cli* occurs. An example of such usage is: "And he did not perceive him, O descendant of Kakutstha" (*sa ca kākutstha nābudhat*).
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, the "Unfolding of the Series," in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the "Series on the Distinguishing Mark" (*viśeṣakasara*):
When two similar things are perceived through their difference in properties, there may arise a "distinguishing mark."

Even though the distinction has not been concealed, when the specific feature fails to manifest due to similarity, and a manifestation of that specific feature occurs by some cause, it is called a "distinguisher" (viśeṣaka), being the opposite of the universal (sāmānya).

Just as, by Your grace, although the marks such as the four arms are common to both You and the liberated, the recently liberated ones indeed distinguish You by Lakṣmī residing upon Your chest. (1849)

In this case, although there is no concealment of the distinction between the liberated souls and the Blessed Lord, since they are similar in having four arms, a lack of perception of their specific difference might arise; therefore, the Blessed Lord's specific distinction is made manifest by His chest being radiant with Lakṣmī. This is the *viśeṣaka* (distinguishing feature).

O Lord, just as among the dark-hued lotuses and other such things that shine with their own luster, the splendor of the fragrance of the lotus is difficult to perceive even by you, so too is Padmā difficult to comprehend.

Here, by means of the *tadguṇa* ornament—consisting of the Goddess Padmā’s relinquishing her own quality in order to assume the blackness of the Lord—a distinct manifestation arises through the fragrance of the lotus she holds, even within a blueness that is common to other divine women; thus, this differs from the previous example. Both of these ornaments are found at the very beginning of Dīkṣita’s work.

The predecessors, however, say: "When difference (*bheda*) and dissimilarity (*vaiṣamya*) manifest, two distinct figures of speech should not be postulated; rather, there is merely the absence of the figures already mentioned. This is because the manifestation of difference and generic distinction (*vaijātya*) is self-evident, and thus lacks the variety rooted in being the domain of the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*). Nor should it be argued that when difference and particularity manifest through the *mīlita* and *sāmānya* styles, the postulation of a separate figure is justified due to the presence of variety created by the description of an exception (*apavāda*); for even so, the lack of variety remains as it was.
Paṇḍitarāja, however, included this within inference (*anumāna*).
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, the Section on the *Viśeṣaka* (Distinctive) Ornament, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Section on the *Uttara* (Answer) Ornament:
An answer may be either an implied question or a formulated question.
Wherever it is spoken with intentional meaning, there an answer is declared.

Where a question is inferred from an answer that is stated with intentional significance (*sākūta*), there this is the "Answer" (type of *uttara*). This is not inference (*anumāna*), because it lacks the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth. A second type is the answer with intentional significance preceded by the repeated presentation of questions; this alone is designated as "The Hidden Answer" (*gūḍhottara*). As defined in the *Kuvalayānanda*: "An answer accompanied by some intentional significance shall be the 'Hidden Answer'.
This is not "Exclusion" (*parisaṃkhyā*), because here, as in that [other figure], the relationship between the thing to be excluded and the means of exclusion is not intended to be expressed.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"O son of Nanda, why do you search for the cow here and there, wandering about in agitation? She is playing at will in the bower on the bank of the Yamunā; she is easily found there. (1851)

This question posed by the cowherd to the Blessed One, the delight of Nanda—who was searching for a cow that had strayed from its own herd—is intended for the cowherd-maiden who desires Him; it contains the underlying intention: "May we two enjoy our freedom in the bower on the bank of the Kalindi. Here, the cowherd’s inquiry is brought forward, because it would be illogical for her to describe the cow’s location without first asking about the cow.
The second [example] is as follows:
"What are you thinking, O blessed lady? What purpose of mine would be served by your speaking? Speak nevertheless, though I shall listen as if I do not know; Kṛṣṇa, you ask what is strange. (1852)

"What are you thinking of, my dear?"—this is the question of the Blessed Kṛṣṇa directed toward a certain cowherd girl. "What [is it] with you? and so forth, is her reply. Here, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) of the first question is: "If you tell me the cause of your anxiety, then I shall provide a remedy. Regarding the reply, however, the suggested meaning is: "Without actual enjoyment, what remedy could there be for you through mere questions and answers? As for the second question, "I already know your intention."

"Nevertheless, I wish to hear what has been taken from your mouth"—this is the disclosure of the underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*). As for the reply: "You already know my intention; why then do you waste time with repeated questions?"—the beauty of a single answer lies in a question that is merely inferred, whereas it lies in the repeated presentation of both question and answer when the question is explicitly formulated.

The ancients maintain that this figure of speech, *uttarālaṃkāra* (the "Answer Ornament"), is of eight types: since each of its two varieties—question and answer—is fourfold according to whether they are intentional (*sābhiprāya*) or unintentional (*nirabhiprāya*), there are eight forms in total. Among these, in the first instance, the verse beginning with "From there, from here" (*tata itaḥ*), the question inferred is of the form: "Was my cow seen by you? This question is infused with an intention on the part of the Lord Kṛṣṇa—the sovereign of the earth—which, due to the excellence of his speech, takes the form of amorous union (*saṃbhoga*).

The reply as well is imbued with that very same intention. Thus, even in the verse "What are you thinking? where the question is thus formulated, both the question and the answer possess intentional significance. In this manner, other varieties of questions possessing intentional significance may also be cited.
When both the question and the answer are devoid of intentional meaning, an example of an answer that implies a question is as follows:
"If you wish to dwell here or there after attaining great happiness, then abandon this path of sin and resort without hesitation to this mountain-king of serpents. (1853)

The "crooked path" (*vṛjinapatha*) refers to a devious way or a course of misfortune. Here, by means of the answer given to a certain person by someone wishing for his welfare, a question regarding the instruction of one's own welfare by that same agent is inferred; for without such a question, the instruction of welfare would be inappropriate. In this case, both the question and the answer are devoid of ulterior motive, as they are intent solely on communicating knowledge of the matter exactly as it exists.

"If I were to make this supreme vow: 'I shall never, even for the sake of worshipping the Blessed One and His devotees, give away so much as a blade of grass'—this would indeed be a wretched thing, a synonym for miserliness. (1854)

Thus, the meaning is that an exceedingly high wager has been made by him, such that he has made this vow. The sense is: "This very person is indeed a wretch; what other wretch could there be besides him? He further qualifies this very person as "kadarya" (miserly). The term *arya* refers to a Vaiśya, as established by the rule "aryaḥ svāmivaiśyayoḥ. A *kadarya* is one who is both base (*kutsita*) and an *arya*; here, the word *ku-* is replaced by *kad-* according to the rule "koḥ kattatpuruṣe'ci. The intention is that this is a synonym for that [miser], having merely undergone a change of form.

The meaning is that a Vaiśya is already miserly by nature; therefore, what need is there to mention his miserliness when he is in a state of contempt? In the alternative sense, *paṇaḥ* refers to the word *paṇa*. From the root *kṛ*, the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *ādi* (Pāṇini 5.4.44). If this very word *kṛpaṇaḥ*—which is synonymous with *kadarya* (miser)—is the one that follows immediately (*paraḥ*), then [the question arises]: "What is a *kṛpaṇa*? This question is to be inferred here, as it is listed as a synonym for *kadarya* in the verse: "In the sense of a miser: *kṛpaṇa*, *kṣudra*, *kiṃpaca*, *animitampaca*."

The lack of intentional significance (*anākūtatva*) in both the question and the answer is exactly as before; however, the distinguishing feature is the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) that has been demonstrated.
An example of an answer to a question posed within that very same context is as follows:

"What is to be gone to? The serpent-mountain (Ahi-giri). What is to be contemplated? The conduct of the Lord of the Bull-mountain (Vṛṣādri-pati). Who is to be saluted? The lotus-eyed one (Abja-akṣa). Where is it to be enjoyed? In this beloved land. (1855)
What is that supreme Brahman to be meditated upon? What is its nature, form, and qualities to be known? What is its glory to be sung? And what is the nectar-like name of it to be drunk? (1856)

"Svarūparūpaguṇam" is a collective dvandva compound. "Abhidhānanibham" means that of which the pretext (*nibha*) is the name; herein all the questions are contained. As before, both the question and the answer are devoid of intentional meaning (*nirabhiprāyatā*).
"Who are you? Or who are you? Why do you travel alone?"—thus I ask. You, Govinda, are indeed one who provides much assistance; you ask, and I understand your words. (1857)

In this context, Kṛṣṇa’s question, “Who are you? contains the intention that she is worthy of his own enjoyment. The cowherd girl’s reply, “Who am I? What do you have to do with me? contains the intention that his question is merely a futile inquiry. Kṛṣṇa’s further question, “Why do you go alone? intends to ascertain her independence and ease of movement. His subsequent reproachful response, beginning with “It is said that you...,” contains the intention that she is fickle by mere words alone and not actually a reckless woman who wanders at will.
And this verse deserves to serve as an illustration of all four types of composed riddles, according to the distinction between the skill and lack of skill of the speaker.

In this matter, Jagannātha states that in this figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*), the very essence (*jīvātu*) consists in the repeated composition of questions and answers, since it is precisely through this that the emergence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) occurs. Therefore, a single question followed by a single answer does not constitute the ground for this figure of speech. Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases where the question is inferred; for while the inferred question is indeed one, and the answer is likewise one because it is not explicitly composed as such, the "inferred" nature intended here is not the state of being implied by the answer. Rather, he declared that it refers merely to the fact that [the subsequent answer] arises from hearing a preceding answer within a series of questions and answers.

"Where will you go? To the Mountain of Serpents; what supreme, wondrous reality is there? Of what nature is that glorious place, and what is that glory whose manifestation is this entire universe? (1858)

In this context, the question "What is there? is said to be "suggested" (*unnīta*) because it arises from hearing the answer "A mountain of snakes. Although the first question is not suggested, it is nevertheless included for the purpose of eliciting the answer. Thus, according to this view, the examples of suggested questions shown previously are not actually examples at all. Furthermore, the two-fold nature of this figure of speech is not to be understood by the distinction between a question being "suggested" or "stated," but rather by the distinction between its being "suggested" (*unnīta*) or "not suggested" (*anunnīta*).

In reality, however, when the question and answer are pregnant with underlying intention (*ākūta*), the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) arises from that alone; thus, there is no requirement for repeated mention. But in the absence of such intention, the wonder produced by repeated mention is required in the case of a formulated question (*nibaddha-praśna*). However, in the case of an implied question (*ākṣipta-praśna*), if sensitive readers (*sahṛdayas*) perceive the wonder created by the implication of the question, then let there be the status of an ornament (*alaṃkāratva*) even when there is only a single mention.

In that regard, when a question is posed with a hidden intent (*sākūta*), aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) arises even from a single mention, as in: "If you speak sweetly, O fair-faced one, do pearls fall from your mouth? We are but village girls; where, my dear, do we know such polished conversation? (1859)

In this context, the question beginning with "If you converse here... was posed by the Blessed One, the Joy of Nanda (Kṛṣṇa), and it contained an underlying intention (*ākūta*) directed toward bringing about an occasion for amorous enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*). However, the reply beginning with "The conversation is that of a gallant (*nāgaraka*)" was given by the cowherd girl Vallavī with a straightforward mind and was thus devoid of any such intention. The phrase "Do pearls fall from her mouth? is a common worldly expression.
In that very context, when the double entendre (*sākūtatva*) is present in the answer, the aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*) produced by its single mention is as follows:

"O slender-limbed one, can the *suman* flower be obtained in the groves of trees on the slopes of the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā)? For you, O deer-eyed one, such *suman*s are most easily found even among women like yourself. (1860) [Note: The word *suman* is a pun; it means both "flower" and "a woman of good mind/character."]

In this context, the question beginning with "What might be obtained here, my dear? was posed by a certain girl from Vraja of straightforward intellect to the Blessed One, the son of Yaśodā, without any underlying intention (*nirākūta*). The Blessed One’s reply, beginning with "It is most easily obtained," however, contains within it an intention (*ākūta*) regarding the freedom of their mutual enjoyment (*saṃbhoga-svācchandyā*). The aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) produced by the repeated employment of such an intention in the absence of an explicit statement—such as in the phrase "Where will you go?"—has already been discussed. Furthermore, other varieties of this [type of speech] are also possible.

First, there is a twofold division based on whether [the figure] occurs within a verse or outside a verse. Of these, the first type is further divided into two by way of being expressed within a single sentence or expressed across separate sentences.

The author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, the crest-jewel of rhetoricians, states that there are many varieties [of this figure] because both of the two subsequent [questions]—one situated within the verse and one situated outside the verse—are expressed by the single word "uttara" (both as a synonym for "repetition of sound" and as a synonym for "answer"), and because numerous questions receive their answers through a single word, as well as other such modes. This very variety has been separately designated as *citrottarā* (the "painted answer") by the Dīkṣitas.

The *citrottara* (extraordinary answer) is an ornament; it occurs when the answer is not distinct from the question, and that answer which is not different from another [expected] answer is also so regarded.
An answer that is not distinct from the question, and an answer that is not distinct from another answer, is called a "wondrous answer" (citrottarā).
"Just as the Blessed One attained eternal sovereignty by mere intention, so too for one who asks 'how?', that very [intention] is the answer"—thus says a certain poet to someone. (1861)
The Blessed One, by mere volition alone, [brought about] Kaṅka as a sentient being; the repetition is used for the sake of wonder. As it has been said:
"In a promise, in praise, in idle chatter, and even in a threat;
in fear and in wonder, repetition is indeed an ornament."

Thus: the question is "Did he lead [him] to eternal sovereignty? and the answer, which is composed as non-different from the question, is "He led Kaṅka—a specific kind of vulture, namely Jaṭāyu—to [his goal]. In the word *kaṅkam*, the optional *parasavarṇa* (assimilation to the following sound) applies according to the rule *vā padāntasya*.
Just as the grape is surpassed by the sweet speech of Mukunda, so too did a certain king of poets turn the very question itself into an answer for someone else. (1862)

In this case, to the question "Which is the soft one that is surpassed—the *mṛdvī* (the soft one) or the *mṛduḥ* (the soft one)?", the answer "the *mṛdvīkā* (grape), which is *drākṣā* (grape), is surpassed" is an answer identical to the question.
When a certain woman was asked by her friend, "How does Kamalā, whose abode is the lotus, hold a lotus in her hand as an ornament? she gave this very same answer as a wondrous reply. (1863)

*Kamalālayā* (the abode of Lakṣmī), *padmagehā* (having a lotus as her home), and *kamalā* (Lakṣmī)—the question is: "What (*kam*) ornament (*alam*) does she (*karoti*) make for her hand? The answer, being identical to the question, is "she makes a lotus (*kamalam*)," meaning she makes a lotus as an ornament. This is a *citrottarā* (puzzle-answer) figure; however, because it indicates a needle (*sūcya*) through its indication (*sūcanāt*), the specific figure here is *mudrā* (seal).
Or, for example:
"A man shines upon the mountain of the serpent-king, adorned with a forehead-mark made of musk; tell me, friend, what answer could there be here? There would be only a question in return. (1864)

In the alternative interpretation as a question—“Who, however, is one who has made his excellence manifest? (*kaḥ tu ūrīkṛtalalāmakaḥ*)—the word *tu* signifies either praise or distinction. As the *Medinīkośa* states: “*Tu* is used for filling a verse, distinction, conjunction, emphasis, an alternative, separation, praise, and restriction. Thus, the question is: among these persons upon the mountain-like hoods of the serpent, which person, moreover, shines forth as having made his excellence manifest (*ūrīkṛtalalāmakaḥ*) by virtue of being praiseworthy?

The answer—that the Blessed Lord Śrīnivāsa himself shines as the man who has made a forehead mark with musk and applied decorative tilaka—is composed as non-different from him. According to Amara: "The word *lalāma* denotes a tail, a sectarian mark (*puṇḍra*), a horse, an ornament, preeminence, and a banner."
"Or rather:
'By Hari, whose abode is the mountain and who is the lord of the twice-tongued [serpents], whom was his own chest brought?'—alas, that very question itself provides its own answer. (1865)

The question "Who has led my own chest [to you]? was posed by Hari, whose abode is the mountain and who possesses two tongues (the fire of his wrath) and the lordship over the serpent family; the answer "The heroine has led it" was uttered in a sentence that was not distinct from the question. Here, "heroine" means the beloved Śrī, and "chest" means it was brought to her.
Just as a man might speak the truth, who would dare to say: "What indeed should a man, the leader of the three worlds, say regarding the creation of the three worlds? 1866.

The question is: "What man (puruṣa) would dare to create the three worlds (tribhuvanajananāya trilokīsarjanāya)? The response, as if not knowing, is: "What indeed could he say? Furthermore, another answer is: "The leader (nāyaka), the sovereign (adhīśa), the Puruṣa—the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is heard in the Śruti: 'Now, indeed, the Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa desired, "May I create offspring"'—he would dare."
Or, as if mocking the beloved who had formed the thought, "May she bestow her affection upon me," Lakṣmī, with a smile, seemed to answer that very inquiry. (1867)

"This one is under your control"—this is a self-referential statement made with dramatic gesture (*sābhinaya*). "What joy should he produce in you, in your own mind?"—this is the sense of the question. "In you, the beloved (*kānta*), the dear one (*vallabha*), who are yourself"—such is the underlying meaning. "May he produce joy for me"—this is the sense of the reply. The implication is that, apart from love directed toward you, no other joy is to be desired by my mind. Here too, the question and the answer are composed within a single, inseparable sentence.
Or as in my own *Raṅgarājavilāsa*:
"O friend, bear joy and tell me, who is the wielder of the staff for the clan of the Ten-faced One? To this question posed by her husband, a certain clever woman gave that very same answer. (1868)
The question "Who is the wielder of the staff in the lineage of the Ten-faced one? and the answer "The wielder of the bow" are contained within a single, inseparable sentence.
Tell me, what was severed by the son of Sumitrā with his sword at the mouth of the sister of the Ten-faced one?
You know; recite the syllables in reverse for the question: "What was severed? (kāsinā). 1869.

In this instance, the question "Who are the Kāśīs? becomes an answer when read in reverse; such a peculiarity constitutes a specific excellence (*viśeṣa*). Numerous examples of this kind are to be found in my own compositions, such as the *Śrīnivāsavilāsa* and the *Nṛsiṃhavilāsa*.

Thus has been described the *citrottarālaṅkāra* (the ornament of the "curious answer"), which consists of an answer that is not distinct from the question. An example of an answer that is not distinct from another answer is as follows:
"In his own sovereignty, what kind of thousand-eyed Indra could there even be? Now, tell me, what calamities can there be for those who have turned their faces away from the Daityas? (1870)

In this case, there is a single answer for both questions alike: *vipadaḥ*. It should be understood that in the first question, the answer is provided by the word *vipadaḥ* ending in the singular, joined as an epithet of Indra—meaning "one whose state (*pada*), namely the station of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), has departed. In the second [question], however, the answer is given by the word *vipadaḥ* ending in the plural, meaning "calamities" (*āpadaḥ*).

What kind of majesty shines forth from the one who dwells on the mountain [Mahendra], whose nature is like the wind and who is self-sustaining? Who are those whose pride is humbled by the dark luster of his body’s radiance? Tell me, who are the Malayas? (1871)

Regarding the two questions here—"What is the nature of Śrīnivāsa’s majesty? and "Who are those whose pride is dispelled by the dark luster of his form?"—the answer "alayaḥ" is the same for both. In the first case, "alayaḥ" means "without dissolution," that is, eternal; in the second case, "alayaḥ" means "bees."
Just as the wind blows with the speed of the mount of Lord Siṃhagiri, how does it shine? Whom among the enemies, when shaken by his staff-like arms, would tremble as they are raised up? 1872.

In this case as well, the answer to both questions is the same: *arayaḥ*. It should be understood that for the first question, the meaning is "those devoid of speed," while for the second, it is "enemies."

Just as those seeking wealth might become what they are by taking refuge in Śrīvāsa, what would happen here to those who are afflicted? What would a man of knowledge become, and from that, what kind of prosperity would arise? (1873)

In this regard, the distinction from previous [explanations] is that there is only one answer—“Vibhava” (the Manifestation)—to all three questions. For those seeking wealth (*arthārthin*), who desire unprecedented sovereignty, the answer to the first question is: “Vibhava” means they shall attain power (*prabhava*). For the distressed (*ārta*), who desire the recovery of lost sovereignty, the answer to the second question is: “Vibhava” means they shall regain their lordship (*aiśvarya*). For the man of knowledge (*jñānī*), who worships the Lord while regarding Him alone as both the supreme goal and the means of attainment, the answer to the third question is: “Vibhava” means he becomes free from the cycle of worldly existence (*vigata-saṃsṛti*). Thus it should be understood.

Just as Hari-yaśas [is], what are the clear ones? Of what kind are those possessing that subtle luster? By them, what would the bull-mountain be like? And from where would the highest good arise for one who has become green? 1874.

In this case, the fact that there is only one answer—“Hari”—to all four questions constitutes a distinction from the previous [set]. Regarding the first question, “What is white with the fame of Hari?”...

"Green are the quarters"—this is the answer to the first question. "Of what nature are they? Possessing that same luster; [and] the splendor of Hari’s form"—this is the second [question], to which the answer is: "green" (*harita*), meaning green-colored. We have stated, and shall state again, that the non-distinction between the colors blue (*nīla*) and green (*harita*) is established by poetic convention (*kavisamaya*). "By those green splendors of the body, what would the Vṛṣa-mountain be?"—this is the third [question], to which the answer is: "green" (*harita*), meaning green-colored. Amara states: "The word *pālāśa* means green (*harita*)."

The answer to the question "From where, and for what reason, would the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) arise? is given by the word *turīyasya haritaḥ hareḥ*, which functions as a genitive singular form applicable to all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*).

Tell me: what does the Lord of the Mountain of Serpents bestow by the majesty of the splendor of His body; what does He conquer? What does He cause to resound with His neck in the victory over His enemies; what does He shake—the conch shell? (1875)

What does the Lord of the Mountain of the Serpent (Śrī Śailanātha) bestow? To this question, the answer is "śam" (happiness). What does he conquer by the splendor of his bodily luster? To this, the answer is "kham" (the sky). What does he cause to resound upon the victory over his enemies? To this, the answer is "kam" (the conch). And what does he shake with his neck? To this, the answer is "śaṅkham" (the conch). These four answers are non-different from the four questions. Herein lies the distinction from the previous type: in the first two cases, there is a difference in the words [of the answer], whereas in the latter two, there is no such difference.
Regarding those [puzzles] that exist outside of verse:
"Who dwells on the mountain of serpents? What is the fragrance that satisfies the sense of smell? What was stolen by Hari in secret? O learned one, give only one answer here. (1876)

Here, there is a single answer to all three questions that stands outside the verse itself: "Śrīvāsa. In the first question, "Śrīvāsa" means the Blessed Lord Śrīnivāsa. In the second, "Śrīvāsa" means a specific type of incense produced from the resinous exudations of the Devadāru tree and other such plants. [The word] "Śrīvāsa... [is used].

According to Amarasimha, "vṛkṣadhūpa" refers to both *śrīveṣṭa* and the resin of the *sarala* tree. In the third sense, *śrīvāsaḥ* means "the garment of Śrī" (Lakṣmī). Many other such varieties should be inferred by the intelligent. This first variety, which consists of an answer existing outside the verse (*padyabahirvartin*), occurs only as a variety where the answer is non-different from the answer itself (*uttarābhinna-uttara*).

It does not occur in the first variety where the answer is non-different from the question (*praśnābhinna-uttara*), because since the answer is already composed within the question itself, its existence outside the verse is impossible.

Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*, titled the Chapter on the Ornament of Puzzling Questions (*citrapraśnālaṅkārasara*). Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of Puzzling Questions:
A question is that which is not distinct from another question, or else one that contains another meaning within itself.
Some have described that [work] as being composed of various types of riddles called *citrapraśna*.

Some authorities state that when one question is not distinct from another question, or when it contains a different meaning within itself, it is the figure of speech called *citrapraśna* (the "painted" or "variegated" question). This [example] begins with the Kaustubha gem.

Or rather, how could the heart’s disposition of the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva)—who is indeed a treasury of compassion—not be like that of Kākodara (the serpent Śeṣa)? And his pair of feet possesses the luster of a lotus blossomed by the rays of the autumnal sun. 1877.

In this context, the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) of the Lord of the Kākodara mountain is the subject of the first question; and for the subsequent [verse] beginning with "Śāradā," the phrase "repository of compassion" (*kāruṇyanidhiḥ*) constitutes a single question that is not distinct from the other questions. The meaning of the primary question is "Who is the repository of compassion?"—that is, "Who is the abode of mercy?"—while the meaning of the second is "Who is the repository of *āruṇya*?"—that is, "Who is the locus of redness? We have already stated in the verse on *kaṅka* that the repetition in "kā-kā" is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*).

Regarding the term *vṛkṣadhūpa*, Amara states: "Also *śrīveṣṭa* and the resin of *sarala* [are types of] *vṛkṣadhūpa*. In the third instance, *śrīvāsaḥ* means "the garment of Lakṣmī. Many other such varieties should be inferred by the intelligent. This first variety, which consists of an answer existing outside the verse, occurs only as a variety where the answer is non-different from the verse; it does not occur in the first variety consisting of an answer non-different from the question, because since the answer is already composed within the question itself, its existence outside the verse is impossible.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of the String of Jewels (Alaṅkāramaṇihāra), in the Uttarasaras.
Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of Puzzling Questions (Citrapraśnālaṅkārasara):
A question is that which is either indistinguishable from another question or contains within itself another meaning.
Some have described that [work] as being bound together under the name *Citrapraśna*.

Some say that when one question is not distinct from another question, or when it contains a different meaning within itself, there is the ornament called *citrapraśna* (the "painted" or "variegated" question); this begins with Kaustubha.

Or rather, how could the heart of the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), who is indeed a treasury of compassion, not be like the belly of a black serpent? And his pair of feet possesses the luster of a lotus blossomed by the rays of the autumnal sun.

In this verse, the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) of the Lord of the Kākodara mountain is the subject; thus, the question "Who is the repository of compassion? (*kā āruṇyanidhiḥ*)—which follows the question beginning with "O Śāradā"—is not distinct from the preceding question, but is a single question. The meaning of the first question is "Who is the repository of compassion" (*dayānidhiḥ*); the meaning of the second is "Who is the repository of redness" (*āruṇyanidhiḥ*), that is, the locus of ruddiness. We have already stated in the verse concerning *kaṅka* that the repetition of the word *kāka* is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*).

Just as there may be here on earth a remedy for men afflicted by the three-fold suffering, so too there are two kinds of association: one is association with the wicked, and the other is association with the virtuous who know the essence. 1878.

Here, regarding the two subsequent questions presented in the second half [of the verse], the phrase "kārā-ket" constitutes a single question that is not divided by other inquiries. The meaning of the first question is: "What is *kārā*—a prison—that is a cause of excessive suffering? The meaning of the second question is: "What is *rākā*—the full moon night of the fifteenth day—that is a remover of distress?"

Just as the dark body of the Lord of Vṛṣagiri and the sight of his face turned away from her caused Kālīkā to cast off all hesitation, so too did his fame, directed toward that same object, cause her to abandon her doubts.

In the first half [of the verse], there is a single question consisting of two parts: "the body of the Lord of Vṛṣagiri" and "the sight of his face turned away from her. The meaning of one question is "Who is Kālī? (meaning *kā* + *alī*, "who is the dark one?"), while the other is "Who is *alīkā*? (meaning "who is the unpleasant one?"). In the second half, however, there is a single question consisting of two parts: "her fame" and "the subject of her devotion. The first question is "What is *kāśam*? (meaning "the Kāśa flower"), and "Who (*kā*) has humbled it? (*nyakcakre*).

"What doubt" (kā śaṅkā) regarding the second [question] means that it was "cast down" (nyakcakre), i.e., set aside. The meaning is: "The glory of the Blessed One has cast down the doubt. The intention of the two subsequent [verses] is: "The doubt concerning the supremacy of the Blessed One has been disregarded by us. It should be noted that in the first [verse], *cakre* is used in the active voice (*kartari*) with the perfect tense (*liṭ*), whereas in the second, it is used in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*). The distinction is that in the former case there is one question not distinct from the preceding question, whereas here there are two questions.

"The forest is vast; who will lead me? Tell me the path by which I may go with ease. When the son of Nanda asked this, a certain cowherd girl said, "This way is easy to follow here. (1882)

"Which path (*saraṇi*) leads toward the wilderness (*kāntāra*), the great forest? Tell me that path, that track (*padavī*). [The verb *brū* is transitive with two objects according to the rule *aciñbrūñśāsuji*. "By which path I may go (*yāyām*) so as to proceed easily and without hindrance"—this is the question regarding the way. "Which beloved (*kāntā*) might delight me? Tell me that path, the means of reaching her. "By which beloved, or by which means, I might attain happiness, the pleasure of love"—this contains a further, double meaning.

"This path is easy to traverse; it is traveled with ease"—this is the answer to the question regarding the road. However, in another sense, "this" refers to her: "This very path which you ask about is she, that is, I. Here, in this very place, being easy to traverse and traveled with ease, she brings delight because of the secluded nature of this spot.

Or rather: "O lovely one, if you grant me my desired fortune—which is dense and free from interruption—I shall bestow upon you, O slender-limbed one, the unceasing prosperity that I desire; thus we both shall have our goals fulfilled. (1883)

This verse consists of a dialogue in the form of a question and answer between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the Gopikā. Here, the question is: "O lady of delicate limbs! What desired, uninterrupted abundance (anavarata-sampadaṃ)—that is, continuous prosperity—shall I bestow upon you? The answer, containing a double meaning, is: "O beloved! I shall bestow upon you the desired abundance of the nine gems (navaratna-sampadaṃ). Furthermore, the reply is: "O cloud-like one (ghanabha)! If you grant me my desired fortune (abhīpsita-bhāgya) incessantly and constantly, then I shall have fulfilled my purpose."

"O Cloud! If you grant me that fortune in the form of sexual union—a desired object long prayed for—that is yet to come, then I shall have achieved my purpose and my desires will be fulfilled; such is the pregnant meaning [of her words]."

In this regard, it should be noted that although there exist many varieties of the figure *uttara* (the "answer") as demonstrated by us in accordance with the views of earlier authorities, the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* has adopted only two of those varieties: namely, *citrottarā* (the "wonderful answer") and *gūḍhottarā* (the "hidden answer"). Following that same school of thought, the author of the *Kaustubha*, Veṅkaṭārya, has devised two novel varieties of the figure *praśna* (the "question") as counterparts to those [two types of *uttara*].

This very point has also been demonstrated by us. However, if in this context the second variety—consisting of a question containing another meaning—were to have an answer that is either intentional or unintentional, then it would simply be an example of the figure *uttarālaṃkāra* (the "Answer") as presented earlier in the opinion of the ancients.

Consequently, in the two verses shown—"O Lord of the Earth, removing Bhāmā" and "O Lord of the Earth, you are truly the body of the limbs"—since no answer is actually formulated and the question alone possesses intentionality, they are examples of *citrapraśna* (the "Puzzling Question") alone.

When the first variety of this [figure] is demonstrated in verses such as "Who is the treasury of compassion? and so forth, since it is difficult to discern that one question is not distinct from another question without the provision of an answer, the provision of an answer is indeed necessary. Nevertheless, even though the questions alone remain without an expressed intent, because a striking variety is revealed through the power of *śleṣa* (punning/paronomasia), this is precisely the figure of *citrapraśna* (the "wonderful question"), which is distinguished from the *uttara* (answer) figure shown by earlier authorities.

In the two verses beginning with “*kāntāramayet kāmān*,” however, since both the question and the answer are composed with intentional meaning (*sābhiprāya*), this is indeed a specific variety of the figure *uttarālaṅkāra*. The distinction is that in the examples previously shown according to the method of the ancients, the presence of intentional meaning exists by way of suggestion (*vyaṅgya-maryādayā*), whereas in these two cases, it exists through the power of paronomasia (*śleṣa*). If the *kūṭa* (puzzle) consists solely of the roots of the syllables, then, when those two possess a different meaning based on wordplay (*śleṣa*), one must accept that it is specifically a variety of the *citrapraśna* (puzzle-question), and not the figure of speech *uttara* (answer), because of the presence of a distinct aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*). However, in this case as well, the composition of the answer—just like the composition of the question—is the cause of an excellence of beauty within the figure of speech *uttara*; such is the direction [of the argument].
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, the Lake of Variegated Questions, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Lake of the Subtle Ornament (*sūkṣmālaṅkāra*):
"The subtle (*sūkṣma*) is said to be an intentional action that understands the inner disposition of another."

The figure of speech called *sūkṣma* (the subtle) consists of an intentional action directed toward another person by one who has ascertained that person's underlying intention through gestures and other such signs.
As Nandakiśora gazed at the charming ball held in his hand before him, the cowherd girl with a moon-like face and beautiful pearl-like teeth smiled softly.

In this context, having understood through a gesture—namely, her grasping of the ball—that the intention of the cowherd’s beautiful-browed daughter was to inquire about the time for the secret rendezvous of embracing her breasts, the moonlight began to spread in favor of that purpose; thus, the operation of a gentle smile was composed by her to manifest her own heart’s intent following that, indicating "this is the time for the secret meeting. This is an illustration of the application of *lakṣaṇā* (indication).

If it is argued that the *kūṭa* (puzzle) is merely based on wordplay (*vyañjanaśleṣa*), then it must be accepted that when those two possess a different meaning rooted in paronomasia (*śleṣa*), they constitute a specific variety of the *citrapraśna* (riddle) rather than the figure of speech *uttara* (the answer), because of the presence of a distinct aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*). In this case as well, the composition of an answer—just like the composition of a question—is a cause for an excellence of beauty in the figure of speech *uttara*; such is the direction of the argument.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, the Lake of Variegated Questions, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Lake of the Subtle Ornament (*sūkṣmālaṅkāra*):
"The subtle (*sūkṣma*) is defined as an intentional action that understands the underlying intention of another."

The figure of speech called *sūkṣma* consists of an intentional action directed toward another person by one who has understood that person's underlying intention through gestures and other such signs.
As Nandakiśora gazed at the beautiful ball held in his hand before him, the cowherd girl with a moon-like face and lovely pearl-white teeth smiled softly.

In this context, having understood through a gesture—the act of picking up a ball—that Nanda’s son intended to inquire about the time and place of the secret appointment for seizing her breasts, the cowherd maiden, acting in accordance with his disposition as the moonlight spread forth, employed a gentle smile to manifest the state of her own heart, signifying that it was indeed the time for the tryst; such is the application of the definition [of *lakṣaṇā*].
Just as a woman from Vallava,
while her lover was painting a wood-apple fruit with his own fingernails before her in the Nandana grove, wove a string of pearls into her braided hair.

This too was the conduct of a woman of Vraja who, knowing that this was the time for the secret rendezvous of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s spontaneous pastimes, spoke with an inner intention that "the time for the appointment has arrived amidst the brilliance of the stars in the darkness."

Just as on the moon-like king of mountains known as Vyālācala, that lovely woman—possessing a smiling face and eyes glancing at her pair of blue, jar-like breasts, with her gaze extending toward the chest of the Lord of Śrī—remained there. 1886.

In this context, Nīlā—recognizing through the Lord’s gesture of gazing at her own pair of breasts that his intention consisted of a longing for her enjoyment—performed the act of looking toward Śrīnivāsa’s chest; this act was imbued with the intention of demonstrating the presence of the obstacle in the form of Śrī’s proximity.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, the Chapter on the Subtle (Sūkṣma), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra. Now begins the Chapter on the Concealed (Pihita):
"The Concealed (pihita) is considered to be an intentional action by one who understands the conduct of another."
The figure of speech called *pihita* consists in a purposeful action by one who knows the activity of another.
Just as a woman from the Vallava region,
before her husband Nanda, was scratching a wood-apple fruit with her fingernails held in her own hand, she fashioned a string of pearls into her braided hair.

This too is the action of a woman of Vraja who, knowing the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s disposition toward the time for the tryst of their private dalliance, implies within her gesture the thought: "In this darkness, the appearance of the stars marks the hour for our rendezvous."

Just as on the moon-like king of mountains known as Vyālācala, that lovely woman—her eyes restless upon the pair of her dark, jar-like breasts, her face smiling, and her gaze extending toward the chest of the Lord of Śrī—remained there. (1886)

In this context, Nīlā—knowing the Lord’s intention to be of the nature of eagerness for her own enjoyment through His act of gazing at the pair of her breasts—performs the act of gazing upon the chest of Śrīnivāsa; this act contains the intention of demonstrating the presence of the obstacle in the form of the proximity of Śrī (the Goddess Lakṣmī).
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, the Chapter on the Subtle (Sūkṣma), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra. Now begins the Chapter on the Concealed (Pihita):
"The Concealed (pihita) is considered to be an intentional action by one who knows the ways of others."
The figure of speech called *pihita* consists in concealing the intentional action of one who perceives the activity of another.
Seeing the son of Nanda arrive at her own home in the morning with a perspiring face, Rādhā quickly took up a light, gracefully oscillating fan from her bud-like hand.
*Laghulaya* is *lāmajjaka*. The intention behind seizing the *lāmajjaka* fan is: "I am fanning you because you are exhausted from enjoying other women throughout the entire night."
Or, for example:
Seeing the young Yadava’s cheek stained with turmeric by another young woman, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, concealing her true feelings, placed a jeweled mirror in his hand. (1888)

Here, Rukmiṇī’s action of offering a mirror into his lotus-like hand—pregnant with the intention, "I know that you indulged in private dalliance at night in the house of your rival wife, as inferred from the application of turmeric powder on your cheek"—is composed. The distinction from the previous example is that by the word *pihitākārā* (one whose form is concealed), it is embellished by the figure of speech *mudrā*, which consists in the indication of the name of the figure intended to be suggested.

This [definition] is according to the *Kuvalayānanda*. However, Sarvasvakāra and others define it as follows: "The revelation of a subtle meaning that has been perceived is *sūkṣma* (the subtle). Having thus defined it by encompassing both the intention of another and a factual event—understanding them as "the clever revelation of a subtle meaning which cannot be perceived by those of dull intellect but is perceived by those of sharp intellect"—they cite the following example:

"A clever woman, knowing the lover’s mind was fixed on the time for their secret meeting, closed her play-lotus, which had previously been directed toward his eyes with a significant look. (Note: This verse is an illustration of the figure of speech known as *sūkṣma*, where the heroine perceives the lover's internal thought through his external gesture.)
Seeing the saffron on her neck broken by a stream of sweat-drops trickling from her face,
a certain woman, as if manifesting the masculinity of that slender lady, smiled and drew the outline of a sword upon her hand.

Thus, establishing the presence of the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in these two examples, they did not accept *pihita* as a distinct figure of speech (*alaṃkārāntara*). And this is correct; for they argue that since there is no difference in the employment of intentional action—which is the cause for the diversity of conceiving distinct figures of speech—there can be no distinction [between figures] based merely on a difference in the objects to be revealed, such as an intention or an internal state. Here, the author of the *Vimarśinī* elucidated the intention of the *Alaṃkārabhāṣyakāra*, stating: "That which is the mere perception or the mere manifestation of a subtle matter is indeed this very figure of speech. This, then, is the example: [Example follows]
Just as Ramā was accompanied by her Beloved alone at the swinging door of the pleasure-chamber, so too were the friends of the young woman of the ocean accompanied only by their Beloveds. 1889.

In this instance, the friends have both perceived Lakṣmī’s longing for the enjoyment of her lover and made it manifest by casting side-long glances at the door of the pleasure-chamber; thus, it possesses a twofold significance. Therefore, in such cases, the figure of speech to be designated is *sūkṣma* (the subtle) alone, because it consists in the state of a subtle meaning being perceived and so forth. Even though Lakṣmī’s longing was merely perceived by the friends, it was nonetheless made manifest through her behavior—such as going outside in private.

Nevertheless, in this context, it is merely the perception of the friends' eagerness that constitutes the aesthetic wonder; the actual effort of the friends to go outside does not possess the splendor of being an *alaṃkāra* (poetic figure).
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on Concealment (*pihita*), in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of Pretext (*vyājokti*):
"Pretext (*vyājokti*) is the concealment of one's true form by means of stating another reason."
The poetic figure named *vyājokti* (disguised speech) is the concealment, by means of stating another reason, of a hidden matter that has become manifest through some cause.

Establishing the presence of the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in these two examples, they did not accept *pihita* as a separate figure of speech (*alaṃkārāntara*). And this is correct; for they argue that since there is no difference in the employment of intentional action—which is the cause for the variety in the postulation of distinct figures—there can be no distinction based merely on a difference in the objects to be revealed, such as an intention or a state of affairs. Here, the author of the *Vimarśinī* elucidated the intention of the author of the *Alaṃkārabhāṣya*, who stated: "That which is the mere perception or the mere manifestation of a subtle matter is indeed this very figure of speech. This, then, is the example: [Example follows]

Just as Ramā was accompanied by her Beloved alone at the swinging door of the pleasure-chamber with the restless sidelong glances of the Ocean’s Daughter, so too did her female friends become her sole companions.

In this instance, the eagerness of Śrī for the enjoyment of her lover was perceived by her friends and manifested through the casting of side-glances at the door of the pleasure-chamber; thus, it possesses both meanings [the literal and the suggested]. Therefore, in such cases, the *sūkṣma* (subtle) ornament alone should be stated, because it exists precisely as a subtle matter through its being perceived and so forth. Even though the mere perception of Lakṣmī’s eagerness was manifested by her friends through her behavior—such as departing outside in private—[it remains a case of *sūkṣma*].

Nevertheless, in this context, it is merely the perception of the friends’ eagerness that constitutes the aesthetic charm; there is no such emergence of poetic figure (alaṃkāra) in the mere action of the friends’ departure from her presence.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on Concealment (*pihita*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Figure of Speech *Vyājokti* (Artful Concealment):
"Artful concealment (*vyājokti*) is the hiding of one's true form by stating a different reason."
The concealment of a hidden matter that has become manifest through the statement of some other reason is the poetic figure named *vyājokti* (disguised speech).
"Friend, please straighten this braid of mine, which has been disheveled by the contrary wind," said a certain cowherd girl to her friend as she emerged from a grove on the bank of the Yamunā. (1890)

Here, the concealment of a braid (*dhammilla*) disheveled by the enjoyment of amorous play with the Nandana’s son is achieved through a *vyāja* (pretext) regarding its being disheveled by the contrary wind. This is the distinction between this [figure] and *chekāpahnuti*: in the latter, there is a denial (*apahnava*) by shifting the meaning of the statement; here, there is concealment by describing the appearance (*ākāra*) as being due to another cause. In both the definition and the name of the figure, the inclusion of the term “utterance” (*ukti*) is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any operation that conveys another cause for the purpose of concealing the appearance. Thus: "Seeing Hari approaching on the main road, one woman [concealed her passion] before the garland-seller..."
Then Bhāmā, concealing what was being expressed by his bristling hair, trembling, and other signs, bowed down before him.

"In this case as well, it is indeed *vyājokti* (concealment by pretext). For here, the physical manifestation of horripilation and so forth caused by passion is concealed by a prostration that suggests another cause, namely devotion," so say the Dīkṣitas in the *Kuvalayānanda*. And thus:

"A cowherd girl, returning from a bower on the bank of the Yamunā toward Vraja with a cluster of *ketakī* flowers in her hand, concealed upon her own body the wound made by Śauri’s nails during their private dalliance. (1891)

Thus, even here, according to that [author’s] view, it is indeed *vyājokti* (concealment). For here, the scratching by the Lord’s nails—which resulted from her own amorous play—is concealed by the grasping of the flower-cluster, which suggests another cause: her entry into a thicket of *ketakī* trees abounding in thorns. In reality, however, this is precisely the figure *yukti* (justification), as will be explained during the discussion of the *yukti* alaṃkāra. Furthermore, the mention of "action" (*ceṣṭita*) in the definitions of the figures *sūkṣma* and *pihita* is merely an illustration of the general operation common to both utterance and action. Consequently:
"A crane on a lotus leaf appears like a pearl in an emerald vessel"—having understood this sentiment of mine at our trysting place, she then spoke thus to her friend.

"Look, here the row of swans is as motionless as an ancient verse, like a garland of pure lotuses"— thus did a certain woman speak to her friend, having learned of the thief's intention to meet her there.

In these and other verses of ours as well, the *sūkṣma* (the subtle) ornament prevails. In this particular verse, the intention of the question—"What shall be our place of rendezvous?"—is indicated; thus, when the clever lady of Vraja, who was conversant with that [intention], spoke with significant meaning to her friend regarding the Blessed Lord, the son of Nanda, the *sūkṣma* ornament occurs.

Since, here, by the comparison of the row of swans to a garland of most motionless white lotuses, their lack of movement is indicated; by that [lack of movement], the extreme seclusion of that place is indicated; and by that, it is suggested to him that "this very spot is our rendezvous. Nor should a *dhvani* (suggested sense) be suspected here, because even though the question and answer regarding the rendezvous are manifested through a succession of suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*), they are nonetheless disclosed by the speaker's own words. Thus, this may also be cited as an example of the *pihitālaṃkāra* (the concealed ornament).

Furthermore, another point here should be noted: in the previously cited examples of figures such as *gūḍhottara* (hidden answer) and *sūkṣma* (the subtle), where it is said, "Hurry here and there from that place! What are you thinking, my dear? Who are you, who is yours, and what is yours? Before Nandakiśora, she draws with her own nails," the emotion (*bhāva*) is not revealed by the speaker’s own words; rather, it is to be understood through the power of the beauty of the situation itself, as qualified by the specific nature of the speaker and the person addressed.

In reality, there is no status as an *alaṃkāra* (poetic figure) in that very instance, because it serves as the locus for *dhvani* (suggested meaning). Since earlier authorities have demonstrated that when the underlying emotion (*bhāva*) is made manifest through their own statements, there exists a locus for *alaṃkāra*, they cited examples such as "yatrāsau vetasī pāntha" and so forth; following them, we too have cited similar verses.
Indeed, it is possible to manifest the *bhāva* in these examples by imagining a subsequent verse.

"Why do you search here and there, running about in such agitation? O son of Nanda, where are you looking for the cow? She is playing as she pleases in the bower on the bank of the Yamunā; she is easily found there. (1893)
Thus, a certain woman of Vraja, desiring the son of Nanda who was searching for a cow strayed from her own herd, spoke with intentional meaning to him as he questioned her. (1894)

Thus, therefore, among those examples previously cited by us—such as "the cheeks smeared with the yellow pigment of a young woman" and others—it is only in those cases where there is the manifestation of an emotion (bhāva) that the respective poetic figure (alaṃkāra) exists.
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, the Chapter on Artful Assertion (*vyājokti-sara*), in the *Alaṅkāra-maṇi-hāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Hidden Assertion (*gūḍhokti-sara*):
"Hidden assertion (*gūḍhokti*) occurs when something intended for one person is spoken to another."

That which is intended for someone specific, yet those standing by do not perceive it, and that which is spoken with double meaning (*śleṣa*) for another person—this is the ornament named *gūḍhokti* (the "obscure statement"), as introduced by Dīkṣita.

"Why do you search here and there, running about in such agitation? O son of Nanda, where are you looking for the cow? She is playing as she pleases in the bower on the bank of the Kālindī; she is easily found there. (1893)
Thus, a certain woman of Vraja, desiring the son of Nanda who was searching for a cow strayed from her herd, spoke with significant intent.

Thus, therefore, among those examples previously cited by us—such as "the cheeks smeared with the yellow pigment of a young woman" and so forth—it is only in those cases where there is the manifestation of an emotion (bhāva) that the respective figure of speech (alaṃkāra) exists.
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, the Chapter on Artful Assertion (*vyājokti-sara*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Concealed Assertion (*gūḍhokti-sara*):
"Concealed assertion (*gūḍhokti*) occurs when something intended for one person is spoken to another."

That which is intended to be said regarding someone, but which bystanders do not understand, and which is expressed through double entendre (śleṣa) toward another person—that is the ornament named *gūḍhokti* (the "hidden speech"), as introduced by Dīkṣita.
Just as you have come here longing for the newborn calf, it is certainly because you wish to seize it; yet this dear one wanders not far away—so why do you hasten, O cowherd boy? (1895)

This is spoken by a certain cowherd woman, pointing toward a certain cowherd boy wandering nearby who is eager to catch a calf, regarding the Blessed One, the Delight of Nanda, who is likewise eager to seize her breasts: "O cowherd boy! (In the other sense: O Kṛṣṇa!"—this is the vocative. You have come here with a longing (*lālasā*) born for the calf (*vatse*), that is, for the young grass-eater; as Amara states: "The word *lālase* denotes longing and desire."

Otherwise, you are [here] longing—meaning being eager—for the two breasts which are like calves; for the *Medinī* states: "The word *vatsa* refers to a son, a year, and a calf; it is neuter when referring to the chest. The *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa* states: "He who is *lolupa*, *lolubha*, *lola*, *lampaṭa*, and *lālasa* is [the same]. You have arrived, desiring to seize them—desiring to seize the calf and desiring to seize the breasts. You are [thus].

The analysis of the compound *taṃ jighṛkṣuḥ* is *tau jighṛkṣuḥ*; because of the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *na lokāvyaya...* (Pāṇini 2.3.69), the accusative case is used for the object, and the compound is formed according to the rule *gamyādīnām upasaṃkhyānam*. *Bāḍham* expresses acceptance, meaning "certainly" or "well said. *Eṣa priyaḥ* refers to this beloved one who is the object of affection. In the alternative sense, *eṣa priyaḥ* means my husband; he moves (*carati*) nearby (*avidūre*), that is, in the very vicinity, grazing on grass. This is because the grammatical rule states that *carati* can mean "eating" as well. In the other sense, he wanders about (*sañcarati*).

The sense is: "Why do you hasten so? Why are you in such a hurry? If it is argued that this is indeed *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), because—despite the subject at hand being the son of Nanda—it describes the story of another, an irrelevant young cowherd, we say no. This is not the case, because [the relation] is not manifested through cause and effect, general and particular, or similarity. Nor is it merely a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) between the relevant and the irrelevant; for in that figure, there is an intention to present the irrelevant matter as a point of comparison for the relevant matter. Here, however, there is no such intention regarding the irrelevant matter.
In this instance, the irrelevant matter simply serves to... [suggest] something else.

Since it has been specified for the sake of [another] purpose and because there exists a specific distinction (vicchitti), one must properly resort to *gūḍhokti* (the "concealed statement") as a distinct figure of speech by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). Nor should it be argued that this is merely *dhvani* (suggestion) rather than a figure of speech, on the grounds that the suggested meaning—consisting of the deception of a bystander—is not explicitly revealed by the words themselves; for they say that since that meaning is revealed through *śleṣa* (paronomasia), *dhvani* is impossible here.

O Lord, she whose mind is distressed by the heat of worldly existence and whose heart is moistened with compassion desires nothing else than the majesty of obtaining the play of your sidelong glances. (1896)

"O Lord, O Sovereign of the World, whose heart is moist with compassion! This slender maiden, her mind utterly despondent, desires nothing other than the majesty of obtaining the playfulness of Your sidelong glance—the power of attaining the flow of Your look. Therefore, she is to be protected and guarded by You. This is the prayer directed toward the Blessed One. The hidden meaning (*gūḍhārtha*), however, is as follows: "O Compassionate One, O Lord, [she] has fallen into the torment of the fever of the mind"—this is the analysis of the entire compound word.

The meaning is: by means of a series of mental torments—that is, a succession of the fever of love—this slender woman has become utterly dejected in mind. Regarding the phrase "tvadapāṅga," the word *tvat* is a separate term ending in the ablative singular; thus, *tvat* means "from you. *Apāṅga* means "the bodiless one" (Anaṅga, i.e., Cupid); his *vilāsa* means "his delight" (Rati). The attainment (*lābha*) of that very delight constitutes her "splendor" (*vaibhava*), and from that, she desires nothing else.

Here, by addressing the Lord as "O Protector" (*nātha*), a certain woman of Vraja—desiring nothing other than Rati from Him—conveys to the Blessed One her own state of wretchedness and suffering within saṃsāra, through a mere sidelong glance, in order to deceive a bystander.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, the Chapter on Concealed Expression (Gūḍhokti), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now, the lake of explicit expression (*vivṛtoktisaraḥ*):
if the *vivatoktiśśleṣagūḍha* (the concealed pun of explicit expression) is made explicit by the poet, [it is called *vivṛtokti*].

The meaning concealed by *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is revealed in some manner by the poet’s own statement; this is the sense of *vivṛtokti* (explicit expression). This [term] as well is the innovation of Dīkṣita.
"Just as this Surabhi, born from the Sun, wanders happily following the tracks of the cows on the riverbanks, so too must you protect her," said a certain cowherd girl to the cowherd Kṛṣṇa.

This is the cow Surabhi—according to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *surabhi* refers to a cow in the feminine; it is masculine when referring to the spring (*vasanta*) and the month of Caitra, and is used in all three genders for the meanings 'pleasant' and 'agreeable'. She is grazing comfortably among the trees growing on the banks of the Yamunā, the daughter of the Sun (the meaning being that she is following after those trees). The sense is that she is eating grass, or alternatively, that she is roaming about. The implication is that she should be protected by you so that she does not go elsewhere; she must be tended accordingly. The underlying (inner) meaning, however, is that she is fragrant (*surabhi*).

By this, her status as belonging to the *padminī* (lotus) class of women is indicated. She is gentle (*saumyā*) or charming. "The sheath" has been mentioned; and the sense is "this [sheath] and I too. This is an indirect reference to oneself due to being overcome by passion. The meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) is that it is not only other women, but "I too. Being on the bank of the Yamunā—on the shore of the daughter of the Sun (*ravijā*)—and having come under your power, being fixed upon your form, she is to be protected and gratified by you with the pleasure of love (*ratimukhena*).

Thus a certain gopī spoke to Kṛṣṇa while facing him. This is an instance of *paravañcanā* (deception of another), which is the disclosure of a secret under the guise of another meaning. By means of an implied secondary sense in the form of an instruction to a certain cowherd, the speaker discloses through the word "to Kṛṣṇa" (*abhikṛṣṇam*) her own desired sport with Śrī Kṛṣṇa—a meaning that was intended but kept secret.
Or, for example, a cowherd woman, standing in the way of her husband as he was about to depart for the forest, said to Kṛṣṇa: "Come here and play with these cows at your leisure. (1898)

This is the deceptive speech of a certain cowherd woman, longing to sport with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, directed toward her own husband. For instance, "O cowherd" (he gopa) is the vocative address to her husband. "Come [to me] with sluggish, slow effort"—the sense is that great effort must be exerted when desiring to go a long distance, but not when desiring to go a short distance.

Revealing this very meaning, she says: "Make these cows, the milch-cows (*dhenūḥ*), sport—that is, let them play—right here, in my very presence (*samayā*). This is her address to her husband. However, according to the interpretation of the hidden intention (*gūḍhābhiprāya*), the division of the words is as follows: "O cowherd (*gopāla*), come (*ehi*) with me (*samut-yogam*); let him (*saḥ*) sport (*vilāsaye*) with me; do not go (*mā gāḥ*). The sense is: "O cowherd! You have been waited for by me for such a long duration."

The sense is: "Since you are close to one who dwells in solitude, come to me with joy for union—that is, for our meeting—for the sake of pleasure; reach my side. To dispel the apprehension that she might either amuse herself or not upon suddenly approaching his side, he says, "I shall amuse you" (*vilāsaye*); the sense is, "I shall delight you by bestowing the bliss of love," or "I shall make you full of playful charm. "Do not go"—therefore, do not depart elsewhere now.

"Let this husband go to tend the cattle; we two shall enjoy ourselves at our own pleasure"—this is the underlying intention. This too is a disclosure of what was secret for the purpose of deceiving another. "tiṣṭhamānāḥ" means manifesting their own intention toward Kṛṣṇa. The suffix *taṅ* (ātmanepada) is applied to the root *sthā* by the rule "prakāśanastheyākhyayośca.
Since the designation of "recipient" (*sampradāna*) applies by the rule "ślāghahnuṅsthāśapāṃ jñīpsyamānaḥ," the dative case is used after the word "kṛṣṇa."
"Just as this Punnāga tree loosens the knot of its seed-pod at the tip with its trunk, so too will she rejoice because of that"—at these words of Śauri, the cowherd girl bowed her face. (1899)

This is a speech addressed by the Blessed Śauri, who longs for the embrace of the breasts of the young cowherd girl, toward his female elephant (kareṇu). This Punnāga tree—the preeminent among elephants—is, at its front portion, in the area ahead, loosening with its trunk (śuṇḍā-daṇḍa) the *anduka* bond, that is, the fetter or chain, both of itself and of its mate; such is the sense. "An *anduka* is a fetter (*nigala*), not feminine," according to Amara. It loosens [it].

Therefore, for that reason—namely, due to the loosening of her bonds—that *vaśā* (female elephant; cf. Amarakośa: *kariṇī*, *dhenukā*, *vaśā*) would rejoice (*hṛṣyet*), being desirous of roaming at will. As for the hidden meaning (*gūḍhārtha*), the word division is *agrimabhāḥ gendukabandham*. He whose *agrimā* (foremost) *bhāḥ* (splendor) is such is so described. This *punnāga* (the best of men) is referred to by another term in order to demonstrate his own audacity.

With her hand, she loosens—that is, slackens—the fastening of the bodice, which is the binding of the two breasts determined to be balls; this is an indication of the present used for the future in the sense of immediate proximity. "Asau" (she) refers to you.

In what ought to have been said, the word *vaśā* is used for Gopikā for the purpose of deceiving others. The same should be inferred for the subsequent occurrences of that word and the first-person pronoun. The sense is: "By his power, [I am] mine," referring to him who loosened her bodice; being *vaśā*, meaning dependent [upon him], she would rejoice. The meaning is that she would be delighted by the pleasure of love. Thus, at the words of Śauri—that is, upon hearing the speech of the Blessed One—the cowherd girl became downcast in face. This too is a disclosure of what was hidden for the sake of deceiving others.
In my *Raṅgarājavilāsa*, for example:
Having heard a certain woman say to her own friend, "Beholding this Mādhava, place him today upon your heart like the serpent-king Śeṣa," the young man remained silent. (1900)

This is the speech of a certain clever woman to her friend regarding a matter to be said to a certain lover who, during the festival of the Lord Raṅgarāja, did not know the proper occasion and placed his hand upon her breast amidst the great crowd of people. "Having beheld—that is, having looked all around at and scrutinized limb by limb—this Mādhava, the beloved of Śrī, the Lord of Śrīraṅga, who reclines upon the serpent Śeṣa; keep him in your heart; meditate upon him."

The hidden meaning (*gūḍhārtha*), however, lies in the two words *mā dhavam* and *bhujaṅga-śayam*. O *bhujaṅga*, O libertine! Do not place your hand (*śayam*) upon my heart (*hṛdi*), that is, my breast (*vakṣasi*), having seen this man (*dhavam*) standing at a distance—according to the grammatical rule, "the pronoun *adas* refers to what is distant. The sense is: "Do not let this husband of mine, who is situated nearby, touch my breasts. This too is a disclosure of a secret for the purpose of deceiving another.
Or as it says in my *Nṛsiṃhavilāsa*:

"When a certain woman said to her friend, 'Why do you look at me even though you have not seen my beloved, who is marked with the glorious Śrīvatsa jewel? the king of lechers turned back toward her. (1901)

This is the speech of a certain mature woman to her friend regarding a matter to be told to a certain lover, who—though his husband was standing nearby during the festival crowds of the Lord Nṛsiṃha—failed to perceive him due to being blinded by passion, and instead looked only at himself. [The word *vallabham* refers to the husband.]

"Dayita" means the beloved of the Lord of all worlds; as Amara states: "The word *vallabha* is also used for one who presides over the three [worlds]. He is thus described as one whose jewel is the Kaustubha, which is dense (*ghana*). Why do you look only at me, Śrī, even without beholding that Blessed One who bears the Śrīvatsa mark? The intended meaning is: "Behold the Blessed One as well."

The hidden meaning (gūḍhārtha), however, is as follows: O *kamana* (desirous one)! O lover! Why do you not look at my husband, even though he is present? Or rather: "O dear one (*vatse*), why do you not look at her who possesses a dense (*ghanā*) splendor of jewels (*ratnaśrī*) upon her breast (*vakṣasi*)—or, she who possesses a child (*vatsa*) endowed with a dense splendor of jewels? The sense is: "Do not let him see me in the presence of my husband. This too is merely a disclosure of a secret for the purpose of deceiving another.
The disclosure of concealed bashfulness is as follows:

"O Lord, consider me, who am distressed by love, devoid of fortune, and whose heart is tormented by longing for Govinda"—thus did Śauri perceive the inner disposition of the cowherd girl through her gestures. (1902)

"O fortunate one, remember this wretched woman; find me, whose heart is consumed by longing"—this is the word-division (*padaccheda*) in the first level of meaning. One who possesses *subhaga*—meaning the sixfold divine attributes such as sovereignty—is "the Fortunate One" (*subhaga*). Its vocative is "O Fortunate One," O Lord, O Sovereign of All! Remember this [woman], that is to say, me. The sense is: "Know her to be miserable. Therefore, "find" (attain) me, whose heart is scorched—that is, whose mind is agitated by the three-fold suffering (*tāpatraya*).

"Accept her as one to be protected"—this is the sense. Furthermore, intending another reason for her being his own possession, he says: "she is *viviktā*," meaning she is pure in character (*pavitra-śīlā*) and clear (*svacchā*) because she is not tainted by thoughts of any other refuge; this is the implication. According to Amara, "the words *vivikta*, *pūta*, and *vijana* [mean pure]. The grammatical construction is: "reflecting (*vimṛśan*), i.e., investigating thoroughly, you shall find (*vindeta*). However, according to the interpretation containing the hidden intention (*gūḍhābhiprāya*), the division of the verse is: "O beautiful Govinda, protect (*ava*) me, who am distressed by love (*smaradīnām*), this woman, whose heart is burning (*taptahṛdayām*)."

O Lord, O Beloved! The sense is that you alone are to be petitioned for all human goals (*puruṣārtha*). O Govinda! You, considering me—wretched because of the god of love, and therefore with a heart tormented and a mind weakened by the fever of separation—standing here in solitude in a place free from witnesses; perceiving correctly that "she is now situated in private," please satisfy me. This is the second person singular imperative of the root *ava* used in the sense of pleasing (*prīṇana*).

Here, by means of the explicit, manifest sense consisting of a request to the Blessed One—which conceals the intended sense consisting of a request for union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa through modesty—the phrase "he understood the gesture" (iṅgitam abodhi) brings that other sense into clarity. This is an instance of the disclosure of a concealed meaning encompassed by the power of words (śabda-śakti).
An example of the revelation of a hidden meaning based on the power of the literal sense (*arthaśaktimūlaguptāviṣkaraṇa*) is as follows:

"Alas, you who are indeed a treasure-house of compassion did not deign even with a glance to acknowledge me as I waited for you! As she spoke thus with significant intent, the moon-faced girl of Vraja was embraced by Śauri.

The charge that you, who are said to be a treasure-house of compassion (*kṛpānidhi*), possess contrary characteristics—why is this? To this he says: "Because of [your] perception" (*pratīti*). The sense is: "waiting for you," meaning she has been awaiting you for a long time with the hope of enjoying your company, which has been revolving in her heart. "Not even with a glance did you accept me": let alone the hope of enjoyment, the sense is that you did not even deign to show me favor by extending a mere fragment of a sidelong look. If you are indeed a treasure-house of compassion, why then do you act thus? This is the reproach.

In this very context, by means of such a turn of phrase, [the speaker] has observed you with the thought that the time suitable for your enjoyment—longed for by me—has finally arrived; yet that [time] was not attained. This meaning, which is obtained through the power of the sense (artha-śakti), is what is revealed by the term "with intent" (sākūtam). All of this is an example of the disclosure of what is concealed within a speaker created by the poet.
