The disclosure of poetic concealment (*kaviguptāviṣkaraṇa*) is as follows:
"O you who look upon me with hostility, you constantly delude me with your own virtues! O perverse one, have some mercy; being never separated from you, may I obtain eternal happiness. (1904)

The analysis of the verse is as follows: "Be compassionate toward me; may I not be separated from you. In this context, at the present moment, O you who look askance! O charming one! Do not delude me with your own qualities such as artifice, pride, and the like. Be somewhat compassionate. The sense is: "Do not continue to bewilder me in this way. [May I], being unseparated—meaning not parted—from you, always and without interruption, obtain happiness. In the alternative interpretation, the analysis is: "Be compassionate, or else [be] separated from me by you."

"O Prakṛti!"—this is an address to Mūlaprakṛti (the Root Nature). Amara states: "Pradhāna and Prakṛti [are synonyms] in the feminine. "O Pratīpadarśinī!"—she is so called because she shows everything in a contrary or adverse manner, according to the description: "She has set in motion my beginningless stream of karma; she causes the concealment of the Lord's true nature; she generates erroneous knowledge; and she produces the perception of objects as things to be enjoyed for her own sake. The suffix *ṇini* is applied to the causative form (*ṇijanta*) of the root *dṛś*.

O Perfectly Awakened One, by Your own qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, You constantly delude me, making me see things erroneously. The sense is that You have been taken as my refuge by me—one who says, "I am Your servant, I have come to You for refuge; save me"—according to the manner described in the passage beginning with "I am the slave of Your divine *māyā* composed of the *guṇas*. The word "or" (*vā*) is displaced [and should be read after "dayasva"]. The meaning is: even if there is no intention to exercise complete compassion, please show at least some small measure of mercy.

To the question, "What is the benefit from that?", he says, "By you" (*tvayā*). The sense is: "Separated from you," meaning having attained separation; "this alone is your act of compassion—that I might be released. Then, to the question, "And what of you?", he says, "Eternal" (*nitya*). [The intention is: "May I obtain eternal happiness, the bliss of liberation. Here, first of all, the procedure for appeasing a heroine who has been defiled by jealousy is perceived. However, the intended meaning is a reproach directed at *prakṛti* (Nature) on the part of one who has been defiled by the qualities (*guṇas*) of *prakṛti*.

And that [word] is revealed as being in the vocative case by pronouncing the word *prakṛte*, which ends in the seventh case (locative), preceded by the utterance of another word ending in the vocative, namely *pratīpadarśinī*. The distinction is this: "concealed by a speaker fashioned by the poet" (*kavinibaddhavaktṛgupta*) is for the purpose of deceiving others, whereas "concealed by the poet" (*kavigupta*) is for the purpose of displaying the poet's own maturity.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, the *Vivṛtokti-sara*, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the *Yukti-sara*:
*Yukti* (expedient) is the deception of another through action for the sake of protecting one's own vital secret.

The figure of speech called *yukti* (reasoning) consists of the deception of another by means of some action for the purpose of concealing one's own intention; this too is an innovation of Dīkṣita. Although this figure was not defined in the section on figures of speech in Jayadeva’s *Candrāloka*, nevertheless, in the third chapter (*mayūkha*) dedicated to defining the characteristics of poetry, *yukti* is described as one of those characteristics: "Reasoning (*yukti*) is the establishment of a particular [fact] through the connection with a diverse other matter; for example:
'O cloud, you are someone truly new, since you rain down gold repeatedly.'"
Thus it is said; however, by the initiated, *yukti* is defined in a different manner:
"Yukti is the outmaneuvering of others through action for the sake of protecting one's own vital points."
Just as at evening, a certain cowherd girl who had made an appointment in the cow-pen and was eager for the embrace of Govinda rose up from her kinsmen, taking hold of a creeper. (1905)

In the phrase "he rose" (*uttasthau*), although the root *sthā* is preceded by the prefix *ud*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is not applied because the action of rising does not have "upward motion" as its primary object. "Dāmanīm" refers to a rope for tethering cattle. Here, by means of the act of rising preceded by the taking up of the tethering-rope, there is a desire to deceive his own people through the concealment of the vital point—namely, his longing for an embrace with Govinda—by creating the illusion that he is rising to tether the calf in the evening. This constitutes the concealment of what is about to happen.
Concealment of conduct (*vṛttagopanam*) is as follows:
A certain cowherd girl, her teeth and garment torn by a young cowherd, approached a parrot on the bank of the Yamunā while freely caressing it. (1906)

In this context, there is the deception of others through the act of fondling her lower lip at will, which generates the illusion that it has been bitten by him, thereby concealing the wound from the teeth of the "Joy of Nandana" (Kṛṣṇa) at its most vulnerable point. The epithet *bimboṣṭhī* ("having lips like the bimba fruit") serves as a support for producing the illusion that the parrot might have bitten this very lip, mistaking it for a bimba fruit.

In this regard, the distinction is that in *vyājokti* (disguised speech) there is the concealment of outward appearance (*ākāra*), whereas in *yukti* (artful device) there is the concealment of intention (*āśaya*). Alternatively, the distinction is that in *vyājokti* there is concealment by means of speech, while here [in *yukti*] there is concealment by means of action. And thus, it is established in the *Kuvalayānanda* that even in the verse beginning with "Seeing Hari approaching at the city gate," this is indeed *yukti*.

In this regard, the following must be considered: it is not tenable to claim that there is a distinction between these two [figures] based on the difference between concealment effected by speech and concealment effected by action; for in the section on *vyājokti* (disguised speech), the venerable Dīkṣita himself has clearly demonstrated that the word "speech" (*ukti*) is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the operation of conveying any other means of concealment. Furthermore, in that very same work, in the example beginning with "Seeing him approaching," the definition is likewise clearly shown to apply.

Therefore, the definition of *vyājokti* (the figure of concealment) accepted by the ancients—who did not define *yukti* (the figure of artifice) as a separate ornament—is simply this: the concealment of a matter intended to be expressed for the sake of deceiving another through some action. This action may take the form of speech in some cases and something other than that in others; likewise, the object to be concealed may be an outward appearance in some cases and an internal disposition or the like in others. Thus, a proper distinction is made, and it follows that *yukti* is not distinct from *vyājokti*.

Therefore, since "reasoning alone" applies here in the phrase "having seen him approaching," the writing [of the previous verse] in contradiction with what follows is indeed questionable; for, as they say, a *vyājokti* (disguised statement) is possible according to the aforementioned method with greater parsimony.

In our view, however, since we do not accept that in *vyājokti* (feigned speech) the grasping of a statement consists merely of an operation intended to convey another cause for the purpose of concealing one's true disposition (*ākāra*), we maintain the following distinction: when a true disposition is concealed by means of an operation in the form of a statement, it is *vyājokti*; whereas when a disposition is concealed by means of an operation other than that, it is *ukti* (justification). It is based on this very principle that these two figures have been defined separately. Furthermore, the fact that the author Dīkṣita wrote in his section on *vyājokti* that the verse beginning with "āyāntam ālokya" is indeed *vyājokti* was done in accordance with a different school of thought.

Regarding the statement "it is indeed *yukti*" in that very verse during the discussion on the *yukti* ornament, it should be resolved that this was written there specifically to manifest its own excellence (*svanairbharya*), and thus there is no contradiction with the preceding or following text. Furthermore, in the same manner, even in the verse cited under the section on the *vyājokti* ornament—"From the bower on the bank of the Yamunā, [he goes] to Vraja"—it is actually the *yukti* ornament and not *vyājokti*; such is the direction of the argument.
Thus ends the ninety-third string, "The String of Reasoning," in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins "The String of Worldly Sayings":
this would be a worldly saying (*lokokti*) if it were an imitation of common popular proverbs.

The meaning is as follows: *lokokti* (popular saying) refers to that which is an imitation or mention of the preeminent speech or expression of people—that is, of the world—and its excellence, which consists in being handed down through the tradition of the people of various respective regions according to those respective regions. This *alaṃkāra* (figure of speech) is also the discovery of Dīkṣita alone.
O Blessed One, just as that Pauṇḍraka became an object of derision because he wore your dress—like a jackal who, seeing a leopard, scratches its own body with heated iron. || 1907 ||

Regarding the tiger with a variegated body (*citrakāya*), Amara states: "The five-clawed tiger, the white-lotus [tiger], and the deer-hater are *citrakāya*. The employment of the term *citrakāya* is based on the following distinction: when the concealment of one's own limbs by means of another agent—such as the jackal about to be mentioned—is intended, it is *vyājokti* (the artifice); whereas when the concealment of one's intention is achieved through an action other than that [concealment], it is *yukti* (the expedient). Relying on this very rule, these two figures have been defined separately. Furthermore, the statement by Dīkṣita in his section on *vyājokti* that the verse beginning with "Seeing him approaching" (*āyāntam ālokya*) is indeed an instance of *vyājokti* is made in accordance with a different school of thought.

Regarding the statement "it is indeed *yukti*" in that very verse during the discussion on the *yuktyalaṅkāra*, it should be understood that this was written there specifically to manifest its own excellence; thus, there is no contradiction between the preceding and following texts. And so, even in the verse cited in the section on the *vyājokti* ornament—namely, "From the bower on the bank of the Yamunā, [he goes] to Vraja"—it is actually *yuktyalaṅkāra* and not *vyājokti*; such is the direction of the argument.
Thus ends the ninety-third string, "The String of Logical Arguments," in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins "The String of Proverbs":
A proverb (*lokokti*) occurs when there is an imitation of popular sayings.

The meaning is as follows: "lokokti" (popular saying) refers to that which is an imitation or mention of the preeminent speech or expression of people—that is, of the world—and its excellence, which consists in its being handed down through the tradition of the people of various respective regions according to those specific locales. This ornament (*alaṃkāra*) is also indeed the discovery of Dīkṣita alone.
O Blessed One, just as Pauṇḍraka became an object of derision because he wore your dress—like a jackal who, seeing a tiger’s body, scratches its own body with heated iron. (1907)

*Citrikāya* refers to a tiger; as Amarasimha states: "The five-clawed tiger, the *puṇḍarīka*, and the leopard are enemies of deer. The inclusion of the word *citrikāya* is intended to suggest the act of scratching one's own body with a heated iron rod, preceded by a desire to mark one's limbs—a motif that will be further developed by the jackal’s actions described below. Having seen [the fire], the jackal (*kroṣṭṛ*) is like one who scratches his own body (*kāya*) with heated iron—that is, with a heated iron rod. The rest is clear. Here, in the second half of the verse, there is an imitation of a popular proverb well-known in the dialects of the Karṇāṭaka and Āndhra regions.

Just as one might abandon crookedness even after it has been taught, one can never abandon a heart of demonic nature; for even if bound with bamboo strips, O Blessed One, will a dog's tail ever become straight? (1908)

*Śunaḥpucchaṃ* means *śvāpucchaṃ* (the tail of a dog); the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs according to the rule beginning with *śuno danta-daṃṣṭrā*. Here, there is an imitation of a popular proverb well-known in the Andhra country.

Or rather, O Śauri, perceiving that nothing other than You can thus enable one to cross the ocean of existence, a person rushes toward the world—which is like a great bubble—in the river of the rainy season. (1909)
Here too, there is an imitation of the popular sayings of the people of the Andhra country.
Just as one who, having worshipped you here with great effort for so long, might instead seek a small reward, digs up a mountain and finds only a mouse; || 1910 ||
Or as it is said:

"Even though the Sudarśana discus and other weapons were present, the Daitya was struck down by you with your claws; O Narahari, surely when something can be removed by the claws, what need is there for an axe? (1911)

Just as a wicked man would not sing of Your story merely because he has entered the assembly of the virtuous, O Lord of the World, would a crow, even when confined in a cage, ever utter the *pañcama* note? 1912.
Just as all ritual services rendered to you would be fruitless if one were attached to another deity, O Lord, so too a thousand vows perish through indulgence in even a single instance of self-will.
Just as previously, due to the loss of Your grace, so too now, despite the bestowing of Your supreme grace, we have attained only poverty; thus indeed, there is no kingdom for those born of Pṛthā.

Previously we possessed "akiñcanatā" (the state of having nothing), that is, poverty; now we have attained "akiñcanatā," which means being deprived of other means [of livelihood]. Thus, by describing the "reflection" (pratibimba) starting with "evañca" (and so it is), while disregarding the "original object" (bimba)—namely, that worldly prosperity is far removed from us—this is an instance of *lalitā* (the charming figure). In the previous examples, the manner in which they are enlivened by *upamā* (simile), *nidarśanā* (illustration), and so forth, should be observed by the wise. In all these verses, there is an imitation of the popular proverbs current among the people of those respective regions.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, the "String of Worldly Sayings," in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the "String of Witty Sayings" (*Chekoktisara*):
If a worldly saying contains a hidden inner meaning, it is considered a witty saying (*chekokti*).

Just as when virtuous people sit together in an assembly, a wicked person would not sing of you merely because they are present; O Lord of the World, would a crow, even if confined in a cage, ever utter the *pañcama* note? (1912)

Just as all ritual honors offered to you would be fruitless if there were attachment to another deity, so too, O Lord, if one were to act according to one's own whims, a thousand vows would perish. (1913)
Just as previously, due to the loss of your favor, so too now, despite your extreme grace, we have resorted to absolute poverty; thus, indeed, there is no kingdom for those born of Pṛthā.

Previously we possessed only the state of being "nothing" (akiñcanatā) in the sense of poverty; now, however, we have attained "nothingness" (akiñcanatā) in the sense of being destitute of any other means. Thus, by describing the "reflection" (pratibimba)—beginning with the words "and so"—without even considering the "original object" (bimba), namely that worldly prosperity is far removed from us, this figure is "Lalita" (the Playful). In the previous examples, the manner in which Simile (Upamā), Illustration (Nidarśanā), and others enliven the verse should be observed by the wise. In all these verses, there is an imitation of the popular proverbs of the respective localities.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, the String of Worldly Sayings, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the String of Witty Sayings (*chekoktisara*):
If a worldly saying contains a hidden meaning within its final sense, it is considered a witty saying (*chekokti*).
O lotus-eyed one, may no one whatsoever born in my lineage ever turn away from you; for surely, even a single crippled monkey can bring ruin to an entire forest.

In this context, the popular saying well-known in the Andhra country—that "one who is wavering regarding the statement of the surrendered soul (prapanna), which begins with 'May he not be born in our lineage' and concludes with the summary of its meaning, 'He for whom Vāsudeva is not the deity from birth until death,' is himself a monkey"—is here imitated. For one who turns away from You, the Lord of all lords, is indeed like a monkey due to his extreme fickleness.

For, by being filled with inconceivable, marvelous, and unafflicted knowledge, dispassion, and devotion, he might—by his own arrogance—disturb even his own family, which is as profoundly deep as a great forest; this is another meaning implied within the verse.
Or rather: "O Blessed One, he who has you as his sole refuge trembles even at the sight of a common person; for how could one say that such a crooked course exists within an anthill? (1916)

"Vṛjinagatiḥ" means one who moves crookedly; here, there is an imitation of a popular proverb well-known in the Andhra language. Common folk, being composed of darkness (*tamas*) and swarming with wicked creatures, are as terrifying as anthills; within such a place, what kind of "vṛjinagatiḥ"—that is, a continuous succession of misfortune—might exist? This is the sense implied by the *arthāntaranyāsa*. On this point:
"One should not eat even in the same row as Brahmins or even one's own kin;
for who knows what hidden sin another may possess?"
Thus, it follows the shadow of the meaning of the Smṛti.
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, the Chapter on Chekokti (Pithy Sayings), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Vakrokti (Equivocation):
When a statement intended for one purpose is interpreted in another way by someone else, that is Vakrokti.
If it is expressed through double entendre (śleṣa) or by means of intonation (kāku), it is called "crooked speech" (vakrokti).

The meaning is that *vakrokti* (indirect speech) is an utterance conforming to the manner in which another person’s statement—spoken with one intention—is joined by someone else in a different way. And it is of two kinds, because such a re-joining occurs either through pun (*śleṣa*) or through intonation (*kāku*).
In that regard, an example by way of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is as follows:
"O daughter of the ocean, you should not be angry with me; why should I, who am not the ocean, submerge the crocodile? Thus, Śrī triumphs by deluding Hari with these words. (1922)

With the intention that "no anger should be felt here," another meaning was conceived through a pun by the Goddess Śrī upon the words of the Blessed One, which [otherwise] mean "the crocodile should be cast down."

"Or rather, if you would place your lotus-eye upon me, I shall not take this lotus away; here it is in your hand. May Ramā, thus deluding her own beloved with these words, bestow auspiciousness. 1923.

In this context, regarding the Lord’s request, "You should place your lotus-eye upon me and cast a sidelong glance," there is the invention of an alternative meaning by breaking the compound *nayanābjaṃ* into the words *naya na abjam*—that is, "Do not take away the lotus; rather, this very lotus, the conch, remains right in your hand."
Or as it is said:
"Why do you delay in conversing? O lovely woman, arouse some curiosity! For neither a winnowing-basket nor a plow is to be found here in the vicinity of oil-pressers and plowmen. (1924)

"Why are you angry, O Vanitā? Be gracious toward me, who am bowed before you, O you whose form is silver (Rūpyākṛti). "How could one whose form is silver (Rūpyākṛti) be angry? Thus did the daughter of the ocean mock her beloved.

Regarding the first verse here, the Lord said, "Let some curiosity (*kutūhalam*) arise at the embrace and so forth. Taking this as an opportunity for a double meaning (*arthāntaranyāsa*), one might propose that *kutūhalam* is a compound of *kutū*—meaning a vessel for animal fat or hide—and *halam*—meaning a plow. To this, the reply is given: "A *kutū* is found near an oil-presser and a *hala* near a plowman, but neither is to be found here."

In the second [interpretation], however: "O you two of silvery form" (*he rūpyākṛte*), meaning those of excellent form; "O lady" (*he vanite*), according to Amara: "The word *vanitā* refers to a woman who has engendered excessive passion, or one in whom excessive passion has been engendered. When I am bowed down before you, why do you become angry? Why do you display wrath? This is what the Blessed One said. An alternative meaning is that "silver" (*rūpya*) is that which has the nature of being struck (*āhata*), and "of silvery form" (*rūpyākṛti*) means having a form like that of gold or silver, which are both of "struck form" (*āhatarūpa*). Thus, the meaning is that her form is equal to either gold or silver.

Having interpreted the word *kupyasi* as "you act like base metal" (*kupya*), where base metal refers to copper, bronze, and so forth—distinct from wrought and unwrought gold and silver—the Blessed Mother, the progenitor of the world, gave this reply: "How could silver (*rūpya*) be base metal? The word *rūpya* is derived from the word *rūpa* by adding the suffix *yap* in the sense of "wrought" (*āhata*) or "praiseworthy" (*praśaṃsā*), according to the rule: *rūpād āhatapraśaṃsayor yap*. As Amarasimha states: "Wrought and unwrought gold and silver are called *kośa* and *hiraṇya*; anything other than those two is *kupya*, while both of them are called *rūpya* when wrought."
Just as one might say:

"Having cast aside the bitterness of pride, let your heart become sweet like *mastu* (whey) born from the ocean. [The other replies: "I am not born from *dadhi* (curd), but rather born from the ocean; how then could my heart be *mastu*? (1926).

In this context, having imagined a different meaning for the sentence "May your heart become dear [to me] by casting aside the bitterness of anger"—where the phrase "casting aside the bitterness of pride" means "may it be sweet"—one provides the reply beginning with "I am not born of curd," etc., by conceiving another sense: that which has its bitterness cast out is thus "sweet *mastu*," meaning the whey of curd.
Or, for example:
"O lady with eyes as broad as lotus petals, know that the Supreme Person is situated here; this instruction would be fruitful for one who perceives flesh as tin. (1927)

The response of Śrī is as follows: she imagines another meaning for the Lord’s statement, "Know me, who stand here before you, to be the Supreme Person (puṃs)," by interpreting it to mean, "Only a fool would think my flesh is lead; for her, the instruction that my flesh is not lead is effective. Thus, she replies to Him.
Or as it is said:
"O slender one, let your lover stand at the door for a short while; surely the lover must always remain at every necklace. (1928)

Lakṣmī’s reply—by means of providing another meaning (*arthāntaranyāsa*) to the Lord’s statement, “How long must you remain at the door by the hand of your lover?”—is as follows: even though the necklace has been returned by the jewel-like hero, [the Lord] must indeed stay. In the expression *hārehāre pratihāre*, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound; the absence of the dual ending is according to the rule *tṛtīyāsaptamyorbahulam*.

Just as this Sahajamaru king is exceedingly thirsty for you, the daughter of the ocean of nectar; so too, one who drinks curd produced in a desert while suffering from extreme thirst—this is truly most wonderful.

In this context, the verse beginning with "sahajamarudadhipa" is Śrī’s reply to the Lord’s statement, "sahodaro maghavā yasya sa upendras tvayyatimātraspṛhaḥ," which means "Upendra (Viṣṇu), whose brother is Indra, has excessive longing for you. By assigning a different meaning—namely, "drinking curd in the Maru desert while being naturally thirsty"—she implies that he is "sahajamarudadhipa" (naturally a lord of the Maru desert). These verses, beginning with "na krodhaḥ kāryo'mbudhi," consist of the dialogue between Śrī and Śrīvallabha during a lovers’ quarrel.
"O fair-faced one of Vraja, I cannot remain; I am departing, O jewel of Nanda Gopa's lineage! If you depart, how can he be happy? Thus did Vasudeva address the cowherd girl.

In this context, in order to draw the cowherd maiden toward him, the Blessed One addressed her with the compound vocative "vrajasumukhī. Thereupon, the maiden Vrajasumukhī, by means of a pun (*śleṣa*) on that very word, imagined another meaning—namely, "O Sumukhī, go to Vraja"—and delivered a witty retort to the Blessed One: "I will not stay; I am going, O jewel of the lineage of Nandagopa!"

By that same [method], through the process of complete awakening (*saṃbuddhi*), another meaning is fashioned for the entire compound word *nandagopavaṃśamaṇe*—which was used [by the Lord] as ending in the vocative case—by means of the division: "O jewel of the cowherd clan (*gopavaṃśamaṇe*), Nanda, rejoice!
[The verse says: "If you go away, if you depart while disregarding me who am speaking thus, how could this one, desiring an embrace from you, rejoice?

In this way, the Lord's own desire has been revealed through a very indirect expression (*vakrokti*). This is an instance of "indirect expression enlivened by indirect expression" (*vakroktijīvita-vakrokti*).

Or rather, I think that you have lost your senses, since you converse with me while I am not conversing, O friend; for you tell me, who am truly one whose mind is fixed on Acyuta, that I am one whose mind has strayed—yet you yourself, O friend, are truly one whose mind is fixed on Acyuta.

This verse consists of a dialogue between two beautiful-browed women of Vraja. Here, the first half—beginning with "I think" (*manye*) and so forth—is the speech of one friend to another who is lost in some meditation. "Cyutadhīḥ" means one whose intellect has slipped away; that is to say, one who is unconscious. The second half, beginning with "acyutadhiyam" and ending with "āttha," is the reply of the other woman to her. The remaining sentence, beginning with "ālī" (friend), is the speech of the first woman once again to the one speaking to her.

In this context, seeing her friend giving no reply as she was relating some event with a straightforward mind, [the first woman] said, "Surely you are unconscious. With the intention of saying, "I am not unconscious," she replied, "You are telling me, whose mind is fixed on Acyuta, that my mind has failed in vain. Then the former constructed another meaning: "Friend, it is true that you have a mind fixed on Acyuta; for otherwise, why do you not speak to me who am speaking?"—her heart being attached to Kṛṣṇa.
When the innocent girl said, "Friend, join me in an embrace at the navel like a girdle," the Sairandhrī replied with a smile, "My effort is only to join [the two of us]."

In this context, a certain innocent cowherd girl, with a simple mind, addressed a female artisan who was decorating her, saying, "Arrange for the embrace of the luster of my *sārasana* (girdle). A mature *sairandhrī*, employing the figure of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), devised another meaning for the phrase "the embrace of the luster of the *sārasana*"—namely, "the embrace of Padmanābha," that is, Śrī Kṛṣṇa—and gave this reply: "This effort of decoration is intended precisely to bring about that very embrace."
"O Gopālikā, look here at something! "What should I look at, O Alīke? "I am calling you 'Gopa' (cowherd), O Gopī. "You are simply a fool, O Gopa! 1933.

In this context, the clever woman, the foremost beauty of Vraja, offered a reply—beginning with "What shall I look at on my forehead?"—by employing a pun (*śleṣa*) upon the words spoken by the Blessed Lord, the joy of the Nanda clan: "O Gopālikā, O cowherd girl, look here a little. While the Lord intended, "O Gopālikā [Gopā + alikā], look here a little," she interpreted it as, "O Gopa, on your *alika* (forehead), look a little," and thus provided another meaning. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "O charming one, O fool, O handsome one"—this is the underlying intention (*ākūta*)—"you yourself are the cowherd (*gopa*)."

"I am not a cowherd (gopa), but rather a cowherdess (gopī). Thus, by failing to perceive even the distinction between male and female, you address a woman with a word denoting a man; the implication is that you yourself are merely a cattle-herder (paśupāla). Alternatively, the construction follows the literal meaning: by speaking thus, you are indeed a cowherd. The implication is: "If you were truly an urban gentleman (nāgaraka), how could you speak in such a manner? A cowherd's wife is a *gopālikā*. The suffix *ṅīṣ*—which would normally be applied here to denote a feminine form through connection with a male (*puṃyoga*)—is prohibited by the rule "not after words ending in *pālaka*. Subsequently, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, resulting in the change to *ī* by the rule "from a letter standing before a suffix... (*pratyayasthāt*).

Victorious is Hari, who, speaking to Mura, said: "Indeed, even Śunāsīra (Indra) could be swallowed by me; what need be said of another? Yet he does not wish to swallow the plowshare (sīra), saying 'it is white'. 1934.

Here, with the intention that "even Indra can be swallowed by me," the Lord provides a reply through the conceptualization of another meaning (arthāntaranyāsa) to the words "to swallow" and so forth spoken by Mura; [the sense being: "O Śuna, one who resembles a dog, you cannot swallow Sīra—the Sun—or Sīra—the plough, just as a dog cannot swallow a plough. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *sīra* is masculine when referring to the Sun or a plough. All of this is an example of *vakrokti* (paronomastic speech) involving unmodified punning (*avikṛta-śleṣa*).
Crooked speech (*vakrokti*) consisting of unaltered punning (*śleṣa*) is as follows:

the state of being unaltered in a pun consists in describing a meaning without abandoning the phonemes as they are uttered together; whereas the state of being altered occurs through the insertion or deletion of one or more phonemes.
This Vāmadeva is indeed the Lord of the World, shining even without a beard; if he shines even without a beard, he is undoubtedly that very Lord of the World. || 1935 ||

This verse takes the form of a dialogue between a Śaiva and a Vaiṣṇava. Therein, the Śaiva has stated: "This Vāmadeva, who is peerless, incomparable, most beautiful, and resplendent—this Virūpākṣa alone is the Lord of the World, whom we worship."

According to the Vaiṣṇava view, however, with the intention that Vāsudeva alone is the Lord of the World (*jagadīśa*), the word *asamaḥ*—meaning "unequaled" because it is not accompanied by the letter *ma*—is [interpreted as] "well-adorned" (*suśobhitaḥ*) if it is beautified by the letter *su*, which has displaced the position of the letter *ma*. Then, he alone is Vāmadeva, the Lord of the World; of this there is no doubt. Thus, by effecting the removal of the letter *ma* from the word *vāmadeva* and the insertion of the letter *su* in its place, a different meaning is conceived through punning (*śleṣa*).

Or rather, just as this supreme one who granted boons to the Asura Bāṇa and is skilled at carrying the city of Kāśī—when you ask, "Who is the supreme one here? and I say, "Recite the Veda," what indeed will you understand from much talk? (1936)

This verse as well consists of a dialogue between a Śaiva and a Vaiṣṇava. "The carrying of the city of Kāśī" means its lifting up, that is to say, its protection. "Skilled in that [carrying] and the bestower of boons upon the gods headed by Vīṇā"—this Śiva alone is the supreme, the most excellent; thus it was stated by the Śaiva. Then the Vaiṣṇava said: "Recite the Veda; when you know who is the supreme here, [then you shall know]. [The Śaiva replies: "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords, him, the supreme deity among deities..."

When a Vaiṣṇava replies to the recitation of the Śruti passage, "Agni is the lowest of the deities, Viṣṇu is the highest," by asking, "Who indeed might be the highest?", he substitutes the letter *da* for the letter *va* in the two phrases "bestower of boons upon Bāṇāsura" (*bāṇāsuravaradāyī*) and "skilled in burning the city of Kāśī" (*kāśīpuravahanapaṭu*), reading them instead as "giver of terror to Bāṇāsura" (*bāṇāsuradaradāyī*) and "skilled in burning the city of Kāśī" (*kāśīpuradahanapaṭu*). By thus displacing the *va*s and inserting *da*s, he constructs the meaning that this very Śrī Vāsudeva is the highest.
Therefore, this too is an example of *vikṛta-śleṣa-vakrokti* (perverse punning-circuitous speech).
"O lotus-eyed one, abandon your anger; behold the lover standing before you! Speak softly to this rogue!"—with these words, the Goddess of the Earth eclipsed the Lord of Lakshmi with her wrath.

This is the Lord’s indirect speech (*vakrokti*) intended to appease the Goddess of the Earth, who is troubled by pride. By the term "O fish-eyed one" (*mīnekṣaṇe*), it is suggested that your eyes are naturally clear and bright, and have never been clouded by anger. The sense is that you are standing before me for the sake of a request. The phrase "look at me" (*nirīkṣasva*)—the beloved who desires you—is used to indicate that I am not standing here as a mere indifferent bystander. "Speak softly, O rogue! (*mandaṃ jalpa śaṭha*) is the Goddess of the Earth’s retort; "O rogue" (*śaṭha*) refers to one who acts perversely in secret.

In my presence here, speak softly and not loudly; having done me such great displeasure, do not speak freely as if you were overflowing with intense affection, thinking "I know you"—this is the underlying sentiment.

In this context, regarding the two words *mīnekṣaṇe* and *kamanam*, which have been spoken [by you], take the letter *ma* situated in *mīnekṣaṇe* and the letter *da* in *kamanam*; speak the letter *ma* as the letter *da*. The meaning is: pronounce the letter *ma* as the letter *da*. Then, the form *dīnekṣaṇe kadanam* is produced. Address me, who have been deceived by you, as "O one with darting eyes" (*dīnekṣaṇe*). "Distress" (*kadana*) means mental agony. The sense is: it stands right before you; while you are thus deceiving me, it is clearly manifest before you and does not require further deliberation (*mīmāṃsā*).
Here, by the elision of the letter *m* and the insertion of the letter *d* in its place, another meaning is conceived through a modified pun (*śleṣa*).
Or rather:

He who delights in white speech, by whom the moon was sustained with its pale splendor—he, Vṛṣākapi, the Lord of the three worlds, is sufficient; tell me again, could he possibly be anyone else? (1938)

This too consists of a statement and a counter-statement between a Śaiva and a Vaiṣṇava. He whose luster (*ruci*)—belonging to the ash (*bhasita*)—is white and bright, that is to say, one who is smeared with white ash; by whom, through his naturally pale form possessing a white splendor (*valakṣaśriyā*), the moon (*glauḥ*, *śaśāṅkaḥ*) was held aloft—that is, borne upon his head—he is Vṛṣākapi, Hara, the Lord of the three worlds. Such is the intention of the Śaiva statement.

"Enough with the Vaiṣṇava [sect]! Speak again; say enough; speak having reflected"—this is the meaning. "He alone, as you have said, shall be the Lord of the three worlds"—having accepted this, say "alaṃ," which is without the letter *la*. Because this implies another meaning, by the omission of the letter *la* in your spoken sentence, one who has the luster of a parrot's speech is produced—by whom the chest was held by Śrī, and who is "gaura" (fair)—thus he is described as "one whose luster shines like a parrot," being dark-green like an emerald (*marakata*).
The meaning is as follows: He whose chest is adorned with Śrī (Lakṣmī) is called Vakṣaśśrī; by him, as such, the Earth (Gauḥ) was supported—that is, lifted up—according to the Vedic revelation:

"Thou art lifted up by the Boar, by Kṛṣṇa, the hundred-armed one. That Vṛṣākapi is none other than the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, for Amara states: "Hara and Viṣṇu are both Vṛṣākapis. This has been interpreted with the intention that he is the Lord of the three worlds. The distinction here is merely the elision of the letter *la*.
Just as you say, O learned one, that Śiva alone is indeed the supreme lord of the world, tell me truly: is he not, in fact, Viṣṇu? You yourself know the reality of this matter. (1939)

"You are talkative and loquacious; you say that Śiva alone is indeed the supreme lord of the world. But surely he is Acyuta himself—say that he is the supreme lord of the world! That Śiva is indeed Acyuta, whose very essence is Acyuta. Or, the construction may be: 'He is indeed Acyuta. Acyuta alone is Śiva, the embodiment of auspiciousness, according to the Vedic scripture: 'The eternal, auspicious, and infallible [Acyuta]. Therefore, say that he is the supreme lord of the world. (In this alternative interpretation, *vācā* is a separate word.)

That Śiva is indeed *locyuta* (fallen from his eyes); having attained the non-falling (*acyavana*) from the world, he is the lord of the world—of whom is he the lord? Speak with these words: "Of no one at all. From this very [statement], you understand the truth: while the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the lords of all, is awake, of whom could this [Śiva] be the sovereign? This is the intended meaning. Here too, in this indirect expression (*vakrokti*), there is merely the elision of a syllable (*varṇodvāpa*).

All of this is an illustration of *vakrokti* (indirect speech) based on the punning of words (*śabda-śleṣa*). An example of that which is based on the punning of meaning (*artha-śleṣa*) is as follows:

"Where is the cowherd? Where is the Lord of Beasts? And where does the cow graze today, O slender one? He knows that—'He whose vehicle is the bull'—may this playful speech between Umā and Śiva protect you. (1940)

In this context, the words "Gopāla" and so forth—which were originally a joking remark by Gaurī containing an intention directed toward Kṛṣṇa—were joined with Śrī, who intended to reveal the account of Maheśvara through the phrase "Where is the Lord of Beasts? and so on.

Victorious is Hari as he embraces the cowherd girl: "By what tone [of voice] have you come so swiftly? What do you wish to do, O Kṛṣṇa? Truly, I do not know. "Do you not understand, O lady with arched brows?"—thus he speaks. (1941)

In this context, regarding the women of Vraja who, out of straightforwardness, inquire, "We do not know for what purpose you have come here with such haste," the phrase "na vijānāsi" ("you do not know") is interpreted through a shift in meaning (*arthāntaranyāsa*) by means of an interrogative intonation (*kāku*).
This [type of *vakrokti*] also occurs through the combination of both intonation (*kāku*) and punning (*śleṣa*). For example:

"O son of Bhṛgu, know me to be a chief among Brahmins, more skilled than even the most skillful in battle, O descendant of Daśaratha; and know you, O virtuous Brahmin, to be one whose weapons are ever-ready. [Yet] I honor you highly. (1942)

This is a verse in the form of a dialogue between Bhārgava and Rāghava. Therein, Bhārgava had said three lines—intending to demonstrate his own invincibility and greatness by declaring, "Know me to be one whose stainless weapons, headed by the Brahmā-weapon, are exceedingly proficient in battle"—to which the Lord Rāghava applied a different interpretation, using a tone of irony (*kāku*) and underlying intent (*ākūta*) such as, "O son of Bhṛgu! I highly honor you, O Brahmin," implying, "Oh, how great is your Brahminhood!"

In this very context, O son of Bhṛgu! I consider you to be a *sādhu* (virtuous), *samyak* (proper), *bahu* (much), and *bahula* (abundant) *vipra*—that is, one whose complexion has departed (*vigataprarṇa*). By thus extracting the syllables of the word *pravarṇa*, another meaning is conceived. This being the case, the result is: "one who is more skillful than a thief (*curājipaṭīyāṃsam*), whose chief [quality] is a pale complexion (*vivarṇamukhyam*), and whose weapons have failed (*sannaśastram*). Here, *cura* means theft.

The battle (*āji*) was abundant with that; therein, he [encountered] a leader of the base folk (*pāmaramukhya*), who was more skilled in combat than a thief—according to the maxim, "This is the path practiced by thieves, not one frequented by heroes"—and whose weapons were exhausted, meaning his arms were shattered. (Amara states: "A base person is *vivarṇa*"). ॥

This [figure] is also possible even when another meaning is imagined through a difference in construction (*yojanā*) without the use of double entendre (*śleṣa*) or plaintive intonation (*ākūta*). For example:
"O Rādhā, it is not that I am not attached to you; would I not then dye Nīlā? But I know you well—you are attached to me, O Hari, as you dye Nīlā. (1943)

In this instance, while the Blessed One intended the interpretation: "Devoted as I am to you, I would not be devoted to Nīlā," Rādhā imagined a different meaning by interpreting it according to the literal sound of the words; thus, it constitutes *vakrokti* (paronomastic speech). Although such a form of *vakrokti* has not been analyzed by either earlier or later scholars, nevertheless, because of the presence of such aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*), we have determined that this is indeed *vakrokti*.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter on *vakrokti* (Peculiar Speech) in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the chapter on *svabhāvokti* (Description of Nature):
"The description of the inherent nature residing in genus (*jāti*) and so forth is called *svabhāvokti*."

The poetic figure named *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) is so called because its name is etymologically significant; it consists of a description of the inherent nature residing in things such as genus (*jāti*), and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and substances (*dravya*) are included.

Just as at evening Śauri drives back the herd of cows—whose udders are swollen with milk from the memory of their calves, whose dewlaps swing with rapid motion, and which low with deep, resonant sounds. (1944)

*Gavyām* means a collection of cows; the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *khalagorathāt* under the governing heading *tasya samūhaḥ*. She is described as such because her udders (*ūdhāṃsi*) were very full (*supīvarāṇi*); regarding this, Amara states: *ūdhastu klībamāpīnam*. By the rule *ūdhaso’naṅ*, the substitute *anaṅ* is applied, and by the rule *bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added. The rest is clear in meaning. Here, there is a description of the natural character of the bovine species.

The abode of the golden-hued splendor of the forest thickets of Añjana Mountain—anointing my eyes with the dark, shimmering ichor of a limping deer, and possessing a luster like the plumage of a beautiful peacock—acts as collyrium for my gaze.

This light, which is the radiance of that Hari whose abode is the grove of Añjanagiri, makes my vision "añjanavatī"—that is, it makes it like collyrium. [The suffix] *matup* is elided after the word *añjana* by the rule "vinmatoḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.65), due to the application of the *iṣṭhavadbhāva* operation. Here, there is a description of the inherent nature of a quality (*guṇasvabhāvavarṇana*).
May that divine couple, standing at the wedding altar with the hair on their bodies bristling from the mutual friction of their shoulders, and casting sidelong glances at one another, shine forth.
Herein is the description of the nature of action.

May He who places Ramā upon His chest, who bears the discus and the conch in His hands, and who wears golden garments—the one whose abode is the mountain of the serpent-king—shine forth within my mind. (1947)

We choose for our hearts an indescribable fortune: that certain loveliness ever to be enjoyed by Śiva upon the peak of his bull, wherein the surface of the cheeks blossoms with a measured, white smile, and which bears a tilaka of musk.
In these two verses, there is a description of the essential nature of substances.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, the *Svabhāvokti-sara*, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the *Bhāvika-sara*: when a marvelous object is described, there arises a sense of the past or the future within the present subject matter.
That in which things appear as if directly perceived is considered *bhāvika*.

The *bhāvika* ornament consists of that wherein, through the description of most wonderful deeds, past and future entities appear as if they were present before the eyes. Nor is the appearance of the past and future as if they were perceptible contradictory; for, by the description of such exceedingly marvelous things, an imaginative realization (*bhāvanā*) arises in the hearts of those possessed of *bhāva*. Thus, through the intensity of this imaginative realization, it is indeed possible for even objects that have occurred or will occur to appear as if directly perceived. As in: "In every tree I behold him wearing bark and black antelope skin—sitting, reclining, standing, eating, wandering, and drinking."
Meditating upon Hṛṣīkeśa, he saw the entire world as consisting of Him alone.

In such cases as this, it is not *svabhāvokti* (description of nature), for in that figure there is a sense of perceptibility through the accurate description of the actual nature of a thing; here, however, it is by way of its marvelousness (*adbhutatva*). Nor is it an ornament such as *rasavat* (the presence of rasa), because in those cases the rasa and so forth are apprehended only through the coordination of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and so on. [For example: "Upon the forehead of the bull-bannered Lord, with its playful smile and cheeks blossoming like a white lotus, marked by a tilaka of musk, eternally to be enjoyed—such an indescribable grace within the mind, we choose. (1948)
In these two verses, there is a description of the essential nature of substances.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, the *Svabhāvokti-sara*, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the *Bhāvika-sara*: when a marvelous object is described, the past and future [events] within that subject [are rendered present].
That in which things appear as if directly perceived is considered *bhāvika*.

The poetic figure *bhāvika* is that wherein, through the description of most wonderful deeds, past and future entities appear as if they were present before the eyes. Nor is the appearance of the past and future as if they were perceptible contradictory; for through the description of such extraordinary things, an imaginative realization (*bhāvanā*) arises in the hearts of those possessed of *bhāva*. Thus, by the intensity of this imaginative realization, even objects that are past or yet to come can indeed become manifest as if perceived directly. As it is said: "In every tree I see him wearing bark and black antelope skin—sitting, reclining, standing, eating, wandering, and drinking."
Meditating upon Hṛṣīkeśa, he saw the entire world as consisting of Him alone.

In such cases as these, this is not *svabhāvokti* (description of nature), for in that figure there is a state of appearing as if perceived through the accurate description of the very nature of an object; here, however, it is by way of its marvelousness (*adbhutatva*). Nor is it an ornament such as *rasavat* (possessing rasa) and the like, because in those cases the manifestation of rasa and so forth occurs only through the consideration of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and so on, and not by way of marvelousness. Nor is it *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because there can be no possibility of conceiving past and future things as being present before the eyes. Nor is it *bhrāntimān* (illusion), because the presentation of the object is produced by non-error. Therefore, they say that this is a distinct ornament, transcending all others.

Just as the martial prowess of Narasiṃha, who tore open the breast-slopes of the lord of the sons of Diti with a fierce and formidable loud laugh, remains vivid even today on the Siṃha mountain. (1949)

On the Śeṣācala mountain, known as Siṃhaśikhariṇī—which is to say, Ahobila, which constitutes a portion of that very mountain—there is the manifestation of the Lord Śrī Nṛsiṃha. Through the description of His most wondrous and transcendent great martial prowess (*mahārbhaṭī*), characterized by an intense fury capable of agitating the interior of Hiraṇyakaśipu’s chest, He becomes as if directly perceived through such contemplation. This is the evocation of His terrifying majesty.
Just as Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra, and the others produce joy for the eyes, so too do the primordial sages, even today, bring us delight as they worship Hari on the mountain of the serpent Śeṣa.
This is the manifestation of the greatness of the sacred site.
Or, for example:

"Even now, we behold on this king of mountains, the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), who has mounted his vehicle out of curiosity for the festival procession, the agitation caused by the forest-elephants being seized by crocodiles. (1951)

O Jewel of the Bull-Mounted Lord, even today we behold Brahmā and the other gods at Your gateway, their countless crowns shattered by the blows dealt by the enraged commander of the host during the great conflict.
O Hero of the Raghus, just as you previously saw Vālin and Rāvaṇa defeated, even now I behold the thousand-eyed Indra with his thousand eyes wide open in wonder, exclaiming, "Aha! at the sight.

The analysis is: *ahaha* and *ā*. Both of these are particles (*nipāta*). They function respectively to express the distress born from remembering Vālin and the wonder arising from remembering Rāvaṇa. Regarding the form *ā iti*, there is the preservation of the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule "A particle consisting of a single vowel, except for *aṅ*, [preserves its stem]. This particle is indeed *aṅit* (lacking the *it* designation), because its meaning is remembrance; for it is taught that "in the senses of a sentence and remembrance, [the particle] is *aṅit*. *Ahaha ā* is an *anubhāva* (external manifestation) arising from the commencement of speech, which illuminates both suffering and wonder.

"Aha-ha-ā" means "even now," together with tears born of both sorrow and joy; thus, they are "sahasrāṇi" (accompanied by tears). Because the rule "vopasarjanasya" is optional, the word *saha* does not undergo the change to *sa-* [to form *sāsrāṇi*]. The sense is: "I behold him who possesses such eyes"—that is, one whose eyes are still filled with tears of grief arising from the slaying of Vālin, and whose eyes are filled with tears of delight arising from the slaying of Rāvaṇa. Even now, I see him in that state.

In this alternative interpretation (*pakṣe*), the word *sahasranayana* (thousand-eyed) is *ahahāḥ*: that which has no *ha* (the letter *ha*) is *ahaḥ*; *ahahāḥ* is that whose phoneme is *hā*. The meaning is that by the removal of the letter *ha*, it is constructed with the syllable *hā* right there. For this reason, I behold [Indra] as "possessing a thousand eyes" (*sahasranayana*); the sense is that, according to the aforementioned method, the word *sahasranayana* becomes such [i.e., *ahahāḥ*]. This too is merely a description of the direct perception of a supernatural being; however, the other wonder is its distinction from the previous ones.
All this is a description of the direct perception of present objects; a description of the direct perception of future objects is as follows:
"O Śrīnivāsa, by Your grace, those honors that were to come through the path of light as a result of my daily contemplation dwell this very day within the range of my vision. (1954)

In this context, there is a description of the direct perception of the future wonders—the honors received on the path beginning with light—which are otherwise impossible to see while in the state of bondage.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, the Section on the Bhāvika, in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Section on the Udātta:
that is called *udātta* (the exalted) where a subject matter of great prosperity is described.
Or else, something that characterizes others, or a praiseworthy conduct, is composed.

The figure of speech *udātta* occurs where an object endowed with abundant prosperity is described, or where a praiseworthy deed associated with a great person (*mahāpuruṣa*) is employed as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaka*), as in the example "where this field of Devadatta’s crane is. An *upalakṣaka* is that which makes something known. Since *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) and *bhāvika* (the marvelous) consist of the description of things exactly as they are, the first type of *udātta*, which consists of an object superimposed [upon another] by way of its opposite, finds its proper occasion here.

Among these, the first is *udātta*, characterized by majesty, which consists of the description of an object endowed with inconceivable power, brought forth by the poet’s imagination. The second, however, is the conduct of great men (*mahāpuruṣa*) of noble deeds, which is presented as a subordinate element to another primary subject; it is so called because the conduct of great men is inherently noble.

All this has been a description of the direct perception of present objects; now follows a description of the direct perception of future objects: "O Śrīnivāsa, by Your grace, those honors that were to arise through the path of light (arcis) as a result of my daily contemplation, dwell this very day within the range of my vision. (1954)
In this state of bondage, there is a description of the direct perception of the future wonders—the honors received on the path beginning with light—which would otherwise be impossible to see.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth section, the Chapter on the Bhāvika, in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on the Udātta:
that is Udātta where a subject matter is described as being possessed of great prosperity.
Or else, something indicative of [the subject] or a praiseworthy character is composed.

The figure of speech *udātta* (the Sublime) occurs where an object endowed with abundant prosperity is described, or where the praiseworthy deeds associated with a great person (*mahāpuruṣa*) are depicted as a defining characteristic—as in the expression "where this field of the crane Devadatta is. A "defining characteristic" (*upalakṣaka*) is that which makes something known. Since *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) and *bhāvika* (the vividly real) consist of the description of things exactly as they are, the first type of *udātta*, which consists of an object superimposed [upon another] by way of contrast to those, finds its proper occasion here.

Among these, the first is *udātta*, characterized by majesty (*aiśvarya*), which consists of the description of an object endowed with inconceivable splendor, brought forth by the poet's imagination. The second, however, is the conduct of great men (*mahāpuruṣa*) of noble deeds, which is presented as a subordinate element to another primary subject; it is so called because the conduct of great men is inherently noble.

O Śauri, those who are glanced upon by Your side-long looks dwell together with their wives amidst clusters of houses that are like groves of emerald creepers adorned with sprouts of ruby-stone and encircled by fences of diamond rock.

This is an illustration of *samṛddhi* (prosperity). Here, the definition is applicable because it describes those who possess inconceivable majesty and have been glanced upon by the Blessed One. However, this is not an ornament when describing one who possesses conceivable majesty.

Just as clouds accompanied by lightning appear beautiful upon a mountain peak, so do your pleasure-houses shine upon the Bull-peak mountain, most lovely with their great blue lattices shimmering with inlaid lines of diamonds. (1956)

For here, such a distinction truly arises from the very nature of the dwelling-houses of the Blessed One, who possesses great majesty; therefore, it has been stated that this [work] originates from the creative intuition (*pratibhā*) of the poet. And thus, its name also is meaningful—so says the author of the *Vimarśinī*.
As an indicator of praiseworthy conduct, for example:
"May that mountain be victorious, where, due to a certain circumstance, the King of Ascetics caused the Lord—who bears the lotus and discus—to lay down his weapons."

The king of ascetics, the venerable Rāmānujācārya, on a certain occasion, when he was about to grant a boon once again to King Toṇḍamān for the sake of victory over his enemies, caused Lord Śrīnivāsa—who had laid down His weapons and relinquished His conch and discus—to take up the conch and discus once more. This was done by means of a request for the Lord to assume them in the form of an icon as a condition for the granting of the boon. This constitutes a double object construction (*dvikarmakatā*), similar to the expression, "Janaka took that bow from him. In this context, [the Lord said]:
"Do not fear, my son; may it be well with you; I give the conch and discus to you."
Go with them to that divine city; they two shall slay your enemies for you.
Having spoken thus, he gave [the kingdom] to him and departed along with those two;
and they, having swiftly slain their enemies, established a kingdom free from all thorns.
Together with the king, they both approached the presence of the god;
then the king, having praised the god with numerous hymns, paid him homage.
"Choose a boon, O blessed one," the god said to the king.
"O Lord, best of gods, [I choose this] for the sake of the renown of my bestowing of weapons."
"Do not wear [the marks] upon the image for worship or the stone image, nor on the discus or the conch";
thus entreated, the Lord did not wear those two again.
And both remained invisible, stationed at the sides of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.

In this context, one should also consider the narrative from the *Brahma Purāṇa* contained within the *Veṅkaṭādri-māhātmya*, concerning how the Lord’s Commentator (Rāmānuja) caused Śrīnivāsa to accept the conch and discus; here, the venerable Veṅkaṭādri serves as a distinguishing mark for the noble life-story of the Great Man, namely Bhagavad Rāmānujācārya, who performed the wearing of the conch and discus by Śrīnivāsa—an act worthy of praise.

Or rather, may that mountain reign victorious, upon which the Father of the World, though the bestower of nectar to all the gods, addressed a certain deity as "Father" and begged for the nectar. || 1958 ||

Śrīnivāsa, the progenitor of the world and the bestower of immortality, nectar, or supreme beatitude upon many wise ones—whether gods or scholars—addressed a certain noble and learned sage named Śrīśailapūrṇa as "Father" and requested from him, who was situated at the very distant Tumburu-tīrtha, the service of fetching holy water (*tīrtha*) every day for his own worship; for the word *vārī* signifies the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Desiring to remove such lifelong exertion through his compassion for that man, the Blessed Lord Śrīnivāsa, wearing the guise of a Śabara and accompanied by Śrī, approached him on the path in that very form and requested the holy water. Believing him to be merely a Śabara, the man did not grant the water being brought as an offering worthy of the Blessed One. When he refused to give the water, the Blessed Lord shattered the water-pot held upon the man’s head and, together with his consort, drank the stream of water flowing from it with his own mouth.

When the Śabara returned, having brought the holy water for the worship of the Lord, he found that it had been defiled; consequently, he discarded all the remaining water right there and set out once again toward Tumburu-tīrtha to fetch more. As he was departing, the Lord, out of compassion, revealed His own divine form and said: "From now on, you need not bring water from Tumburu-tīrtha every day for my worship. This much service is sufficient; I am pleased.
Because he was thus addressed by me as "Father" (*tāta*), he is celebrated as *Tātā*.

Having thus granted the boon, he vanished; such is the traditional account (*aitihya*). Herein, the meaning of the verse-quarter, "Addressing someone as 'Father' in the forest region, being thirsty, he begged for a drop of water," is consistent with this. In this instance as well, the life-story of the Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*) has been described in the manner stated above as an integral part of Śeṣācala.

They say that when the life-story of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣacarita) is composed as the principal element (aṅgin) with the intent of conveying the excellence of the subject matter that serves as its subordinate (aṅga), it constitutes a poetic ornament (alaṃkāra); it is not merely presented as a secondary illustration. Thus:
"The King of Mountains, who possesses two thousand eyes, comes within the range of his vision; therein Guha bestowed the wondrous spear (śakti) that strikes terror into his enemies. (1959)

In such cases as this, there is no figure of speech (alaṃkāra). For here, the conduct of the six mothers is intended merely as a secondary characteristic (upalakṣaṇa), and no excellence whatsoever of the mountain is intended to be expressed by means of it.

May that certain man be victorious, whose bell, having become the preceptor of the Upanishads (the heads of the Vedas), revived the world—fainted by the poison of the speakers of evil doctrines—with the nectar of his speech. 1960.
The bell of that Śrīnivāsa, having become the preceptor of the heads of the Vedas,
terrifies the armies of the enemies of the gods and was employed by the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā) for the service of attendance.
It is imagined by people on earth, through an abundance of reasoning,
that the bell of Hara must have merged into its own essence.

The meaning is: "having descended as the Great Preceptor of the Upanishads (Nigamāntamahādeśika)" according to the manner stated above. The rest is clear. Here, with the desire to set forth the great excellence of Śrīnivāsa, who is the primary subject (aṅgin), the life-story of the Lord Nigamāntadeśika—who is his incarnation—is composed as a subordinate element (aṅga).
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of the Exalted (udātta), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Hyperbole (atyukti):
the description of extraordinary, though unreal, qualities such as heroism and the like is intended as hyperbole.

The poetic figure named *atyukti* (hyperbole) is the description of something marvelous, unreal, or improbable, such as valor and the like; by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), qualities such as magnanimity and fame are included.

O Śrīnātha, by Your most wondrous splendor blazing both externally and internally, the mountain of gold was fashioned within the crucible of the cosmic egg, having been melted by the rays of the sun. 1961.

May that certain man be victorious, whose bell, having become the preceptor of the Upanishads (the heads of the Vedas), revived the world—fainted by the poison of the speakers of evil doctrines—with the nectar of his speech. 1960.
The bell of that Śrīnivāsa, having become the preceptor of the heads of the Vedas,
terrifies the armies of the enemies of the wise and is employed by the Lotus-seated One in the service of attendance.
People on earth, by virtue of their abundant reasoning,
imagine that the bell of Hara must have merged into its own self.

The meaning is that he descended as the Great Preceptor of the Vedānta (Nigamāntamahādeśika) according to the manner described above. The rest is clear. Here, with the desire to proclaim the great excellence of Śrīnivāsa—who is the primary subject—the life of the Lord Nigamāntadeśika, who is his incarnation, is composed as a subordinate element.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of the Exalted (*udātta*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Hyperbole (*atyukti*):
the description of extraordinary, yet unreal, valor and other such qualities is intended as hyperbole.

The poetic figure named *atyukti* (hyperbole) is the description of something marvelous, unreal, or improbable, such as heroism; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), qualities like magnanimity and fame are included.
O Śrīnātha, by your most wondrous splendor blazing both within and without, the mountain of gold was fashioned from the crucible of the cosmic egg, having been melted by the rays of the sun.

O Śrīnātha! The sense is that [this fire] is distinct from even the well-known fire, which, though blazing externally and internally with great wonder, performs merely the act of melting particles of gold dust placed within a crucible (*mūṣā*). This is because [your fire] possesses the dual capacity—described below—to both liquefy and solidify the rays of the sun. By "your splendor" (*tejas*), the meaning is by your majesty acting as fire. A "crucible" (*mūṣā*) is indeed a *mūṣikā*, a vessel for melting metallic substances; as Amara states: "A crucible is a metallic melting-pot. (*Taijasāvartanī mūṣā*).

In that [direction], the "light" (ruci) of the sun—the singular number being used with the intention of denoting the genus—means the rays. Having been whirled around and dissolved, the Golden Mountain was fashioned. The sense is that the very rays of the Sun, having been whirled about, were produced as Mount Sumeru through the process of solidification.
Or rather,
by your prowess blazing all around for the sake of creating another cosmic egg, the Golden Mountain is being whirled within this crucible of the world-egg.

For the sake of creating another world-egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)—of the kind described in the passage, "That egg became golden, with a splendor equal to the thousand-rayed sun"—the dative case is used according to the rule *kriyārtha* (Pāṇini 2.3.14). By your blazing majesty on all sides, while this [world] exists, the very shell of the universe (*jagadaṇḍa*) acts as a crucible (*mūṣikā*), and within it the Golden Mountain (*hemādri*) is being revolved and melted.
By the statement that the Golden Mountain is being liquefied within the crucible of the world-egg, the nature of your majesty as fire is understood.

O Sun of the Kakutstha dynasty, by the light of your warriors, which radiates all around beyond the three-quarters of your manifestation, that splendor was constantly fashioned, surpassing the brilliance of the sun and fire.

By the splendor and majesty of Your warriors—Sugrīva, Hanumān, and the others—who flash and blaze all around beyond the eternal manifestation known as the "Three-Footed" (as heard in the Śruti: "Three-quarters of Him are immortality in heaven"), that Three-Footed manifestation was fashioned with a radiance surpassing the sun and fire;
there, beyond the abode of Brahmā, shines His supreme station, that divine realm of light which the gods themselves do not behold.

"That abode of the high-souled Viṣṇu blazes more intensely than the sun and fire"—this authoritative statement is to be considered here. This is an instance of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) regarding valor.
An example of excessive hyperbole (*audāryātyukti*) is as follows:

"The Goddess Śrī herself, having seen that men give boundless wealth obtained through her own side-long glances, comes to their houses of her own accord as a petitioner and does not depart from there. (1964)

In this context, by the statement that even Śrī herself comes to the houses of those who have attained wealth through her own sidelong glances and does not depart from there, there is an exaggeration (atiśayokti) of the generosity of her devotees; furthermore, by the phrase "does not depart from there," the inexhaustibility of the prosperity of her devotees is suggested.

O Mother, according to the degree of their need, men whose prosperity has been uplifted by you go to the gatekeeper; if a beggar goes there, let him go, for even the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) goes there to beg.

"Even Kubera goes to the doors of those people who have acquired wealth through your side-glance for the sake of alms"—this is an exaggeration of his magnanimity; yet another meaning is also perceived: "The Great Lord (Maheśvara) has become a beggar."
An example of hyperbolic praise (*kīrtyatyukti*) is as follows:

"Agitated by the waves of the ocean of fame belonging to the multitude of people who have taken refuge in you, the clusters of cosmic-egg-pumpkins are tossed about, repeatedly sinking and surfacing. (1966)

This is *atyukti* (hyperbole). If it is asked, "What is the distinction between this and *atiśayokti* (poetic exaggeration)?"—know that the difference is this: in *atiśayokti*, there is merely the statement of what is unreal; whereas in *atyukti*, because of the qualifying term "marvelous" (*adbhuta*) applied to the untrue, it is the statement of what is absolutely unreal. For this very reason, Daṇḍin [wrote]:
"O lady of faultless limbs, as these two breasts of yours expand, there is not enough space within the interval of your vine-like arms."
Thus, this very thing, when refined by the narration of particulars,
becomes lovely to everyone who follows the course of worldly life.

Thus, having stated that the description of the extreme fullness of the breasts is already established in the world, and that it becomes lovely and beautiful precisely through such a statement of specific qualities— that is, through being adorned by an expression of excellence—
it is intended that the subject be superimposed as if transcending the world.
By means of that [superimposition], the discerning are exceedingly satisfied, but other people are not.
Having said this, [the sage continued]:
"This orb of your breasts was fashioned by the Creator with very little space, without even considering that such a thing as this would come to pass."
"This is illogical"—this has been stated as "the Gauḍa-endearing" (gauḍopalālitam).
Thus, the distinction from hyperbole (atiśayokti) is shown through the term "exaggeration" (atyukti).

Now, one might ask: what is the difference between the figure of speech *udātta* and *atyukti*? For there appears to be no distinction, since in the previously cited example of *udātta*, such as "the moat of diamond-stones" (*vajraśilāvāla*), there is likewise a description of an unimaginable abundance that lies solely within the domain of a poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*). To this, they reply: "The [distinction lies in] the attainment..."

"Exaggeration (*udātta*) consists in the overstatement of excellence, while *atyukti* (hyperbole) consists in the overstatement of valor. Others, however, having defined the figure *udātta* as "the description of an impossible object that lies solely within the domain of a poet's most wonderful creative intuition," argue that *atyukti* need not be defined separately; for since there is no evidence for a distinction between such descriptions of excellence, valor, nobility, and so forth, and the various types of hyperbole (*atyukti*) based on such excellence, valor, nobility, and so forth, they are not distinct.
Vaidyanātha, however, described the intention of the Dīkṣitas as being that the difference between these two lies in their being either factual or non-factual.
Thus ends the hundredth chapter, the Chapter on Hyperbole (Atyukti), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Etymological Interpretation (Nirukti):
Nirukti is the conceptualization of a different meaning for a name based upon its etymological derivation (yoga).

Nirukti is the poetic figure consisting of the description of a different meaning for a name that, by virtue of its etymological derivation (*yoga*), denotes a specific meaning. Although this was not defined as an *alaṃkāra* by the ancients, it is nonetheless described as such in the third chapter of Jayadeva’s *Candrāloka*:
"Nirukti is the etymological explanation of a name; it may be true or false. Through such deeds, I know you to be truly the 'Maker of Night' (*doṣākara*)."

Thus, that which was established as *nirukti* (etymological definition) by being presented as a characteristic of poetry (*kāvyalakṣaṇa*) has been categorized by Dīkṣitas as a figure of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*) with some degree of distinction; accordingly, we too have defined this as an ornament. While the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) provided here is true in accordance with the established usage of the name, the etymological derivation [of others] has been imagined otherwise [and is therefore false].

O Lord of the World, just as you afflict these people like one who is merciless in the endless forest of worldly existence, it is true here that you are indeed Janārdana; what doubt can there be in this? (1967)

"Exaggeration (*udātta*) consists in the overstatement of excellence, while *atyukti* (hyperbole) consists in the overstatement of heroism. Others, however, having defined the figure *udātta* as "the description of an improbable matter that falls solely within the domain of a poet’s most wonderful creative intuition," argue that *atyukti* need not be defined separately; for since such descriptions of excellence, heroism, nobility, and so forth occur in various ways through the attainment of wealth, valor, magnanimity, etc., there is no evidence for a distinction between them.
Vaidyanātha, on the other hand, described the intention of the Dīkṣitas as being that the difference between these two lies in their being either factual or non-factual.
Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, the Chapter on Hyperbole (Atyukti), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Etymological Interpretation (Nirukti):
Nirukti is the conceptualization of a different meaning for a name based upon its etymological derivation.

Nirukti is the poetic figure consisting of the description of a different meaning for a name that, by virtue of its etymological application (*yoga*), denotes a specific sense. Although this was not defined as a poetic figure by the ancients, it is nevertheless described as such in the third chapter of Jayadeva’s *Candrāloka*:
"Nirukti is the etymological derivation of a name, whether true or false;
I know you to be truly the 'maker of faults' (*doṣākara*) because of such deeds."

Thus, that which was established as a definition of poetry (*kāvyalakṣaṇa*)—namely, *nirukti* itself—was categorized by Dīkṣitas as a figure of sense (*arthālaṃkāra*) with a slight modification; following their lead, we too have defined this ornament accordingly. While the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) provided here is indeed true in accordance with the established usage of the name, the etymological derivation [offered by others] has been conceived otherwise and is therefore false.

O Lord of the World, just as you afflict these people like one who is merciless in the endless forest of worldly existence, it is true here that you are Janārdana; what doubt can there be in this? (1967)

In this context, there is the conceptualization of another meaning for the name *Janārdana*—which is etymologically derived as "he who is entreated by people (*jana*) for all human goals (*puruṣārtha*)"—through its application according to the method described above.
O Daughter of the Ocean of Nectar, because the interior of Your speech is exceedingly clear and sweet, sugar (sitā) became white by that very quality; thus it is said that "it is sugar" (sita). 1968.

O daughter of the ocean of nectar! This [verse] intends to follow those very qualities that were desired even within the essence of speech. By that very quality—the essence of your words characterized by the aforementioned attributes—sugar (*śarkarā*) was made white (*sitā*); it was bound with a rope (*rajjvā*), acting as the instrument, for the purpose of punishing transgressions in accordance with their merit. But in the ultimate sense, by that very quality—namely, clarity and sweetness—it is "white" (*viśadā*) and "bound" (*baddhā*). [The root] *ṣiñ* means "to bind"; the suffix *kta* is used in the passive sense, meaning "well-bound."

The sense is that it is precisely because of its theft from the foremost of the goddesses (Śrī Vāgīśvarī), who is distinguished by the aforementioned attributes, that sugar attains its clarity and sweetness. For this very reason—because it was thus bound—it was called "sitā" (white/bound) and sung of as such by lexicographers in the statement, "sugar is sitā. Here, the word "sitā," which is a name for sugar, is derived through etymological reasoning (*yogataḥ*) to produce a different meaning [from its conventional one].
O Lord, that which served as a place of rest for the moon as it entered by way of its path is called the *candraśālā*, the turret atop your residence. (1969)
In this case, the interpretation of the name "Candraśālā" through its etymological derivation (*yoga*) results in a different meaning than its literal sense.
Or rather: O Hari, since your insight is so skillful in manifesting the names and forms of the universe, I know you to be the Lord of Śeṣaśaila, truly denoted by the word "Sat" (Being).

O you whose insight (*prekṣā*)—for *prekṣā* means wisdom (*prajñā*), according to Amara’s lexicon where it says "prekṣā, upalabdhi, cit, and saṃvit"—is preeminent; or, in the alternative sense, [O you] in whom there is excellent vision (*prakṛṣṭā īkṣā*), that is, the resolve stated in such passages as "It thought: May I become many," and who are most proficient in that grammar—the system of words—in which all names (*nāman*), meaning nominal stems (this being an illustration for verbal roots as well), and their forms (*rūpa*), that is, their essential natures, exist as the manifold names and forms (*viśvāni nāmarūpāṇi*).

Elsewhere, she is preeminent in the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) of the entire universe consisting of the sentient and insentient, and in the creation of the diverse worlds such as the gods and the assignment of their respective names. Therefore—because of her intellect being so exceedingly skillful in the method of such differentiation, or (in your case) because of your possessing such a resolve—the one denoted by the word *sat* is he who is called "the wise one" (*san vidvān*), as Amarasimha states: "The wise man is *sat*."
