In this context, regarding the phrase "Being alone, my dear," the word *sat* (Being) refers to the Supreme Self by taking as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) existence characterized by fitness for connection with the means of valid cognition. "On your mountain" means on the speech—namely, the *Mahābhāṣya*—of the Lord Ananta, who has descended as Patañjali, the protector of the world. "The Lord" means the capable one, one who is proficient in the study, understanding, and propagation of that [work]; the locative case is used according to the rule beginning with "the master, the lord, the ruler."

The construction is as follows: "In truth" means in a manner that is certain; "elsewhere," I recognize You, the Lord of Śeṣagiri, the Lord of Veṅkaṭādri, as the Truth—the Supreme Brahman described as "Truth and Knowledge. Here, by the method stated, another meaning for the term *Śeṣagirīśvara* is conceived through its etymological derivation (*yoga*).
O jewel among women with lotus-like eyes, I believe that the fish was deprived of its essence by the luster of your eyes; therefore, the wise call it *visāra* (the "devoid-of-essence"). 1971.
By your lotus-eye, with its white, brilliant, and dark luster, the fish here had its essence destroyed; therefore, people on earth spoke of it as the "dispersion" (*visāra*) of that [lotus]. 1972.

These two verses, which convey the same meaning, have as their sole essence the demonstration of a variety in their sequential order. Regarding the term *visāra*, Amara states in his list of synonyms for fish that it means "a small fish" (*śakulī*). Here, however, by means of the etymological derivation (*yoga*) of the word *mīna* (fish) from the aforementioned method, another meaning is imagined.

Just as a cloud, desiring to conceal its own radiance, was likely struck upon the cheek by Hari, so too do its teeth fall away under the guise of hailstones; therefore, they call this cloud "A-mu" (the toothless one).
The construction of another meaning by demonstrating the etymological derivation (*yoga*) of the word *nīrada* as "one whose teeth (*rada*) have fallen out."
Or rather,
O Acyuta, since the earth has been purified by your very fame, the celestial river, knowing the futility of its own birth, has become known by the meaningful name Mandākinī.

“Mandā” means unfortunate, lazy, or inactive; “akīnī” means suffering; and according to the *Viśva* lexicon, “akaṃ” means both suffering and sin. Here, by means of the etymological derivation (*yoga*) of the name Mandākinī, another meaning is conceived.

O Nṛhari, just as the tree of heaven (Svaru), having been surpassed by you with your magnificent jewel, became [the sacrificial wood] Svaru, so too, desiring to conquer you, it was split by your claws and thus acquired its name according to its literal meaning (*anvartha-abhidha*).

The celestial tree (Svastaru), that wish-fulfilling branch, was surpassed by you with your noble jewel; it was cast down by your magnanimity. Thereupon, in order to exact revenge, it became a thunderbolt (dambholi) and turned into a sacrificial stake (svaru).

According to Amara, *svaru* means "a hundred-fold peak" (*śatakoṭi*) or "a thunderbolt" (*śamba*). Desiring to conquer you, he was split and torn by your claws; therefore, he became known by a name true to its meaning (*anvarthābhidha*), for his *aru*—his wound—was excellent (*suṣṭhu*), thus he was called *Svaru*, signifying a "severe wound" (*balavadvraṇa*). According to Amara, "wound" (*vraṇa*) is synonymous with *īrma* and *aru*. The address "O Nṛhari" (Man-lion) contains the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) regarding the extreme sharpness of the tips of your claws, which are capable of splitting even a thunderbolt (*dambholi*).

Here, the term *svastaru*—that is, one whose phonemes are *sa*, *va*, *ra*, *sta*, *ru*, *śa*, *pa*, *rā*, *sta*, *taḥ*, *parā*, *kṛ*, *taḥ*, *staḥ*, *staḥ*—is thus described. Consequently, the further sense that he became a *svaru* (wooden sacrificial chip) by becoming the word *svaru* according to the aforementioned method is also highly striking. In this instance, the imaginative construction of another meaning for the name *svaru* through its etymological derivation (*yoga*) is a blend with the figure of speech *viṣama* (the incongruous).
Just as gold that is shaken from afar by the weight of its own glorious luster and slightly distressed by the wind is called "Kārtasvara" by poets—this is known by us. || 1976 ||

It cried out; it uttered a sound that was slightly pained or distressed (*kārta*). In this way, the term is explained, for by the rule "īṣadarthe," the substitute *kā* is applied to *ku*. Here, a different meaning is conceived through the etymological derivation (*yoga*) of the name *Kārtasvara*.

Or rather, as she went with her brother to the heart of Hari, the ocean—which was her birthplace—was surely sealed by Lakṣmī; that is why they call it the "Jagat-samudra" (the world-ocean). || 1977 ||

The departure from the birth-house together with his brother Kaustubha and the ocean’s status as a mine of jewels (*ratnākara*) indicate the necessity of sealing [the text]. Here, a different meaning is conceived through the etymological derivation (*yoga*) of the name *samudra*. The word *samudra* is derived from the root *undī* (meaning "to moisten") with the prefix *sam*, formed by the addition of the suffix *rak* according to the rule *sphāyitañci* etc. It has been explained by some as "one in which excellent *udras* (a species of aquatic creature) exist. Through that etymology, another meaning is conceived.
Just as Hari seized the rays of the moon—who desired to surpass the luster of his own face—so too is he known for his pure hands; otherwise, how could he possess such stainless hands?

The true meaning is that *karān* refers to hands and rays (*kiraṇān*). He "cut" (*avadāyiṣṭa*) or "severed" (*kṛṇatti sma*) them; this is derived from the root *do* in the sense of "cutting," belonging to the *divādi* class, used here in the active voice (*kartari*) with the present tense suffix (*laṭ*). Otherwise, in the absence of such cutting of the hands—that is, by virtue of having pure hands, being free from the fault of seizing the property of others, and having clean hands—it implies having bright rays; such is the actual state of affairs. This person is known for his "pure-handedness"—meaning either having severed hands or having white rays; such is the ultimate reality. According to Amara: "Cut (*kṛtta*), sliced (*dāta*), divided (*dita*), and severed (*chita*)."

The suffix *kta* is applied to the root *dyati* in the sense of the object (*karman*). By the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti*, there is the substitution of *ā*. The rest is clear. Here, regarding the name "avadātakara" (the one with white rays), which possesses as its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) the state of having white rays, there is a description of another meaning through etymological derivation (*yoga*) according to the method stated above.

Just as Indra, wishing to steal the beauty of his own gentle smile, extends his rays toward the moon, Hari instantly cut them down; therefore, the moon is renowned as "Sita-kara" (the one with white rays).

*asinaut abadhnāt*, from the root *ṣiñ* in the sense of "binding," in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense. *Sitakaraḥ* means "one whose hands are bound. Here, by the aforementioned method, a different meaning is produced for the name *sitakaraḥ* through its etymological derivation (*yoga*).
O Mother,
by your splendor, which illuminates the ten directions like hundreds of lamps, the lightning— its own radiance eclipsed— has truly acquired its name "Vidyut" (the one whose light is destroyed).

The word *vidyut* is derived from the root *dyut* with the suffix *kvip* due to its inclusion in the *dyut-saṃpad-ādi* group; thus, *vidyut* means "that which has lost its luster," i.e., "lusterless. Alternatively, it is derived from the root *dyut* in the sense of "shining" (*dyuta dīptau*) with the suffix *kvip* in the active sense according to the rule "bhujabhāsa-ādi"; thus, *vidyut* means "that which shines intensely. As the *Medinīkośa* states: "In the feminine, *vidyut* refers to lightning or twilight; in the masculine/feminine/neuter, it means 'lusterless'. The rest is clear. Here, a different meaning is conceived for the name *vidyut* through its etymological derivation (*yoga*).

Just as a serpent, O Acyuta, though challenged to fight with your two arms from which Rāhu has been cast out, did not venture forth; therefore those who know the true nature of things call that [arm] a "nāga" (serpent). 1981.
In this case, based on the etymological derivation (*yoga*) that "he does not come" (*na āgacchati*), another meaning has been postulated for the name "Nāga."
O Mother, because he struck at your feet and, shedding blood from his head, vanished from the world, he became known as Lohitaka; thus, this ruby is indeed that very [blood]. (1982)

O Mother! Because his head was struck—that is, hit by Your foot—for the purpose of removing the luster from Your feet, he, shedding—that is, vomiting—blood from his head, became hidden from the world, having gone into concealment within the world.

The sense is that, due to the humiliation caused by his head bleeding from the blow of your foot, he was so ashamed that he could not show his face to anyone and has hidden himself away somewhere. Therefore, it follows that this ruby—*padmarāga*, *lohitaka*—was so called because he was "red-headed" (*lohitaṃ rudhiraṃ ke śirasi yasya sa tathoktaḥ*), meaning one whose head was red with blood; such was his name.

In ultimate reality, however, that [name] is so called because within—that is, between—the two syllables of the word *loka* (the letters *la* and *ka*), there are the sounds *hi* and *ta*. There is an identity (*tādātmya*) between the word and its meaning. *Lohitaka* is simply *lohita*; it is its name, formed by the suffix *kan* in the sense of the base itself according to the rule "after *lohita*, when referring to a gem" (*lohitān maṇau*). Amara states: "The red jewel is *lohitaka*. Here, the fact that the name *lohitaka*, which was established through the suffix *kan* in its own primary sense, is conceived as having a different meaning through a different etymological derivation (*yogāntara*) constitutes a distinct aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), which is quite evident.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, the Chapter on Etymology (*nirukti*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Chapter on Negation (*pratiṣedha*):
negation is the description of a negation that has been perceived.

That well-known restatement of a negation—which, because it is already known, is by itself useless, yet attains beauty by implying another meaning—is the figure of speech called *pratiṣedha* (negation).

O Lord of Ramā, Your devotees have been made cool by Your own incomparable compassion, in a way that neither the moon, nor nectar, nor the Malaya breeze, nor even the snow-capped mountain can achieve. (1983)

In this context, the fact that the devotees of the Lord were not created from the Moon and others is already well known; yet, as it is being proclaimed here, the sense is that because they surpassed even the Moon and others in coolness, and because they were so humiliated by having their heads bleed from the blow of Your foot, they were ashamed to show their faces to anyone and hid themselves away somewhere. Therefore, "this" refers to the ruby (*padmarāga*), the red gem; it follows that he was "lohitaka. *Lohitaka* means one whose head (*ke*) has blood (*lohita*)—that is, one with that name. He was [the Moon] so called.

In ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), however, that [name] is so called because between the two syllables *lo* and *ka*—that is, in the middle—is placed the syllable *hi*, consisting of the sounds *h* and *i*. There is an identity (*tādātmya*) between the word and its meaning: *lohita* itself is *lohitaka*; this is its name, formed by the addition of the suffix *kan* in the sense of the base itself according to the rule "after *lohita*, when referring to a gem" (*lohitan maṇau*). Amara states: "A red jewel is *lohitaka*. Here, the fact that the name *lohitaka*, which was established through the suffix *kan* in its own primary sense, is conceived as having a different meaning through another etymological derivation (*yogāntara*) constitutes a distinct aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), which is quite evident.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, the Chapter on Etymology (Niruktisara), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Chapter on Negation (Pratiṣedhasara):
negation is the description of a negation that has been perceived.

That well-known restatement of a negation (*niṣedhānuvāda*) which, being already known and thus inherently useless by itself, acquires beauty by implying another meaning, is the figure of speech called *pratiṣedha* (negation).

O Lord of Rama, Your devotees have been made cool by nothing other than Your own incomparable compassion—neither by the moon, nor by nectar, nor by the Malaya breeze, nor even by the bearer of snow. (1983)
In this context, the well-known absence of being created by the moon and others among the devotees of the Blessed One,

when being celebrated, clarifies the meaning that their coolness (*śaiśirya*) surpasses even that of the moon and such; and this is revealed by the qualifying epithet "cool with incomparable compassion," which demonstrates their distinction from the moon and others who possess only limited coolness.
Or rather: "O Śauri, these senses of mine are as difficult to subdue as Arjuna’s horses; behold them, O Lord, and restrain them if they run only along the wrong path. (1984)

"Arjuna’s chariot-horses" refers to the horses that pull the chariot. "If the master is capable, yet they run off course"—the construction is: "restrain these senses; let us see you restrain them. Here, the fact that the speaker's senses lack the status of being Arjuna’s chariot-horses is well known; its mention serves to reveal their difficult-to-restrain nature and the impossibility of controlling them. And this is brought to light by the poet himself through the power of the epithets such as "difficult to tame" (*durdāntāni*).

Just as neither the ten-faced Rāvaṇa nor Vālī were difficult for me to overcome, so too this multitude of my faults is hard to assail; O Lord, how can you be a great archer without piercing these? 1985.

Here too, the absence of the multitude of faults in the speaker—such as having ten faces and so forth—is indeed perceived; being thus proclaimed, it manifests his invincibility, which is further revealed by the very expression "he who is difficult to overcome" (*sudurādharṣa*).
"This is neither milk nor curd, nor cream, nor even butter from the daughter of Nanda; alas, what is this of Hari?"—this bitter distaste in my mind must be cast away. (1986)

The construction is as follows: "What is this? means "What object is this?"—[the answer being] "It is from Hari. The "astringent of the mind" (*manasaḥ kaṣāyam*) refers to the latent impressions of passion and so forth, and also to a decoction prepared from well-known substances like neem; as Amara states: "The word *kaṣāya* is masculine [only] when referring to a decoction, and neuter when referring to an extract. Here, the speaker intends a sarcasm: while the absence of milkiness and such qualities in the astringent of his own mind is well known, you show your preference for taking away the most delicious milk and the like, rather than for removing our most loathsome mental astringency.
And that [feeling] is manifested by the two qualifiers "extremely bitter" and "to be abandoned," as well as by the substantive "bitterness."
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, the Chapter on Prohibition (*pratiṣedhasara*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Prescription (*vidhisara*):
that is the figure of speech called Prescription (*vidhyalaṃkṛti*) wherein something already established is prescribed.

That which is a prescription of what is already known, yet not contradicted by its lack of utility, becomes more beautiful by containing another meaning within it—that is the ornament named *vidhi*. As they say:
"When there is a prescription of a matter already known, which is devoid of utility, yet possesses elegance by containing another intention within it..."
Those who have thoroughly studied the science of literature call this the figure of speech known as *vidhi* (prescription). Thus [it is said].

O Blessed One, I shall speak the truth as it is: You are the Lord, and the individual soul (jīva) is indeed the individual soul, O Hari. O Protector of the World, what intelligent person would consider the Lord of the Universe and His servant to be non-different? 1987.
Fresh butter! Alas, what is this of Hari? This bitter mental impurity of mine must be utterly abandoned. (1986)

The construction is as follows: "What is this? means "What object is this? [and the answer is] "It is Hari. The term *kaṣāya* refers to the impurity of the mind, that is, the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) such as passion (*rāga*), and also to a decoction prepared from well-known substances like neem; as Amara states: "The word *kaṣāya* is used for astringent extract (*niryāsa*) as well, and is not feminine. Here, the speaker intends a sarcasm: while the absence of milk and other qualities in the impurity of the speaker’s mind is well known, you show your preference only for taking away delicious milk and the like, and not for removing our most loathsome mental impurities.
And that [feeling] is manifested by the two qualifiers "extremely bitter" and "to be abandoned," as well as by the substantive "bitterness."
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, the Chapter on Prohibition (*pratiṣedhasara*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Prescription (*vidhisara*):
that is the figure of speech called Prescription (*vidhyalaṅkāra*) wherein something already established is prescribed.

That which is an injunction whose method is already known, yet which—though sublated by its lack of utility—is made more beautiful by containing another meaning within it, is the figure of speech called *vidhi*. As they say: "When there is an injunction of a matter already known, which is devoid of utility, yet possesses aesthetic charm by containing another underlying intention..."
Those who have thoroughly studied literary aesthetics call this the figure of speech known as *vidhi* (prescription). Thus [it is said].

O Blessed One, I shall speak the truth as it is: You are the Lord, and the individual soul is indeed the individual soul, O Hari. O Protector of the World, what intelligent person would consider the Lord of the Universe and His servant to be non-different? (1987)

In this context, the prescription of the Supreme Self as the Supreme Self and the individual self as the individual self—being sublated by its own lack of utility—implies their absolute difference in nature due to such attributes as His being the Lord of all and the other’s being subordinate to Him, His omniscience, and so forth. This is made manifest by the second half of the verse beginning with "He is the Lord of the universe," and so on.
Or as it is said:
"From this day forward, indeed, you are truly you and we are truly we; you are subject to the senses, while we are solely obedient to the Blessed Lord. (1988)

In this context, the formulation "you" and "we"—specifically the repeated use of "you" and "we"—is inappropriate; it implies, by way of implication (*arthāntaranyāsa*), a mutual incompatibility characterized by the inability to harmonize, such as being servants of the senses versus being the sole servants of the Lord. This is made manifest by the second half of the verse:
"From this day forward, O people, 'you' are you and 'we' are we;
there is no longer any association between us and you."
You are devoted to wealth and pleasure, while we are devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
we are the servants of Viṣṇu, whereas you are the servants of the senses.
This is what should be reflected upon:
"O Blessed One, whatever bond has been created for a living being by you through merit and demerit—whether it be favorable or even unfavorable—that is indeed nothing but a bond. (1989)

O Blessed One! Regarding the binding—that is, the bondage—of a living being (*jantu*) or creature (*prāṇin*) caused by merit and demerit, or by good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta-karman*), which has been performed by You: whether that binding be favorable, producing worldly and otherworldly happiness as the fruit of merit; or unfavorable, producing the three types of suffering, hell, and so forth, as the fruit of sin—it is indeed merely a binding, regardless of how it is. For even a shackle made of gold does not fail to serve as a bond; the notion that only an iron one is a binder is neither seen nor heard. This is the intended meaning.

The meaning is that the word *nahanam* (binding), whether read in its natural order (*anuloma*) as "the binding" or read in reverse order (*pratiloma*) as "nahanam," results in the same form, *nahanam*, in both cases. Here, the prescription of the "binding-ness" of the binding—which is otherwise untenable—implies that it acts as an obstacle to the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). And this [obstructiveness] is revealed by the qualification of being produced by merit and demerit (*puṇya-apuṇya-karaṇakatva*).

"Then the wise one, having shaken off both merit and demerit, being stainless, attains supreme equality"—by such scriptural passages, it is indeed taught that the attainment of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) occurs immediately after the shaking off of merit and demerit. Alternatively, the injunction regarding the binding with those [fetters] implies that they are difficult to release by anyone other than the Blessed One. "In the past, these beings were bound by the Supreme One through His supreme meditative absorption (*samādhi*);
by Him alone are they to be released; no one else is capable of releasing them."

Thus, on the basis of this authority, such passages as "And his karmans perish when that which is both high and low is seen" are also favorable to this view. Although in these examples of injunctions and prohibitions there exists a suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha) characterized by the transference of the literal sense (arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya), they do not receive the designation of *dhvani* (suggestive poetry); for those suggested meanings are disclosed by the author's own statement: "Incomparably compassionate and cool, [I am] the Lord of the World and His servant."

If it is argued that since injunction and prohibition were previously mentioned as sub-varieties of the figure *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), it is not appropriate to enumerate them as separate figures of speech, we reply: it was previously stated that those two constitute varieties of *ākṣepa* when they are sublated; however, let it be understood here that they function as figures of speech when they are established.
Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, the "String of Rules," in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.

The sense is this: whether it causes the suffering of the threefold afflictions, hell, and so forth, or not, a bond is indeed a bond, regardless of its nature. For even a shackle made of gold does not fail to serve as a restraint; it is neither seen nor heard that only an iron one is a binder.

The meaning is that in the case of the word *nahanam* (binding), whether it is recited in its natural order (*anuloma*) as "nahanam" or in its reverse order (*pratiloma*) as "nahanam," it results in the same form, "nahanam," in both instances. Here, the prescription of "binding-ness" for what is already a binding is logically untenable; this implies its nature as an obstacle to the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). And that [obstructive nature] is further illuminated by the qualification that it is brought about by merit and demerit (*puṇya-apuṇya*).

"Then the wise one, having shaken off both merit and demerit, being stainless, attains supreme equality"—by such scriptural passages as these, it is indeed taught that the attainment of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) occurs immediately after the shaking off of merit and demerit. Alternatively, the injunction regarding the binding of those [souls] implies their difficulty of liberation by anyone other than the Blessed Lord. "The bound souls were previously bound by the Supreme One through His supreme meditative power (*samādhi*);
they must be liberated by Him alone; no other is capable of liberating them."

On the basis of such authority, passages such as "And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen" are also favorable to this view. Although these examples of injunctions and prohibitions contain suggested meanings (*vyaṅgyārtha*) characterized by the transference of the expressed sense (*saṃkramitavācya-lakṣaṇa*), they do not receive the designation of *dhvani* (suggestive poetry), because those suggested meanings are disclosed by the author's own statement: "O Lord of the World, you who are cool with incomparable compassion, [you and] your servant."

If it is argued that since injunction (*vidhi*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) were previously mentioned as sub-varieties of the figure *ākṣepa*, it is not appropriate to enumerate them as separate figures, we reply: it was previously stated that those two constitute varieties of *ākṣepa* when they are sublated; however, in this context, let it be understood that they function as figures when they are established.
Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, the Chapter on Prescriptive Rules (vidhisara), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Chapter on Causes (hetusara):
When a cause is stated together with its effect, it is called *hetu* (the figure of speech "Cause").

The meaning is that the description of an effect together with its cause is the figure of speech called *hetu*. This was treated by Jayadeva in the third chapter (*mayūkha*) of his *Candrāloka* as a definition of poetry under the name "Effect" (*kārya*). For example:
"If there is the attainment of a result from an activity, whether in reality or otherwise—this cool-rayed moon rises for the sake of shattering the pride of fair-browed women."
Thus it is said; however, this too has been included among the figures of speech (alaṃkāras) by the initiated [authorities] on account of its marvelousness.
Just as your incarnation into the world is for its protection, of this there is no doubt; yet, O Lord of Ramā, my doubt is this: why do you delay in protecting me? (1990)
Here, there is a simultaneous description of both the cause and the effect—namely, the protection of the world and the descent [of the Lord].

Just as an emerald upon the crest of a serpent, having attained a certain divine splendor, exerts itself greatly to make the world free from the mud [of impurity] by acting as a clearing nut (*katakaphala*). (1991)

On the crest of the serpent-king (the mountain), that which is somehow transcendent—that is, the emerald (gārutmata)—assumes the state of a *kataka* fruit (the clearing nut). This means it assumes the status of the supreme among gods (*amarādyatā*), namely the state of being the Abode of Śrī (*śrīnivāsatva*). It bears the nature of the *kataka*, the fruit of a specific tree that clarifies turbid water, such that the world (*bhuvana*)—both the universe and the water—is rendered with its mud and impurity cast down and surpassed. Oh, what a marvel! That the emerald, having attained the status of the Abode of Śrī, should assume the nature of the *kataka* fruit.

Regarding the word *marakataka* (emerald): the state of being "not preceded by *mara*" (*amarādya*) refers to that which does not have the letters *ma* and *ra* as its initial syllables (*ādyau varṇau*). Having attained that state—namely, the condition of being *amarādya*—the word *marakataka* assumes the nature of *kataka* (myrobalan). This is because, upon the removal of the initial *ma* and *ra*, the form *kataka* is produced; this further meaning is strikingly beautiful.

Here, the description of the cause—the assumption of the nature of *kataka*—is presented alongside its effect—the sinking of the world’s mud—based on a pun (*śleṣa*), which is reinforced by an apparent contradiction (*virodha*).

O Blessed One, just as one who has attained the state of being a virtuous lamp through the consecration of a glorious kingdom shines forth to dispel darkness, so does your own great lamp of the Ākula lineage shine brilliantly to dispel the gloom.

"O Blessed One, he is one who abides in auspiciousness (*śubha*), or who causes auspiciousness to proceed; thus he is a *śubhavartī*. His state is *śubhavartitva*. In the alternative sense, it is the state of one whose wick (*varti*) or condition (*daśā*) is auspicious. According to the *Ratnamālā*: 'Wick (*varti*) refers to the wick of a lamp, anointing the body, or the polishing of a gem. He has attained great splendor (*suśrī*) through the royal consecration (*rājyābhiṣeka*). In the compound *suśrīrājya*, the *repha* is elided by the rule *ro ri*, and a long vowel is substituted by the rule *ḍhralope*. In the alternative sense, the word division is: 'one of great luster (*sumahāḥ*) due to the consecration with clarified butter (*ājyābhiṣeka*), the family lamp. Here, *mahaḥ* means a beautiful festival (*utsava*)."

He who possesses that [state] is so described; according to the expression "let there be a constant festival for them," he is one characterized by uninterrupted festivities, or one of great splendor. Amara states in his lexicon of various meanings ending in -as: "mahaḥ" [means] both "festival" and "splendor. He is the lamp of his lineage (*kuladīpaḥ*), illuminating his own family. He is yours (*bhavadīyaḥ*), a man (*nā* = *pumān*). In the alternative sense, he is yours, and he is both very great (*sumahān*) and an undisturbed, imperishable lamp (*anākuladīpaḥ*).

The meaning is "a lamp. It shines for the purpose of dispelling—that is, for the removal of—darkness, both as the quality of *tamas* and as physical gloom. Here, within a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) concerning both the relevant (the devotee) and the irrelevant (the lamp), there is a simultaneous description of the cause—the light of the Lord’s devotee and the light of that great lamp—and the effect, which is the dispelling of darkness.

O lotus-eyed one, he by whom you have been placed within his sight—having been proclaimed as one who possesses the application of divine collyrium—is indeed able to perceive even a hidden matter. 1993.

He who bears celestial collyrium is called Añjanādri; the state of being such is "tattā," by which [state he is so designated]. In the alternative sense, *divyam* means praiseworthy; that which is *añjanam* (collyrium) is its *dhārā*, meaning a *vartiḥ* (ointment-stick), specifically a line of eye-collyrium. The state of being such is "tattā," by which [it is so designated]. According to the *Viśva* and *Medinī* lexicons: "*Vartiḥ* refers to the preparation of medicine and a line of eye-collyrium. You are renowned by which wise person (*sudṛk*)—one who possesses clear vision—[you] were placed in his sight, that is, seen; thus, that wise person is a *jñānī* (knower).

The meaning is that [the eye] possesses a vision capable of directly perceiving objects that are otherwise beyond the senses. Indeed, it is able to know—that is, to perceive—even a hidden object, which is the true meaning of the scripture (śāstra-tattvārtha), and in the secondary sense, a treasure (nidhi) in the form of wealth. Here, there is a simultaneous description of the cause and its effect—the perception of Śrīnivāsa and the knowledge of the true meaning of reality—through the application of the analogy of collyrium and the eye, and the discovery of a treasure, both of which are expressed through double meanings (śleṣa).

Just as the King of Kosala, who was the slayer of Bhūri— a producer of auspiciousness for the world— slew Rāvaṇa, so too did he slay Hiraṇyākṣa, who was likewise a source of misfortune for the worlds.

Sītā is the auspicious land of her birth; her abductor was the ten-faced Rāvaṇa. He by whom the King of Kosala was slain—that very King of Kosala, the son of Daśaratha—is *asaḥ*, meaning he is not [that person], i.e., he does not possess the form of the King of Kosala. According to the rule *etattadoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.132), because of the exclusion *anañsamāse*, there is no elision of the *su*-case ending of the word *tat*. Alternatively, *asaḥ* means "devoid of its own sound" (*savarṇa*); thus, the King of Kosala is the King of Kola (*kolarāṭ*). This means he was formerly the best of boars (*varāhaśreṣṭha*).

The meaning is as follows: he slew Hiraṇyākṣa, who was such a destroyer of the earth that produces auspiciousness—the earth being that which brings about welfare and bestows security upon the world—for the sake of the auspiciousness and well-being of the worlds. Here, there is the presentation of the possessor of the effect (the world's welfare) together with its cause (the slaying of Rāvaṇa and Hiraṇyākṣa).

Just as he who places his trust in you, O Emperor, regarding both your being and your deeds as one, deserves to attain the status of sovereign over the entire, ancient realm that is the teacher of all castes.

O Emperor, O King of Kings, O Blessed One! Regarding the statement, "In the word *samrāṭ*, the *m* [of *samaḥ*] becomes *m*," the *m* of *samaḥ* remains precisely *m*. It does not become an *anusvāra*. As stated in the *Ratnamālā*: "The term *samrāṭ* refers to Agni, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the Sun, as well as one who is a sovereign lord of a realm (*maṇḍaleśvara*). Such authorities as, "This is the world of Brahman, O Emperor," and "Viṣṇu, the great one consisting of Brahman, is the King of Kings over all," are to be considered here. That person who, regarding You as the object, possesses a single, uniform disposition and action—this also implies speech and mental activity—[attains You].

The meaning is that he is non-contradictory (*avisaṃvādī*), according to the principle stated as: "One [aspect] of the Great-Souled Ones is in speech, one in mind, and one in action. He extends *pratyaya*—meaning either trust or meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Such a person is worthy of attaining the status of a sovereign emperor (*sāmrājyapada*), a position of supreme sovereignty (*ādhirājya*), which is mature (*vṛddha*) and fully developed (*abhivṛddhimat*) through all the social orders (*varṇa*), such as the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others, and is thus preeminent (*guru*).

The sense is that one who offers devotion to you, the Sovereign (*samrāj*), through identification with the three instruments (*karaṇatrayasārūpyeṇa*), attains the glory of sovereignty according to the principle of "the nature of his resolve" (*tatkratu-naya*). In another interpretation, the address "O Sovereign! is an invocation using the word *samrāj* itself; the meaning is: "that person [who offers devotion] to you, the word *samrāj*."

That man who extends—that is, prescribes—the single suffix for both the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), namely the suffix *ṣyañ* ordained by the rule "after words denoting qualities and [the class beginning with] *brāhmaṇa*, in the sense of the object and [the abstract state]," deserves to obtain the status of universal sovereignty (*sāmrājyapada*), which is designated as "vṛddha" according to the rule "that whose first vowel among its vowels is *vṛddhi* is called *vṛddha*," and which is characterized by all its syllables (*varṇa*) being heavy (*guru*).

The meaning is that the person who prescribes the suffix *ṣyañ* after the word *samrāj* attains the status of "Sāmrājya," a term which is both "vṛddha" (possessing the first vowel of its class) and "the guru (preceptor/teacher) of all castes. This description is applied because the word *sāmrājya*, being formed in the manner stated, is indeed "vṛddha" and is the "guru of all castes. In both these interpretations, there is a description of the cause—the prescription of the suffix after *samrāj*—along with its effect, which is the attainment of the status of *sāmrājya*.

Just as a virtuous tree, fragrant with blossoms, gentle in its nature, yielding good fruit, and providing auspicious shade, brings comfort to one weary from the coming and going of worldly existence who has approached its very foot, so does the Blessed One bring happiness to such a person.

He whose mind is *sāmoda* (full of fragrance), *saumya* (gentle), *anugra* (gracious), *sumanas* (well-disposed), and *śobhana* (beautiful)—or alternatively, he from whom the *sāmodas*, *saumyas*, and *sumanasas* (the gods or the ever-wise) [proceed]. In the other sense, the meaning is "possessing fragrant and delicate flowers. He is *suphalada* (bestowing excellent fruit), granting all fruits culminating in the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); in the other sense, he is so called because he gives fruits that have reached full maturity.

He who possesses a shadow that is sinless, which turns back all suffering, and which is both radiance and non-glare—he, the Blessed One, is like a "good tree" (sattaru), such as a mango tree or other auspicious tree, for one exhausted by the coming and going of *saṃsṛti*—the wandering to and fro in cyclic existence—or, in another sense, by the coming and going on the path of right progression (*samyaksṛti*), he provides rest at his own root for one who has come to him, approached his feet, and sought refuge at his base.

And it brings happiness to the person who has come for its sake. Here too, there is a description of the cause and the effect—the attainment of the Blessed One’s bliss—through their simultaneity (*sāhitya*). The distinction is this: in the previous examples, the effect was directly indicated by the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) or the *tumun* suffix; here, however, it is merely implied. If it is asked, "What is the difference between this and *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of the causal indicator)? it is said in reply: in *kāvyaliṅga*, there exists a relationship of the prover and the proven (*upapādaka-upapādya-bhāva*) between the cause and the effect; here, however, it is the relationship of the instigator and the instigated (*prayojaka-prayojya-bhāva*) that provides the aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*).

Furthermore, the status of this as an ornament (*alaṃkāra*) arises precisely from the excellence of beauty when [the meaning] is understood through implication (*gamyatā*), and not from the direct employment of words expressive of it; in this regard, both [theories] are exactly equal. In the example provided here, the distinction lies in its being mixed with a simile (*upamā*).
Just as a man seeking a treasure of glory resorts to worldly existence itself, yet, finding only its fruit— worldly prosperity— he wanders about together with ghosts.

A man who neglects you—the treasure-house of fortune, the possessor of all wealth, and the abode of Śrī—flees from worldly existence (*bhava*) and resorts only to *paśupati* (Śiva). The fruit of this is that while seeking prosperity (*bhūti*), he attains only ruin (*bhūti*). [The suffix] *śatṛ* is used here in the sense of cause according to the rule "lakṣaṇahetvoḥ"; here, "cause" refers to the result. Thus, the meaning is: "in order to attain prosperity. In the alternative sense, it means: "while seeking ashes (*bhūti*), he obtains them," that is, becoming smeared with ashes.

The meaning is that the very fact that he wanders together with *piśācas*—that is, equally with them, except for those *piśācas* who are the attendants of Rudra and belong to a specific class of divine beings—is his [karmic] fruit. Here too, the description of the cause and its effect—the existence and the wandering—is interwoven with *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Some wise ones have declared that the identity of the cause and the effect is the figure of speech called *hetu*;
the meaning is that certain ancient authorities have stated that the description of the non-difference between cause and effect constitutes the *hetu* ornament.

Like the family instruction bestowed by the Thirty [Gods], like the protection afforded to the pair of ear-leaf ornaments of the celestial damsels, a certain manifestation of the Lord of the Veṅkaṭa mountain—expert in the preservation of the world—was beheld. 1998.
In this context, the identity between the Blessed One—the cause for the training and so forth that benefits the gods—and that which possesses the cause for such training and so forth is described.

Or rather, may we behold that indescribable mass of splendors, which delights the lotus-eyes, which has been intensely cultivated by the wise, and which has rescued the life of the elephant seized by the crocodile. 1999.
Here too, the oneness of the Blessed One with the fruit of that life—namely, the saving of the life of the elephant seized by the crocodile—is described.

O Blessed One, I perceive this face of yours—its cheeks filled with a smile, radiant with the brilliance of white light, and shimmering with a tilaka—to be nothing other than bliss itself manifesting. 2000.

The construction is as follows: "I perceive this throbbing face of yours to be nothing but bliss (*ānanda*). In the alternative sense, it means: "I perceive the face (*ānana*) to be 'bliss' (*ānanda*) devoid of the throbbing of the syllable *adaḥ* (i.e., without the manifestation of the letter *da*). The meaning is that one knows the word "face" (*ānana*) to have been formed by removing the letter *da* from the word "bliss" (*ānanda*). Here too, there is an identity between the cause of bliss—the Lord’s face—and the effect, which is bliss itself. This constitutes another aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), distinguished from the previous example.

If it is asked, "How can the designation of non-difference be considered an *alaṃkāra* (poetic figure) when it lacks aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*)?", we say no. For its status as an *alaṃkāra* is beyond dispute, since its charm is unavoidable when it conveys the production of an effect through the necessity of that effect and its swiftness, while being independent of any other auxiliary causes. The distinction here is this: in *rūpaka*, the designation of non-difference arises from similarity (*sādṛśya*), whereas here it arises from the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). We have already explained the difference between this and *rūpakātiśayokti* in that very same place.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, the Chapter on Cause (hetu), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
